translations.an10.13:1: There are, monks, these ten fetters. Which ten? The five lower fetters and the five higher fetters. What are the five lower fetters? Self-identity view, doubt, dependence on rituals and practices, sensual desire, and ill-will - these are the five lower fetters.
translations.an10.15:1: As far as, monks, there are beings, whether footless or two-footed or four-footed or many-footed, whether having form or formless, whether percipient or non-percipient or neither percipient nor non-percipient, the Tathagata, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, is declared the foremost among them; in the same way, whatever wholesome things there are, all are based upon diligence, converge upon diligence. Diligence is declared the foremost among them.
translations.an10.15:2: Just as, monks, all the footprints of living creatures, all enter into the footprint of the elephant, and the elephant's footprint is declared the foremost among them, due to its size; in the same way, whatever wholesome things there are, all are based upon diligence, converge upon diligence. Diligence is declared the foremost among them.
translations.an10.15:3: Just as, monks, all the rafters of a peaked roof, all converge upon the peak, and the peak is declared the foremost among them; in the same way, whatever wholesome things there are, all are based upon diligence, converge upon diligence. Diligence is declared the foremost among them.
translations.an10.15:7: Just as, monks, all the minor kings are vassals of the king, the wheel-turning monarch, and the wheel-turning monarch is declared the foremost among them; in the same way, whatever wholesome things there are, all are based upon diligence, converge upon diligence. Diligence is declared the foremost among them.
translations.an10.15:8: Just as, monks, all the stars' radiance does not amount to one sixteenth of the moon's radiance, and the moon's radiance is declared the foremost among them; in the same way, whatever wholesome things there are, all are based upon diligence, converge upon diligence. Diligence is declared the foremost among them.
translations.an10.15:9: Just as, monks, in the autumn, when the sky is clear and the sun is shining, it illuminates all that is in the sky, dispels all darkness, and shines, blazes, and radiates; in the same way, whatever wholesome things there are, all are based upon diligence, converge upon diligence. Diligence is declared the foremost among them.
translations.an10.17:1: Live with a protector, monks, not without a protector. One without a protector lives in suffering. These ten things, monks, are protectors. Which ten? Here, a monk is virtuous, he dwells restrained by the Patimokkha, endowed with conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, and he trains in the training rules, having undertaken the training rules.
translations.an10.17:2: Again, monks, a monk is learned, he has heard much, he has retained what he has heard, and he has stored up what is good and salutary, the words of the teachings, connected with the goal, connected with the Dhamma, which lead to the complete and perfect enlightenment, which are well-spoken, well-repeated, connected with the knowledge, and which are to be seen, to be understood, and to be realized by the wise. Whatever monk is learned, having heard much, and having retained what he has heard, this too is a thing that is a protector.
translations.an10.17:3: Again, monks, a monk has good friends, good companions, and good associates. Whatever monk has good friends, good companions, and good associates, this too is a thing that is a protector.
translations.an10.18:10: Again, monks, a monk is mindful, endowed with the highest mindfulness and awareness, remembering and recollecting what was done and said long ago. 'This monk is mindful, endowed with the highest mindfulness and awareness, remembering and recollecting what was done and said long ago,' thus the senior monks, the monks of middle standing, and the new monks think, 'He should be told, he should be advised.' The senior monks, the monks of middle standing, and the new monks, having compassion for him, having sympathy for him, and having concern for him, will only bring about growth in wholesome things, and not decline. This too is a thing that is a protector.
translations.an10.18:11: Again, monks, a monk is wise, endowed with the wisdom that leads to arising and passing away, the noble, penetrating, and leading to the complete destruction of suffering. 'This monk is wise, endowed with the wisdom that leads to arising and passing away, the noble, penetrating, and leading to the complete destruction of suffering,' thus the senior monks, the monks of middle standing, and the new monks think, 'He should be told, he should be advised.' The senior monks, the monks of middle standing, and the new monks, having compassion for him, having sympathy for him, and having concern for him, will only bring about growth in wholesome things, and not decline. This too is a thing that is a protector.
translations.an10.18:2: Live with a protector, monks, not without a protector. One without a protector lives in suffering. These ten things, monks, are protectors. Which ten? Here, a monk is virtuous, he dwells restrained by the Patimokkha, endowed with conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, and he trains in the training rules, having undertaken the training rules. 'This monk is virtuous, he dwells restrained by the Patimokkha, endowed with conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, and he trains in the training rules, having undertaken the training rules,' thus the senior monks, the monks of middle standing, and the new monks think, 'He should be told, he should be advised.' The senior monks, the monks of middle standing, and the new monks, having compassion for him, having sympathy for him, and having concern for him, will only bring about growth in wholesome things, and not decline. This too is a thing that is a protector.
translations.an10.18:4: Again, monks, a monk has good friends, good companions, and good associates. 'This monk has good friends, good companions, and good associates,' thus the senior monks, the monks of middle standing, and the new monks think, 'He should be told, he should be advised.' The senior monks, the monks of middle standing, and the new monks, having compassion for him, having sympathy for him, and having concern for him, will only bring about growth in wholesome things, and not decline. This too is a thing that is a protector.
translations.an10.18:5: Again, monks, a monk is easy to correct, endowed with the qualities that make one easy to correct, patient, and obedient to advice. 'This monk is easy to correct, endowed with the qualities that make one easy to correct, patient, and obedient to advice,' thus the senior monks, the monks of middle standing, and the new monks think, 'He should be told, he should be advised.' The senior monks, the monks of middle standing, and the new monks, having compassion for him, having sympathy for him, and having concern for him, will only bring about growth in wholesome things, and not decline. This too is a thing that is a protector.
translations.an10.18:6: Again, monks, a monk is skilled and diligent in various tasks shared among his fellow monks, and is able to do them without difficulty, examining them with a mind that is not lazy. The senior monks think that this monk should be spoken to and instructed, as do the middle-ranking and new monks. For one who is favored by senior, middle-ranking, and new monks, there is only growth in wholesome qualities, and no decline. This too is a condition that is not barren.
translations.an10.18:7: Again, monks, a monk is eager to hear the teaching and is delighted by the Dhamma and the Vinaya. The senior monks think that this monk should be spoken to and instructed, as do the middle-ranking and new monks. For one who is favored by senior, middle-ranking, and new monks, there is only growth in wholesome qualities, and no decline. This too is a condition that is not barren.
translations.an10.18:8: Again, monks, a monk lives with energy applied to the abandoning of unwholesome qualities and the acquisition of wholesome qualities, and is strong, firm, and unshakeable in his efforts. The senior monks think that this monk should be spoken to and instructed, as do the middle-ranking and new monks. For one who is favored by senior, middle-ranking, and new monks, there is only growth in wholesome qualities, and no decline. This too is a condition that is not barren.
translations.an10.18:9: Again, monks, a monk is content with whatever robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicine and provisions he receives. The senior monks think that this monk should be spoken to and instructed, as do the middle-ranking and new monks. For one who is favored by senior, middle-ranking, and new monks, there is only growth in wholesome qualities, and no decline. This too is a condition that is not barren.
translations.an10.20:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was living in the Kuru country at a town called Kammāsadhamma, which was a market town of the Kuru people.
translations.an10.20:10: And how, monks, is a monk one whose body is tranquil? Here, a monk, having given up pleasure and pain, and with the disappearance of former pleasure and pain, enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is without pleasure and pain and is characterized by purity of mindfulness and equanimity. It is in this way that a monk is one whose body is tranquil.
translations.an10.20:11: And how, monks, is a monk one whose mind is fully freed? Here, a monk's mind is freed from sensual desire, his mind is freed from ill will, and his mind is freed from delusion. It is in this way that a monk is one whose mind is fully freed.
translations.an10.20:2: Monks, there are these ten abidings of a noble one, in which noble ones have dwelled, dwell, and will dwell. What ten? Here, a monk is one who has given up the five hindrances, is endowed with the six factors, guards the one thing, is devoted to the four things, is a speaker of the truth, is unshaken in his exertion, is one whose body is tranquil, whose mind is fully freed, and whose wisdom is fully freed.
translations.an10.20:3: And how, monks, is a monk one who has given up the five hindrances? Here, a monk has given up sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. It is in this way that a monk is one who has given up the five hindrances.
translations.an10.20:4: And how, monks, is a monk endowed with the six factors? Here, a monk, having seen a form with his eye, is not delighted by it, nor is he displeased; he dwells with mindfulness and equanimity. Having heard a sound with his ear... Having smelled an odor with his nose... Having savored a taste with his tongue... Having felt a tactile sensation with his body... Having cognized a mental phenomenon with his mind, he is not delighted by it, nor is he displeased; he dwells with mindfulness and equanimity. It is in this way that a monk is endowed with the six factors.
translations.an10.20:5: And how, monks, is a monk one who guards the one thing? Here, a monk is endowed with mindfulness, guarding his mind. It is in this way that a monk is one who guards the one thing.
translations.an10.20:6: And how, monks, is a monk devoted to the four things? Here, a monk serves only one thing, he is devoted to only one thing, he is dependent on only one thing, and he is resolved on only one thing. It is in this way that a monk is devoted to the four things.
translations.an10.20:7: And how, monks, is a monk a speaker of the truth? Here, a monk has given up and abandoned various speculations about the past and the future, such as: 'The world is eternal' or 'The world is not eternal', 'The world is finite' or 'The world is infinite', 'The soul and the body are the same' or 'The soul and the body are different', 'There is a self after death' or 'There is no self after death', 'There both is and is not a self after death' or 'There neither is nor is not a self after death'. All these speculations are given up, abandoned, and rejected. It is in this way that a monk is a speaker of the truth.
translations.an10.20:8: And how, monks, is a monk unshaken in his exertion? Here, a monk has given up sensual desire, ill will, and delusion. It is in this way that a monk is unshaken in his exertion.
translations.an10.20:9: And how, monks, is a monk one whose wisdom is fully freed? Here, a monk has given up thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty. It is in this way that a monk is one whose wisdom is fully freed.
translations.an10.24:1: On one occasion the Venerable Mahācunda was living in the Ceti country, in a town called Sahajāti. There the Venerable Mahācunda addressed the monks: 'Friends, monks...'
translations.an10.24:10: Just as, friend, a person who is wealthy, who has wealth, would talk about wealth, a person who has many possessions, who has many possessions, would talk about many possessions, a person who has many enjoyments, who has many enjoyments, would talk about many enjoyments. If, in any kind of wealth acquisition, he is able to acquire wealth, grains, silver, or gold, then he is to be known as one who, being wealthy, talks about wealth, being a person with many possessions, talks about many possessions, being a person with many enjoyments, talks about many enjoyments. Why is that? Because, indeed, he is able to acquire wealth, grains, silver, or gold in any kind of wealth acquisition.
translations.an10.24:2: A bhikkhu who makes a claim to knowledge, saying: 'I know this doctrine, I see this doctrine.' If, friend, that bhikkhu is overcome by greed, hatred, delusion, anger, hostility, denigration, domineering, envy, miserliness, or evil desires, then he is to be known as one who does not understand the doctrine in such a way that greed does not overcome him, and yet greed overcomes him; he does not understand the doctrine in such a way that hatred does not overcome him, and yet hatred overcomes him; he does not understand the doctrine in such a way that delusion does not overcome him, and yet delusion overcomes him; he does not understand the doctrine in such a way that anger does not overcome him, and yet anger overcomes him; he does not understand the doctrine in such a way that hostility does not overcome him, and yet hostility overcomes him; he does not understand the doctrine in such a way that denigration does not overcome him, and yet denigration overcomes him; he does not understand the doctrine in such a way that domineering does not overcome him, and yet domineering overcomes him; he does not understand the doctrine in such a way that envy does not overcome him, and yet envy overcomes him; he does not understand the doctrine in such a way that miserliness does not overcome him, and yet miserliness overcomes him; he does not understand the doctrine in such a way that evil desires do not overcome him, and yet evil desires overcome him.
translations.an10.24:3: A bhikkhu who makes a claim to development, saying: 'I have developed my body, I have developed my virtue, I have developed my mind, I have developed my wisdom.' If, friend, that bhikkhu is overcome by greed, hatred, delusion, anger, hostility, denigration, domineering, envy, miserliness, or evil desires, then he is to be known as one who does not understand the doctrine in such a way that greed does not overcome him, and yet greed overcomes him; he does not understand the doctrine in such a way that hatred does not overcome him, and yet hatred overcomes him; he does not understand the doctrine in such a way that delusion does not overcome him, and yet delusion overcomes him; he does not understand the doctrine in such a way that anger does not overcome him, and yet anger overcomes him; he does not understand the doctrine in such a way that hostility does not overcome him, and yet hostility overcomes him; he does not understand the doctrine in such a way that denigration does not overcome him, and yet denigration overcomes him; he does not understand the doctrine in such a way that domineering does not overcome him, and yet domineering overcomes him; he does not understand the doctrine in such a way that envy does not overcome him, and yet envy overcomes him; he does not understand the doctrine in such a way that miserliness does not overcome him, and yet miserliness overcomes him; he does not understand the doctrine in such a way that evil desires do not overcome him, and yet evil desires overcome him.
translations.an10.24:5: Just as, friend, a person who is poor, who has no wealth, would talk about wealth, a person who has no possessions, who has no possessions, would talk about many possessions, a person who has no enjoyments, who has no enjoyments, would talk about many enjoyments. If, in any kind of wealth acquisition, he is not able to acquire wealth, grains, silver, or gold, then he is to be known as one who, being poor, talks about wealth, being a person with no possessions, talks about many possessions, being a person with no enjoyments, talks about many enjoyments. Why is that? Because, indeed, he is not able to acquire wealth, grains, silver, or gold in any kind of wealth acquisition.
translations.an10.24:9: A bhikkhu who makes a claim to knowledge and development, saying: 'I know this doctrine, I see this doctrine, I have developed my body, I have developed my virtue, I have developed my mind, I have developed my wisdom.' If, friend, that bhikkhu is not overcome by greed, hatred, delusion, anger, hostility, denigration, domineering, envy, miserliness, or evil desires, then he is to be known as one who understands the doctrine in such a way that greed does not overcome him, and yet greed does not overcome him; he understands the doctrine in such a way that hatred does not overcome him, and yet hatred does not overcome him; he understands the doctrine in such a way that delusion does not overcome him, and yet delusion does not overcome him; he understands the doctrine in such a way that anger does not overcome him, and yet anger does not overcome him; he understands the doctrine in such a way that hostility does not overcome him, and yet hostility does not overcome him; he understands the doctrine in such a way that denigration does not overcome him, and yet denigration does not overcome him; he understands the doctrine in such a way that domineering does not overcome him, and yet domineering does not overcome him; he understands the doctrine in such a way that envy does not overcome him, and yet envy does not overcome him; he understands the doctrine in such a way that miserliness does not overcome him, and yet miserliness does not overcome him; he understands the doctrine in such a way that evil desires do not overcome him, and yet evil desires do not overcome him.
translations.an10.29:1: As far as the kingdom of Kosala, as far as the kingdom of King Pasenadi of Kosala has been conquered, King Pasenadi of Kosala is the highest authority. But, bhikkhus, even for King Pasenadi of Kosala, there is a change for the worse, a decline. Seeing this, bhikkhus, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that. Becoming disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate towards the highest, and even more so towards the lower.
translations.an10.29:10: One perceives forms internally, and sees external forms that are blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, and blue in color. Just as, for example, the flower of the uva plant is blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, and blue in color, or just as the cloth from Baranasi, which is smooth on both sides, is blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, and blue in color; in the same way, one perceives forms internally, and sees external forms that are blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, and blue in color. 'I know and see these forms, having overcome them,' such is one's perception. This is the fifth basis for overcoming.
translations.an10.29:11: One perceives forms internally, and sees external forms that are yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in color. Just as, for example, the flower of the kanikara plant is yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in color, or just as the cloth from Baranasi, which is smooth on both sides, is yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in color; in the same way, one perceives forms internally, and sees external forms that are yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in color. 'I know and see these forms, having overcome them,' such is one's perception. This is the sixth basis for overcoming.
translations.an10.29:12: One perceives forms internally, having perceived them externally, limited, beautiful or ugly. Suppose there were a red kanavera flower or a red cloth from Benares, with a smooth surface on both sides: in the same way, one perceives forms internally, having perceived them externally, limited, beautiful or ugly. ‘I know and see that I have overcome them,’ such is one’s perception. This is the seventh basis for overcoming.
translations.an10.29:13: One perceives forms internally, having perceived them externally, limitless, beautiful or ugly. Suppose there were a white lotus or a white cloth from Benares, with a smooth surface on both sides: in the same way, one perceives forms internally, having perceived them externally, limitless, beautiful or ugly. ‘I know and see that I have overcome them,’ such is one’s perception. This is the eighth basis for overcoming. These, monks, are the eight bases of overcoming.
translations.an10.29:14: The best of these eight bases of overcoming is that one perceives forms internally, having perceived them externally, limitless, beautiful or ugly. ‘I know and see that I have overcome them,’ such is one’s perception. There are beings who perceive in this way. For those who perceive in this way, there is a change in their perception. Seeing this, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with it. Becoming disenchanted, they become dispassionate, and through dispassion, they are liberated.
translations.an10.29:15: There are, monks, these four paths. What four? A difficult path with difficult direct knowledge, a quick path with difficult direct knowledge, an easy path with difficult direct knowledge, an easy path with quick direct knowledge—these, monks, are the four paths.
translations.an10.29:16: The best of these four paths is an easy path with quick direct knowledge. There are beings who follow this path. For those who follow this path, there is a change in their perception. Seeing this, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with it. Becoming disenchanted, they become dispassionate, and through dispassion, they are liberated.
translations.an10.29:17: There are, monks, these four perceptions. What four? One perceives a small limited perception, one perceives a large limited perception, one perceives an immeasurable perception, one perceives the base of nothingness, perceiving ‘there is nothing’. These, monks, are the four perceptions.
translations.an10.29:18: The best of these four perceptions is that one perceives the base of nothingness, perceiving ‘there is nothing’. There are beings who perceive in this way. For those who perceive in this way, there is a change in their perception. Seeing this, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with it. Becoming disenchanted, they become dispassionate, and through dispassion, they are liberated.
translations.an10.29:2: As far as the moon and sun move, illuminating the quarters with their radiance, so far is a thousandfold world system. In that thousandfold world system, there are a thousand moons, a thousand suns, a thousand Sineru mountains, a thousand Jambudīpa continents, a thousand Aparagoyāna regions, a thousand Uttarakuru regions, a thousand Pubbavideha regions, four thousand great oceans, four thousand great kings, a thousand gods of the four great kings, a thousand gods of the Thirty-Three, a thousand Yāma gods, a thousand Tusita gods, a thousand Nimmānaratī gods, a thousand Paranimmitavasavattī gods, a thousand Brahmā worlds. As far as a thousandfold world system, Mahābrahmā is considered the highest. But even Mahābrahmā has a change in his perception. Seeing this, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with it. Becoming disenchanted, they become dispassionate, and through dispassion, they are liberated.
translations.an10.29:20: There are, monks, some ascetics and brahmins who teach the ultimate purification. The best of those who teach the ultimate purification is one who, having completely transcended the base of nothingness, dwells in the base of neither perception nor non-perception. They teach the Dhamma having realized it for themselves. There are beings who teach in this way. For those who teach in this way, there is a change in their perception. Seeing this, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with it. Becoming disenchanted, they become dispassionate, and through dispassion, they are liberated.
translations.an10.29:3: There is a time, monks, when the world contracts. When the world contracts, most beings are reborn in the Ābhassara heaven. There they are mind-made, filled with joy, self-luminous, and they move through the air. They remain for a long time, and their lifespan is very long. When the world contracts, the Ābhassara gods are considered the highest. But even the Ābhassara gods have a change in their perception. Seeing this, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with it. Becoming disenchanted, they become dispassionate, and through dispassion, they are liberated.
translations.an10.29:4: There are, monks, these ten bases of meditation. What ten? One perceives the earth kasina above, below, and all around, immeasurable and without duality; one perceives the water kasina … the fire kasina … the air kasina … the blue kasina … the yellow kasina … the red kasina … the white kasina … the space kasina … the consciousness kasina above, below, and all around, immeasurable and without duality. These, monks, are the ten bases of meditation.
translations.an10.29:5: This is the best among these ten kasina bases, that is, the consciousness kasina, when one perceives it as above, below, across, undivided, and immeasurable. There are beings who perceive it in this way. For those who perceive it in this way, there is a change for the better. Seeing this, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with it. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate, and through dispassion, he is liberated from it, and not from anything inferior.
translations.an10.29:6: There are eight bases of mastery, bhikkhus. What eight? A bhikkhu perceives forms internally and sees small forms externally, limited and of a beautiful color; he discerns and knows them, thinking: 'I have mastered these and I see them.' This is the first base of mastery.
translations.an10.29:7: A bhikkhu perceives forms internally and sees limitless forms externally, of a beautiful color; he discerns and knows them, thinking: 'I have mastered these and I see them.' This is the second base of mastery.
translations.an10.29:8: A bhikkhu perceives the formless internally and sees small forms externally, limited and of a beautiful color; he discerns and knows them, thinking: 'I have mastered these and I see them.' This is the third base of mastery.
translations.an10.29:9: A bhikkhu perceives the formless internally and sees limitless forms externally, of a beautiful color; he discerns and knows them, thinking: 'I have mastered these and I see them.' This is the fourth base of mastery.
translations.an10.51:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Savatthi in Jeta's Grove, Anathapindika's Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: 'Bhikkhus!' 'Venerable sir,' the bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an10.51:3: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu skilled in the examination of his own mind? Just as a woman or a man, young, youthful, and fond of adornments, would look at their own face in a clean and bright mirror or in a bowl of clear water, and see a smudge or a mark on it, they would make an effort to remove it. If they do not see a smudge or a mark on it, they would be satisfied, thinking: 'My face is clean, my face is pure.' In the same way, a bhikkhu examines his own mind: 'Am I often covetous or not? Am I often hateful or not? Am I often deluded or not? Am I often lethargic or not? Am I often restless or not? Am I often doubtful or not? Am I often angry or not? Am I often defiled in mind or not? Am I often faithless or not? Am I often lazy or not? Am I often unenergetic or not? Am I often unconcentrated or not?'
translations.an10.51:4: If, upon examination, a bhikkhu knows: 'I am often covetous, hateful, deluded, lethargic, restless, doubtful, angry, defiled in mind, faithless, lazy, and unenergetic,' then he should make an effort to abandon those same unwholesome, unprofitable states. Just as one would make an effort to remove a burn from one's scalp or head, in the same way, the bhikkhu should make an effort to abandon those unwholesome states, with desire, effort, enthusiasm, exertion, without being complacent, with mindfulness and clear comprehension.
translations.an10.54:2: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu skilled in the examination of his own mind? Just as a woman or a man, young, youthful, and fond of adornments, would look at their own face in a clean and bright mirror or in a bowl of clear water, and see a smudge or a mark on it, they would make an effort to remove it. If they do not see a smudge or a mark on it, they would be satisfied, thinking: 'My face is clean, my face is pure.' In the same way, a bhikkhu examines his own mind: 'Do I gain internal peace of mind? Do I not gain internal peace of mind? Do I gain the higher understanding of the Dhamma through wisdom? Do I not gain the higher understanding of the Dhamma through wisdom?'
translations.an10.54:5: If, upon examination, a bhikkhu knows: 'I do not gain internal peace of mind, I do not gain the higher understanding of the Dhamma through wisdom,' then he should make an effort to acquire those same wholesome states, with desire, effort, enthusiasm, exertion, without being complacent, with mindfulness and clear comprehension. Just as one would make an effort to remove a burn from one's scalp or head, in the same way, the bhikkhu should make an effort to acquire those wholesome states. Later on, he will gain both internal peace of mind and the higher understanding of the Dhamma through wisdom.
translations.an10.54:6: If, upon examination, a bhikkhu knows: 'I gain internal peace of mind, I gain the higher understanding of the Dhamma through wisdom,' then he should make an effort to establish himself in those same wholesome states for the destruction of the corruptions.
translations.an10.58:1: If, monks, wanderers of other sects were to ask you: 'What are the roots of all things, what is the origin of all things, what is the arising of all things, what is the meeting place of all things, what is the resort of all things, what is the supreme of all things, what is the most excellent of all things, what is the end of all things, what is the conclusion of all things, what is the final goal of all things?' and you were to answer them thus, how would you answer these wanderers of other sects?
translations.an10.58:2: Then, monks, listen and pay attention, I will speak.
translations.an10.59:1: Therefore, monks, you should train thus: 'Our minds will be developed in accordance with our going forth, no evil unwholesome things will take possession of our minds; our minds will be developed in accordance with the perception of impermanence, the perception of non-self, the perception of ugliness, the perception of danger, the perception of abandoning, the perception of fading away, the perception of cessation; we will develop the perception of the world as empty, the perception of the origin and passing away of the world, the perception of the cessation of the world.'
translations.an10.60:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. At that time the Venerable Girimānanda was sick, suffering, and gravely ill.
translations.an10.60:10: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of cessation? Here, Ānanda, a monk gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects: 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the giving up of all attachments, the destruction of craving, cessation, nibbāna.' This, Ānanda, is called the perception of cessation.
translations.an10.60:11: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of non-delight in all worlds? Here, Ānanda, a monk gives up and lives giving up the attachments, the underlying tendencies, and the inclinations of the mind that are the basis for the world.
translations.an10.60:12: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of non-intention in all formations? Here, Ānanda, a monk is repelled by, disgusted with, and disenchanted with all formations.
translations.an10.60:13: And what, Ānanda, is mindfulness of breathing? Here, Ānanda, a monk gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down cross-legged, holding his body straight, and establishes mindfulness in front of him. He breathes in mindful, breathes out mindful. Breathing in a long breath, he knows 'I am breathing in a long breath'; breathing out a long breath, he knows 'I am breathing out a long breath'. Breathing in a short breath, he knows 'I am breathing in a short breath'; breathing out a short breath, he knows 'I am breathing out a short breath'. He trains thus: 'I will breathe in experiencing the whole body'; 'I will breathe out experiencing the whole body'; 'I will breathe in calming the bodily formation'; 'I will breathe out calming the bodily formation'; 'I will breathe in experiencing rapture'; 'I will breathe out experiencing rapture'; 'I will breathe in experiencing pleasure'; 'I will breathe out experiencing pleasure'; 'I will breathe in experiencing the mental formation'; 'I will breathe out experiencing the mental formation'; 'I will breathe in calming the mental formation'; 'I will breathe out calming the mental formation'; 'I will breathe in experiencing the mind'; 'I will breathe out experiencing the mind'; 'I will breathe in gladdening the mind'; 'I will breathe in concentrating the mind'; 'I will breathe in liberating the mind'; 'I will breathe in observing impermanence'; 'I will breathe in observing fading away'; 'I will breathe in observing cessation'; 'I will breathe in observing relinquishment.' This, Ānanda, is called mindfulness of breathing.
translations.an10.60:14: If, Ānanda, you were to teach these ten perceptions to the monk Girimānanda, there is a chance that Girimānanda, having heard them, will recover from his illness.
translations.an10.60:2: The Venerable Ānanda said to the Buddha: 'The Venerable Girimānanda is sick, suffering, and gravely ill. It would be good, sir, if the Buddha would visit the Venerable Girimānanda out of compassion.' 'If, Ānanda, you were to teach these ten perceptions to the monk Girimānanda, there is a chance that Girimānanda, having heard them, will recover from his illness.
translations.an10.60:3: What are the ten? The perception of impermanence, the perception of non-self, the perception of ugliness, the perception of danger, the perception of abandoning, the perception of fading away, the perception of cessation, the perception of non-delight in all worlds, the perception of non-intention in all formations, and mindfulness of breathing.
translations.an10.60:4: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of impermanence? Here, Ānanda, a monk gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects: 'Form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent.' Thus he lives observing impermanence in these five aggregates of clinging. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of impermanence.
translations.an10.60:5: And what, Ananda, is the perception of non-self? Here, Ananda, a monk who has gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects: 'The eye is not self, forms are not self, the ear is not self, sounds are not self, the nose is not self, odors are not self, the tongue is not self, flavors are not self, the body is not self, tactile sensations are not self, the mind is not self, mental phenomena are not self.' Thus he dwells observing non-self in these six internal and external bases. This, Ananda, is called the perception of non-self.
translations.an10.60:6: And what, Ananda, is the perception of foulness? Here, Ananda, a monk reflects on this very body from the soles of the feet up, from the top of the hair down, surrounded by skin, as being full of many kinds of unclean things: 'In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, stomach, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints, and urine.' Thus he dwells observing foulness in this body. This, Ananda, is called the perception of foulness.
translations.an10.60:7: And what, Ananda, is the perception of danger? Here, Ananda, a monk who has gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects: 'This body is afflicted with many sufferings and many dangers. In this body various afflictions arise, such as eye disease, ear disease, nose disease, tongue disease, body disease, headache, backache, stomachache, and fever, as well as diseases of the stomach and intestines, and diseases of the head, and diseases caused by bile, phlegm, and wind, and diseases resulting from a change of season, and diseases caused by bad fortune, and diseases caused by deeds, and cold and heat and hunger and thirst.' Thus he dwells observing danger in this body. This, Ananda, is called the perception of danger.
translations.an10.60:8: And what, Ananda, is the perception of abandonment? Here, Ananda, a monk does not tolerate a sensual thought that has arisen, but abandons it, removes it, and destroys it. He does not tolerate a malicious thought that has arisen, but abandons it, removes it, and destroys it. He does not tolerate a cruel thought that has arisen, but abandons it, removes it, and destroys it. He does not tolerate any evil, unwholesome thoughts that have arisen, but abandons them, removes them, and destroys them. This, Ananda, is called the perception of abandonment.
translations.an10.61:1: In the past, monks, it is not known whether ignorance was first and knowledge afterwards, or whether knowledge was first and ignorance afterwards.
translations.an10.61:2: I say, monks, that ignorance has a nutriment, not that it has no nutriment. And what is the nutriment for ignorance? The five hindrances are its nutriment. I say, monks, that the five hindrances have a nutriment, not that they have no nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the five hindrances? The three kinds of misconduct are their nutriment.
translations.an10.61:3: Thus, monks, association with the unwholesome completes lack of faith, lack of faith completes unwise attention, unwise attention completes lack of restraint of the senses, lack of restraint of the senses completes the three kinds of misconduct, the three kinds of misconduct complete the five hindrances, and the five hindrances complete ignorance. In this way, monks, ignorance is nourished by a nutriment and grows.
translations.an10.61:4: Just as, monks, the rain that falls on the top of a mountain flows down and fills the clefts and gullies, and the clefts and gullies fill the pools, and the pools fill the lakes, and the lakes fill the streams, and the streams fill the rivers, and the rivers fill the great ocean; in the same way, monks, ignorance is nourished by a nutriment and grows.
translations.an10.61:7: Thus, monks, association with the wholesome completes faith, faith completes wise attention, wise attention completes restraint of the senses, restraint of the senses completes good conduct, good conduct completes the four foundations of mindfulness, the four foundations of mindfulness complete the seven factors of enlightenment, and the seven factors of enlightenment complete knowledge and liberation. In this way, monks, knowledge and liberation are nourished by a nutriment and grow.
translations.an10.7:1: Then the Venerable Ananda approached the Venerable Sariputta, and having approached, he exchanged greetings with him. After the exchange of greetings, he sat down to one side and said to the Venerable Sariputta:
translations.an10.7:2: Is it possible, friend Sāriputta, that a monk could attain such concentration that he would not perceive earth as earth, water as water, fire as fire, air as air, the base of the infinity of space as the base of the infinity of space, the base of the infinity of consciousness as the base of the infinity of consciousness, the base of nothingness as the base of nothingness, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this world as this world, the other world as the other world; and yet he would still be perceptive?
translations.an10.7:4: But how is it possible, friend Sāriputta, that a monk could attain such concentration that he would not perceive earth as earth … and yet he would still be perceptive?  One time, friend Ānanda, I was staying right here in Sāvatthī in the Blind Men’s Grove.  There I attained such concentration that I did not perceive earth as earth, water as water, fire as fire, air as air, the base of the infinity of space as the base of the infinity of space, the base of the infinity of consciousness as the base of the infinity of consciousness, the base of nothingness as the base of nothingness, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this world as this world, the other world as the other world; and yet I was still perceptive.
translations.an3.10:1: Endowed with three things, monks, a person throws off these three fetters and is cast into hell as if brought there.  What three?  He is immoral, and his immoral conduct is not abandoned; he is envious, and his envy is not abandoned; he is miserly, and his miserliness is not abandoned.  Endowed with these three things, a person throws off these three fetters and is cast into hell as if brought there.
translations.an3.12:5: Again, monks, in whatever quarter a monk understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’, ‘This is the origin of suffering’, ‘This is the cessation of suffering’, ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering’.  This, monks, is the second thing that is a source of comfort to a monk as long as life lasts.
translations.an3.15:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was living in the Deer Park at Isipatana near Benares.  There the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Monks …'
translations.an3.15:2: ‘In the past, monks, there was a king named Sacred.  Then King Sacred addressed a wheelwright: “I have need of a chariot, wheelwright.  Can you make me a new chariot in six months?”  “I can, your majesty”, the wheelwright replied to King Sacred.  Then, monks, the wheelwright finished one wheel in six months.  Then King Sacred addressed the wheelwright: “I have need of a chariot, wheelwright.  The new chariot is finished.  Can you finish a second wheel in these six days?”  “I can, your majesty”, the wheelwright replied.  The wheelwright finished the second wheel in six days and, taking the new chariot, approached King Sacred.  Having approached, he said to King Sacred: “Your majesty, the new chariot is finished.”  “What difference is there, good wheelwright, between the wheel that was finished in six months and the wheel that was finished in six days?”  “I do not see any difference, your majesty.”  “There is a difference, your majesty.  May your majesty see the difference.”'
translations.an3.15:3: Then, monks, the wheelwright spun the wheel that was finished in six days.  Having spun it, it went as far as the impetus of the effort, then fell to the ground, rolling.  Then, monks, the wheelwright spun the wheel that was finished in six months.  Having spun it, it went as far as the impetus of the effort, then stood firm, axle-bound.
translations.an3.15:5: It may be, monks, that you think: ‘The wheelwright was someone else at that time.’  But, monks, it should not be regarded in that way.  I was the wheelwright at that time.  At that time I was skilled in woodwork, in the defects in wood, and in the seasoning of wood.  Now, monks, I am the arahant, the fully awakened one, skilled in bodily crookedness, in the defects of bodily crookedness, and in the straightening of the body, skilled in verbal crookedness, in the defects of verbal crookedness, and in the straightening of speech, skilled in mental crookedness, in the defects of mental crookedness, and in the straightening of the mind.  Any monk or nun in whom bodily crookedness is not abandoned, in whom the defects of bodily crookedness and the seasonings of bodily crookedness are not abandoned, in whom verbal crookedness is not abandoned, in whom the defects of verbal crookedness and the seasonings of verbal crookedness are not abandoned, in whom mental crookedness is not abandoned, in whom the defects of mental crookedness and the seasonings of mental crookedness are not abandoned, such ones, monks, are fallen into this Dhamma and Vinaya, like the wheel finished in six days.
translations.an3.15:6: Any monk or nun in whom bodily crookedness is abandoned, in whom the defects of bodily crookedness and the seasonings of bodily crookedness are abandoned, in whom verbal crookedness is abandoned, in whom the defects of verbal crookedness and the seasonings of verbal crookedness are abandoned, in whom mental crookedness is abandoned, in whom the defects of mental crookedness and the seasonings of mental crookedness are abandoned, such ones, monks, are established in this Dhamma and Vinaya, like the wheel finished in six months.
translations.an3.1:3: Thus, monks, the fool is prone to fear, the wise person is not prone to fear.  The fool has much to fear, the wise person has nothing to fear.  The fool is subject to much suffering, the wise person is subject to little suffering.  There is no fear for the wise person, no suffering for the wise person.
translations.an3.20:1: A person of bad character, monks, endowed with three qualities, soon attains to great wealth in possessions. What three? Here, monks, a person of bad character is farsighted, able, and has connections. And how, monks, is a person of bad character farsighted? Here, monks, a person of bad character knows his goods: 'This goods is of such a kind, is being sold at such a price, will have such a profit, and such a return.' Thus, monks, a person of bad character is farsighted.
translations.an3.20:2: And how, monks, is a person of bad character able? Here, monks, a person of bad character is skilled in buying and selling goods. Thus, monks, a person of bad character is able.
translations.an3.20:3: And how, monks, does a person of bad character have connections? Here, monks, those householders or sons of householders who are wealthy, rich, and prosperous, think of a person of bad character thus: 'This person of bad character is farsighted and able, and is capable of supporting a wife and children, and of providing for us from time to time.' They provide him with possessions, saying: 'Come, good person of bad character, engage in business, support a wife and children, and provide for us from time to time.' Thus, monks, a person of bad character has connections. Endowed with these three qualities, a person of bad character soon attains to great wealth in possessions.
translations.an3.20:4: Similarly, monks, a monk endowed with three qualities soon attains to great wealth in wholesome things. What three? Here, monks, a monk is farsighted, able, and has connections. And how, monks, is a monk farsighted? Here, monks, a monk truly understands: 'This is suffering, this is the origin of suffering, this is the cessation of suffering, and this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.' Thus, monks, a monk is farsighted.
translations.an3.20:5: And how, monks, is a monk able? Here, monks, a monk dwells with energy applied to the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states, strong, firm in exertion, and not giving up in wholesome things. Thus, monks, a monk is able.
translations.an3.22:1: There are, monks, these three kinds of sick persons found in the world. What three? Here, monks, some sick person, whether he gets suitable food or does not get suitable food, whether he gets suitable medicine or does not get suitable medicine, whether he gets suitable attendance or does not get suitable attendance, does not recover from that illness.
translations.an3.22:3: Here, monks, some sick person, whether he gets suitable food or not, whether he gets suitable medicine or not, whether he gets suitable attendance or not, recovers from that illness.
translations.an3.22:4: Now, monks, that sick person who, whether he gets suitable food or not, whether he gets suitable medicine or not, whether he gets suitable attendance or not, recovers from that illness, is said to have a curable illness, curable food, curable medicine, and curable attendance. And, monks, other sick persons, too, should be given attendance in dependence on him. These, monks, are the three kinds of sick persons found in the world.
translations.an3.22:5: Similarly, monks, there are these three kinds of persons found in the world, like the sick. What three? Here, monks, some person, whether he sees the Tathagata or does not see the Tathagata, whether he hears the Dhamma and Vinaya taught by the Tathagata or does not hear the Dhamma and Vinaya taught by the Tathagata, does not enter upon the fixed course of the wholesome things.
translations.an3.22:6: Here, monks, some person, whether he sees the Tathagata or not, whether he hears the Dhamma and Vinaya taught by the Tathagata or not, enters upon the fixed course of the wholesome things.
translations.an3.24:1: There are, monks, these three persons who are very helpful to another person. What three? Here, monks, a person who, having come to another person, goes for refuge to the Buddha, goes for refuge to the Dhamma, and goes for refuge to the Sangha, is very helpful to that person.
translations.an3.24:2: Again, monks, a person who, having come to another person, truly understands: 'This is suffering, this is the origin of suffering, this is the cessation of suffering, and this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering,' is very helpful to that person.
translations.an3.24:3: Again, monks, a person who, having come to another person, having destroyed the corruptions, lives in the corruption-free emancipation of mind and emancipation of wisdom, having personally realized it by his own direct knowledge, is very helpful to that person. These, monks, are the three persons who are very helpful to another person.
translations.an3.2:1: A person of bad character, monks, is known by three things, and a person of good character is known by three things. A person of bad character is known by three things. What three? By bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct. A person of bad character is known by these three things.
translations.an3.2:2: A person of good character, monks, is known by three things. What three? By bodily good conduct, verbal good conduct, and mental good conduct. A person of good character is known by these three things.
translations.an3.30:4: A person of little wisdom, stupid, and unwise, even if he goes to the bhikkhus from time to time, is not able to grasp the beginning, the middle, and the end of a talk, and wisdom is not evident in him.
translations.an3.30:5: He is not able to grasp the beginning, the middle, and the end of a talk, and wisdom is not evident in him, and he cannot understand, and wisdom is not evident in him.
translations.an3.30:6: A person of high wisdom, monks, is called superior, even if he goes to the bhikkhus from time to time.
translations.an3.30:8: And a person of great wisdom, monks, is also called superior, even if he goes to the bhikkhus from time to time.
translations.an3.32:4: There is the case, Ānanda, where a monk thinks, 'This is peace, this is exquisite, that is, the stilling of all fabrications, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the ending of craving, detachment, cessation, Nibbāna.' It is in this way, Ānanda, that a monk's appropriate concentration is to be developed. Just as this body, though it is made up of various parts, is held together by the system of tendons, so too, a monk's appropriate concentration is to be developed for the ending of the corruptions. And if a monk has developed this concentration, then there will be no 'I am' or 'This is mine' or 'I shall be' with regard to this conscious body or with regard to any external signs. And if a monk has developed this concentration, then there will be no 'I am' or 'This is mine' or 'I shall be' while attaining the liberation of the mind or the liberation by wisdom.
translations.an3.33:1: Then Venerable Sāriputta approached the Buddha, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him, 'I could teach the Dhamma in brief or in detail or in both brief and detailed ways. But there will be those who understand.' 'It is time, Bhagavā, it is time, Sugata, for the Bhagavā to teach the Dhamma in brief or in detail or in both brief and detailed ways. There will be those who understand.',
translations.an3.33:2: Therefore, Sāriputta, you should train yourselves: 'There will be no
translations.an3.34:10: Whatever action, monks, is rooted in delusion, caused by delusion, originated from delusion, and produced from delusion: when delusion has vanished, that action is abandoned, uprooted, pulled out of the ground like a palmyra tree, and becomes non-recurrent in the future.
translations.an3.34:1: There are, monks, these three origins of actions which lead to their production. What three? Greed is the origin of actions which lead to their production, hatred is the origin of actions which lead to their production, and delusion is the origin of actions which lead to their production.
translations.an3.34:11: Suppose, monks, seeds that are intact, unbroken, and unspoiled, and which have a sprout, are planted in well-prepared soil in a favorable season. A man would burn them with fire, and having burned them with fire, he would reduce them to ashes. Having reduced them to ashes, he would winnow them in a strong wind or wash them away in a swift stream. In this way, monks, those seeds would be destroyed, uprooted, pulled out of the ground like a palmyra tree, and become non-recurrent in the future. In the same way, monks, whatever action is rooted in non-greed, caused by non-greed, originated from non-greed, and produced from non-greed: when greed has vanished, that action is abandoned, uprooted, pulled out of the ground like a palmyra tree, and becomes non-recurrent in the future.
translations.an3.33:3: And, Sāriputta, when a monk has no conceit or self-importance regarding this conscious body, and no conceit or self-importance regarding all external objects, and when he dwells having abandoned conceit and self-importance by realizing liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom; this, Sāriputta, is called a monk who has cut off craving, broken the bonds, and by rightly understanding self-importance, has made an end of suffering. This was said by me, Sāriputta, in the Pārāyana, in response to a question about the rising of the sun:
translations.an3.34:5: Suppose, monks, seeds that are intact, unbroken, and unspoiled, and which have a sprout, are planted in well-prepared soil in a favorable season. A god would provide a proper rainfall. In this way, monks, those seeds would grow, increase, and develop. In the same way, monks, whatever action is rooted in greed, caused by greed, originated from greed, and produced from greed: wherever that action ripens, there it produces its effect. Wherever that action produces its effect, there the doer of that action experiences the result, either in this life or in the next, or in some subsequent existence.
translations.an3.34:13: Rooted in greed, rooted in hatred, and rooted in delusion, whatever action one does, whether small or large; the result of that action is experienced here and now, and there is no other place for it to ripen.
translations.an3.34:2: Whatever action, monks, is rooted in greed, caused by greed, originated from greed, and produced from greed: wherever that action ripens, there it produces its effect. Wherever that action produces its effect, there the doer of that action experiences the result, either in this life or in the next, or in some subsequent existence.
translations.an3.34:9: Whatever action, monks, is rooted in non-hatred, caused by non-hatred, originated from non-hatred, and produced from non-hatred: when hatred has vanished, that action is abandoned, uprooted, pulled out of the ground like a palmyra tree, and becomes non-recurrent in the future.
translations.an3.35:3: I will ask you a question, young man. Answer as you like. What do you think, young man? Suppose this householder or his son has a roofed house with a peaked roof, with windows shut, and with a door closed. A couch is spread in it with its legs removed, with its bolts removed, and with its supports removed; it has a mattress and a pillow, and it is covered with a woolen blanket. A oil lamp is burning there, and four wives, who are attractive and of a pleasant appearance, are attending upon him. What do you think, young man? Would he sleep comfortably or not? How would it be for him?
translations.an3.33:4: The abandoning of sensual perceptions, the overcoming of both sorrow and aversion, the dispelling of sloth, and the abandoning of restlessness and worry.
translations.an3.34:6: Whatever action is rooted in hatred... whatever action is rooted in delusion, caused by delusion, originated from delusion, and produced from delusion: wherever that action ripens, there it produces its effect. Wherever that action produces its effect, there the doer of that action experiences the result, either in this life or in the next, or in some subsequent existence. These, monks, are the three origins of actions which lead to their production.
translations.an3.35:4: What do you think, young man? Would feelings of lust and grief arise in that householder or his son due to which, being overwhelmed by those feelings of lust and grief, he would experience suffering?
translations.an3.35:8: One who has attained nibbana, a brahmin, always sleeps in happiness; One who is not attached to sensual pleasures, cooled, without acquisitions.
translations.an3.39:10: Living thus, knowing the teaching without acquisitions; In health, youth, and life, I have abandoned the intoxications.
translations.an3.39:2: I had three mansions, one for the winter, one for the summer, and one for the rainy season. I lived in the rainy season mansion, surrounded by musicians, without going down to the lower mansion. Just as a servant or a worker or a menial is given a meal of broken rice in another's home, in the same way, I was given a meal of rice and meat in my father's home.
translations.an3.39:3: Then it occurred to me: 'An uninstructed ordinary person, subject to old age, not having gone beyond old age, seeing another who is old, would be repelled, humiliated, and disgusted, looking down on himself. I too am subject to old age, not having gone beyond old age. If I, who am subject to old age, not having gone beyond old age, were to see another who is old, I would be repelled, humiliated, and disgusted, which would not be fitting.' Then, having reflected thus, I abandoned all intoxication with youth.
translations.an3.39:4: An uninstructed ordinary person, subject to illness, not having gone beyond illness, seeing another who is ill, would be repelled, humiliated, and disgusted, looking down on himself: 'I too am subject to illness, not having gone beyond illness. If I, who am subject to illness, not having gone beyond illness, were to see another who is ill, I would be repelled, humiliated, and disgusted, which would not be fitting.' Then, having reflected thus, I abandoned all intoxication with health.
translations.an3.39:5: An uninstructed ordinary person, subject to death, not having gone beyond death, seeing another who has died, would be repelled, humiliated, and disgusted, looking down on himself: 'I too am subject to death, not having gone beyond death. If I, who am subject to death, not having gone beyond death, were to see another who has died, I would be repelled, humiliated, and disgusted, which would not be fitting.' Then, having reflected thus, I abandoned all intoxication with life.
translations.an3.39:7: A monk who is intoxicated with youth, health, or life, having turned away from the training, falls into decline.
translations.an3.39:8: Subject to illness, subject to old age, and subject to death; Ordinary people are repelled by things that are in accordance with their nature.
translations.an3.39:9: I would be repelled by that, in such things; But it is not fitting for one who lives like me.
translations.an3.40:1: There are, monks, these three kinds of mastery. What three? Mastery over oneself, mastery over the world, and mastery over the Dhamma. And what, monks, is mastery over oneself? Here, a monk, living in the wilderness, or at the foot of a tree, or in an empty hut, reflects: 'I did not go forth from the household life into homelessness for the sake of robes, almsfood, lodging, or to become something. I have gone forth from the household life into homelessness having pierced the multitude of suffering, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair, pierced by suffering. I will surely know the end of this whole mass of suffering.' He reflects: 'My energy will be aroused, my mindfulness will be established, my body will be tranquil, my mind will be concentrated and one-pointed.' He makes himself his own master, abandons the unwholesome, develops the wholesome, abandons what is blameworthy, develops what is blameless, and purifies himself. This, monks, is called mastery over oneself.
translations.an3.40:3: And what, monks, is mastery over the Dhamma? Here, a monk, living in the wilderness, or at the foot of a tree, or in an empty hut, reflects: 'I did not go forth from the household life into homelessness for the sake of robes, almsfood, lodging, or to become something. I have gone forth from the household life into homelessness having pierced the multitude of suffering, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair, pierced by suffering. I will surely know the end of this whole mass of suffering.' The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, to be known by the wise, each for himself. There are my fellow monks who know and see. If I, having gone forth in this well-expounded Dhamma and discipline, were to live lazily, heedlessly, it would not be fitting.' He reflects: 'My energy will be aroused, my mindfulness will be established, my body will be tranquil, my mind will be concentrated and one-pointed.' He makes the Dhamma his master, abandons the unwholesome, develops the wholesome, abandons what is blameworthy, develops what is blameless, and purifies himself. This, monks, is called mastery over the Dhamma. These, monks, are the three kinds of mastery.
translations.an3.40:4: There is no secrecy in the world, no one conceals an evil deed; The man himself knows, whether he speaks the truth or lies.
translations.an3.40:5: It is good, indeed, that you have examined yourself; One who sees the evil in himself, and conceals it, is a fool.
translations.an3.40:6: The gods and the Tathagatas see the foolish and unwise person wandering in the world; Therefore, one who is master of himself, master of the world, and wise, is a meditator, master of the Dhamma, and a follower of the Dhamma; One who is intent on the truth does not decline, a sage.
translations.an3.48:1: Monks, relying on the Himalayas, the king of mountains, large sal trees grow by means of three increases. What three? They grow by means of branches, leaves, and roots. Monks, relying on the Himalayas, the king of mountains, large sal trees grow by means of these three increases.
translations.an3.48:2: In the same way, monks, relying on the believer, the family man, the people in the house grow by means of three increases. What three? They grow by means of faith, virtue, and wisdom. The people in the house, monks, relying on the believer, the family man, grow by means of these three increases.
translations.an3.48:3: Just as a mountain, a rock in the forest, Trees leaning against it grow;
translations.an3.51:1: Then two old brahmins, advanced in years, aged, of great age, eighty, ninety, one hundred years from birth, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged greetings, they sat down at one side. As they sat down at one side, those brahmins said to the Blessed One: "We are brahmins, old, advanced in years, aged, of great age, eighty, ninety, one hundred years from birth; we are not given to skillful things, not given to wholesomeness, not given to what inspires confidence. Teach us, Master Gotama, advise us, Master Gotama, for our long-term benefit and happiness"
translations.an3.51:2: "You are old, brahmins, advanced in years, aged, of great age, eighty, ninety, one hundred years from birth; you are not given to skillful things, not given to wholesomeness, not given to what inspires confidence. This world is swept away by old age, illness, and death. When the world is being swept away by old age, illness, and death, one who is self-controlled in body, speech, and mind is a shelter, a refuge, and a support for the departed.
translations.an3.51:3: Life is short, The decaying have no shelter; Seeing the fear of death, Do deeds that bring happiness.
translations.an3.52:4: The world is on fire, With old age and death; It is being burned by giving, What is given is well-placed.
translations.an3.60:1: Then the brahmin Saṅgāravo approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged greetings, he sat down at one side. As he sat down at one side, the brahmin Saṅgāravo said to the Blessed One: "We are brahmins, Master Gotama. We perform sacrifices and have sacrifices performed. There, Master Gotama, both the one who performs the sacrifice and the one for whom the sacrifice is performed, all of them are endowed with a meritorious practice that brings many rewards, that is, the procedure of the sacrifice. But this one, Master Gotama, who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness, who tames, calms, and extinguishes himself alone, is endowed with a meritorious practice that brings one reward, that is, the procedure of going forth",
translations.an3.60:10: Here, brahmin, someone does not predict based on a sign, nor does he predict having heard the sound of humans, non-humans, or deities: 'Your mind will be like this, your mind will be like that, your heart will be like this.' He predicts many things, but they do not turn out as predicted.
translations.an3.60:11: Here, brahmin, someone does not predict based on a sign, nor does he predict having heard the sound of humans, non-humans, or deities. But having thought, having reflected, having heard the sound of his own thoughts, he predicts: 'Your mind will be like this, your mind will be like that, your heart will be like this.' He predicts many things, but they do not turn out as predicted.
translations.an3.60:12: Here, brahmin, someone does not predict based on a sign, nor does he predict having heard the sound of humans, non-humans, or deities, nor does he predict having heard the sound of his own thoughts. But having entered a concentration without thought, without reflection, he knows, having encompassed it with his mind: 'This person's mental formations have been arranged thus, this person's heart will think in this way, this person will think thus.' He predicts many things, and they turn out as predicted. This, brahmin, is called the miracle of instruction.
translations.an3.60:13: And what, brahmin, is the miracle of instruction? Here, brahmin, someone instructs thus: 'Think in this way, do not think in that way; attend to your mind in this way, do not attend to your mind in that way; abandon this, and dwell having entered upon that.' This, brahmin, is called the miracle of instruction. These, brahmin, are the three miracles. Of these three miracles, brahmin, which one do you approve of as the most excellent and sublime?
translations.an3.60:14: "There, Master Gotama, as for the miracle that someone experiences here, various kinds of psychic power ... as far as the Brahma world, having control over one's body, this miracle is like a magical illusion, it is like a dream.
translations.an3.5:1: A fool, monks, can be known by three things.  What three?  He does not give a thoughtful answer to a question, he does not give a thoughtful rejection to a question, and when another's thoughtful rejection of a question is adorned with phrases and words, and is clear and pleasing, he does not approve of it.
translations.an3.60:16: Whatever marvel, Bhante Gotama, one might expect from one who instructs thus: 'Think in this way, do not think in that way; attend to this, do not attend to that; abandon this, and live having undertaken that' — this is the greatest marvel, the most extraordinary and sublime of the three marvels.
translations.an3.60:17: It is amazing, Bhante Gotama, it is marvelous. Whatever the Blessed One has said, we have come to know these three marvels in the Blessed One. For the Blessed One has many kinds of psychic power, and he experiences them ... up to the Brahma world. The Blessed One has a mind that is without thought, without examination, and he knows the cessation of thought: 'When this person's mental formations are stilled, the mind of this person will think of that thought next.' The Blessed One instructs thus: 'Think in this way, do not think in that way; attend to this, do not attend to that; abandon this, and live having undertaken that.'
translations.an3.60:18: 'I shall answer you, brahmin, and I shall explain. I have many kinds of psychic power, and I experience them ... up to the Brahma world. I have a mind that is without thought, without examination, and I know the cessation of thought: 'When this person's mental formations are stilled, the mind of this person will think of that thought next.' I instruct thus: 'Think in this way, do not think in that way; attend to this, do not attend to that; abandon this, and live having undertaken that.'
translations.an3.60:19: 'But, Bhante Gotama, is there any other monk who possesses these three marvels, apart from the Blessed One?' 'Not one hundred, brahmin, nor two hundred, nor three hundred, nor four hundred, nor five hundred, but more than that, are the monks who possess these three marvels.' 'Where do those monks live now, Bhante Gotama?' 'In this very Sangha of monks.'
translations.an3.60:2: I ask you, brahmin, about this. Please answer as you think fit. What do you think, brahmin? When a Tathagata, an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One, appears in the world, he says: 'This is the path, this is the practice, by which I have reached the unsurpassed, sublime, perfect enlightenment; come, practice like this, and you too will reach the unsurpassed, sublime, perfect enlightenment.' The Teacher teaches the Dhamma, and others practice accordingly; there are many hundreds, many thousands, many hundreds of thousands of them.
translations.an3.60:3: What do you think, brahmin? Is the path of merit, the path of good deeds, that leads to enlightenment, a single path or multiple paths?
translations.an3.60:4: Then Venerable Ananda said to the brahmin Sangarava: 'Of these two paths, brahmin, which one do you think is more fruitful, more beneficial, and more sublime?' The brahmin Sangarava said to Venerable Ananda: 'Both the Blessed One and Venerable Ananda are my teachers, my refuges.'
translations.an3.60:5: Venerable Ananda asked the brahmin Sangarava again: 'I am not asking, brahmin, who your teachers and refuges are. I am asking: of these two paths, brahmin, which one do you think is more fruitful, more beneficial, and more sublime?' The brahmin Sangarava said to Venerable Ananda again: 'Both the Blessed One and Venerable Ananda are my teachers, my refuges.'
translations.an3.60:7: Then the Blessed One thought: 'Even if Venerable Ananda asks the brahmin Sangarava for the third time, he will not be able to get an answer. I should intervene.' The Blessed One said to the brahmin Sangarava: 'What conversation, brahmin, has arisen among the king's men, who are sitting together in the royal capital?' 'This conversation has arisen, Bhante Gotama, among the king's men, who are sitting together in the royal capital:
translations.an3.60:8: There are, brahmin, these three marvels. What three? The marvel of psychic power, the marvel of teaching, and the marvel of instruction. And what, brahmin, is the marvel of psychic power? Here, brahmin, some person has many kinds of psychic power, and he experiences them: 'Being one, he becomes many; being many, he becomes one; he appears and disappears; he goes unhindered through walls, through ramparts, through mountains, as if through space; he dives in and out of the earth, as if it were water; he walks on water, as if it were earth; he travels through space, cross-legged, as if he were a bird; with his hand he touches and strokes the sun and the moon, so powerful and mighty; he exercises mastery over his body, as far as the Brahma world.' This, brahmin, is called the marvel of psychic power.
translations.an3.60:9: And what, brahman, is the miracle of instruction? Here, brahman, someone gives a signal and says: 'Your mind is thus, your mind is thus, your heart is thus.' And no matter how much he gives the signal, the mind is just so, not otherwise.
translations.an3.61:13: These four noble truths, monks, are taught by me, unrefuted, untainted, unadulterated, unrejected by wise ascetics and brahmins. This is what was said. And with reference to what was it said? When there is consciousness, name-and-form comes to be; from name-and-form, the six sense bases; from the six sense bases, contact; from contact, feeling. I declare that feeling is suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path to the cessation of suffering.
translations.an3.61:14: And what, monks, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress are suffering; not getting what one wants is suffering. In short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. This, monks, is called the noble truth of suffering.
translations.an3.61:15: And what, monks, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? With ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, becoming; with becoming as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress come to be. This is the origin of the entire mass of suffering.
translations.an3.61:16: And what, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? With the complete fading away and cessation of ignorance, the cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, the cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, the cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, the cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, the cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, the cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, the cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, the cessation of becoming; with the cessation of becoming, the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease. This is the cessation of the entire mass of suffering.
translations.an3.61:3: In the past, monks, a wise person, having considered the matter, did not say: 'This is to be done, this is not to be done.' When the true and false are not clearly seen, and one lives without self-control, there is no personal doctrine of a recluse that is in accordance with the Dhamma.
translations.an3.61:8: These three, monks, are the bases of speculation that wise men speculate about, master, and proclaim, and which, carried to their conclusion, lead to the doctrine of non-action.
translations.an3.61:9: This Dhamma, monks, has been taught by me, unrefuted, untainted, unadulterated, unrejected by wise ascetics and brahmins. And what is the Dhamma that has been taught by me, unrefuted, untainted, unadulterated, unrejected by wise ascetics and brahmins? The six elements, monks, have been taught by me; the six sense bases have been taught by me; the eighteen mental examinations have been taught by me; the four noble truths have been taught by me.
translations.an3.62:1: The uninstructed worldling, monks, speaks of three fearsome things that are without a mother and a father. What three? There is a time, monks, when a great conflagration occurs. When a great conflagration occurs, villages, towns, and cities are burned. And when villages, towns, and cities are being burned, a mother cannot find her child, nor can a child find its mother.
translations.an3.62:2: Again, monks, there is a time when a great rain cloud occurs. When a great rain cloud occurs, a great flood arises. When a great flood arises, villages, towns, and cities are swept away. And when villages, towns, and cities are being swept away, a mother cannot find her child, nor can a child find its mother.
translations.an3.62:3: Again, monks, there is a time when fear arises, a terror, and the people of the countryside flee to the towns, the people of the towns flee to the cities, and the people of the cities flee to the countryside. And when fear arises, a terror, and the people of the countryside are fleeing to the towns, the people of the towns are fleeing to the cities, and the people of the cities are fleeing to the countryside, a mother cannot find her child, nor can a child find its mother. These, monks, are the three fearsome things that are without a mother and a father, spoken of by the uninstructed worldling.
translations.an3.62:4: The uninstructed ordinary person, monks, says that there are three kinds of fears that are fearsome and not fearsome to one who is not a protector of the truth. What are these three? There is a time, monks, when a great conflagration occurs. When a great conflagration occurs, villages and towns and cities are burned.
