When villages and towns and cities are being burned, there is a time when a mother does not find her child, nor a child its mother. The uninstructed ordinary person says that this is the first kind of fear that is fearsome and not fearsome to one who is not a protector of the truth.
translations.an3.62:5: Again, monks, there is a time when a great rain cloud occurs. When a great rain cloud occurs, a great flood arises. When a great flood arises, villages and towns and cities are swept away. When villages and towns and cities are being swept away, there is a time when a mother does not find her child, nor a child its mother. The uninstructed ordinary person says that this is the second kind of fear that is fearsome and not fearsome to one who is not a protector of the truth.
translations.an3.62:6: Again, monks, there is a time when fear arises due to a threat from a wild beast, and the people of the countryside flee to the towns. When fear arises due to a threat from a wild beast, and the people of the countryside are fleeing to the towns, there is a time when a mother does not find her child, nor a child its mother. The uninstructed ordinary person says that this is the third kind of fear that is fearsome and not fearsome to one who is not a protector of the truth. These, monks, are the three kinds of fears that are fearsome and not fearsome to one who is not a protector of the truth.
translations.an3.62:7: There are, monks, three fears that are not fearsome to one who is a protector of the truth. What are these three? The fear of old age, the fear of illness, and the fear of death. A mother does not get to have her living child and say: 'I am living, may my child live.' Nor does a child get to have its living mother and say: 'I am living, may my mother live.'
translations.an3.62:8: A mother does not get to have her ailing child and say: 'I am ailing, may my child not ail.' Nor does a child get to have its ailing mother and say: 'I am ailing, may my mother not ail.'
translations.an3.62:9: A mother does not get to have her dying child and say: 'I am dying, may my child not die.' Nor does a child get to have its dying mother and say: 'I am dying, may my mother not die.' These, monks, are the three fears that are not fearsome to one who is a protector of the truth.
translations.an3.63:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosalan country with a large community of monks, and he arrived at a brahmin village called Venāgapura. The brahmin householders of Venāgapura heard: 'The ascetic Gotama, the Sakyan son who went forth from the Sakyan clan, has arrived at Venāgapura.'
translations.an3.63:11: 'It is wonderful, Master Gotama, it is marvelous! Who else could be the recipient of such great offerings, such great hospitality, unobstructed and unrestricted, except for Master Gotama?'
translations.an3.63:2: Then the brahmin householders of Venāgapura approached the Blessed One. Having approached, some of them paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side, some exchanged greetings with him and sat down to one side, some saluted him with their hands placed together and sat down to one side, some announced their name and clan and sat down to one side, and some sat down to one side in silence.
translations.an3.63:5: 'There are, brahmin, these three kinds of high and lofty beds that I am now the recipient of, unobstructed and unrestricted. What are these three? The divine high and lofty bed, the brahmin high and lofty bed, and the noble high and lofty bed. These, brahmin, are the three kinds of high and lofty beds that I am now the recipient of, unobstructed and unrestricted.'
translations.an4.10:10: Beings roam in samsara, going from birth to death; having fully understood sensual pleasures and all the fetters of existence;
translations.an4.10:9: Bound by sensual desire, bound by the fetter of existence; bound by wrong view, led by ignorance;
translations.an4.18:1: 'There are, monks, these four modes of going forth that do not lead to going forth. What are these four? One does not go forth due to desire, nor due to hatred, nor due to delusion, nor due to fear— These, monks, are the four modes of going forth that do not lead to going forth.'
translations.an4.1:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Blessed One was living among the Vajjians at Bhanda Village.
translations.an4.1:4: 'Morality, concentration, and wisdom, and the highest liberation; these things, understood by the Buddha, the renowned Gotama,'
translations.an4.24:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāketa in the Grove of the Blind Men's Grove.
translations.an4.24:2: 'Whatever, monks, is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought, and pondered in the mind by this community of gods and humans, with its asuras, brahmas, and recluses and brahmins, I know it all.'
translations.an4.24:5: If I were to say, 'I know and I do not know,' that would be equivalent to that.
translations.an4.24:7: Thus, monks, the Tathagata is one who knows and sees what can be known and seen. He does not think, 'I have seen,' or 'I have not seen,' or 'I shall see,' or 'I shall not see.' He does not think, 'I have heard,' or 'I have not heard,' or 'I shall hear,' or 'I shall not hear.' He does not think, 'I have sensed,' or 'I have not sensed,' or 'I shall sense,' or 'I shall not sense.' He does not think, 'I have known,' or 'I have not known,' or 'I shall know,' or 'I shall not know.' Thus, monks, the Tathagata is one who knows and sees what can be known and seen, and he is not different from that. I say that there is no one who is more excellent or superior to him.
translations.an4.24:8: Whatever is seen, heard, or sensed, Is considered true by the foolish; But for one who is wise and mindful, That is not the truth, nor is it false.
translations.an4.28:1: There are, monks, these four noble lineages, ancient, original, and traditional, which are uncalculable and incalculable from the beginning. What four? Here, monks, a monk is content with any robe, and he speaks in praise of contentment with robes. He does not commit any offense on account of robes, and he is not agitated if he does not get a robe. If he gets a robe, he uses it unattached, uninfatuated, and aware of the drawbacks, knowing its purpose and using it wisely. He does not become self-complacent or complacent about others on account of his contentment with robes. Whoever is skilled, diligent, and mindful in this, he is called a monk who stands in the ancient, noble lineage.
translations.an4.28:4: Again, monks, a monk is delighted with development and devoted to development, delighted with relinquishment and devoted to relinquishment. He does not become self-complacent or complacent about others on account of his delight in development and devotion to development, or his delight in relinquishment and devotion to relinquishment. Whoever is skilled, diligent, and mindful in this, he is called a monk who stands in the ancient, noble lineage. These, monks, are the four noble lineages, ancient, original, and traditional, which are uncalculable and incalculable from the beginning.
translations.an4.28:5: A monk endowed with these four noble lineages, whether he lives in the eastern direction or the western direction, the northern direction or the southern direction, he lives without being overcome by discontent. Why is that? Because, monks, a wise person is the conqueror of discontent.
translations.an4.28:6: The wise do not tolerate discontent, nor does discontent tolerate the wise; The wise tolerate discontent, for the wise are the conquerors of discontent.
translations.an4.31:1: There are, monks, these four wheels, by which the wheel of the noble ones turns, and by which the noble ones quickly attain greatness and abundance in wealth. What four? Living in a suitable place, associating with good people, making a suitable effort, and having done good deeds in the past. These, monks, are the four wheels, by which the wheel of the noble ones turns, and by which the noble ones quickly attain greatness and abundance in wealth.
translations.an4.32:1: There are, monks, these four means of support. What four? Giving, kind words, beneficial actions, and equality of treatment. These, monks, are the four means of support.
translations.an4.32:2: Giving, kind words, and beneficial actions, And equality of treatment in all things; These are the means of support in the world, Like the wheels of a chariot that carry it along.
translations.an4.32:3: These means of support do not perish, Not even a mother's love for her child; One may gain honor or veneration, Even a father's love for his child.
translations.an4.33:1: The lion, the king of beasts, emerges from his lair in the evening. Having emerged, he stretches. Having stretched, he looks around in all four directions. Having looked around, he lets out a mighty roar three times. Having let out a mighty roar, he goes to his hunting ground. Whatever animals, monks, that are living on the ground and hear the sound of the lion's roar, they mostly experience fear, terror, and anxiety. They enter into holes, or they enter into burrows, or they enter into the forest, or the birds fly up into the sky. Whatever elephants, monks, that are bound by strong ropes and stakes in the villages, towns, and capital cities, they break and destroy those bonds and, frightened and terrified, they run away in all directions. Such, monks, is the great power and great majesty of the lion, the king of beasts.
translations.an4.33:2: In the same way, monks, when the Tathagata, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, appears in the world, he teaches the Dhamma: 'This is the truth, this is the origin of the truth, this is the cessation of the truth, and this is the path leading to the cessation of the truth.' Whatever gods, monks, that are long-lived, beautiful, and happy, living in high and spacious mansions, they hear the Tathagata's teaching of the Dhamma and mostly experience fear, terror, and anxiety: 'We are impermanent, it seems, and we thought we were permanent; we are unstable, it seems, and we thought we were stable; we are without a core, it seems, and we thought we had a core. We are impermanent, unstable, and without a core, and we are encompassed by the truth.' Such, monks, is the great power and great majesty of the Tathagata.
translations.an4.33:3: When the Buddha sets in motion the wheel of Dhamma, He is the teacher of the world, without a peer.
translations.an4.33:4: The cessation of the truth and its origin, And the noble path that leads to the cessation of suffering; The cessation of the truth and its origin, And the noble path that leads to the cessation of suffering.
translations.an4.34:1: There are, monks, these four things that are supreme and unsurpassed. What four? Whatever beings there are, whether footless or two-footed, four-footed or many-footed, whether they have form or are formless, whether they are percipient or non-percipient, or neither percipient nor non-percipient, the Tathagata, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, is declared the supreme among them. Those who have faith in the Buddha are supreme among those who have faith. The result of having faith in the supreme is supreme.
translations.an4.34:2: Whatever conditioned things there are, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared the supreme among them. Those who have faith in the Noble Eightfold Path are supreme among those who have faith. The result of having faith in the supreme is supreme.
translations.an4.34:3: Whatever conditioned or unconditioned things there are, the destruction of craving is declared the supreme among them, that is, the destruction of craving, the removal of craving, the abandonment of craving, the rejection of craving, the elimination of craving, the destruction of craving, the cessation of craving, Nibbana. Those who have faith in the destruction of craving are supreme among those who have faith. The result of having faith in the supreme is supreme.
translations.an4.34:4: Whatever groups or assemblies there are, the Sangha of the Tathagata's disciples is declared the supreme among them, that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight individuals, this Sangha of the Buddha's disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of respect, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Those who have faith in the Sangha are supreme among those who have faith. The result of having faith in the supreme is supreme. These, monks, are the four things that are supreme and unsurpassed.
translations.an4.34:5: The supreme among those who have faith is one who knows the supreme Dhamma; those who have faith in the Buddha are supreme, and they are worthy of gifts and unsurpassed.
translations.an4.34:6: Those who have faith in the Dhamma are supreme, and they attain the peace of the destruction of craving; those who have faith in the Sangha are supreme, and they attain the unsurpassed field of merit.
translations.an4.34:7: The gift given to the supreme is the supreme gift, and it yields the supreme fruit; the supreme life, beauty, fame, and happiness are the result of giving to the supreme.
translations.an4.35:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was living in the Kalandakanivapa in Rajagaha. Then the brahmin Vassakara, the chief minister of Magadha, approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. After exchanging greetings and pleasant conversation, he sat down at one side and said to the Blessed One:
translations.an4.35:2: We consider one who is endowed with four things to be a wise and intelligent person. What four? Here, Master Gotama, one is well-versed in the knowledge of various texts and understands the meaning of what has been spoken: 'This is the meaning of that statement, this is the meaning of that statement.' One is mindful and able to recall and remember even what was said long ago; in regard to the duties to be performed by one who is a member of a household, one is skilled and diligent, able to manage and organize, able to dispel any fear that may arise. We consider one who is endowed with these four things to be a wise and intelligent person. If it is allowable, Master Gotama, please approve of this; if it is not allowable, please refute it.
translations.an4.35:6: One who knows the death-free, the liberation from the snare of death, who shows the way that is beneficial to gods and humans, who teaches the Dhamma, and who, having seen and heard it, is pleasing to many people.
translations.an4.36:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Magadha country and arrived at a village of the brahmins of the Kosalans. The brahmin Doṇa saw the Blessed One sitting at the foot of a tree, and he approached him and exchanged greetings. After exchanging greetings, Doṇa sat down at one side and said to the Blessed One:
translations.an4.36:2: 'Will you be a god?' 'I will not be a god, brahmin.' 'Will you be a gandhabba?' 'I will not be a gandhabba, brahmin.' 'Will you be a yakkha?' 'I will not be a yakkha, brahmin.' 'Will you be a human being?' 'I will not be a human being, brahmin.'
translations.an4.36:4: 'If, brahmin, I were to be a god because I have not abandoned the corruptions, then I would be a god. But I have abandoned the corruptions, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm tree that has been destroyed, so that they cannot arise in the future. If I were to be a gandhabba... a yakkha... a human being because I have not abandoned the corruptions, then I would be a gandhabba... a yakkha... a human being. But I have abandoned the corruptions... Just as a lotus or a water lily or a water flower, though born in the water and grown up in the water, yet remains unsoiled by the water, even so, brahmin, though I was born in the world and grew up in the world, yet I remain unsoiled by the world. Remember me, brahmin, as the Buddha.'
translations.an4.37:1: A monk who is endowed with four things is not capable of decline, but is close to Nibbana. What four? Here, a monk is virtuous, restrained by the rules of the Patimokkha, and is endowed with good conduct and a sense of shame; he is restrained in his senses, and is moderate in eating; he is devoted to wakefulness.
translations.an4.37:2: And how, monks, is a monk virtuous? Here, a monk is virtuous, and he is restrained by the rules of the Patimokkha, and is endowed with good conduct and a sense of shame; he is restrained in his senses, and is moderate in eating. He trains himself in the training rules, and is skilled in the rules of the Patimokkha. In this way, monks, a monk is virtuous.
translations.an4.37:3: And how, monks, is a monk one who guards the doors of his senses?  Here, monks, a monk having seen a form with his eye, does not grasp at the general appearance or the details of it.  If, while doing so, the sense door of the eye, which is not guarded, were to be taken over by lustful thoughts and unwholesome states, he practices restraint, guards the sense door of the eye, and achieves restraint over the sense door of the eye.  Having heard a sound with his ear...  Having smelled a smell with his nose...  Having tasted a taste with his tongue...  Having felt a touch with his body...  Having cognized a mental object with his mind, he does not grasp at the general appearance or the details of it.  If, while doing so, the sense door of the mind, which is not guarded, were to be taken over by lustful thoughts and unwholesome states, he practices restraint, guards the sense door of the mind, and achieves restraint over the sense door of the mind.  Thus, monks, a monk is one who guards the doors of his senses.
translations.an4.37:4: And how, monks, is a monk one who is moderate in eating?  Here, monks, a monk reflects and eats, not for amusement, nor for intoxication, nor for putting on weight, nor for beautification, but only for the maintenance and nourishment of this body, for keeping it alive, for aiding the spiritual life, thinking: 'I will destroy the old feeling and not create a new one, and I will maintain myself, be blameless, and live in comfort.'  Thus, monks, a monk is one who is moderate in eating.
translations.an4.37:5: And how, monks, is a monk one who is devoted to wakefulness?  Here, monks, a monk during the day, having washed his feet, minds his manners and sits down in a cross-legged position, keeping his body straight, having established mindfulness in front of him.  At the end of the night, at the end of the first watch, he gets up and walks back and forth, and at the end of the night, at the end of the last watch, having washed his feet, he minds his manners and sits down in a cross-legged position, keeping his body straight, having established mindfulness in front of him.  Thus, monks, a monk is one who is devoted to wakefulness.  Endowed with these four qualities, a monk is not liable to decline, and he gains proximity to nibbana.
translations.an4.37:6: A monk established in virtue,  guarded in his senses,  moderate in eating,  and devoted to wakefulness.
translations.an4.37:7: Living thus, ardent,  day and night, untiring;  He develops the wholesome,  and reaches the highest peace.
translations.an4.38:1: A monk, monks, who is endowed with the complete and utter destruction of all speculative views about the past, the future, and the present, is called 'one who has destroyed all speculative views about the past, the future, and the present.'  And how, monks, is a monk one who has destroyed all speculative views about the past, the future, and the present?  Here, monks, a monk has abandoned and rejected all speculative views about the past, the future, and the present, such as: 'The world is eternal' or 'The world is not eternal', 'The world is finite' or 'The world is infinite', 'The soul and the body are the same' or 'The soul is one thing and the body another', 'The Tathagata exists after death' or 'The Tathagata does not exist after death', 'The Tathagata both exists and does not exist after death' or 'The Tathagata neither exists nor does not exist after death.'  Thus, monks, a monk has destroyed all speculative views about the past, the future, and the present.
translations.an4.38:4: And how, monks, is a monk one who is tranquil?  Here, monks, a monk has abandoned conceit, which is cut off at the root, made like a palm tree that has been destroyed, and is no longer subject to future arising.  Thus, monks, a monk is one who is tranquil.  A monk who has destroyed all speculative views about the past, the future, and the present is called 'one who has destroyed all speculative views about the past, the future, and the present, and is tranquil.'
translations.an4.38:5: Desire for sensual pleasure, desire for existence,  and desire for non-existence, along with the underlying tendency to these desires;  These are the underlying tendencies to views,  and the accumulation of latent tendencies.
translations.an4.38:6: For one who has abandoned all passion,  and is liberated by the destruction of craving;  These underlying tendencies to views  are abandoned and eliminated.
translations.an4.52:1: There are, monks, these four streams of merit, streams of good deeds, that are pleasant, desirable, and that bring happiness, and that lead to what is liked, desired, and agreeable, and to one's own happiness and well-being.  What four?  Here, monks, a noble disciple has faith in the Buddha, and this faith is based on knowledge: 'The Blessed One is the Exalted One, the Fully Awakened One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Leader of Persons to be Tamed, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Awakened One, the Blessed One.'  This, monks, is the first stream of merit, stream of good deeds, that is pleasant, desirable, and that brings happiness, and that leads to what is liked, desired, and agreeable, and to one's own happiness and well-being.
translations.an4.52:2: Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple has faith in the Dhamma, and this faith is based on knowledge: 'The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, to be seen here and now, timeless, inviting all to come and see, leading to the goal, to be known by the wise, each for himself.'  This, monks, is the second stream of merit, stream of good deeds, that is pleasant, desirable, and that brings happiness, and that leads to what is liked, desired, and agreeable, and to one's own happiness and well-being.
translations.an4.52:3: Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple has faith in the Sangha, and this faith is based on knowledge: 'The Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples has entered on the good way, the straight way, the true way, and the proper way; that is to say, the four pairs of persons, the eight individuals; this Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, and worthy of reverence; it is the supreme field for merit for the world.'  This, monks, is the third stream of merit, stream of good deeds, that is pleasant, desirable, and that brings happiness, and that leads to what is liked, desired, and agreeable, and to one's own happiness and well-being.
translations.an4.52:4: Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with the noble virtues, which are unbroken, unsplit, unspotted, unblemished, freeing, praised by the wise, and conducive to concentration.  This, monks, is the fourth stream of merit, stream of good deeds, that is pleasant, desirable, and that brings happiness, and that leads to what is liked, desired, and agreeable, and to one's own happiness and well-being.  These, monks, are the four streams of merit, streams of good deeds, that are pleasant, desirable, and that bring happiness, and that lead to what is liked, desired, and agreeable, and to one's own happiness and well-being.
translations.an4.52:5: For one whose faith in the Tathagata is firm and well-established;  and whose virtue is beautiful,  praised by the noble ones.
translations.an4.52:6: They call one who has faith in the Sangha and has a correct view 'not poor', and their life is not in vain.
translations.an4.53:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering on a road between Madhura and Verañja. A large number of householders and their wives were also wandering on that road between Madhura and Verañja. The Blessed One turned off the road and sat down at the root of a certain tree. The householders and their wives saw the Blessed One sitting at the root of the tree and approached him. After paying homage to the Blessed One, they sat down on one side. As they sat on one side, the Blessed One said to them:
translations.an4.53:10: Both are faithful and generous, mindful and righteous; they are the benefactors, speaking kindly to each other.
translations.an4.53:11: They are content and have few wishes, they are not jealous, and they have the same virtues; they are friends to each other, with no ill-will.
translations.an4.53:2: “There are four cohabitations, householders. What four? A fool lives with a fool, a fool lives with a wise person, a wise person lives with a fool, a wise person lives with a wise person.
translations.an4.53:3: And how, householders, does a fool live with a fool? Here, a master is a killer of living beings, a thief, a sensualist, a liar, a drinker, and unrighteous, with a mind corrupted by stinginess, abusing and reviling ascetics and brahmins; and his wife is also a killer of living beings, a thief, a sensualist, a liar, a drinker, and unrighteous, with a mind corrupted by stinginess, abusing and reviling ascetics and brahmins. This, householders, is how a fool lives with a fool.
translations.an4.53:8: The master is unrighteous, jealous, and abusive; the wife is virtuous, generous, and without attachment; even she lives with her husband, the fool.
translations.an4.53:9: The master is virtuous, generous, and without attachment; the wife is unrighteous, jealous, and abusive; even she lives with her husband, the wise person.
translations.an4.5:1: “There are four persons, monks, to be found in the world. What four? The person who goes with the stream, the person who goes against the stream, the person who stands firm, and the person who has crossed over and stands on dry land, unshakable, a brahmin.
translations.an4.5:2: And what, monks, is the person who goes with the stream? Here, a certain person indulges in sensual pleasures and does evil deeds. This, monks, is called the person who goes with the stream.
translations.an4.5:3: And what, monks, is the person who goes against the stream? Here, a certain person does not indulge in sensual pleasures and does not do evil deeds; and even with pain and sadness, with tears and lamentation, he lives the perfect and pure spiritual life. This, monks, is called the person who goes against the stream.
translations.an4.5:4: And what, monks, is the person who stands firm? Here, a certain person, through the destruction of the five lower fetters, is reborn spontaneously and will attain final nibbana there, without returning from that world. This, monks, is called the person who stands firm. And what, monks, is the person who has crossed over and stands on dry land, unshakable, a brahmin? Here, a certain person, through the destruction of the taints, has realized for himself with direct knowledge the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he lives. This, monks, is called the person who has crossed over and stands on dry land, unshakable, a brahmin. These, monks, are the four persons to be found in the world.
translations.an4.5:5: Those people who are heedless in sensual pleasures, unrepelled by sensual pleasures, return again and again to birth and decay, driven by craving, going with the stream.
translations.an4.5:6: Therefore the wise person, established in mindfulness, does not indulge in sensual pleasures or in evil; and even with pain, he gives up sensual pleasures, and is called one who goes against the stream.
translations.an4.5:7: The person who has abandoned the five defilements, is fully trained, and is not liable to fall away; who has mastered his mind and has controlled his faculties, is called one who stands firm.
translations.an4.62:2: “There are four kinds of happiness that can be attained by a layperson who enjoys sensual pleasures, at the proper time and in the proper season. What four? The happiness of ownership, the happiness of wealth, the happiness of debtlessness, and the happiness of blamelessness.
translations.an4.62:3: And what, householder, is the happiness of ownership? Here, a clansman has wealth acquired by energetic striving, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous and lawfully gotten. He thinks: 'I have wealth acquired by energetic striving... lawfully gotten.' He feels happiness and joy. This, householder, is called the happiness of ownership.
translations.an4.62:5: And what, householder, is the happiness of debtlessness? Here, a clansman has no debts to anyone, whether small or large. He thinks: 'I have no debts to anyone, whether small or large.' He feels happiness and joy. This, householder, is called the happiness of debtlessness.
translations.an4.62:6: And what, householder, is the happiness of blamelessness? Here, a noble disciple is endowed with blameless bodily action, blameless verbal action, and blameless mental action. He thinks: 'I am endowed with blameless bodily action, blameless verbal action, and blameless mental action.' He feels happiness and joy. This, householder, is called the happiness of blamelessness. These, householder, are the four kinds of happiness that can be attained by a layperson who enjoys sensual pleasures, at the proper time and in the proper season.
translations.an4.62:7: Having known the happiness of debtlessness, and then the happiness of ownership, one enjoys the happiness of wealth, and then one sees with wisdom.
translations.an5.23:1: These five, monks, are corruptions of gold, by which corrupted gold is not malleable, nor ductile, nor radiant, but brittle and not properly workable. What five? Iron, copper, tin, lead, and silver. These five, monks, are corruptions of gold... If the gold is freed from these five corruptions, it is malleable, ductile, radiant, not brittle, and properly workable. Whatever ornament one wishes, whether a ring, earrings, or a gold chain, it serves the purpose.
translations.an5.23:2: In the same way, monks, there are these five corruptions of the mind, corrupted by which the mind is not malleable, nor ductile, nor radiant, but brittle and not properly concentrated for the destruction of the taints. What five? Sensual desire, ill-will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. These five, monks, are corruptions of the mind... If the mind is freed from these five corruptions, it is malleable, ductile, radiant, not brittle, and properly concentrated for the destruction of the taints. When one's mind is concentrated, one can witness whatever dhamma one wishes to witness, in each and every (meditation) object.
translations.an5.23:3: If one wishes: 'May I experience various mystic powers... may I, having been one, become many; or, having been many, become one... may I go unhindered through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through air; may I dive in and out of the earth as if it were water; may I walk on water as if it were earth; may I travel through the air like a bird; may I, with my body, touch and stroke the moon and sun, so powerful and mighty, and may I exercise control over my body as far as the world of Brahma', one can witness it, in each and every (meditation) object.
translations.an5.23:4: If one wishes: 'May I, with the divine ear, hear both divine and human sounds, whether near or far', one can witness it, in each and every (meditation) object.
translations.an5.23:5: If one wishes: 'May I understand the minds of other beings, other persons... may I understand a mind with passion as a mind with passion, a mind without passion as a mind without passion... a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion, a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion... a contracted mind as contracted, a distracted mind as distracted... an exalted mind as exalted, an unexalted mind as unexalted... a surpassable mind as surpassable, an unsurpassable mind as unsurpassable... a concentrated mind as concentrated, an unconcentrated mind as unconcentrated... a liberated mind as liberated, an unliberated mind as unliberated', one can witness it, in each and every (meditation) object.
translations.an5.25:1: Monks, right view supported by these five factors is accompanied by the fruit of stream-entry and the benefits of stream-entry, and is accompanied by the fruit of the cessation of effluents and the benefits of the cessation of effluents.
translations.an5.26:1: Monks, there are these five bases of liberation, where the mind of a monk who is heedful, zealous, and resolute, and who dwells, is liberated, or the unexhausted taints are exhausted, or the unattained supreme security from bondage is attained.
translations.an5.26:3: Again, monks, a monk teaches the Dhamma to others in detail, as he has heard and studied it. To the extent that the monk teaches the Dhamma to others in detail, as he has heard and studied it, he experiences the meaning and the Dhamma. He feels joy, and being joyful, rapture arises. With a rapturous mind, his body becomes tranquil, and being tranquil, he feels pleasure. With a pleased mind, he becomes concentrated. This, monks, is the second basis of liberation, where the mind of a monk who is heedful, zealous, and resolute, and who dwells, is liberated, or the unexhausted taints are exhausted, or the unattained supreme security from bondage is attained.
translations.an5.26:4: Again, monks, a monk recites the Dhamma in detail, as he has heard and studied it. To the extent that the monk recites the Dhamma in detail, as he has heard and studied it, he experiences the meaning and the Dhamma. He feels joy, and being joyful, rapture arises. With a rapturous mind, his body becomes tranquil, and being tranquil, he feels pleasure. With a pleased mind, he becomes concentrated. This, monks, is the third basis of liberation, where the mind of a monk who is heedful, zealous, and resolute, and who dwells, is liberated, or the unexhausted taints are exhausted, or the unattained supreme security from bondage is attained.
translations.an5.26:6: Again, monks, a monk has no teacher, nor does he have a co-resident who is a teacher, who teaches him the Dhamma in detail, as learned and as practiced, nor does he teach the Dhamma in detail to others, nor does he recite the Dhamma in detail, nor does he think about the Dhamma with his mind, nor does he examine it. But he has a certain concentration sign that is well-practiced, well-attended to, well-considered, and well-penetrated by wisdom. In whatever way, monks, a monk has a concentration sign that is well-practiced, well-attended to, well-considered, and well-penetrated by wisdom, in that way he is one who experiences the meaning and one who experiences the Dhamma. For one who experiences the meaning and the Dhamma, joy arises. For one who is joyful, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. For one with a tranquil body, pleasure arises. For one who is pleased, the mind becomes concentrated. This, monks, is the fifth emancipation, where the mind of an unemancipated monk, who is heedful, ardent, and resolute, becomes emancipated, or where the unexhausted corruptions are exhausted, or where the unattained supreme security from bondage is attained.
translations.an5.27:1: Cultivate concentration, monks, for one who is concentrated and mindful, five knowledges arise of themselves. What five? The knowledge arises of itself that this concentration is presently pleasant and will result in a pleasant outcome in the future. The knowledge arises of itself that this concentration is noble and free from defilements. The knowledge arises of itself that this concentration is not cultivated by an impure person. The knowledge arises of itself that this concentration is peaceful, sublime, and gained by one who is mindful, and that it is not accompanied by mental constructs. The knowledge arises of itself that I enter this concentration mindfully and emerge from it mindfully.
translations.an5.28:1: I will teach you, monks, the development of the five-factored noble concentration. Listen and pay attention, I will speak.
translations.an5.28:10: Just as, monks, a skilled charioteer, standing on level ground, at a crossroads, with a well-trained horse, holding the reins in his left hand and the whip in his right hand, can go wherever he wants, and return whenever he wants. In the same way, monks, a monk who has developed the five-factored noble concentration can direct his mind to whatever he wants, and can attain mastery over it, wherever he wants, with a mindful and aware mind.
translations.an5.28:15: If he wishes: 'May I, with the divine eye, which is pure and surpasses the human, see beings passing away and being reborn...,' he can attain mastery over it, wherever he wants, with a mindful and aware mind.
translations.an5.28:7: When a monk has developed the five-factored noble concentration in this way, and has made it a habit, he can direct his mind to whatever he wants, and can attain mastery over it, wherever he wants, with a mindful and aware mind.
translations.an5.28:8: Just as, monks, a water jar, placed on a level surface, full to the brim, and even, if a strong man were to pour water into it from any side, the water would flow in. In the same way, monks, a monk who has developed the five-factored noble concentration in this way, and has made it a habit, can direct his mind to whatever he wants, and can attain mastery over it, wherever he wants, with a mindful and aware mind.
translations.an5.28:9: Just as, monks, a pond, on level ground, with four sluice gates, full to the brim, and even, if a strong man were to open the sluice gates from any side, the water would flow out. In the same way, monks, a monk who has developed the five-factored noble concentration in this way, and has made it a habit, can direct his mind to whatever he wants, and can attain mastery over it, wherever he wants, with a mindful and aware mind.
translations.an5.2:1: There are, monks, these five powers of a trainee. What five? The power of faith, the power of moral shame, the power of moral dread, the power of energy, and the power of wisdom.
translations.an5.2:2: And what, monks, is the power of faith? Here, a noble disciple is endowed with faith, and has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathagata: 'The Blessed One is indeed the Enlightened One, the Knower of the Worlds, the Guide of those who need guidance, the Teacher of gods and humans, the Awakened One, the Blessed One.' This is called the power of faith.
translations.an5.2:3: And what, monks, is the power of moral shame? Here, a noble disciple has a sense of moral shame, and is ashamed of bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct, and is ashamed of the acquisition of unwholesome and unskillful things. This is called the power of moral shame.
translations.an5.2:4: And what, monks, is the power of moral dread? Here, a noble disciple has a sense of moral dread, and dreads bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct, and dreads the acquisition of unwholesome and unskillful things. This is called the power of moral dread.
translations.an5.2:5: And what, monks, is the power of energy? Here, a noble disciple is endowed with energy, and strives to abandon unwholesome things, and to develop wholesome things, and is strong, firm, and unshakeable in his efforts to develop wholesome things. This is called the power of energy.
translations.an5.2:6: And what, monks, is the power of wisdom? Here, a noble disciple is endowed with wisdom, and is possessed of the wisdom that leads to the arising of the ariyan penetration, and to the realization of the supreme security from bondage. This is called the power of wisdom. These, monks, are the five powers of a trainee.
translations.an5.30:1: Thus have I heard—on one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosalan country with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and he arrived at a Kosalan brahmin village called Icchānaṅgala. The Blessed One stayed there in the Icchānaṅgala woodland. The brahmin householders of Icchānaṅgala heard: 'The ascetic Gotama, the Sakyan son who went forth from the Sakyan clan, has arrived at Icchānaṅgala and is staying in the Icchānaṅgala woodland.'
translations.an5.30:3: 'Let the Blessed One accept our invitation, let the Fortunate One accept our invitation; the time for the Blessed One's meal has come. Wherever the Blessed One will go now, the brahmin householders of the villages and towns will go there too, just as the water flows down from a high place. Just as, when the god rains heavily, the water flows down from a high place, so too, wherever the Blessed One will go now, the brahmin householders of the villages and towns will go there too. What is the reason for this? The reason is, sir, that the Blessed One has a good reputation for virtue and wisdom.'
translations.an5.31:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying in the Ānāthapiṇḍika monastery... Then Princess Sumanā, accompanied by five hundred chariots and five hundred royal princes, approached the Blessed One; having approached, she bowed down to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Princess Sumanā said to the Blessed One:
translations.an5.31:10: Just so, a virtuous person, a faithful person, excels in the world by means of generosity, surpassing all the stingy people.
translations.an5.31:11: Just as a cloud fills the earth with water and showers down on it, a disciple of the Fully Awakened One, endowed with vision, excels by means of generosity.
translations.an5.31:12: Just so, a disciple of the Fully Awakened One, endowed with vision, excels by means of generosity, surpassing the stingy by five factors.
translations.an5.31:2: 'There are, sir, two disciples of the Blessed One who have equal faith and virtue and wisdom—one who gives and one who does not give. After the breakup of the body, after death, they will be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. Will there be any distinction or difference between them, sir, as they have become devas?'
translations.an5.31:3: 'There will be, Sumanā,' the Blessed One said. 'The giver, Sumanā, excels the non-giver, having become a deva, in five ways: in celestial life span, in celestial beauty, in celestial pleasure, in celestial fame, and in celestial power.'
translations.an5.31:4: 'But, sir, if they were to come back to this world and be reborn as human beings, will there be any distinction or difference between them, sir, as they have become human beings?' 'There will be, Sumanā,' the Blessed One said. 'The giver, Sumanā, excels the non-giver, having become a human being, in five ways: in human life span, in human beauty, in human happiness, in human fame, and in human power.'
translations.an5.31:5: 'But, sir, if both of them were to go forth from the household life into homelessness, will there be any distinction or difference between them, sir, as they have gone forth?' 'There will be, Sumanā,' the Blessed One said. 'The giver, Sumanā, excels the non-giver, having gone forth, in five ways...'
translations.an5.31:6: 'But, sir, if both of them were to attain arahantship, will there be any distinction or difference between them, sir, as they have attained arahantship?' 'Here, Sumanā, I say there is no difference, inasmuch as they have attained liberation.'
translations.an5.31:9: Just as the moon, free from clouds, shines in the sky, outshining all the stars in the world with its radiance.
translations.an5.34:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof. Then General Sīha approached the Blessed One; having approached, he bowed down to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, General Sīha said to the Blessed One: 'Can the Blessed One teach me the immediate result of giving?'
translations.an5.34:2: 'It can be done, Sīha,' the Blessed One said. 'The giver, Sīha, the donor, is dear and charming to the people. And this, Sīha, is the immediate result of giving.'
translations.an5.34:8: One who gives is dear, and many people respect him; his reputation grows, and his fame increases. Unenvious, he conquers the assembly, and he is a wise and non-stingy person.
translations.an5.34:9: Therefore the wise give gifts, having removed the stain of stinginess, and they are happy. Established in a long-lasting and divine state, they delight together with the devas.
translations.an5.36:1: There are these five seasonable gifts. Which five? One gives a gift to a visitor; one gives a gift to a guest; one gives a gift to one who is ill; one gives a gift during a famine; one gives a gift to the virtuous first, [saying,] 'May those who are virtuous receive it first.' These are the five seasonable gifts.
translations.an5.36:2: The wise, who are free from stinginess, give at the proper time. Having given at the proper time, to the noble ones, to those who are straightforward, the gift bears great fruit.
translations.an5.36:3: The mind of one who gives is clear and joyful, and his reward is great. Those who rejoice in that gift, who give assistance, share in the merit, and their reward is not less.
translations.an5.37:1: When a donor gives food, they give five things to the recipients. What five? They give life, beauty, happiness, strength, and intelligence. Having given life, they have a share in life, either divine or human; having given beauty, they have a share in beauty, either divine or human; having given happiness, they have a share in happiness, either divine or human; having given strength, they have a share in strength, either divine or human; having given intelligence, they have a share in intelligence, either divine or human. When a donor gives food, they give these five things to the recipients.
translations.an5.37:2: One who gives life, strength, and intelligence, one who gives beauty and intelligence, is a giver of happiness, and they attain happiness.
translations.an5.38:2: Just as a large banyan tree, on a crossroads, is a refuge for the birds all around, so a faithful disciple is a refuge for many people: for monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.
translations.an5.38:3: Like a tree with branches, leaves, and trunk, and with fruit, they are a refuge for the birds.
translations.an5.38:4: The birds delight in the beautiful tree, and those who eat the fruit eat the fruit. In the same way, people delight in a virtuous person, and those who are faithful and have a tranquil mind are refreshed.
translations.an5.38:5: Just as a tree with a straight trunk, with branches and leaves, is a pleasant place, so a faithful person, endowed with virtue, is a pleasant and gentle person.
translations.an5.38:6: Those who are free from passion, hatred, and delusion, who are without taint, give gifts to such a person, and they are the fields of merit in the world.
translations.an5.41:1: There are these five gifts of wealth. Which five? A noble disciple, with wealth acquired by energetic striving, amassed by the strength of their arms, and earned by the sweat of their brow, righteously, makes themselves happy and pleased, and properly maintains that pleasure. They make their mother and father happy and pleased, and properly maintain that pleasure. They make their wife and children, slaves, and workers happy and pleased, and properly maintain that pleasure. This is the first gift of wealth.
translations.an5.41:4: Furthermore, a noble disciple, with wealth acquired by energetic striving, amassed by the strength of their arms, and earned by the sweat of their brow, righteously, gives a gift to their relatives, to guests, to their ancestors, to the king, and to the devas. This is the fourth gift of wealth.
translations.an5.41:5: Furthermore, a noble disciple, with wealth acquired by energetic striving, amassed by the strength of their arms, and earned by the sweat of their brow, righteously, gives a gift to those self-controlled and virtuous monks and brahmans who are devoted to abstention, who are humble, and who are established in patience and gentleness. They give a gift that is lofty, of long standing, and conducive to happiness, leading to heaven and the higher states. This is the fifth gift of wealth. These are the five gifts of wealth.
translations.an5.41:6: If a noble disciple's wealth, which they have given to these five gifts of wealth, decreases, they think, 'My wealth, which I have given to the gifts of wealth, is decreasing.' They are not worried about it. If a noble disciple's wealth, which they have given to these five gifts of wealth, increases, they think, 'My wealth, which I have given to the gifts of wealth, is increasing.' They are not worried about it, and they are happy in both cases.
translations.an5.41:7: I have enjoyed my wealth, I have used it, I have given generous gifts, and I have given to the highest recipients; I have given to those who are self-controlled and established in the holy life.
translations.an5.41:8: Whatever wealth I desired, I have obtained it, and I have done what is not to be regretted. The wise one, living at home, has obtained the goal.
translations.an5.43:1: Then the householder Anathapindika went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down to one side.
translations.an5.43:4: A noble disciple should not desire long life, nor should they pray for or delight in long life. A noble disciple who desires long life should follow a path that leads to a long life. One who follows such a path will attain long life, either divine or human, and will be fortunate.
translations.an5.43:5: A noble disciple should not desire beauty, nor should they pray for or delight in beauty. A noble disciple who desires beauty should follow a path that leads to beauty. One who follows such a path will attain beauty, either divine or human, and will be fortunate.
translations.an5.43:6: A noble disciple should not desire happiness, nor should they pray for or delight in happiness. A noble disciple who desires happiness should follow a path that leads to happiness. One who follows such a path will attain happiness, either divine or human, and will be fortunate.
translations.an5.43:7: The noble disciple does not deserve, householder, to ask for or delight in fame, nor to seek for the sake of fame. The noble disciple should follow the path that leads to the cessation of fame. Having followed the path that leads to the cessation of fame, they attain the attainment of fame, whether divine or human, and they become fortunate.
translations.an5.43:9: Long life, beauty, fame, and heavenly bliss, And lofty noble birth; By longing I wish for these, And they are of utmost excellence, beyond compare.
translations.an5.49:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One, and having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
translations.an5.49:2: Now on that occasion, Queen Mallikā had died. Then a certain man approached King Pasenadi of Kosala and told him: “Your Majesty, Queen Mallikā has died.” When this was said, King Pasenadi of Kosala became distressed, saddened, and bent over, and he sat down, leaning on his staff.
translations.an5.51:3: There is no possibility, monks, that a monk who does not abandon these five hindrances, corruptions of the mind that weaken wisdom, could know and see as it really is: ‘My welfare is for my own sake, or for the sake of others, or for the sake of both.’ Suppose a river were to flow from a mountain, flowing swiftly and carrying everything along. If a man were to open the mouths of the river on both sides, the current in the middle of the river would be split, divided, and dispersed, and it would not flow far, swiftly, or carry everything along. So too, monks, there is no possibility that a monk who does not abandon these five hindrances could know and see as it really is: ‘My welfare is for my own sake, or for the sake of others, or for the sake of both, or for the sake of supreme knowledge and vision.’
translations.an5.56:1: Then a certain monk approached his preceptor and said: ‘I am pleased, venerable sir, and my body is at ease, but the directions do not appear to me, the teachings do not appear to me, my mind is lethargic and sleepy, and I am not delighted with the spiritual life, and I have doubts about the teachings.’
translations.an5.56:3: ‘It is, monk, that when one is not guarded in the senses, not moderate in eating, and not devoted to wakefulness, and one does not develop the mind in the development of the factors of enlightenment, day and night, one’s body becomes complacent, the directions do not appear, the teachings do not appear, one’s mind is lethargic and sleepy, and one is not delighted with the spiritual life, and one has doubts about the teachings. Therefore, monk, you should train yourself thus: “I will be guarded in the senses, moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness, and I will develop the mind in the development of the factors of enlightenment, day and night.” You should train yourself thus, monk.’
translations.an5.56:4: Then that monk, having been advised by the Blessed One, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and departed. Then that monk, living alone, diligent, ardent, and resolute, soon realized for himself, by his own direct knowledge, the supreme culmination of the spiritual life, and having seen it, he dwelled in it. He understood: ‘Birth is destroyed, the spiritual life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, and there is no further becoming.’ And that monk became an arahant.
translations.an5.57:10: ‘I am not the only one who is dear and pleasing to all my dear and pleasing ones, but rather all beings are dear and pleasing to all their dear and pleasing ones, insofar as they are born, die, and transmigrate.’ As he frequently reflects on this, the path arises. He develops and cultivates this path, and as he develops and cultivates it, all his fetters are abandoned, and his underlying tendencies are eliminated.
translations.an5.57:11: ‘I am not the only one who is the owner of my actions, the heir of my actions, born of my actions, related to my actions, and dependent on my actions, such that whatever action I perform, good or bad, I will be the heir of that action; but rather all beings are the owners of their actions, the heirs of their actions, born of their actions, related to their actions, and dependent on their actions, such that whatever action they perform, good or bad, they will be the heirs of that action.’ As he frequently reflects on this, the path arises. He develops and cultivates this path, and as he develops and cultivates it, all his fetters are abandoned, and his underlying tendencies are eliminated.
translations.an5.57:15: I have mastered all, I have seen the safe refuge; I have enthusiasm for renunciation, And I have seen Nibbāna.
translations.an5.57:7: A noble disciple reflects: ‘I am not the only one who is subject to old age and has not transcended it, but rather all beings are subject to old age and have not transcended it, insofar as they are born, die, and transmigrate.’ As he frequently reflects on this, the path arises. He develops and cultivates this path, and as he develops and cultivates it, all his fetters are abandoned, and his underlying tendencies are eliminated.
translations.an5.57:8: ‘I am not the only one who is subject to illness and has not transcended it, but rather all beings are subject to illness and have not transcended it, insofar as they are born, die, and transmigrate.’ As he frequently reflects on this, the path arises. He develops and cultivates this path, and as he develops and cultivates it, all his fetters are abandoned, and his underlying tendencies are eliminated.
translations.an8.13:1: The king's good horse, the king's excellent horse, is endowed with eight factors. What eight? There is the case where the king's good horse is well-born on both sides, maternal and paternal. He is born in a good area. Whatever they feed him — grass or hay — he eats with relish, without complaining. He is disgusted by dung and urine. He is comfortable in his living quarters, and does not stray when yoked to the chariot. The charioteer can easily control him. He has a good gait. He thinks, 'I will convey the king, I will not convey another.' When going, he goes on a straight path. He is steadfast, his strength lasting until the end of his life. Endowed with these eight factors, the king's good horse is the king's excellent horse, and is reckoned as one of the king's possessions.
translations.an8.14:1: I will teach you, monks, eight faults of a horse and eight faults of a horseman. Listen and pay close attention to what I will say.
translations.an8.14:2: And which are the eight faults of a horse and the eight faults of a horseman? There is the case where a certain horse, when told to go, is sluggish, and when goaded by the horseman, turns back, and with his hind legs, pushes the chariot. There is this kind of horse. This, monks, is the first fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:3: Furthermore, there is the case where a certain horse, when told to go, is sluggish, and when goaded by the horseman, jumps over, breaks the yoke, and splits the pole. There is this kind of horse. This, monks, is the second fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:4: Furthermore, there is the case where a certain horse, when told to go, is sluggish, and when goaded by the horseman, lets out a fart, and defecates, while standing in the chariot. There is this kind of horse. This, monks, is the third fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:5: Furthermore, there is the case where a certain horse, when told to go, is sluggish, and when goaded by the horseman, takes a wrong path, and overturns the chariot. There is this kind of horse. This, monks, is the fourth fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:6: Furthermore, there is the case where a certain horse, when told to go, is sluggish, and when goaded by the horseman, kicks with his hind legs, and strikes the horseman's chest and feet. There is this kind of horse. This, monks, is the fifth fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:7: Furthermore, there is the case where a certain horse, when told to go, is sluggish, and when goaded by the horseman, does not obey, does not obey the horseman, and with his teeth, bites the horseman's hand, and goes wherever he wants. There is this kind of horse. This, monks, is the sixth fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:8: Furthermore, there is the case where a certain horse, when told to go, is sluggish, and when goaded by the horseman, neither goes forward nor turns back, but stands still, stuck in one place. There is this kind of horse. This, monks, is the seventh fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:9: Furthermore, there is the case where a certain horse, when told to go, is sluggish, and when goaded by the horseman, draws in his front and hind legs, and sits down right there, on all fours. There is this kind of horse. This, monks, is the eighth fault of a horse. These, monks, are the eight faults of a horse and the eight faults of a horseman.
translations.an8.19:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was living in the land of the Vajjians, in the village of Nalanda, at the base of the Pavarika tree.
translations.an8.22:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was living among the Vajjians at Hatthigama. There the Blessed One addressed the monks, saying: 'Monks, the excellent horseman of Hatthigama possesses eight wonderful and marvelous qualities.'
translations.an8.22:10: If I were to say, venerable sir, that the Blessed One had spoken of me first, it would not be surprising if the Blessed One were to say: 'There is no bondage by which the excellent horseman of Hatthigama, being bound, would come back to this world again.' This, venerable sir, is the eighth wonderful and marvelous quality that I see.
translations.an8.22:11: These, venerable sir, are the eight wonderful and marvelous qualities that I see. But I do not know: 'Which eight wonderful and marvelous qualities has the Blessed One declared?'
translations.an8.22:12: Then the monk, having received almsfood at the residence of the excellent horseman of Hatthigama, rose from his seat and departed. Then, returning from his alms round after his meal, he approached the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, sat down to one side. As he was sitting down to one side, the monk reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had with the excellent horseman of Hatthigama.
translations.an8.22:2: Then a certain monk, having dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of the householder Uggaha, the one with the elephant village. Having arrived, he sat down on a prepared seat. Then the householder Uggaha, the one with the elephant village, approached the monk and, having bowed, sat down to one side. The monk, sitting to one side, said to the householder Uggaha, the one with the elephant village: 'You, householder, have been endowed by the Blessed One with eight wonderful and amazing things. What are those eight wonderful and amazing things with which you have been endowed by the Blessed One?'
translations.an8.22:3: 'I do not know, venerable sir, what those eight wonderful and amazing things are with which I have been endowed by the Blessed One. However, the eight wonderful and amazing things that are evident to me, please listen to them, pay attention, and I will speak.' The monk replied to the householder Uggaha, the one with the elephant village: 'Very well, householder.' The householder Uggaha, the one with the elephant village, said: 'When I, venerable sir, was wandering in the elephant forest and saw the Blessed One from a distance for the first time, as soon as I saw him, my mind was pleased, and my intoxication with liquor disappeared. This, venerable sir, is the first wonderful and amazing thing that is evident to me.'
translations.an8.22:4: I, venerable sir, being pleased in mind, approached the Blessed One. The Blessed One taught me step by step, namely: the talk on giving, the talk on virtue, and the talk on heaven; he explained the drawbacks of sensual pleasures, the advantages of renunciation, and the corruption of sensual pleasures. When the Blessed One knew that I was attentive, with a mind that was pliable, free from obstacles, uplifted, and pleased, he revealed to me the teaching of the Buddhas, which is directly visible, namely: suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path. Just as a clean cloth, free from black spots, would properly take the dye; in the same way, in that very seat, there arose in me the dust-free, stainless eye of the Dhamma: 'Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease.' I, venerable sir, having seen the Dhamma, having attained the Dhamma, having known the Dhamma, having penetrated the Dhamma, having overcome doubt, having given up speculation, being free from wavering, took refuge in the Teacher, the Dhamma, and the Sangha, and I undertook the five precepts. This, venerable sir, is the second wonderful and amazing thing that is evident to me.
translations.an8.22:5: I had, venerable sir, four young daughters. Then I, venerable sir, approached those daughters and said to them: 'I, sisters, have undertaken the five precepts. Whoever wishes may enjoy the wealth and do meritorious deeds here, or may go to her own relatives. What is the use of a man to you?' When I had spoken thus, my eldest daughter said to me: 'We, venerable sir, are dependent on a man.' Then I, venerable sir, having called a man, took my daughter by the left hand and the man by the right hand, and I gave her to him. I, venerable sir, do not know of any change of mind in giving away my daughter. This, venerable sir, is the third wonderful and amazing thing that is evident to me.
translations.an8.22:6: The wealth in my family, venerable sir, is evident to me. And that wealth is not divided among those who are virtuous and of good character. This, venerable sir, is the fourth wonderful and amazing thing that is evident to me.
translations.an8.22:7: When, venerable sir, I approach a monk, I approach him respectfully, not disrespectfully. If that venerable one teaches me the Dhamma, I listen respectfully, not disrespectfully. If that venerable one does not teach me the Dhamma, I teach him the Dhamma. This, venerable sir, is the fifth wonderful and amazing thing that is evident to me.
translations.an8.22:8: It is not surprising, venerable sir, that deities invite the Sangha and say: 'The monk is freed from both bonds, freed by wisdom, a seer of the body, one who has attained the view, one who has attained faith, one who has attained the Dhamma, one who follows the Dhamma, one who follows faith, one who is virtuous, of good character, one who is of bad character, of bad deeds.' When I, venerable sir, am attending to the Sangha, I do not know of any such mind arising in me: 'I will give a little to this one, a lot to that one.' But I, venerable sir, give with an equal mind. This, venerable sir, is the sixth wonderful and amazing thing that is evident to me.
translations.an8.22:9: It is not surprising, venerable sir, that deities invite me and say: 'The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One.' When they say this, I, venerable sir, say to those deities: 'Whether you deities say this or not, the Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One.' I, venerable sir, do not know of any elation of mind: 'These deities approach me, I converse with deities.' This, venerable sir, is the seventh wonderful and amazing thing that is evident to me.
translations.an8.23:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Āḷavi, at the Aggāḷa shrine. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Monks, Hatthaka of Āḷavaka is endowed with eight wonderful and amazing things. What eight? Hatthaka of Āḷavaka, monks, has faith, is virtuous, has a sense of shame, has a fear of wrongdoing, is learned, is generous, and is wise— Hatthaka of Āḷavaka is endowed with these eight wonderful and amazing things.' The Blessed One said this. Having said this, the Sugata got up from his seat and entered his dwelling.
translations.an8.23:2: Then a certain monk, having dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of Hatthaka of Āḷavaka. Having arrived, he sat down on a prepared seat. Then Hatthaka of Āḷavaka approached the monk and, having bowed, sat down to one side. The monk, sitting to one side, said to Hatthaka of Āḷavaka:
translations.an8.23:3: You, friend, have been endowed by the Blessed One with these seven wonderful and marvelous things.  Which seven?  ‘One with faith, monks, is a person of few ailments, a person of good health, a person with much joy, a person with much faith, a person with much wisdom, a person with much learning, a person with much generosity.’  You, friend, have been endowed with these seven wonderful and marvelous things by the Blessed One.
translations.an8.23:4: Then that monk, having received almsfood at the residence of Hatthaka of Alavi, rose from his seat and left.  Then that monk, after his alms round, returned from his alms round and approached the Blessed One.  Having approached the Blessed One and bowed down to him, he sat down to one side.  Sitting to one side, that monk said to the Blessed One:
translations.an8.24:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was living in the Aggalava cetiya in Alavi.  Then Hatthaka of Alavi, accompanied by five hundred lay followers, approached the Blessed One, and having approached him, he bowed down to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.  Sitting to one side, Hatthaka of Alavi said to the Blessed One:  “This is a large assembly, Hatthaka.  How do you gather such a large assembly?”  “I gather this large assembly, sir, by means of the four means of gathering a crowd taught by the Blessed One.  I gather one who should be gathered by giving by giving, one who should be gathered by kind words by kind words, one who should be gathered by beneficial help by beneficial help, and one who should be gathered by equality of treatment by equality of treatment.  Riches appear in my family, sir.  I think that one should listen to this when one is poor.”  “Well said, Hatthaka!  This is the way to gather a large assembly.  All those in the past who gathered a large assembly did so by these same four means of gathering a crowd.  All those in the future who will gather a large assembly will do so by these same four means of gathering a crowd.  All those who gather a large assembly now do so by these same four means of gathering a crowd.”
translations.an8.26:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was living in the Jivaka Ambavana in Rajagaha.  Then Jivaka Komarabhacca approached the Blessed One, and having approached him, he bowed down to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.  Sitting to one side, Jivaka Komarabhacca said to the Blessed One:  “How far, sir, does one qualify as a lay follower?”  “As far, Jivaka, as one has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha, that far one qualifies as a lay follower.”
translations.an8.26:2: “How far, sir, does one qualify as a virtuous lay follower?”  “As far, Jivaka, as a lay follower abstains from the destruction of life, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, and abstains from liquor, wine, and intoxicants that cause negligence, that far one qualifies as a virtuous lay follower.”
translations.an8.26:3: “How far, sir, does one qualify as a lay follower who has set out on the path for his own benefit and not for the benefit of others?”  “As far, Jivaka, as a lay follower is endowed with faith himself and does not persuade others to be endowed with faith, is endowed with virtue himself and does not persuade others to be endowed with virtue, is endowed with a sense of shame himself and does not persuade others to be endowed with a sense of shame, is endowed with a sense of fear of wrongdoing himself and does not persuade others to be endowed with a sense of fear of wrongdoing, is endowed with learning himself and does not persuade others to be endowed with learning, is endowed with generosity himself and does not persuade others to be endowed with generosity, is endowed with wisdom himself and does not persuade others to be endowed with wisdom.  That far, Jivaka, one qualifies as a lay follower who has set out on the path for his own benefit and not for the benefit of others.”
translations.an8.28:5: Furthermore, the four foundations of mindfulness are developed and well-developed in a bhikkhu who has destroyed the taints.  And, friends, when the four foundations of mindfulness are developed and well-developed in a bhikkhu who has destroyed the taints, this is the power of a bhikkhu who has destroyed the taints, by means of which he declares the destruction of the taints:  ‘My taints are destroyed.’
translations.an8.28:6: Furthermore, the four bases for spiritual power are developed and well-developed in a bhikkhu who has destroyed the taints, the five spiritual faculties are developed and well-developed, the seven factors of enlightenment are developed and well-developed, and the noble eightfold path is developed and well-developed.  And, friends, when the noble eightfold path is developed and well-developed in a bhikkhu who has destroyed the taints, this is the power of a bhikkhu who has destroyed the taints, by means of which he declares the destruction of the taints:  ‘My taints are destroyed.’
translations.an8.2:1: Monks, there are these eight causes and conditions that lead to the acquiring of the knowledge that is in conformity with the noble path, to the clear realization of the noble path that has not been realized, to the increase, to the expansion, to the full development of the noble path that has been realized.  What eight?  Here, monks, a monk lives in dependence on a teacher or a fellow monk in the holy life who is learned and has a good understanding of the teachings, one who is able to declare, teach, describe, establish, reveal, expound, and exhibit the noble path.  This, monks, is the first cause and condition that leads to the acquiring of the knowledge that is in conformity with the noble path, to the clear realization of the noble path that has not been realized, to the increase, to the expansion, to the full development of the noble path that has been realized.
translations.an8.2:11: He instructs him in the Dhamma by means of a twofold knowledge—knowledge of the body and knowledge of the mind.  The monk knows and sees what he has known and seen.  This Dhamma leads to affection, respect, development, and unity.
translations.an8.2:15: He speaks the Dhamma to him in a way that is not untimely, not unrelated, and not unmoderated.  He speaks the Dhamma to him in a way that is suitable, and he does not despise the noble silence.  The monk knows and sees what he has known and seen.  This Dhamma leads to affection, respect, development, and unity.
translations.an8.2:2: He lives depending on a teacher or a fellow monk who is learned and has mastered the teachings, and in whom faith and reverence have been established, and who is capable of instructing, exhorting, and guiding him. From time to time, he approaches them and asks: ‘What is this, venerable sir? What is the meaning of this?’ The venerable monks then clear up any doubts he may have, and they instruct him in the teachings that are intricate and subtle. This, monks, is the second factor that contributes to the growth and fulfillment of the initial stage of the holy life, which has not been attained but can be attained, and to the growth and fulfillment of the initial stage of the holy life that has been attained.
translations.an8.2:4: He is virtuous, and he dwells restrained by the rules of the Patimokkha, endowed with conduct and resort, and seeing danger in the slightest faults. He trains in the training rules. This, monks, is the fourth factor that contributes to the growth and fulfillment of the initial stage of the holy life, which has not been attained but can be attained, and to the growth and fulfillment of the initial stage of the holy life that has been attained.
translations.an8.2:5: He is learned, and he bears in mind and retains the teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with their meaning and phrasing. The teachings that are entirely perfect and pure, and that proclaim the holy life, are well-learned by him, and he has retained them in mind, recited them verbally, and penetrated them by view. This, monks, is the fifth factor that contributes to the growth and fulfillment of the initial stage of the holy life, which has not been attained but can be attained, and to the growth and fulfillment of the initial stage of the holy life that has been attained.
translations.an8.2:6: He has energy, and he dwells applying himself to the abandonment of unwholesome states and to the acquisition of wholesome states, and he is steadfast, firm in his effort, and not shaking off the burden of wholesome states. This, monks, is the sixth factor that contributes to the growth and fulfillment of the initial stage of the holy life, which has not been attained but can be attained, and to the growth and fulfillment of the initial stage of the holy life that has been attained.
translations.an8.2:7: He gains the ear of the Sangha, and he is not one who talks excessively or excessively talks about things that are not relevant. He teaches the Dhamma, or he recites it, or he remains silent, and he does not despise noble silence. This, monks, is the seventh factor that contributes to the growth and fulfillment of the initial stage of the holy life, which has not been attained but can be attained, and to the growth and fulfillment of the initial stage of the holy life that has been attained.
translations.an8.2:8: He dwells contemplating the rise and fall of the five aggregates of clinging: ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the passing away of form; such is feeling, such is the origin of feeling, such is the passing away of feeling; such is perception, such is the origin of perception, such is the passing away of perception; such are the formations, such is the origin of the formations, such is the passing away of the formations; such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.’ This, monks, is the eighth factor that contributes to the growth and fulfillment of the initial stage of the holy life, which has not been attained but can be attained, and to the growth and fulfillment of the initial stage of the holy life that has been attained.
translations.an8.2:9: His fellow monks think of him in this way: ‘This venerable one lives depending on the teacher or a fellow monk who is learned and has mastered the teachings, and in whom faith and reverence have been established, and who is capable of instructing, exhorting, and guiding him. This venerable one knows and sees.’ This, too, is a factor that contributes to the growth and fulfillment of the qualities that are dear, cherished, and conducive to the holy life, and that lead to unity and harmony.
translations.an8.30:1: On one occasion, the Blessed One was dwelling in the Bhagga country at the deer park in the Bhesakala forest in the village of Migadaya. At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha was dwelling in the Ceti country, in the eastern part of the wood. Then, while the Venerable Anuruddha was alone in seclusion, a reflection arose in his mind: ‘This Dhamma is for one who is content, not for one who is discontent. This Dhamma is for one who is satisfied, not for one who is dissatisfied. This Dhamma is for one who is secluded, not for one who is fond of company. This Dhamma is for one who has energy, not for one who is lazy. This Dhamma is for one who has mindfulness established, not for one who is unmindful. This Dhamma is for one who is concentrated, not for one who is unconcentrated. This Dhamma is for one who is wise, not for one who is unwise.’
translations.an8.30:10: When you, Anuruddha, think about these eight thoughts of a great man and attain the four jhanas, which are the higher states of consciousness, and the blissful dwellings that are experienced in this life, you will be like a wealthy householder or his son who has a peaked-roofed mansion, with windows on all sides, shutters, and a door, and which is covered, secure, and protected from the wind. In the same way, when you are dwelling in a dwelling at the root of a tree, you will be content, and your mind will be at peace, and you will be free from distress, and you will be able to attain nibbana.
translations.an8.30:11: When you, Anuruddha, think about these eight thoughts of a great man and attain the four jhanas, which are the higher states of consciousness, and the blissful dwellings that are experienced in this life, you will be like a wealthy householder or his son who has a couch that is spread with a layer of wool, with a layer of soft material, and with a layer of blankets, and which has a canopy above and red cushions at the head and the foot.
