In the same way, when you are dwelling in a bed of grass, you will be content, and your mind will be at peace, and you will be free from distress, and you will be able to attain nibbana.
translations.an8.30:12: When you, Anuruddha, think about these eight thoughts of a great man and attain the four jhanas, which are the higher states of consciousness, and the blissful dwellings that are experienced in this life, you will be like a wealthy householder or his son who has various medicines, such as ghee, butter, oil, honey, and molasses. In the same way, when you are dwelling in a dwelling that is free from filth, you will be content, and your mind will be at peace, and you will be free from distress, and you will be able to attain nibbana. Therefore, Anuruddha, you should dwell in the Ceti country, in the eastern part of the wood, for the coming rainy season.
translations.an8.30:13: Then the Bhagava, having advised the Venerable Anuruddha with this advice—just as a strong man might extend a bent arm or bend an extended arm—disappeared from among the cetis in Pacinavamsadaya and appeared in front of the Venerable Anuruddha in the Bhaggas, in the Susumara mountain, in the Bhesakala forest, in the deer park. The Bhagava sat down in the appointed seat. The Bhagava, having sat down, addressed the monks: 'I will teach, monks, eight thoughts of a great man. Listen to that... And what, monks, are the eight thoughts of a great man? This Dhamma is for one who has few wishes, not for one who has many wishes; this Dhamma is for one who is content, not for one who is discontent; this Dhamma is for one who is secluded, not for one who is fond of socializing; this Dhamma is for one who is energetic, not for one who is lazy; this Dhamma is for one whose mindfulness is established, not for one whose mindfulness is not established; this Dhamma is for one who is concentrated, not for one who is not concentrated; this Dhamma is for one who is wise, not for one who is unwise; this Dhamma is for one who delights in non-proliferation, not for one who delights in proliferation.
translations.an8.30:2: Then the Bhagava, having known the thought in the mind of the Venerable Anuruddha—just as a strong man might extend a bent arm or bend an extended arm—disappeared from among the cetis in Pacinavamsadaya and appeared in front of the Venerable Anuruddha in the Bhaggas, in the Susumara mountain, in the Bhesakala forest, in the deer park. The Bhagava sat down in the appointed seat. The Venerable Anuruddha also bowed to the Bhagava and sat down to one side. The Bhagava, having sat down to one side, said to the Venerable Anuruddha:
translations.an8.30:22: Then the Venerable Anuruddha spent the Rains Retreat in that same place, among the cetis in Pacinavamsadaya. Then the Venerable Anuruddha, alone, heedful, ardent, and resolute, in no long time—having realized for himself with direct knowledge, having attained the end of the holy life, and having known and seen it for himself—lived having known and seen the end of the holy life. He said: 'My birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more coming back to any state of being.' And a certain Venerable Anuruddha was an arahant. Then the Venerable Anuruddha, having attained arahantship, at that time recited these verses:
translations.an8.30:23: 'As I had thought, the Teacher is unsurpassed in the world; With a mind-made body, I approached him with psychic power.'
translations.an8.30:24: 'As I had thought, the Buddha taught me further; The Buddha, free from proliferation, taught a Dhamma free from proliferation.'
translations.an8.30:3: 'Well done, Anuruddha. Well done, Anuruddha, that you thought that great thought: 'This Dhamma is for one who has few wishes, not for one who has many wishes; this Dhamma is for one who is content, not for one who is discontent; this Dhamma is for one who is secluded, not for one who is fond of socializing; this Dhamma is for one who is energetic, not for one who is lazy; this Dhamma is for one whose mindfulness is established, not for one whose mindfulness is not established; this Dhamma is for one who is concentrated, not for one who is not concentrated; this Dhamma is for one who is wise, not for one who is unwise.' Therefore, Anuruddha, you should also think this eighth great thought: 'This Dhamma is for one who delights in non-proliferation, not for one who delights in proliferation.''
translations.an8.30:4: When, Anuruddha, you think these eight great thoughts, then, Anuruddha, to whatever extent you wish, you will live having entered the first jhana, which is accompanied by thought and examination, and is born of seclusion, and is filled with joy and happiness.
translations.an8.30:5: When, Anuruddha, you think these eight great thoughts, then, Anuruddha, to whatever extent you wish, you will live having entered the second jhana, which has internal confidence and singleness of mind, without thought and examination, and is born of concentration, and is filled with joy and happiness.
translations.an8.30:6: When, Anuruddha, you think these eight great thoughts, then, Anuruddha, to whatever extent you wish, you will live having entered the third jhana, in which one is equanimous and mindful, and one experiences happiness with the body, which the noble ones declare: 'One who is equanimous and mindful, and who dwells happily.'
translations.an8.30:7: When, Anuruddha, you think these eight great thoughts, then, Anuruddha, to whatever extent you wish, you will live having entered the fourth jhana, in which one has given up pleasure and pain, and in which the previous pleasure and pain have passed away, and one experiences a state that is neither painful nor pleasant, and one is mindful and has a sense of detachment.
translations.an8.39:1: 'The eighth, monks, are the meritorious, wholesome, and blissful things that are the basis of bliss, that are auspicious, and that have a blissful result, and that lead to a heavenly world. What are the eight? Here, monks, a noble disciple has gone for refuge to the Buddha. This, monks, is the first meritorious, wholesome, and blissful thing that is the basis of bliss, that is auspicious, and that has a blissful result, and that leads to a heavenly world, and is desirable, lovely, and pleasant.'
translations.an8.39:2: Again, monks, a noble disciple has gone for refuge to the Dhamma. This, monks, is the second meritorious, wholesome, and blissful thing... and is desirable, lovely, and pleasant.
translations.an8.39:3: Again, monks, a noble disciple goes for refuge to the community. This, monks, is the third gift, a gift of merit, a gift of good, a source of happiness, leading to heaven, and resulting in happiness, and it conduces to what is desirable, lovely, and pleasing, and to one's own welfare and happiness. There are, monks, these five great gifts, original, long-standing, traditional, ancient, and unadulterated, not taken up as a result of speculation, and which are not adulterated by recluses and brahmins, and clever people. What are the five? Here, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned the destruction of life, abstains from the destruction of life. He, having abstained from the destruction of life, gives to immeasurable beings freedom from fear, freedom from hatred, and freedom from oppression. Having given to immeasurable beings freedom from fear, freedom from hatred, and freedom from oppression, he becomes a partaker of immeasurable freedom from fear, freedom from hatred, and freedom from oppression. This, monks, is the first gift, a great gift, original, long-standing, traditional, ancient, and unadulterated, not taken up as a result of speculation, and which is not adulterated by recluses and brahmins, and clever people. This, monks, is the fourth gift of merit, a gift of good, a source of happiness, leading to heaven, and resulting in happiness, and it conduces to what is desirable, lovely, and pleasing, and to one's own welfare and happiness.
translations.an8.39:7: Having abandoned the basis for intoxication, namely, intoxicating drinks and drugs, he abstains from the basis for intoxication, namely, intoxicating drinks and drugs. He, having abstained from the basis for intoxication, namely, intoxicating drinks and drugs, gives to immeasurable beings freedom from fear, freedom from hatred, and freedom from oppression. Having given to immeasurable beings freedom from fear, freedom from hatred, and freedom from oppression, he becomes a partaker of immeasurable freedom from fear, freedom from hatred, and freedom from oppression. This, monks, is the fifth gift, a great gift, original, long-standing, traditional, ancient, and unadulterated, not taken up as a result of speculation, and which is not adulterated by recluses and brahmins, and clever people. This, monks, is the eighth gift of merit, a gift of good, a source of happiness, leading to heaven, and resulting in happiness, and it conduces to what is desirable, lovely, and pleasing, and to one's own welfare and happiness.
translations.an8.40:1: The destruction of life, monks, when developed and cultivated, leads to hell, to the animal realm, and to the realm of ghosts. The result of the destruction of life is that, for a human being, it leads to a short life span.
translations.an8.40:2: The taking of what is not given, monks, when developed and cultivated, leads to hell, to the animal realm, and to the realm of ghosts. The result of the taking of what is not given is that, for a human being, it leads to poverty and lack of wealth.
translations.an8.40:3: Sexual misconduct, monks, when developed and cultivated, leads to hell, to the animal realm, and to the realm of ghosts. The result of sexual misconduct is that, for a human being, it leads to enmity and hatred.
translations.an8.40:4: False speech, monks, when developed and cultivated, leads to hell, to the animal realm, and to the realm of ghosts. The result of false speech is that, for a human being, it leads to being deceived and misled.
translations.an8.40:5: Slanderous speech, monks, when developed and cultivated, leads to hell, to the animal realm, and to the realm of ghosts. The result of slanderous speech is that, for a human being, it leads to separation from friends.
translations.an8.40:6: Harsh speech, monks, when developed and cultivated, leads to hell, to the animal realm, and to the realm of ghosts. The result of harsh speech is that, for a human being, it leads to unlovely and unpleasant speech.
translations.an8.40:7: Idle chatter, monks, when developed and cultivated, leads to hell, to the animal realm, and to the realm of ghosts. The result of idle chatter is that, for a human being, it leads to speech that is not worthy of confidence.
translations.an8.6:2: For an uninstructed ordinary person, monks, gain and loss, fame and ill-fame, blame and praise, pleasure and pain arise. For an instructed noble disciple, monks, gain and loss, fame and ill-fame, blame and praise, pleasure and pain also arise. What, monks, is the distinction, the difference, the distinction in this case between an uninstructed ordinary person and an instructed noble disciple?
translations.an8.6:4: His mind, monks, is not overcome by gain, his mind is not overcome by loss, his mind is not overcome by fame, his mind is not overcome by ill-fame, his mind is not overcome by blame, his mind is not overcome by praise, his mind is not overcome by pleasure, his mind is not overcome by pain. He is not delighted by gain, he is not tormented by loss; he is not delighted by fame, he is not tormented by ill-fame; he is not delighted by praise, he is not tormented by blame; he is not delighted by pleasure, he is not tormented by pain. He, monks, who is thus free from delight and aversion, is not freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I say that he is not freed from suffering.
translations.an8.6:7: Gain and loss, fame and ill-fame, blame and praise, pleasure and pain: these things, among humans, are impermanent, and subject to change.
translations.an8.6:8: Knowing this, a wise and intelligent person, mindful and discerning, observes the changing nature of things. The mind is not disturbed by pleasant things, and is not repelled by unpleasant things.
translations.an8.7:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on Mount Gijjhakūṭa, not far from the village of Devadatta. There the Buddha addressed the monks, saying: “It is good, monks, that a monk from time to time reflects on his own decline and another's decline. It is good that a monk from time to time reflects on his own success and another's success. Devadatta, overcome by eight bad qualities, has fallen into decline, is headed for misery, and will be destroyed for a long time.
translations.an8.7:2: What eight? For Devadatta, overcome by gain, has fallen into decline, is headed for misery, and will be destroyed for a long time. Overcome by loss ... by fame ... by disrepute ... by praise ... by criticism ... by pleasure ... by ill will ... by friendship with bad people, Devadatta has fallen into decline, is headed for misery, and will be destroyed for a long time. These are the eight bad qualities by which Devadatta, overcome, has fallen into decline, is headed for misery, and will be destroyed for a long time.
translations.an8.7:3: It is good, monks, that a monk, having gained gain, should live having overcome it, having gained loss ... fame ... disrepute ... praise ... criticism ... pleasure ... ill will ... having gained friendship with bad people, should live having overcome it.
translations.an8.8:4: Then Sakka, lord of the gods, just like a strong man extending or flexing his arm, disappeared among the gods of the Thirty-Three in the Sudassana Hall on Mount Meru. Then Sakka, lord of the gods, approached Venerable Uttara; having approached, he bowed to Venerable Uttara and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of the gods, said to Venerable Uttara:
translations.an8.8:5: “Is it true, sir, that Venerable Uttara taught the monks the Dhamma thus: ‘It is good, friends, that a monk from time to time reflects on his own decline, another's decline, his own success, and another's success’?” “It is, lord of the gods.” “But whose idea was this, sir, Venerable Uttara's or the Buddha's, the Arahant, the Fully Awakened One's?” “I will give you a simile, lord of the gods, and by means of this simile, some wise people here will understand the meaning of what was said.
translations.an8.8:6: Suppose, lord of the gods, a great crowd of people were bringing grain from a village or town to a granary. If someone were to approach that great crowd of people and ask: ‘Where did you get this grain from?’, how would that great crowd of people answer? They would answer: ‘We got it from that great granary.’ In the same way, lord of the gods, whatever is well spoken is the word of the Buddha, the Arahant, the Fully Awakened One. Having taken it up, we and others speak it.
translations.an8.8:7: “It is amazing, sir, it is marvelous! This statement by Venerable Uttara: ‘Whatever is well spoken is the word of the Buddha, the Arahant, the Fully Awakened One. Having taken it up, we and others speak it.’ At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on Mount Gijjhakūṭa, not far from the village of Devadatta. There the Buddha addressed the monks, saying:
translations.mn108:1: I have heard that at one time Venerable Ānanda was staying near Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground, not long after the Buddha's final Nibbāna.
translations.mn108:13: “There are, brahmin, ten qualities that inspire confidence, proclaimed by the Buddha, who knew and saw, the Arahant, the Fully Awakened One. When we see these qualities in him, we pay homage to him, respect him, and venerate him. Having paid homage, respected, and venerated him, we live in dependence on him. What are the ten?
translations.mn108:14: Here, brahmin, a monk is virtuous, with well-defined principles, living controlled by the monastic code, perfect in conduct and behavior, seeing danger in the smallest faults, and trains in the rules of training.
translations.mn108:15: He is learned, with a good memory, and has mastered the teachings. He is a bearer of the teachings, a versed reciter of the teachings, and a teacher of the teachings. The teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life - such teachings are much learned by him, retained in mind, and mentally inspected, and well-penetrated by view.
translations.mn108:17: He gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas, which are the higher states of consciousness, and the blissful meditations in this life.
translations.mn108:18: He experiences various kinds of psychic power - having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and disappears; he goes unhindered through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through air; he dives in and out of the earth as if it were water; he walks on water as if it were earth; he travels through the air like a bird with his wings outstretched; with his hand he touches and strokes the moon and sun, so powerful and mighty; he exercises control over his body as far as the world of Brahmā.
translations.mn108:19: With the divine ear, which is purified and surpasses the human ear, he hears both kinds of sounds, divine and human, whether near or far.
translations.mn108:2: Now at that time King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha was planning to attack Rājagaha, and was seeking to know if King Pajjota would come to his aid.
translations.mn108:20: He discerns the minds of other beings, other persons, as having mind, as not having mind. He discerns a mind with passion as a mind with passion, a mind without passion as a mind without passion, a mind with aversion as a mind with aversion, a mind without aversion as a mind without aversion, a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion, a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion, a contracted mind as a contracted mind, a distracted mind as a distracted mind, a mind that is enlarged as a mind that is enlarged, a mind that is not enlarged as a mind that is not enlarged, a mind that is superior as a mind that is superior, a mind that is not superior as a mind that is not superior, a mind that is concentrated as a mind that is concentrated, a mind that is not concentrated as a mind that is not concentrated, a mind that is liberated as a mind that is liberated, a mind that is not liberated as a mind that is not liberated.
translations.mn108:23: With the destruction of the corruptions, he has realized for himself with direct knowledge the uncorrupted liberation of mind, the uncorrupted liberation by wisdom, in this very life. These, brahman, are the ten inspiring things that the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-awakened One, has declared. Wherever these things are found, we pay homage, we honor, we respect, and we venerate them; having paid homage, having honored, having respected, and having venerated them, we live in dependence on them.
translations.mn108:25: Then the brahman Vassakara, the chief minister of Magadha, said to the Venerable Ananda: 'Where, sir Ananda, are you living now?' 'I am living now, brahman, in the Veḷuvana.' 'Is the Veḷuvana, sir Ananda, a pleasant place, quiet, free from noise, with an atmosphere of seclusion, suitable for retreat, and with few visitors, just as it is protected by the guardians, the protectors?' 'Yes, brahman, the Veḷuvana is a pleasant place, quiet, free from noise, with an atmosphere of seclusion, suitable for retreat, and with few visitors, just as it is protected by the guardians, the protectors.' 'Yes, sir Ananda, the Veḷuvana is a pleasant place, quiet, free from noise, with an atmosphere of seclusion, suitable for retreat, and with few visitors, just as it is protected by the meditators, the practitioners of meditation. You, sir, are a meditator, a practitioner of meditation.
translations.mn108:28: 'The Blessed One, sir Ananda, praised and commended meditation. Let us go now, sir Ananda; we have much to do, much work to be done.' 'You may go, brahman, at your convenience.' Then the brahman Vassakara, the chief minister of Magadha, having delighted in and approved of the Venerable Ananda's words, rose from his seat and departed.
translations.mn108:3: Then the Venerable Ananda, having dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe and entered Rājagaha for alms. The Venerable Ananda thought: 'It is too early to go for alms in Rājagaha. What if I were to go to the residence of the brahman Gopakamoggallāna, where he is staying?'
translations.mn108:4: Then the Venerable Ananda went to the residence of the brahman Gopakamoggallāna, where he was staying. The brahman Gopakamoggallāna saw the Venerable Ananda coming in the distance. Having seen him, he said to the Venerable Ananda: 'Come, sir Ananda. Welcome, sir Ananda. It has been a long time since you have taken the opportunity to come here. Please sit down, sir Ananda, this seat is prepared.' The Venerable Ananda sat down on the prepared seat. The brahman Gopakamoggallāna took another, lower seat and sat down to one side.
translations.mn108:5: The brahman Gopakamoggallāna said to the Venerable Ananda: 'Is there, sir Ananda, even one monk who has attained in every respect, in all aspects, and in all circumstances, the states that the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-awakened One, had attained?' 'There is no monk, brahman, who has attained in every respect, in all aspects, and in all circumstances, the states that the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-awakened One, had attained. For the Blessed One is the originator of the path, the producer of the path, the declarer of the path, the knower of the path, the seer of the path, the guide on the path. His disciples now live following the path, having attained it afterwards.'
translations.mn108:7: The brahman Gopakamoggallāna asked the Venerable Ananda: 'Has the Blessed One, sir Ananda, appointed a refuge, saying:
translations.mn117:11: And what, monks, is wrong intention? Intention of sensual desire, intention of ill-will, intention of harm— this, monks, is wrong intention.
translations.mn108:9: ‘But, Ananda, what is the reason for our being in harmony?’ ‘We are not without a refuge, brahman; we are with a refuge, brahman; we are with the refuge of the Dhamma.’
translations.mn117:10: There, monks, right view goes first. And how, monks, does right view go first? One recognizes wrong intention as wrong intention and right intention as right intention, and this is right view.
translations.mn117:12: And what, monks, is right intention? I say that there are two kinds of right intention: there is right intention that is influenced by sensual desire, has a destination in acquisitions, and is of the dark side; and there is right intention that is noble, taintless, and has a supramundane destination as its destination.
translations.mn117:13: And what, monks, is right intention that is influenced by sensual desire, has a destination in acquisitions, and is of the dark side? Intention of renunciation, intention of non-ill-will, intention of non-cruelty: this, monks, is right intention that is influenced by sensual desire, has a destination in acquisitions, and is of the dark side.
translations.mn117:14: And what, monks, is right intention that is noble, taintless, and has a supramundane destination as its destination? The thinking, thought, intention, mental absorption, mental fixation, and verbal formation of one who has the noble, taintless, and supramundane mind, and who is developing the noble path: this, monks, is right intention that is noble, taintless, and has a supramundane destination as its destination.
translations.mn117:15: One who is striving for the abandoning of wrong intention, who is making an effort for the entering upon of right intention, has a mind that is rightly directed for the sake of the arising of the noble path. One who is mindful abandons wrong intention and enters upon right intention; this is one's right mindfulness. These three things — right view, right effort, and right mindfulness — follow upon right intention, that is, they have right intention as their guide.
translations.mn117:16: Of these three things, right view is the forerunner. And how is right view the forerunner? One who has right view understands wrong speech as wrong speech and right speech as right speech: this is one's right view.
translations.mn117:18: And what, monks, is right speech? I say that there are two kinds of right speech: there is right speech that is influenced by sensual desire, has a destination in acquisitions, and is of the dark side; and there is right speech that is noble, taintless, and has a supramundane destination as its destination.
translations.mn117:19: And what, monks, is right speech that is influenced by sensual desire, has a destination in acquisitions, and is of the dark side? Abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from idle chatter: this, monks, is right speech that is influenced by sensual desire, has a destination in acquisitions, and is of the dark side.
translations.mn117:20: And what, monks, is right speech that is noble, taintless, and has a supramundane destination as its destination? The abstaining, the avoidance, the refraining from the four kinds of verbal misconduct of one who has the noble, taintless, and supramundane mind, and who is developing the noble path: this, monks, is right speech that is noble, taintless, and has a supramundane destination as its destination.
translations.mn117:22: Of these three things, right view is the forerunner. And how is right view the forerunner? One who has right view understands wrong action as wrong action and right action as right action: this is one's right view.
translations.mn117:24: And what, monks, is right action? I say that there are two kinds of right action: there is right action that is influenced by sensual desire, has a destination in acquisitions, and is of the dark side; and there is right action that is noble, taintless, and has a supramundane destination as its destination.
translations.mn117:25: And what, monks, is right action that is influenced by sensual desire, has a destination in acquisitions, and is of the dark side? Abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from misconduct in sensual pleasures: this, monks, is right action that is influenced by sensual desire, has a destination in acquisitions, and is of the dark side.
translations.mn117:28: Of these three things, right view is the forerunner. And how is right view the forerunner? One who has right view understands wrong livelihood as wrong livelihood and right livelihood as right livelihood: this is one's right view.
translations.mn117:29: And what, monks, is wrong livelihood? Scheming, talking, hinting, belittling, pursuing gain with gain: this, monks, is wrong livelihood.
translations.mn117:30: And what, monks, is right livelihood? I say that there are two kinds of right livelihood: there is right livelihood that is influenced by sensual desire, has a destination in acquisitions, and is of the dark side; and there is right livelihood that is noble, taintless, and has a supramundane destination as its destination.
translations.mn117:31: And what, monks, is right livelihood that is influenced by sensual desire, has a destination in acquisitions, and is of the dark side? Here, a noble disciple having abandoned wrong livelihood, makes his living by right livelihood: this, monks, is right livelihood that is influenced by sensual desire, has a destination in acquisitions, and is of the dark side.
translations.mn117:34: Of these things, right view is the forerunner. And how is right view the forerunner? For one with right view, right intention follows. For one with right intention, right speech follows. For one with right speech, right action follows. For one with right action, right livelihood follows. For one with right livelihood, right effort follows. For one with right effort, right mindfulness follows. For one with right mindfulness, right concentration follows. For one with right concentration, right knowledge follows. For one with right knowledge, right liberation follows. Thus, monks, the learner is endowed with the eight factors, and the arahant is endowed with the ten factors. And, monks, through right knowledge, many evil, unwholesome things are abandoned, and the development and perfection of wholesome things takes place.
translations.mn117:35: Of these things, right view is the forerunner. And how is right view the forerunner? For one with right view, wrong view is eliminated. And whatever evil, unwholesome things arise from wrong view, those too are eliminated. From right view, many wholesome things develop and reach perfection. For one with right intention, wrong intention is eliminated... For one with right speech, wrong speech is eliminated... For one with right action, wrong action is eliminated... For one with right livelihood, wrong livelihood is eliminated... For one with right effort, wrong effort is eliminated... For one with right mindfulness, wrong mindfulness is eliminated... For one with right concentration, wrong concentration is eliminated... For one with right knowledge, wrong knowledge is eliminated... For one with right liberation, wrong liberation is eliminated. And whatever evil, unwholesome things arise from wrong liberation, those too are eliminated. From right liberation, many wholesome things develop and reach perfection.
translations.mn117:2: “Monks, I will teach you the noble right concentration with its supports and requisites. Listen and attend closely, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” those monks replied to the Bhagavā. The Bhagavā said this:
translations.mn117:36: Thus, monks, there are twenty skillful qualities and twenty unskillful qualities— the Great Forty Dhamma Teaching that has been promulgated, which no ascetic or brahmin or god or Mara or Brahma or anyone else in the world can surpass.
translations.mn117:4: There, monks, right view goes first. And how does right view go first? One understands wrong view as wrong view and right view as right view— this is one's right view.
translations.mn117:5: And what, monks, is wrong view? 'There is no gift, no offering, no sacrifice, no fruit or result of good or bad deeds, no this world, no other world, no mother, no father, no spontaneously born beings, and no ascetics or brahmins who, having realized this world and the other world by their own superknowledge, make it known to others'— this, monks, is wrong view.
translations.mn117:6: And what, monks, is right view? I say, monks, that there are two kinds of right view: there is right view that is affected by the taints, part of the path, and involved with acquisitions; and there is right view that is noble, taintless, and supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:7: And what, monks, is right view that is affected by the taints, part of the path, and involved with acquisitions? 'There is gift, offering, and sacrifice, and there is fruit and result of good and bad deeds, and there is this world and the other world, and there is mother and father, and there are spontaneously born beings, and there are ascetics and brahmins who, having realized this world and the other world by their own superknowledge, make it known to others'— this, monks, is right view that is affected by the taints, part of the path, and involved with acquisitions.
translations.mn117:8: And what, monks, is right view that is noble, taintless, and supramundane, a factor of the path? The wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor, and the path factor of right view in one whose mind is noble, whose mind is taintless, and who is developing the noble path— this, monks, is called right view that is noble, taintless, and supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:9: One makes an effort to abandon wrong view, to develop right view; this is one's right effort. Mindful, one abandons wrong view and develops right view; this is one's right mindfulness. These three things— right view, right effort, and right mindfulness— follow upon and circle around right view.
translations.mn118:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Savatthi in the Eastern Monastery, the palace of Migara's mother, together with many well-known elder disciples, including the Venerable Sariputta, the Venerable Maha Moggallana, the Venerable Maha Kassapa, the Venerable Maha Kaccana, the Venerable Maha Kotthita, the Venerable Maha Kappina, the Venerable Maha Cunda, the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Revata, the Venerable Ananda, and other well-known elder disciples.
translations.mn118:15: Mindfulness of breathing, monks, when developed and cultivated, is very fruitful and beneficial. Mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness.
translations.mn118:17: Here, monks, a monk who has gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down cross-legged, holding his body straight, and establishes mindfulness in front of him.
translations.mn118:18: When breathing in long, he knows 'I am breathing in long'; when breathing out long, he knows 'I am breathing out long'. When breathing in short, he knows 'I am breathing in short'; when breathing out short, he knows 'I am breathing out short'. He trains himself thinking 'I will breathe in experiencing the whole body'; he trains himself thinking 'I will breathe out experiencing the whole body'. He trains himself thinking 'I will breathe in calming the bodily process'; he trains himself thinking 'I will breathe out calming the bodily process'.
translations.mn118:19: He trains himself thinking 'I will breathe in experiencing rapture'; he trains himself thinking 'I will breathe out experiencing rapture'. He trains himself thinking 'I will breathe in experiencing pleasure'; he trains himself thinking 'I will breathe out experiencing pleasure'. He trains himself thinking 'I will breathe in experiencing the mental process'; he trains himself thinking 'I will breathe out experiencing the mental process'. He trains himself thinking 'I will breathe in calming the mental process'; he trains himself thinking 'I will breathe out calming the mental process'.
translations.mn118:2: Now at that time the elder monks were advising and instructing the new monks. Some elder monks were advising and instructing ten new monks, some were advising and instructing twenty new monks, some were advising and instructing thirty new monks, and some were advising and instructing forty new monks. And those new monks, being advised and instructed by the elder monks, knew great progress and distinction.
translations.mn118:20: He trains himself thinking 'I will breathe in experiencing the mind'; he trains himself thinking 'I will breathe out experiencing the mind'. He trains himself thinking 'I will breathe in gladdening the mind'; he trains himself thinking 'I will breathe out gladdening the mind'. He trains himself thinking 'I will breathe in concentrating the mind'; he trains himself thinking 'I will breathe out concentrating the mind'. He trains himself thinking 'I will breathe in liberating the mind'; he trains himself thinking 'I will breathe out liberating the mind'.
translations.mn118:21: He trains himself thinking 'I will breathe in contemplating impermanence'; he trains himself thinking 'I will breathe out contemplating impermanence'. He trains himself thinking 'I will breathe in contemplating dispassion'; he trains himself thinking 'I will breathe out contemplating dispassion'. He trains himself thinking 'I will breathe in contemplating cessation'; he trains himself thinking 'I will breathe out contemplating cessation'. He trains himself thinking 'I will breathe in contemplating relinquishment'; he trains himself thinking 'I will breathe out contemplating relinquishment'.
translations.mn118:23: And how, monks, is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness?
translations.mn118:24: When, monks, a monk, while breathing in long, knows 'I am breathing in long', or, while breathing out long, knows 'I am breathing out long';  while breathing in short, knows 'I am breathing in short', or, while breathing out short, knows 'I am breathing out short';  trains thus: 'I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body', or, 'I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body';  trains thus: 'I shall breathe in calming the bodily formation', or, 'I shall breathe out calming the bodily formation';  in this way, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.  I say, monks, that this, too, is a certain body among bodies, that is, breathing in and out.  Therefore, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.
translations.mn118:25: When, monks, a monk trains thus: 'I shall breathe in experiencing joy', or, 'I shall breathe out experiencing joy';  trains thus: 'I shall breathe in experiencing pleasure', or, 'I shall breathe out experiencing pleasure';  trains thus: 'I shall breathe in experiencing the mental formation', or, 'I shall breathe out experiencing the mental formation';  trains thus: 'I shall breathe in calming the mental formation', or, 'I shall breathe out calming the mental formation';  in this way, monks, a monk dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.  I say, monks, that this, too, is a certain feeling among feelings, that is, the mindful attention to breathing in and out.  Therefore, monks, a monk dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.
translations.mn118:26: When, monks, a monk trains thus: 'I shall breathe in experiencing the mind', or, 'I shall breathe out experiencing the mind';  trains thus: 'I shall breathe in gladdening the mind', or, 'I shall breathe out gladdening the mind';  trains thus: 'I shall breathe in concentrating the mind', or, 'I shall breathe out concentrating the mind';  trains thus: 'I shall breathe in liberating the mind', or, 'I shall breathe out liberating the mind';  in this way, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.  I do not, monks, say that mindfulness of breathing is for one who is forgetful and lacks clear comprehension.  Therefore, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.
translations.mn118:27: When, monks, a monk trains thus: 'I shall breathe in contemplating impermanence', or, 'I shall breathe out contemplating impermanence';  trains thus: 'I shall breathe in contemplating dispassion', or, 'I shall breathe out contemplating dispassion';  trains thus: 'I shall breathe in contemplating cessation', or, 'I shall breathe out contemplating cessation';  trains thus: 'I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment', or, 'I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment';  in this way, monks, a monk dwells contemplating dhammas in dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.  He, having seen with wisdom the removal of covetousness and displeasure, is one who looks on with equanimity.  Therefore, monks, a monk dwells contemplating dhammas in dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.
translations.mn118:28: Developed and cultivated in this way, monks, mindfulness of breathing fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness.
translations.mn118:29: How, monks, are the four foundations of mindfulness developed and cultivated so as to fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment?
translations.mn118:3: At that time, the Blessed One was sitting in the open, surrounded by the community of monks, on the Uposatha day, the fifteenth, during the Pavāraṇā festival, on the full moon night.  Then the Blessed One, having looked around the silent community of monks, addressed the monks:
translations.mn118:30: When, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world, his mindfulness is established in that moment, and he is not forgetful.  When, monks, a monk's mindfulness is established in that moment, and he is not forgetful, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness is established in him in that moment.  He develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness in that moment, and the development of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness comes to fulfillment in him in that moment.
translations.mn118:31: He, having thus established himself, examines with wisdom that dhamma, examines it, and investigates it, and by means of that investigation, he gains a thorough understanding of it.  When, monks, a monk, having thus established himself, examines with wisdom that dhamma, examines it, and investigates it, and by means of that investigation, he gains a thorough understanding of it, the enlightenment factor of investigation of dhammas is established in him in that moment.  He develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of dhammas in that moment, and the development of the enlightenment factor of investigation of dhammas comes to fulfillment in him in that moment.
translations.mn118:33: For one who has established energy, unworldly joy arises.  When, monks, unworldly joy arises in a monk who has established energy, the enlightenment factor of joy is established in him in that moment.  He develops the enlightenment factor of joy in that moment, and the development of the enlightenment factor of joy comes to fulfillment in him in that moment.
translations.mn118:34: For one who has joy, both the body and the mind become tranquil.  When, monks, both the body and the mind of a monk with joy become tranquil, the enlightenment factor of tranquility is established in him in that moment.  He develops the enlightenment factor of tranquility in that moment, and the development of the enlightenment factor of tranquility comes to fulfillment in him in that moment.
translations.mn118:35: For one with a tranquil body, the mind becomes concentrated and happy.  When, monks, the mind of a monk with a tranquil body becomes concentrated and happy, the enlightenment factor of concentration is established in him in that moment.  He develops the enlightenment factor of concentration in that moment, and the development of the enlightenment factor of concentration comes to fulfillment in him in that moment.
translations.mn118:36: When a monk's mind is well-established in this way, he carefully attends to it.  When, bhikkhus, a monk's mind is well-established in this way, the enlightenment factor of equanimity is developed, the enlightenment factor of equanimity is frequently practiced, the enlightenment factor of equanimity is made much of, in him.
translations.mn118:4: ‘I, bhikkhus, have developed and cultivated this path; I have developed and cultivated this path to a great extent.  Therefore, bhikkhus, you should strive still more for what is unattained, for the attainment of what is not yet attained, for the realization of what is not yet realized.  I shall come to Sāvatthī during the coming month of Kattika.’
translations.mn118:40: When developed and cultivated in this way, bhikkhus, the four establishments of mindfulness fulfill the seven enlightenment factors.
translations.mn118:41: And how, bhikkhus, are the seven enlightenment factors developed and cultivated so that they fulfill the knowledge and liberation?
translations.mn118:6: Those elder monks, bhikkhus, advise and instruct the new monks a great deal.  Some elder monks advise and instruct ten monks, some advise and instruct twenty monks, some thirty, some forty.
translations.mn118:9: There are, bhikkhus, monks in this monk community who are arahants, whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, destroyed the fetters of being, and are completely liberated through final knowledge—there are such monks in this monk community.
translations.mn11:13: In a Dhamma and Vinaya that has not been well taught, there is no proper faith in the Teacher, no proper faith in the Dhamma, no fulfillment of the precepts, no affection and respect for one's fellow monks.  What is the reason for this?  It is because such a Dhamma and Vinaya is poorly taught, not leading out, not leading to the cessation of the corruptions.
translations.mn11:14: The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, who knows and sees, teaches the knowledge of the utter destruction of all acquisitions—of sensual acquisition, of acquisition through views, of acquisition through precepts and practices, of acquisition through the theory of a self.
translations.mn11:15: In a Dhamma and Vinaya that has been well taught, there is proper faith in the Teacher, proper faith in the Dhamma, fulfillment of the precepts, affection and respect for one's fellow monks.  What is the reason for this?  It is because such a Dhamma and Vinaya is well taught, leading out, leading to the cessation of the corruptions, leading to the complete destruction of suffering.
translations.mn11:2: ‘Here, bhikkhus, is one who has gone forth, here is a second who has gone forth, here is a third who has gone forth, here is a fourth who has gone forth; the wanderers of other sects are empty, hollow, and devoid of meaning.’  This, bhikkhus, is the proper lion's roar.
translations.mn11:6: There are, bhikkhus, two views: the view of existence and the view of non-existence.  Whatever recluses or brahmins hold the view of existence, they are opposed to the view of non-existence; whatever recluses or brahmins hold the view of non-existence, they are opposed to the view of existence.
translations.mn11:7: Whatever recluses or brahmins do not understand as it really is the origin and the passing away, the satisfaction, the danger, and the escape from these two views, they are attached, they are repelled, they are obsessed, they are enslaved, they are fettered, they are not freed, they are not released; they do not escape from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; they do not escape from suffering, I say.
translations.mn11:9: There are, bhikkhus, four kinds of acquisition.  What four?  Acquisition through sensual desires, acquisition through views, acquisition through precepts and practices, acquisition through the theory of a self.
translations.mn12:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Vesālī at the Gabled Hall in the Great Forest.
translations.mn12:10: Here, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata knows as it really is the places and the non-places, the occasions and the non-occasions.  And it is because the Tathāgata knows as it really is the places and the non-places, the occasions and the non-occasions, that he is able to roar his lion's roar in the assemblies, to set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma.
translations.mn12:19: Again, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata, through the destruction of the corruptions, having realized for himself with direct knowledge the uncorrupted liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, dwells in the knowledge and vision of that liberation.  And it is because the Tathāgata, through the destruction of the corruptions, having realized for himself with direct knowledge the uncorrupted liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, dwells in the knowledge and vision of that liberation, that he is able to roar his lion's roar in the assemblies, to set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma.
translations.mn12:2: Now at that time Sunakkhatta, the Licchavi, had recently left this Dhamma and Vinaya.  He was speaking in the assembly hall at Vesālī, saying: ‘There is no superhuman state, no distinction in knowledge and vision, attainable by the monk Gotama.  The monk Gotama teaches a Dhamma that is hammered out by reasoning, following his own line of inquiry as it occurs to him, and he has no superhuman state, no distinction in knowledge and vision.’
translations.mn12:20: These, Sāriputta, are the ten Tathāgata powers, possessed by a Tathāgata, by which he claims a bull's voice, by which he roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, by which he sets in motion the Wheel of Dhamma.
translations.mn12:22: There are, Sāriputta, four kinds of intrepidity of a Tathāgata, by which, possessed of these four kinds of intrepidity, he claims a bull's voice, by which he roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, by which he sets in motion the Wheel of Dhamma.  What are the four?
translations.mn12:23: They might say of me: 'These things are not fully awakened to by the Tathagata.' But I do not see any sign of this, Sāriputta. Not seeing any such sign, I live in security, fearlessness, and intrepidity.
translations.mn12:24: They might say of me: 'These corruptions are not fully awakened to by the Tathagata.' But I do not see any sign of this, Sāriputta. Not seeing any such sign, I live in security, fearlessness, and intrepidity.
translations.mn12:25: They might say of me: 'These things that hinder one from the goal, when attended to, do not lead to hindrance.' But I do not see any sign of this, Sāriputta. Not seeing any such sign, I live in security, fearlessness, and intrepidity.
translations.mn12:26: They might say of me: 'The Dhamma taught by the Tathagata does not lead to the complete destruction of suffering for one who practices it.' But I do not see any sign of this, Sāriputta. Not seeing any such sign, I live in security, fearlessness, and intrepidity.
translations.mn12:32: There are, Sāriputta, these four modes of generation. What four? Egg-born generation, womb-born generation, moisture-born generation, and spontaneous generation.
translations.mn12:33: And what, Sāriputta, is egg-born generation? There are, Sāriputta, certain beings who are born from an egg; this, Sāriputta, is called egg-born generation. And what, Sāriputta, is womb-born generation? There are, Sāriputta, certain beings who are born from a womb; this, Sāriputta, is called womb-born generation. And what, Sāriputta, is moisture-born generation? There are, Sāriputta, certain beings who are born in a rotten fish, or in a rotten corpse, or in a cesspit, or in a sewer; this, Sāriputta, is called moisture-born generation. And what, Sāriputta, is spontaneous generation? The devas, some non-human beings, and some human beings are spontaneously born; this, Sāriputta, is called spontaneous generation. These, Sāriputta, are the four modes of generation.
translations.mn12:35: There are, Sāriputta, these five destinations. What five? Hell, the animal realm, the realm of ghosts, human beings, and the devas.
translations.mn12:36: I understand hell, Sāriputta, and the path that leads to hell, and the practice that leads to hell; and I also understand how one who practices accordingly is reborn in hell after the breakup of the body, after death. I understand the animal realm, Sāriputta, and the path that leads to the animal realm, and the practice that leads to the animal realm; and I also understand how one who practices accordingly is reborn in the animal realm after the breakup of the body, after death. I understand the realm of ghosts, Sāriputta, and the path that leads to the realm of ghosts, and the practice that leads to the realm of ghosts; and I also understand how one who practices accordingly is reborn in the realm of ghosts after the breakup of the body, after death. I understand human beings, Sāriputta, and the path that leads to human beings, and the practice that leads to human beings; and I also understand how one who practices accordingly is reborn among human beings after the breakup of the body, after death. I understand the devas, Sāriputta, and the path that leads to the devas, and the practice that leads to the devas; and I also understand how one who practices accordingly is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world, after the breakup of the body, after death. I understand Nibbana, Sāriputta, and the path that leads to Nibbana, and the practice that leads to Nibbana; and I also understand how one who practices accordingly, through the destruction of the corruptions, enters upon the corruption-free liberation of mind, the liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, dwells in it.
translations.mn12:4: The angry person is a foolish person, Sāriputta. This statement of his is spoken out of anger. The foolish person, Sāriputta, thinks he will disparage the Tathagata, but he actually praises him. The praise of the Tathagata is this, Sāriputta: 'The Dhamma taught by the Tathagata leads to the complete destruction of suffering for one who practices it.'
translations.mn12:43: If someone were to say of me, Sāriputta, who knows and sees thus: 'There is no further excellence of knowledge and vision for the ascetic Gotama; the Dhamma taught by the ascetic Gotama is limited, and he teaches it based on his own speculation, his own ingenuity,' and if one were not to abandon that statement, not to abandon that thought, not to relinquish that view, one would be reborn in hell. Just as a monk who is accomplished in virtue, concentration, and wisdom would not seek anything else, so too, Sāriputta, I say that one who does not abandon that statement, thought, and view would be reborn in hell.
translations.mn12:44: I, Sāriputta, have practiced the holy life, endowed with four factors: I have been a practitioner of austerities, a supreme practitioner of austerities; I have been a practitioner of scrupulousness, a supreme practitioner of scrupulousness; I have been a practitioner of seclusion, a supreme practitioner of seclusion; I have been a practitioner of non-possessiveness, a supreme practitioner of non-possessiveness.
translations.mn12:46: But, Sāriputta, I have this drawback in my practice of scrupulousness: for more than a hundred years, a drop of semen has been stored up in my body, accumulated and built up. Just as a drop of oil is stored up in a sesame seed, so too, Sāriputta, a drop of semen has been stored up in my body for more than a hundred years. But, Sāriputta, it does not occur to me: 'Let me wipe away this drop of semen with my hand, or let someone else wipe it away with their hand.' This, Sāriputta, is the drawback I have in my practice of scrupulousness.
translations.mn12:47: But, Sāriputta, I have this drawback in my practice of seclusion: I walk back and forth, Sāriputta, and I walk back and forth, and even for a drop of water, my compassion is established: 'Let me not harm any small living being.' This, Sāriputta, is the drawback I have in my practice of seclusion.
translations.mn12:49: For I, Sāriputta, approach those cowsheds that have been left empty by the cowherds, and I eat the dung of the young calves. As long as I have not finished my own dung, I eat my own dung. This, Sāriputta, is my great disgusting food.
translations.mn12:5: For it will not occur to the foolish person, Sāriputta, who has gone for seven days without seeing me: 'The Blessed One is an arahant, a fully awakened one, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a sublime one, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of devas and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.'
translations.mn12:50: For I, Sāriputta, have entered a certain terrifying forest. There, Sāriputta, in that terrifying forest, it is terrifying - whoever enters that forest without aversion will have their hair stand on end. For I, Sāriputta, spend the night in the open and the day in the forest during the cold winter months; and during the hot summer months, I spend the day in the open and the night in the forest. It occurs to me, Sāriputta, a verse that was not previously heard: 'With ears plugged and nose plugged, alone in a terrifying forest; like a bull, not leaning on anything, a sage with controlled senses.'
translations.mn12:51: For I, Sāriputta, lie down on a mattress of grass, covering myself with my robe. It occurs to me, Sāriputta, that when I approach the villages, they throw clods of earth at me, and they throw sticks and stones, and they pour dust into my ears and nose. But I, Sāriputta, do not recognize any evil intention in them. This, Sāriputta, is my abiding in equanimity.
translations.mn12:52: There are, Sāriputta, certain ascetics and brahmins who say: 'Purification comes from food.' They say: 'We will eat millet.' They eat millet, and millet flour, and millet water - they eat various preparations of millet. But I, Sāriputta, know that I have eaten only one kind of millet as food. It may occur to them, Sāriputta, that the millet was very large at that time. But it should not be seen in that way, Sāriputta. For the millet was just as small then as it is now. When I, Sāriputta, eat only one kind of millet as food, my body becomes extremely thin. Just as, for example, the joints of a skeleton are visible, so too my joints are visible due to eating so little. Just as, for example, the tendons of a skeleton are visible, so too my tendons are visible due to eating so little. Just as, for example, the vertebrae of a skeleton are visible, so too my vertebrae are visible due to eating so little. Just as, for example, the bones of the ribs are visible, so too my ribs are visible due to eating so little. Just as, for example, the bones of the spine are visible, so too my spine is visible due to eating so little. Just as, for example, the sockets of the eyes are visible, so too my eye sockets are visible due to eating so little. Just as, for example, the skin of the head is tight, so too my scalp is tight and shriveled due to eating so little. So I, Sāriputta, thinking 'I will defecate or urinate', squat down right there, due to eating so little. So I, Sāriputta, massaging my limbs with my hands, make the putrid roots of the hair fall out, due to eating so little.
translations.mn12:56: I, Sāriputta, did not attain the knowledge and vision of the unsurpassed, the supreme, the highest, the ultimate, by means of that practice, that way of life, that painful practice. Why is that? Because that noble knowledge is not attainable by that means, and the noble knowledge that is attainable leads to the complete destruction of suffering.
translations.mn12:57: There are, Sāriputta, certain ascetics and brahmins who say: 'Purification comes from the cycle of existence.' But, Sāriputta, the cycle of existence is not easy to transcend, which I have not transcended before, in this long time, except for the pure abodes of the gods. And I, Sāriputta, would not be reborn in this world again, even if I were to cycle through the pure abodes of the gods.
translations.mn12:6: For it will not occur to the foolish person, Sāriputta, who has gone for seven days without seeing me: 'The Blessed One has various kinds of psychic powers, which he experiences - being one, he becomes many, and being many, he becomes one; he appears and disappears; he goes unimpeded through walls, through ramparts, and through mountains as if through the air; he dives in and out of the earth as if it were water; he walks on water as if it were earth; he travels through the air like a bird with its wings; with his hand he touches and strokes the moon and sun, which are so powerful and mighty; he has mastery over his body as far as the brahmalokas.'
translations.mn12:60: There are, Sāriputta, certain ascetics and brahmins who say: 'Purification comes from sacrifice.' But, Sāriputta, the sacrifice is not easy to perform, which I have not performed before, in this long time, except for the king or a wealthy brahmin or a wealthy householder.
translations.mn12:61: There are, Sāriputta, certain ascetics and brahmins who say: 'Purification comes from tending the fire.' But, Sāriputta, the fire is not easy to tend, which I have not tended before, in this long time, except for the king or a wealthy brahmin or a wealthy householder.
translations.mn12:62: There are, Sāriputta, certain recluses and brahmins who declare and believe as follows: 'As long as a person is young, youthful, and endowed with the foremost of life, they are endowed with the highest wisdom and insight. But as one ages, grows old, and becomes advanced in years, one's wisdom and insight decline.' This, Sāriputta, is not the correct view. I, Sāriputta, am now old, aged, and advanced in years, with eighty years having passed. Yet, I have four disciples who are over a hundred years old, endowed with the highest life, wisdom, and insight. Just as a skilled archer, well-trained and practiced, can shoot an arrow straight and true, so too are these disciples endowed with the highest wisdom and insight. If they were to ask me a question about the four foundations of mindfulness, I would answer them, and they would understand my answer without needing to ask a second or third time. The teaching of the Tathāgata, the explanation of the Dhamma, and the answering of questions are not limited. If my disciples were to care for me with a bed, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata's wisdom and insight would not decline.
translations.mn12:7: This, Sāriputta, is a quality that does not belong to the Tathāgata, and which the foolish man would not ascribe to me: 'The Tathāgata has the divine ear, the purified and surpassing hearing, with which he hears both divine and human sounds, near and far.'
translations.mn12:8: This, Sāriputta, is a quality that does not belong to the Tathāgata, and which the foolish man would not ascribe to me: 'The Tathāgata has the knowledge of the minds of others, and knows the mind of another as being with passion or without passion, with hatred or without hatred, with delusion or without delusion, contracted or expanded, surpassable or unsurpassable, concentrated or unconcentrated, liberated or unliberated.'
translations.mn12:9: There are, Sāriputta, ten powers of a Tathāgata, possessed by which a Tathāgata claims the lion's seat, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the wheel of Dhamma. What are these ten?
translations.mn135:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Blessed One was living in Sāvatthī, at Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery.
translations.mn135:13: Here, young man, someone does not give to a recluse or brahmin food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, or bedding. As a result of this action, they are reborn in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in a lower realm, in hell. If they are not reborn in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in a lower realm, in hell, and instead are reborn among humans, they will have a lack of wealth wherever they are reborn. This, young man, is a path that leads to a lack of wealth, namely, not giving to a recluse or brahmin food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, or bedding.
translations.mn135:2: Then Subha, the young man, son of Todeyya, approached the Blessed One, and after exchanging greetings, sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Subha, the young man, son of Todeyya, asked the Blessed One:
translations.mn135:20: Beings are the owners of their actions, heirs to their actions, born from their actions, related to their actions, and have their actions as their refuge. It is action that distinguishes beings as superior or inferior.
translations.mn135:3: What is the reason, Master Gotama, what is the cause, why human beings are seen to be inferior and superior? For human beings are seen to be short-lived and long-lived, often ill and rarely ill, ugly and beautiful, of little account and of great account, poor and wealthy, low-born and high-born, foolish and wise. What is the reason, Master Gotama, what is the cause, why human beings are seen to be inferior and superior?
translations.mn135:4: Beings are the owners of their actions, heirs to their actions, born from their actions, related to their actions, and have their actions as their refuge. It is action that distinguishes beings as superior or inferior. I do not understand the meaning of the Blessed One's brief statement, or the detailed explanation of the brief statement. Please, Master Gotama, explain the Dhamma so that I can understand the meaning of the Blessed One's brief statement and the detailed explanation of the brief statement. Very well, young man, listen and pay attention, I will speak.
translations.mn135:5: Here, young man, someone is a killer of living beings, brutal, with a blooded hand, a killer of creatures, and devoid of compassion for living beings.  Through that action, that deed, that transgression, they experience a decrease in their lifespan, a decrease in their beauty, a decrease in their happiness, a decrease in their strength, and a decrease in their wealth.  If they do not experience a decrease in their lifespan, a decrease in their beauty, a decrease in their happiness, a decrease in their strength, and a decrease in their wealth, then they will experience a short lifespan wherever they are reborn.  This path, young man, leads to a short lifespan, namely, being a killer of living beings, brutal, with a blooded hand, a killer of creatures, and devoid of compassion for living beings.
translations.mn135:6: Here, young man, someone abstains from killing living beings, laying down the rod, laying down the sword, and is scrupulous, merciful, and compassionate towards all living beings.  Through that action, that deed, that transgression, they experience an increase in their lifespan, an increase in their beauty, an increase in their happiness, an increase in their strength, and an increase in their wealth.  If they do not experience an increase in their lifespan, an increase in their beauty, an increase in their happiness, an increase in their strength, and an increase in their wealth, then they will experience a long lifespan wherever they are reborn.  This path, young man, leads to a long lifespan, namely, abstaining from killing living beings, laying down the rod, laying down the sword, and being scrupulous, merciful, and compassionate towards all living beings.
translations.mn13:10: If, monks, a certain person has risen, or is making an effort, or is striving, and their possessions increase, they experience suffering and grief due to the need to protect those possessions: 'What if kings take them away, or thieves take them away, or fire burns them, or water sweeps them away, or unworthy heirs take them away?'  And then, while they are protecting and guarding their possessions, kings take them away, or thieves take them away, or fire burns them, or water sweeps them away, or unworthy heirs take them away.  They lament, they grieve, they beat their chest, and they become deluded: 'What I had is no more.'  This, monks, is a visible danger of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering, a result of sensual pleasures, a source of sensual pleasures, a condition for sensual pleasures, and a cause of sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:11: Again, monks, sensual pleasures are the cause, the source, the condition, and the cause of sensual pleasures, and due to this, kings quarrel with kings, nobles quarrel with nobles, brahmins quarrel with brahmins, householders quarrel with householders, a mother quarrels with her child, a child quarrels with its mother, a father quarrels with his child, a child quarrels with its father, a brother quarrels with his brother, a brother quarrels with his sister, a sister quarrels with her brother, and a friend quarrels with their friend.  There, they become quarrelsome and argumentative, and they come to blows with each other, even with sticks, and with clods of earth, and with swords.  There, they die, and they experience death and suffering.  This, monks, is a visible danger of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering, a result of sensual pleasures, a source of sensual pleasures, a condition for sensual pleasures, and a cause of sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:12: Again, monks, sensual pleasures are the cause, the source, the condition, and the cause of sensual pleasures, and due to this, they take up a sword, and they prepare a bow and arrow, and they rush into battle, even with arrows flying, and with swords clashing, and with spears flashing.  There, they are pierced by arrows, and they are cut by swords, and they have their heads cut off by swords.  There, they die, and they experience death and suffering.  This, monks, is a visible danger of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering, a result of sensual pleasures, a source of sensual pleasures, a condition for sensual pleasures, and a cause of sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:13: Again, monks, sensual pleasures are the cause, the source, the condition, and the cause of sensual pleasures, and due to this, they take up a sword, and they prepare a bow and arrow, and they rush into battle, even with arrows flying, and with swords clashing, and with spears flashing.  There, they are pierced by arrows, and they are cut by swords, and they are splashed with hot oil, and they are crushed by a falling rock, and they have their heads cut off by swords.  There, they die, and they experience death and suffering.  This, monks, is a visible danger of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering, a result of sensual pleasures, a source of sensual pleasures, a condition for sensual pleasures, and a cause of sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:15: Again, monks, sensual pleasures are the cause, the source, the condition, and the cause of sensual pleasures, and due to this, they engage in bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct.  Having engaged in bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct, they experience a decrease in their lifespan, a decrease in their beauty, a decrease in their happiness, a decrease in their strength, and a decrease in their wealth, and they are reborn in a lower realm, in a bad destination, in a state of suffering, in hell.  This, monks, is a danger of sensual pleasures that leads to the next world, a mass of suffering, a result of sensual pleasures, a source of sensual pleasures, a condition for sensual pleasures, and a cause of sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:16: And what, monks, is the escape from sensual pleasures?  The elimination of desire and passion for sensual pleasures, the abandonment of desire and passion for sensual pleasures - this is the escape from sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:17: Whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand sensual pleasures, their enjoyment, their danger, and their escape, as they really are, they will not understand sensual pleasures, nor will they be able to instruct others to understand sensual pleasures as one who has practiced them.  This is not possible.  But whatever ascetics or brahmins do understand sensual pleasures, their enjoyment, their danger, and their escape, as they really are, they will understand sensual pleasures, and they will be able to instruct others to understand sensual pleasures as one who has practiced them.  This is possible.
translations.mn13:18: And what, monks, is the enjoyment of forms?  Suppose, monks, a king's daughter, or a brahmin's daughter, or a householder's daughter, fifteen or sixteen years old, neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too fat, neither too dark nor too fair - at that time, she is considered most beautiful.  'Yes, venerable sir.'  The pleasure and joy that arise from that beautiful form - this is the enjoyment of forms.
translations.mn13:19: And what, monks, is the danger in forms? Suppose, monks, a sister sees her brother, after a long time, eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old, broken, decrepit, bent, supporting himself with a stick, frail, with youthfulness gone, with teeth broken, with hair grey, with bald head, with wrinkled skin, with limbs bent. What do you think, monks? Has that former beauty, that former loveliness disappeared, and is the danger evident? 'Yes, venerable sir.' This, monks, is the danger in forms.
translations.mn13:2: Then a number of monks, having dressed in the morning, after putting away their bowls and robes, went to the park of the wanderers of other sects. After going there, they exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects and sat down to one side. Those wanderers of other sects said to them:
translations.mn13:20: Again, monks, a sister sees her brother, afflicted with a disease, suffering, gravely ill, lying in his own urine, with excrement, being lifted up by others, being laid down by others. What do you think, monks? Has that former beauty, that former loveliness disappeared, and is the danger evident? 'Yes, venerable sir.' This, monks, is the danger in forms.
translations.mn13:23-28: Again, monks, a sister sees her brother's corpse, thrown in a charnel ground, a skeleton with flesh and blood, a skeleton without flesh but with blood, a skeleton without flesh and blood, a skeleton with tendons, a skeleton without tendons, but with bones held together by the tendons, a skeleton without tendons and bones held together, scattered in various directions, a hand-bone, a foot-bone, a shin-bone, a thigh-bone, a hip-bone, a back-bone, a rib-bone, a breast-bone, a shoulder-bone, a neck-bone, a jaw-bone, a tooth-bone, a skull-bone. What do you think, monks? Has that former beauty, that former loveliness disappeared, and is the danger evident? 'Yes, venerable sir.' This, monks, is the danger in forms.
translations.mn13:29: Again, monks, a sister sees her brother's corpse, thrown in a charnel ground, a skeleton with white bones, a heap of bones more than a year old, a skeleton with bones that have been bleached and are like a conch shell. What do you think, monks? Has that former beauty, that former loveliness disappeared, and is the danger evident? 'Yes, venerable sir.' This, monks, is the danger in forms.
translations.mn13:3: 'The ascetic Gotama teaches the complete understanding of sensual pleasures; we also teach the complete understanding of sensual pleasures. The ascetic Gotama teaches the complete understanding of forms; we also teach the complete understanding of forms. The ascetic Gotama teaches the complete understanding of feelings; we also teach the complete understanding of feelings. What distinction, what excellence, what difference is there between the ascetic Gotama and us, that this teaching and this instruction should be given?'
translations.mn13:30: And what, monks, is the escape from forms? The removal of desire and lust for forms, the abandonment of desire and lust for forms - this is the escape from forms.
translations.mn13:32: And what, monks, is the attraction in feelings? Here, monks, a monk, having separated himself from sensual pleasures, having separated himself from unwholesome states, enters and remains in the first jhana, which is accompanied by thought and examination, and has the joy and pleasure born of seclusion. At that time, monks, the monk does not think of his own affliction, nor of the affliction of others, nor of the affliction of both; at that time he feels a feeling that is without affliction. I say, monks, that the attraction in feelings is the highest.
translations.mn13:36: And what, monks, is the danger in feelings? The fact that feelings are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change - this, monks, is the danger in feelings.
translations.mn13:37: And what, monks, is the escape from feelings? The removal of desire and lust for feelings, the abandonment of desire and lust for feelings - this, monks, is the escape from feelings.
translations.mn13:4: Then those monks neither approved nor disapproved of the words of those wanderers of other sects; without approving or disapproving, they rose from their seats and went away, thinking: 'We will know the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One.'
translations.mn13:6: One should say to those wanderers of other sects: 'Friends, what is the attraction in sensual pleasures, what is the danger, and what is the escape? What is the attraction in forms, what is the danger, and what is the escape? What is the attraction in feelings, what is the danger, and what is the escape?' When asked thus, monks, those wanderers of other sects will not be able to give an answer, and besides, they will fall into trouble. What is the reason for this? It is because they are without a basis.
translations.mn13:8: And what, monks, is the danger in sensual pleasures?  Here, a clansman makes his living by some craft, such as by calculating, accounting, computing, farming, trading, cow-keeping, archery, being a royal servant, or by some other craft.  He is oppressed by heat and cold, by hunger and thirst, and by flies and mosquitoes.  He is afflicted by the rigors of the seasons, by bodily pains, and by troubles with his wife and children.  This, monks, is the danger in sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering, a source of suffering, a reason for suffering, a condition for suffering, a basis for suffering.
translations.mn13:9: If, monks, that clansman's efforts do not succeed, he sorrows, grieves, and laments, he weeps and beats his breast, and becomes distraught: 'I have no gain, my efforts are fruitless.'  This, monks, is also the danger in sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering, a source of suffering, a reason for suffering, a condition for suffering, a basis for suffering.
translations.mn140:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Magadhan country and arrived at a potter's village called Kumbhakara.
translations.mn140:12: 'One should not be negligent, one should protect the truth, one should be generous, and one should train in the virtues.'  This is what was said, but with what reason was it said?
translations.mn140:14: And what, monk, is the earth element?  The earth element may be internal or external.  And what, monk, is the internal earth element?  Whatever internal, personal, earth element is hard, solid, and sustained, such as head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinew, bone, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, stomach, feces, or whatever else is internal, personal, earth element, hard, solid, and sustained.  This, monk, is called the internal earth element.  Both the internal earth element and the external earth element are simply earth element.  It should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'  Having seen it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the earth element and one's mind is liberated from the earth element.
translations.mn140:15: And what, monk, is the water element?  The water element may be internal or external.  And what, monk, is the internal water element?
