Whatever internal, personal, water element is watery and sustained, such as bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints, and urine, or whatever else is internal, personal, water element, watery and sustained.  This, monk, is called the internal water element.  Both the internal water element and the external water element are simply water element.  It should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'  Having seen it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the water element and one's mind is liberated from the water element.
translations.mn140:16: And what, monk, is the fire element?  The fire element may be internal or external.  And what, monk, is the internal fire element?  Whatever internal, personal, fire element is fiery and sustained, such as that by which one is warmed, aged, and consumed, and that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is fully digested, or whatever else is internal, personal, fire element, fiery and sustained.  This, monk, is called the internal fire element.  Both the internal fire element and the external fire element are simply fire element.  It should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'  Having seen it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the fire element and one's mind is liberated from the fire element.
translations.mn140:17: And what, monk, is the air element?  The air element may be internal or external.  And what, monk, is the internal air element?  Whatever internal, personal, air element is airy and sustained, such as up-going winds, down-going winds, winds in the belly, winds in the bowels, winds that course through all the limbs, in-breath and out-breath, or whatever else is internal, personal, air element, airy and sustained.  This, monk, is called the internal air element.  Both the internal air element and the external air element are simply air element.  It should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'  Having seen it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the air element and one's mind is liberated from the air element.
translations.mn140:18: And what, monk, is the space element?  The space element may be internal or external.  And what, monk, is the internal space element?  Whatever internal, personal, space element is space and sustained, such as the holes of the ears, the nostrils, the mouth, and that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is swallowed, and that by which it is absorbed, and that by which it is excreted, or whatever else is internal, personal, space element, space and sustained.  This, monk, is called the internal space element.  Both the internal space element and the external space element are simply space element.  It should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'  Having seen it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the space element and one's mind is liberated from the space element.
translations.mn140:2: 'If you, potter, were to stay in this shed for one night,' he said.  'I have no shed, sir.  There is a monk who has arrived first and is staying here.  If he gives permission, you may stay here, sir, as you like.'
translations.mn140:20: Then, with mindfulness of the body established, with an immeasurable mind, he abides pervading one quarter with equanimity, likewise the second, the third, and the fourth, and so above, below, around, and everywhere, and to all as to himself, he abides pervading the entire world with equanimity, abundant, expansive, measureless, free from enmity and oppression. Just as a skilled goldsmith or his apprentice, having heated gold and cleaned it, would then shape it, mold it, and prepare it; in the same way, the monk's mind is pliable, malleable, and luminous. Whatever idea or concept he wishes to apply to it, it serves his purpose, just like gold that has been heated, cleaned, shaped, molded, and prepared.
translations.mn140:23: If he feels a pleasant feeling, he knows it as such; he knows it is impermanent, he knows it is not to be identified with, he knows it is not to be delighted in. If he feels a painful feeling, he knows it as such; he knows it is impermanent, he knows it is not to be identified with, he knows it is not to be delighted in. If he feels a neutral feeling, he knows it as such; he knows it is impermanent, he knows it is not to be identified with, he knows it is not to be delighted in.
translations.mn140:29: ‘One should not be negligent of wisdom, one should constantly honor the truth, one should constantly practice generosity, and one should train in patience.’ This is what was said, and it was said in reference to this.
translations.mn140:3: At that time, a certain clansman named Pukkusati was living in that potter's shed, having gone forth from home to homelessness with faith in the Buddha. The Buddha approached the Venerable Pukkusati and said: 'If you, monk, would stay in this potter's shed for one night.' 'The shed is narrow, sir, but let the monk stay as he likes.'
translations.mn140:30: ‘Where consciousness does not become established and has no growth, that is where the sage is at peace.’ This is what was said, but in reference to what?
translations.mn140:31: ‘I am,’ this is a conceit; ‘I am this,’ this is a conceit; ‘I shall be,’ this is a conceit; ‘I shall not be,’ this is a conceit; ‘I shall be material,’ this is a conceit; ‘I shall be immaterial,’ this is a conceit; ‘I shall be percipient,’ this is a conceit; ‘I shall be non-percipient,’ this is a conceit; ‘I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient,’ this is a conceit. Conceit is a disease, a tumor, a dart. The sage has transcended all conceits. The sage is at peace, not born, not aging, not dying, not alarmed, not hankering.
translations.mn140:32: ‘Where consciousness does not become established and has no growth, that is where the sage is at peace.’ This is what was said, and it was said in reference to this. Remember this concise explanation of the six elements, monk.
translations.mn140:33: Then the Venerable Pukkusati rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, and prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, saying: 'Forgive me, sir, for my transgression, which was foolish, stupid, and unskillful, in that I did not recognize the Buddha when I should have. May the Buddha forgive my transgression, and may I be restrained in the future.' 'You have seen your transgression, monk, as a transgression, and you have made amends in accordance with the Dhamma. We forgive your transgression. For it is growth in the Noble One's discipline that, having seen one's transgression as such, one makes amends in accordance with the Dhamma and exercises restraint in the future.'
translations.mn140:34: ‘I would like to receive the going forth and ordination in the Buddha's presence.’ 'Do you have the complete set of robes?' 'I do not have the complete set of robes, sir.' 'The Tathagata does not give the going forth to one who does not have the complete set of robes.'
translations.mn140:35: Then the Venerable Pukkusati, having delighted in and approved of the Buddha's words, rose from his seat, bowed down to the Buddha, and circumambulated him. He then went in search of a set of robes. While he was searching for robes, a cow attacked and killed him.
translations.mn140:4: The Buddha entered the potter's shed, sat down on a prepared seat, and, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body straight, established mindfulness in front of him, and spent most of the night sitting. The Venerable Pukkusati also spent most of the night sitting. The Buddha thought: 'This clansman is sitting nicely. I will ask him a question.' The Buddha then asked the Venerable Pukkusati:
translations.mn140:5: ‘For whom did you go forth, monk? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you like?’ 'I, sir, have gone forth having heard of the ascetic Gotama, the Sakyan son, the Sakyan. The good report about the Buddha Gotama has spread:
translations.mn140:6: Then the following thought occurred to the Blessed One: 'This young man is from a good family and has gone forth from a good family.  What if I were to teach him the Dhamma?', the Blessed One said to the Venerable Pukkusati: 'I will teach you the Dhamma, monk.  Listen carefully and pay attention, I will speak.', 'Yes, Venerable Sir,' the Venerable Pukkusati replied to the Blessed One.
translations.mn140:7: 'The six elements, monk, are: earth, water, fire, air, space, and consciousness.  The six bases for contact are: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.  There are eighteen mental examinations;  the four bases of spiritual power are: the basis of spiritual power consisting of desire, the basis of spiritual power consisting of energy, the basis of spiritual power consisting of mind, and the basis of spiritual power consisting of investigation.  One should not be negligent in wisdom, should guard the truth, and should be devoted to renunciation, and one should train in serenity.' - This is the explanation of the elements.
translations.mn146:12: 'This is a comparison that I have given to illustrate the meaning.  The meaning is this: 'the internal fleshly body' is a term for the internal bases; 'the external leather body' is a term for the external bases; 'the internal sinew, the internal bone, the internal cartilage' is a term for the fetter of delight; 'the three leather thongs' is a term for the noble wisdom that cuts, tears, shreds, and splits the internal defilement, the internal fetter, and the internal bond.
translations.mn146:13: There are, nun, these seven factors of enlightenment, which, when developed and cultivated, lead a monk to the destruction of the corruptions, to the realization of liberation, to the realization of wisdom, and to the attainment of the supreme peace.  What seven?  Here, nun, a monk develops the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, which is based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and which matures in release.  He develops the factor of enlightenment that is investigation of phenomena...  He develops the factor of enlightenment that is energy...  He develops the factor of enlightenment that is joy...  He develops the factor of enlightenment that is tranquility...  He develops the factor of enlightenment that is concentration...  He develops the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity, which is based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and which matures in release.  These, nun, are the seven factors of enlightenment, which, when developed and cultivated, lead a monk to the destruction of the corruptions, to the realization of liberation, to the realization of wisdom, and to the attainment of the supreme peace.
translations.mn146:14: Then the Venerable Nandaka instructed those nuns with this teaching, and dismissed them, saying: 'Go, nuns, it is time.'  Then those nuns, having delighted in and approved of the Venerable Nandaka's words, rose from their seats, bowed down to the Venerable Nandaka, and circumambulated him.  They went to the Blessed One, bowed down to him, and stood to one side.  The Blessed One said to them: 'Go, nuns, it is time.'  Then those nuns bowed down to the Blessed One, circumambulated him, and departed.
translations.mn146:3: At that time, the elder monks were instructing the nuns in the doctrine.  The Venerable Nandaka did not want to instruct the nuns in the doctrine.  Then the Blessed One said to the Venerable Ananda: 'Who is available to instruct the nuns in the doctrine today?'  'All the monks are available, Venerable Sir, but the Venerable Nandaka does not want to instruct the nuns in the doctrine.', 'Instruct the nuns, Nandaka, advise the nuns, and speak the Dhamma to the nuns.'
translations.mn146:4: 'Instruct the nuns, Nandaka, advise the nuns, and speak the Dhamma to the nuns.'  'Yes, Venerable Sir,' the Venerable Nandaka replied, and early in the morning, he put on his robe and, taking his bowl and outer robe, went into Savatthi for alms.  After walking for alms in Savatthi, he returned in the evening, and those nuns saw him coming from a distance.  Having seen him, they prepared a seat and water for his feet.  The Venerable Nandaka sat down on the prepared seat, and they washed his feet.  Those nuns then bowed down to the Venerable Nandaka and sat down to one side.  Seated to one side, the Venerable Nandaka said to them:
translations.mn146:5: 'There will be a question-and-answer session, nuns.  If one does not know, one should say: 'I do not know.'  If one does know, one should say: 'I know.'  If one has doubts or uncertainty about something, one should ask: 'How is this, Sir?  What is the meaning of this?'
translations.mn147:1: Thus I have heard— on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling in Sāvatthī at Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s park.  Then, when the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this thought occurred to him: “Rāhula’s faculties are mature, his mind is mature, his wisdom is mature; what if I were to teach him the higher wisdom for the destruction of the corruptions?”  Then the Blessed One, having risen early, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms.  Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī and returned after his meal, he addressed the Venerable Rāhula: “Take a sitting cloth, Rāhula; let us go to the Andhavana for the day’s abiding.” “Yes, sir,” the Venerable Rāhula replied, and having taken a sitting cloth, he followed close behind the Blessed One.
translations.mn147:2: At that time, many thousands of deities were following the Blessed One, saying: 'Today the Blessed One will make the venerable Rāhula attain the destruction of the corruptions.' Then the Blessed One entered the Andhavana and sat down at the root of a certain tree, having folded his legs crosswise. The venerable Rāhula also bowed down to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to the venerable Rāhula: 'What do you think, Rāhula, is the eye permanent or impermanent?' 'Impermanent, sir.' 'Is what is impermanent suffering or happiness?' 'Suffering, sir.' 'Is what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, fit to be regarded as:
translations.mn148:40: Seeing thus, monks, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with forms, disenchanted with eye-consciousness, disenchanted with eye-contact, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with craving.
translations.mn148:16: This, monks, is the path that leads to the origination of identity: one regards the eye as 'this is mine, this I am, this is my self'
translations.mn149:2: I will teach you, monks, the great sixfold base. Listen and pay attention, I will speak.
translations.mn148:3: There are, monks, six internal bases that are to be understood, six external bases that are to be understood, six consciousness-bodies that are to be understood, six contact-bodies that are to be understood, six feeling-bodies that are to be understood, six craving-bodies that are to be understood.
translations.mn149:11: And what, monks, are the things that are to be fully understood by direct knowledge? The five clinging-aggregates are to be mentioned: the form clinging-aggregate, the feeling clinging-aggregate, the perception clinging-aggregate, the volitional formations clinging-aggregate, the consciousness clinging-aggregate. These things are to be fully understood by direct knowledge.
translations.mn148:34: Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises, the meeting of the three is contact, and from contact as a condition, feeling arises, whether pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
translations.mn148:22: This, monks, is the path that leads to the cessation of identity: one regards the eye as 'this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self'
translations.mn149:3: The eye, monks, is not known as it truly is, forms are not known as they truly are, eye-consciousness is not known as it truly is, eye-contact is not known as it truly is, the feeling that arises from eye-contact, whether pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, is not known as it truly is.
translations.mn149:8: For one who is attached, obsessed, and infatuated, the five clinging-aggregates in the future will increase.
translations.mn148:2: I will teach you, monks, the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with its own meaning and phrasing, entirely complete and pure, the holy life.
translations.mn149:9: The eye, monks, is seen as it really is, forms are seen as they really are, eye-consciousness is seen as it really is, eye-contact is seen as it really is, and whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition, whether pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, that too is seen as it really is. One is not infatuated with the eye, nor with forms, nor with eye-consciousness, nor with eye-contact, nor with whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition. For one who is not infatuated, the five aggregates of clinging are diminished. One's craving, which brings renewal of being, accompanied by delight and lust, and which finds delight in this and that, is abandoned. One's physical and mental energies are abandoned, one's physical and mental distresses are abandoned, one's physical and mental fevers are abandoned. One experiences physical and mental pleasure.
translations.mn19:11: Whatever a monk keeps thinking about and pondering, that becomes the inclination of his mind. If a monk keeps thinking about and pondering renunciation, he abandons sensual thoughts, develops thoughts of renunciation, and his mind inclines to thoughts of renunciation. If a monk keeps thinking about and pondering non-ill-will... non-harming, he abandons harmful thoughts, develops thoughts of non-harming, and his mind inclines to thoughts of non-harming.
translations.mn19:12: Just as, monks, in the last month of the hot season, when all the crops are ripening, a cowherd would guard his cows, standing at the root of a tree or in a open area, simply keeping an eye on them, thinking, 'These are cows.' In the same way, I simply kept an eye on these things, thinking, 'These are things.'
translations.mn19:13: My energy, monks, was aroused, unrelenting, my mindfulness was established, unmuddled, my body was calm, unaroused, my mind was concentrated, one-pointed.
translations.mn19:14: I, monks, separated from sensual desires, separated from unwholesome things, entered and remained in the first jhana, which is accompanied by thinking and pondering, and has the joy and pleasure born of seclusion.
translations.mn19:24: This, monks, was the third knowledge I achieved in the last watch of the night: the destruction of ignorance, the arising of knowledge, the disappearance of darkness, the arising of light, as happens for one who is heedful, ardent, and resolute.
translations.mn19:25: Suppose, monks, a large herd of deer were to live in a forest, and a man were to appear, desiring their harm, desiring their suffering, desiring their lack of safety. He would close off the safe path, block the safe path, open up the wrong path, and increase the wrong path. In the same way, a large herd of deer would, in the future, fall into misfortune. But suppose, monks, a man were to appear, desiring the welfare of the deer, desiring their happiness, desiring their safety. He would open up the safe path, close off the wrong path, decrease the wrong path, and increase the safe path. In the same way, a large herd of deer would, in the future, grow and thrive.
translations.mn19:26: This simile, monks, has been given to make the meaning clear. The large herd of deer, monks, is a term for living beings. The man desiring their harm, desiring their suffering, desiring their lack of safety, monks, is a term for Māra, the wicked one. The wrong path, monks, is a term for the wrong eightfold path, that is, wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration. The wrong path, monks, is a term for delight and lust. The wrong path, monks, is a term for ignorance. The man desiring their welfare, desiring their happiness, desiring their safety, monks, is a term for the Tathāgata, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one. The safe path, monks, is a term for the noble eightfold path, that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. Thus, monks, I have opened up the safe path, closed off the wrong path, decreased the wrong path, and increased the safe path.
translations.mn19:3: As I, monks, was dwelling heedful, ardent, and resolute, a sensual thought arose. I understood: 'This sensual thought has arisen in me. It leads to one's own affliction, to the affliction of others, to the affliction of both, and it obstructs wisdom, promotes vexation, and does not lead to nibbana.' When I considered, 'It leads to one's own affliction,' I understood its meaning. When I considered, 'It leads to the affliction of others,' I understood its meaning. When I considered, 'It leads to the affliction of both,' I understood its meaning. When I considered, 'It obstructs wisdom, promotes vexation, and does not lead to nibbana,' I understood its meaning. So I, monks, abandoned, removed, and eliminated the sensual thought that had arisen, and I did not tolerate it.
translations.mn19:6: Whatever a monk keeps thinking about and pondering, that becomes the inclination of his mind. If a monk keeps thinking about and pondering sensual thoughts, he abandons thoughts of renunciation, develops sensual thoughts, and his mind inclines to sensual thoughts. If a monk keeps thinking about and pondering malicious thoughts... violent thoughts, he abandons thoughts of non-violence, develops violent thoughts, and his mind inclines to violent thoughts.
translations.mn19:7: Just as, monks, in the last month of the rainy season, in the autumn, when the crops are ripening and the cowherd protects his cows, he keeps a close eye on them, hitting and prodding them with his stick, keeping them in and holding them back.  What is the reason for this?  The cowherd sees that there is a danger of death or imprisonment for them.  I, too, monks, have seen the danger of unwholesome things, the defilement of wholesome things, and the advantage of renunciation.
translations.mn19:8: As I, monks, was dwelling heedful, ardent, and resolute, the thought of renunciation arose in me.  I understood: 'This thought of renunciation has arisen in me.  It does not lead to affliction, nor to the affliction of others, nor to the affliction of both; it leads to wisdom, dispels darkness, and tends towards Nirvana.'  Whether by night or by day, monks, as I ponder and reflect on this thought, I do not see any danger arising from it.  Even if I were to ponder and reflect on it for a long time, my body would become tired, my mind would become distracted, and my mind would become restless.  So I, monks, settle my mind, calm it, unify it, and concentrate it.
translations.mn1:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Ukkaṭṭhā, in the suburb of Subhagavane, at the root of a sal tree.  There the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Monks!'  'Yes, venerable sir,' the monks replied.  The Blessed One said:
translations.mn1:10: He perceives Brahma as Brahma; having perceived Brahma as Brahma, he conceives of Brahma, he conceives of himself as Brahma, he conceives of Brahma as 'mine', he delights in Brahma.  What is the reason for this?  I say it is because he has not fully understood it.
translations.mn1:11: He perceives radiance as radiance; having perceived radiance as radiance, he conceives of radiance, he conceives of himself as radiance, he conceives of radiance as 'mine', he delights in radiance.  What is the reason for this?  I say it is because he has not fully understood it.
translations.mn1:123: If a monk, monks, is an arahant, one who has destroyed the corruptions, has lived the holy life, has done what had to be done, has laid down the burden, has attained the goal, has destroyed the fetters of becoming, and is freed by right knowledge, he too perceives earth as earth; having perceived earth as earth, he does not conceive of earth, he does not conceive of himself as earth, he does not conceive of earth as 'mine', he does not delight in earth.  What is the reason for this?  It is because his ignorance has been destroyed, and he is without delusion.
translations.mn1:13: He perceives the highest deva worlds as the highest deva worlds; having perceived the highest deva worlds as the highest deva worlds, he conceives of the highest deva worlds, he conceives of himself as the highest deva worlds, he conceives of the highest deva worlds as 'mine', he delights in the highest deva worlds.  What is the reason for this?  I say it is because he has not fully understood it.
translations.mn1:14: He perceives the conqueror as the conqueror; having perceived the conqueror as the conqueror, he conceives of the conqueror, he conceives of himself as the conqueror, he conceives of the conqueror as 'mine', he delights in the conqueror.  What is the reason for this?  I say it is because he has not fully understood it.
translations.mn1:147: The Tathagata, too, monks, who is an arahant and a fully enlightened Buddha, perceives earth as earth; having perceived earth as earth, he does not conceive of earth, he does not conceive of himself as earth, he does not conceive of earth as 'mine', he does not delight in earth.  What is the reason for this?  It is because the Tathagata has fully understood it.
translations.mn1:171: The Tathagata, too, monks, who is an arahant and a fully enlightened Buddha, perceives earth as earth; having perceived earth as earth, he does not conceive of earth, he does not conceive of himself as earth, he does not conceive of earth as 'mine', he does not delight in earth.  What is the reason for this?  It is because he knows that delight is the root of suffering, and that the origin of suffering is birth, existence, and decay.  Therefore, monks, I say that the Tathagata, having destroyed all cravings, having abandoned all defilements, has attained the supreme enlightenment.
translations.mn1:19: He perceives what is seen as what is seen; having perceived what is seen as what is seen, he conceives of what is seen, he conceives of himself as what is seen, he conceives of what is seen as 'mine', he delights in what is seen.  What is the reason for this?  I say it is because he has not fully understood it.
translations.mn1:2: I shall teach you, monks, the root of all things.  Listen and pay attention, I shall speak.
translations.mn1:20: He perceives what is heard as what is heard; having perceived what is heard as what is heard, he conceives of what is heard, he conceives of himself as what is heard, he conceives of what is heard as 'mine', he delights in what is heard.  What is the reason for this?  I say it is because he has not fully understood it.
translations.mn1:22: He perceives what is known as what is known; having perceived what is known as what is known, he conceives of what is known, he conceives of himself as what is known, he conceives of what is known as 'mine', he delights in what is known.  What is the reason for this?  I say it is because he has not fully understood it.
translations.mn1:23: He perceives unity as unity; having perceived unity as unity, he conceives of unity, he conceives of himself as unity, he conceives of unity as 'mine', he delights in unity.  What is the reason for this?  I say it is because he has not fully understood it.
translations.mn1:24: He perceives diversity as diversity; having perceived diversity as diversity, he conceives of diversity, he conceives of himself as diversity, he conceives of diversity as 'mine', he delights in diversity.  What is the reason for this?  I say it is because he has not fully understood it.
translations.mn1:25: He perceives all as all; having perceived all as all, he conceives of all, he conceives of himself as all, he conceives of all as 'mine', he delights in all.  What is the reason for this?  I say it is because he has not fully understood it.
translations.mn1:27: If a monk, monks, is a trainee, one who has not yet reached the goal, but is striving for the highest security from bondage, he too perceives earth as earth; having perceived earth as earth, he does not conceive of earth, he does not conceive of himself as earth, he does not conceive of earth as 'mine', he does not delight in earth.  What is the reason for this?  It is because it should be fully understood by him.
translations.mn1:3: Here, monks, an untaught ordinary person who has not seen the noble ones, is not proficient in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and is not trained in the Dhamma of the noble ones — perceives earth as earth; having perceived earth as earth, he conceives earth, he conceives in earth, he conceives from earth, he conceives earth as 'mine', he delights in earth. What is the reason for this? I say it is because he has not fully understood it.
translations.mn1:4: He perceives water as water; having perceived water as water, he conceives water, he conceives in water, he conceives from water, he conceives water as 'mine', he delights in water. What is the reason for this? I say it is because he has not fully understood it.
translations.mn1:5: He perceives fire as fire; having perceived fire as fire, he conceives fire, he conceives in fire, he conceives from fire, he conceives fire as 'mine', he delights in fire. What is the reason for this? I say it is because he has not fully understood it.
translations.mn1:51: And, monks, even a monk who is an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge — he too perceives earth as earth; having perceived earth as earth, he does not conceive earth, he does not conceive in earth, he does not conceive from earth, he does not conceive earth as 'mine', he does not delight in earth. What is the reason for this? I say it is because he has fully understood it.
translations.mn1:7: He perceives the base of infinite space as the base of infinite space; having perceived the base of infinite space as the base of infinite space, he conceives the base of infinite space, he conceives in the base of infinite space, he conceives from the base of infinite space, he conceives the base of infinite space as 'mine', he delights in the base of infinite space. What is the reason for this? I say it is because he has not fully understood it.
translations.mn1:8: He perceives the base of nothingness as the base of nothingness; having perceived the base of nothingness as the base of nothingness, he conceives the base of nothingness, he conceives in the base of nothingness, he conceives from the base of nothingness, he conceives the base of nothingness as 'mine', he delights in the base of nothingness. What is the reason for this? I say it is because he has not fully understood it.
translations.mn1:9: He perceives the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; having perceived the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he conceives the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he conceives in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he conceives from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he conceives the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as 'mine', he delights in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. What is the reason for this? I say it is because he has not fully understood it.
translations.mn20:2: Monks, a monk who is intent on the mind should from time to time give attention to five signs. What are the five?
translations.mn22:12: Therefore, monks, you should understand the meaning of what I have said, and you should remember it accordingly. If you do not understand the meaning of what I have said, you should ask me or the other wise monks.
translations.mn22:14: I have taught you the Dhamma like a raft, monks, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping. You should let go even of the Dhamma, not to mention non-Dhamma.
translations.mn22:18: When this was said, a certain monk asked the Blessed One: 'Can there be anxiety about something that does not exist outside?' 'There can be, monk', the Blessed One replied. 'Here, a monk thinks:
translations.mn22:25: Is it the case, monks, that when there is a self, one perceives ‘my self’? “Yes, venerable sir.” Is it the case, monks, that when there is what belongs to a self, one perceives ‘my self’? “Yes, venerable sir.” But when, monks, both self and what belongs to a self are not found in truth and reality, and there is the view ‘that is the world, that is the self, I will be permanent, stable, eternal, unchanging after death, the same for all eternity’—is this not, monks, a complete and perfect foolishness? “It is, venerable sir, a complete and perfect foolishness.”
translations.mn22:20: ‘Can there be, venerable sir, agitation about what is not internal?’ ‘There can, monks’, the Blessed One said. Here, a certain monk has this view: ‘that is the world, that is the self, I will be permanent, stable, eternal, unchanging after death, the same for all eternity’. He hears the teaching of the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, which is for the abandoning of all views, the relinquishing of all bases for views, the removal of all latent tendencies, the calming of all mental formations, the abandoning of all attachments, the destruction of craving, the fading away of passion, the cessation of suffering, the realization of nibbāna. He thinks: ‘I will be annihilated, I will perish, I will no longer exist’. He grieves, laments, and wails, and falls into confusion. Thus, monks, there can be agitation about what is not internal.”
translations.mn22:23: Monks, you should abandon that view of self, by abandoning which view of self sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise. Do you see, monks, that view of self, by abandoning which view of self sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise? “We do not, venerable sir.” “Good, monks. I too do not see that view of self, by abandoning which view of self sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise.”
translations.mn22:19: ‘But can there be, venerable sir, no agitation about what is external?’ ‘There can, monks’, the Blessed One said. Here, a certain monk does not have this view: ‘it is mine, it is not mine; it will be mine, I do not have it’. He does not grieve, lament, or wail, and he does not fall into confusion. Thus, monks, there can be no agitation about what is external.”
translations.mn22:24: Monks, you should abandon that dependence on views, by abandoning which dependence on views sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise. Do you see, monks, that dependence on views, by abandoning which dependence on views sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise? “We do not, venerable sir.” “Good, monks. I too do not see that dependence on views, by abandoning which dependence on views sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise.”
translations.mn22:27: Therefore, monks, whatever form, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, all form should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'  Whatever feeling...  Whatever perception...  Whatever volitional formations...  Whatever consciousness, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, all consciousness should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'
translations.mn22:28: Seeing thus, monks, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, disenchanted with consciousness,
translations.mn22:29: being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate, through dispassion he is liberated, and in the liberated one there is the knowledge: 'I am liberated.'  'Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming back to this state.'
translations.mn22:30: This, monks, is called a monk who has removed the crossbar, who has filled in the moat, who has broken the pillar, who has removed the door bolt, who has a noble vision, who has a noble understanding, and who is freed from all sensual pleasures.
translations.mn22:31: And how, monks, is a monk one who has removed the crossbar?  Here, monks, a monk's ignorance is abandoned, its root is cut off, it is like a palm tree that has been destroyed, it will not grow again, and it will not arise in the future.  In this way, monks, a monk is one who has removed the crossbar.
translations.mn22:32: And how, monks, is a monk one who has filled in the moat?  Here, monks, a monk's rebirth-producing and corruption-producing tendencies are abandoned, their root is cut off, they are like a palm tree that has been destroyed, they will not grow again, and they will not arise in the future.  In this way, monks, a monk is one who has filled in the moat.
translations.mn22:33: And how, monks, is a monk one who has broken the pillar?  Here, monks, a monk's craving is abandoned, its root is cut off, it is like a palm tree that has been destroyed, it will not grow again, and it will not arise in the future.  In this way, monks, a monk is one who has broken the pillar.
translations.mn22:34: And how, monks, is a monk one who has removed the door bolt?  Here, monks, a monk's five lower fetters are abandoned, their root is cut off, they are like a palm tree that has been destroyed, they will not grow again, and they will not arise in the future.  In this way, monks, a monk is one who has removed the door bolt.
translations.mn22:35: And how, monks, is a monk one who has a noble vision, who has a noble understanding, and who is freed from all sensual pleasures?  Here, monks, a monk's 'I am' conceit is abandoned, its root is cut off, it is like a palm tree that has been destroyed, it will not grow again, and it will not arise in the future.  In this way, monks, a monk is one who has a noble vision, who has a noble understanding, and who is freed from all sensual pleasures.
translations.mn22:38: If, monks, others honor, respect, and venerate the Tathagata, the Tathagata does not feel joy, pleasure, or satisfaction.  If, monks, others honor, respect, and venerate the Tathagata, the Tathagata thinks: 'Whatever they do to me, they do to what has already been fully understood.'
translations.mn22:39: Therefore, monks, if others abuse, scold, and harass you, you should not feel angry, resentful, or displeased.  Therefore, monks, if others honor, respect, and venerate you, you should not feel joy, pleasure, or satisfaction.  Therefore, monks, if others honor, respect, and venerate you, you should think: 'Whatever they do to me, they do to what has already been fully understood.'
translations.mn22:40: Therefore, monks, abandon what is not yours;  abandoning what is not yours will be for your long-term benefit and happiness.
translations.mn22:42: The Dhamma has been well-expounded by me, monks, revealed, opened, and shown;  it is like a ladder with the rungs cut off.  In the Dhamma that has been well-expounded by me, revealed, opened, and shown, those monks who are arahants, whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, who have done what had to be done, who have laid down the burden, who have achieved their goal, who are liberated by wisdom, who are fully freed, there is no more progress to be made.
translations.mn22:43: The Dhamma has been well-expounded by me, monks, revealed, opened, and shown;  it is like a ladder with the rungs cut off.  In the Dhamma that has been well-expounded by me, revealed, opened, and shown, those monks who have abandoned the five lower fetters, all of them are stream-enterers, they will not be reborn, and they will not be subject to the cycle of suffering.
translations.mn22:44: The Dhamma has been well-expounded by me, monks, revealed, opened, and shown;  it is like a ladder with the rungs cut off.  In the Dhamma that has been well-expounded by me, revealed, opened, and shown, those monks who have abandoned the three fetters, greed, hatred, and delusion, all of them are once-returners, they will only return to this world once and then make an end of suffering.
translations.mn22:45: The Dhamma has been well-expounded by me, monks, revealed, opened, and shown;  it is like a ladder with the rungs cut off.  In the Dhamma that has been well-expounded by me, revealed, opened, and shown, those monks who have abandoned the three fetters, all of them are stream-enterers, they are not subject to falling, and they are bound for enlightenment.
translations.mn22:46: The Dhamma has been well-expounded by me, monks, revealed, opened, and shown;  it is like a ladder with the rungs cut off.  In the Dhamma that has been well-expounded by me, revealed, opened, and shown, those monks who follow the Dhamma, who follow faith, all of them are bound for enlightenment.
translations.mn22:6: For what reason, foolish man, do you not understand that I have taught the Dhamma in many ways, that I have spoken of the things that are obstacles, that I have spoken of the things that are obstacles? And yet you are not devoted to giving up obstacles. I have spoken of sensual pleasures as unattractive, as causing much suffering and distress, and as having much greater drawbacks. I have spoken of sensual pleasures as being like a skeleton ... like flesh ... like a grass torch ... like a charcoal pit ... like a dream ... like borrowed goods ... like a fruit tree ... like a sword stake ... like a snake's head ... like a poisonous snake, as causing much suffering and distress, and as having much greater drawbacks. But you, foolish man, through your own misdeed, you revile us and you harm yourself, and you accumulate much demerit. This, foolish man, will be for your long-term harm and suffering.
translations.mn22:7: Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'What do you think, monks? Is this monk Ariṭṭha, who is prone to giving in to his instincts, able to stand firm in this Dhamma and Vinaya?' 'Let it be, sir; no, sir.' When this was said, the monk Ariṭṭha, who was prone to giving in to his instincts, sat silent, embarrassed, with his shoulders hunched and his head down, staring at the ground, unable to respond. Then the Blessed One, knowing that the monk Ariṭṭha was sitting silent, embarrassed, with his shoulders hunched and his head down, staring at the ground, unable to respond, said to him: 'You will be known, foolish man, by this evil and corrupt view of yours. I will question the monks about this.'
translations.mn22:9: There is no possibility, monks, of sensual desire being given up by someone who has not gone beyond sensual desire, beyond the perception of sensual desire, beyond the thoughts of sensual desire.
translations.mn26:10: And what, monks, is the source of suffering? A son is a source of suffering, a wife is a source of suffering, a servant is a source of suffering, a thief is a source of suffering, an enemy is a source of suffering. These are the sources of suffering, the acquisitions that are suffering. A person who is bound by these sources of suffering, who is infatuated with them, who is attached to them, seeks only for sources of suffering.
translations.mn26:11: And what, monks, is the source of corruption? A son is a source of corruption, a wife is a source of corruption, a servant is a source of corruption, a thief is a source of corruption, an enemy is a source of corruption, gold and silver are sources of corruption. These are the sources of corruption, the acquisitions that are corruption. A person who is bound by these sources of corruption, who is infatuated with them, who is attached to them, seeks only for sources of corruption. This, monks, is an unwise search.
translations.mn26:13: I, too, monks, before my enlightenment, when I was not yet enlightened and was still a bodhisattva, used to search for the source of birth, used to search for the source of aging, used to search for the source of illness, used to search for the source of death, used to search for the source of suffering, used to search for the source of corruption, being myself subject to birth, aging, illness, death, suffering, and corruption. Then it occurred to me: 'Why do I, being myself subject to birth, search for the source of birth? Why do I, being myself subject to aging, search for the source of aging? ... Why do I, being myself subject to corruption, search for the source of corruption? What if I, being myself subject to birth, were to search for the unborn, the unexcelled security from bondage, nibbāna, having known the danger in birth? ... What if I, being myself subject to corruption, were to search for the uncorrupted, the unexcelled security from bondage, nibbāna, having known the danger in corruption?'
translations.mn26:14: At that time, monks, I was a young man, with a wealth of black hair, and I had a long life ahead of me. I was endowed with a good physique, and my parents, who were not wanting me to leave, were tearful and grieving. I shaved off my hair and beard, put on yellow robes, and went forth from home into homelessness.
translations.mn26:17: I, monks, searching for the unsurpassed, safe-from-bondage state, wandered from place to place in the Magadha region. I came to a delightful place, with a beautiful park and a lovely grove, and a river with clear water, pleasant and with a suitable fording place, and a village nearby for alms. Then it occurred to me: 'This is a delightful place, with a beautiful park and a lovely grove, and a river with clear water, pleasant and with a suitable fording place, and a village nearby for alms. It is suitable for a clansman who is intent on striving.' So I sat down there, thinking: 'This is suitable for striving.'
translations.mn26:21: Then, monks, having known the brahman's invitation and having known the kindness towards beings, I surveyed the world with the buddha-eye. I saw beings with little dust in their eyes, with much dust in their eyes, with sharp faculties, with dull faculties, with good qualities, with bad qualities, with docile qualities, with stubborn qualities, some who saw the danger in the next world and were afraid of it, and some who did not see the danger in the next world and were not afraid of it. Just as in a pond of water, some lotus flowers are born in the water, grow in the water, and are not soiled by the water, some are born in the water, grow in the water, and are soiled by the water, and some are born in the water, grow in the water, and rise above the water, untouched by it; in the same way, I saw beings with little dust in their eyes, with much dust in their eyes, with sharp faculties, with dull faculties, with good qualities, with bad qualities, with docile qualities, with stubborn qualities, some who saw the danger in the next world and were afraid of it, and some who did not see the danger in the next world and were not afraid of it. Then, monks, I spoke to the brahman Sahampati in verse: 'The doors to the deathless are open for those who hear, let them release their faith; I do not speak to those with violent thoughts, the supreme dhamma is taught to humans and brahmans.' Then, monks, the brahman Sahampati, having said 'I have been given the opportunity by the Blessed One to hear the teaching of the dhamma', bowed to me, circled around me, and disappeared.
translations.mn26:25: A certain wanderer, Upaka, saw me on the road between Gaya and the Bodhi tree, and having seen me, he said: 'Your faculties are clear, your complexion is pure and bright. Under whom have you lived as an ascetic, who is your teacher, and whose dhamma do you like?' When this was said, I replied to the wanderer Upaka in verse: 'I am the conqueror of all, I am all-knowing, I am not dependent on anyone; I have destroyed craving, I am liberated by my own knowledge, I am one who has attained. I do not have a teacher, I do not have an equal, I am the highest in the world, I am the teacher, I am the one who has attained the highest. I will roll the wheel of dhamma in the city of Kasi, I will beat the drum of the deathless in the blind world.' 'As you say, friend, you are the conqueror of the infinite.' 'Those who have attained the destruction of the corruptions are the conquerors, I have conquered the evil dhammas, therefore I am the conqueror', I said. When this was said, the wanderer Upaka said 'good luck to you, friend' and, shaking his head, took a bypath and left.
translations.mn26:26: Then, monks, I wandered by stages and arrived at the deer park in Isipatana near Benares, where the group of five monks were living. The group of five monks saw me coming from afar and, having seen me, they discussed among themselves: 'This ascetic Gotama is coming, he is living a life of abundance, he is devoted to abundance, he is not worthy of respect, he should not be greeted, his bowl and robes should not be accepted, and a seat should not be prepared for him, unless he wishes to sit.' As I approached, the group of five monks were unable to greet me in the usual way. Some of them greeted me, some offered me my bowl and robes, and some prepared a seat for me. They also addressed me by name and as 'friend'.
translations.mn26:28: When this was said, I said to the group of five monks: 'Do you recognize me as having lived like this before?' 'No, venerable sir.' 'I am the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one. Please listen, I will teach you the dhamma, I have attained the deathless. If you practice as instructed, you will soon realize, for the sake of which sons of good families leave their homes and become homeless, the highest goal of the holy life, you will see it for yourselves, you will attain it, and you will live having realized it.'
translations.mn26:29: I was unable to instruct the group of five monks. I advised two of the monks, and the other three went for alms. Whatever the three monks brought back from their alms round, the six of them would eat. I also advised those three monks, and two of them went for alms. Whatever the two monks brought back from their alms round, the six of them would eat.
translations.mn26:30: Then, monks, the group of five monks, being advised and instructed by me, seeing the danger in birth and seeking the unborn, the highest security from bondage, nibbana, they realized the unborn, the highest security from bondage, nibbana. Seeing the danger in aging and seeking the ageless, the highest security from bondage, nibbana, they realized the ageless, the highest security from bondage, nibbana. Seeing the danger in illness and seeking the illness-free, the highest security from bondage, nibbana, they realized the illness-free, the highest security from bondage, nibbana. Seeing the danger in death and seeking the deathless, the highest security from bondage, nibbana, they realized the deathless, the highest security from bondage, nibbana. Seeing the danger in sorrow and seeking the sorrow-free, the highest security from bondage, nibbana, they realized the sorrow-free, the highest security from bondage, nibbana. Seeing the danger in defilement and seeking the undefiled, the highest security from bondage, nibbana, they realized the undefiled, the highest security from bondage, nibbana. And their knowledge and vision arose: 'Our liberation is unshakable, this is our last birth, there will be no further becoming.'
translations.mn26:31: Monks, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure. Which five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, and connected with sensual pleasure; sounds cognizable by the ear... aromas cognizable by the nose... flavors cognizable by the tongue... tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, and connected with sensual pleasure. These, monks, are the five strands of sensual pleasure.
translations.mn26:34: Just as a wilderness path, monks, is made by the repeated treading of many feet, and a cart path is made by the repeated passing of many carts, so too, a monk, having separated himself from sensual pleasures, having separated himself from unwholesome states, enters and remains in the first jhana, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and filled with joy and pleasure born of seclusion. This, monks, is called a monk who has blinded Māra, who has destroyed the eye of Māra, who has gone beyond the range of Māra, who has gone beyond the sight of the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:35: Again, monks, a monk, having surpassed the thought and examination of ideas, enters and remains in the second jhana, which is accompanied by internal confidence and unification of mind, and is without thought and examination, and is filled with joy and pleasure born of concentration. This, monks, is called... the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:36: Again, monks, a monk, having surpassed joy, dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences pleasure with the body, and enters and remains in the third jhana, which the noble ones declare as 'equanimous, mindful, and dwelling in pleasure'. This, monks, is called... the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:37: Again, monks, a monk, having surpassed pleasure and pain, and having previously abandoned both happiness and sadness, enters and remains in the fourth jhana, which is without pleasure or pain, and is accompanied by equanimity and mindfulness. This, monks, is called... the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:38: Again, monks, a monk, having surpassed all perception of forms, and having terminated the perception of sensory reactions, and having ceased the perception of diversity, thinks 'space is infinite' and enters and remains in the base of infinite space. This, monks, is called... the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:39: Again, monks, a monk, having surpassed the base of infinite space, thinks 'consciousness is infinite' and enters and remains in the base of infinite consciousness. This, monks, is called... the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:4: Then the Blessed One went to the park of the brahmin Rammaka. At that time, many monks were sitting in the park of the brahmin Rammaka, engaged in a discussion on the Dhamma. The Blessed One stood outside the door, waiting for the discussion to end. When the discussion had ended, the Blessed One cleared his throat and knocked on the door. The monks opened the door for the Blessed One. The Blessed One entered the park of the brahmin Rammaka and sat down on a prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Monks, what were you discussing when I arrived? What was the subject of your conversation?' 'We were discussing the Dhamma, sir, and we were waiting for the Blessed One to arrive.' 'Good, monks. This is fitting for you, sons of good families, who have gone forth from home to homelessness, to sit together and discuss the Dhamma. When you are gathered together, there are two things to do: either discuss the Dhamma or observe noble silence.'
translations.mn26:40: Again, monks, a monk, having surpassed the base of infinite consciousness, thinks 'there is nothing' and enters and remains in the base of nothingness. This, monks, is called... the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:41: Again, monks, a monk, having surpassed the base of nothingness, enters and remains in the base of neither perception nor non-perception. This, monks, is called... the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:5: Monks, there are two kinds of search: the noble search and the ignoble search. And what, monks, is the ignoble search? Here, monks, someone who is subject to birth searches for what is subject to birth; someone who is subject to aging searches for what is subject to aging; someone who is subject to illness searches for what is subject to illness; someone who is subject to death searches for what is subject to death; someone who is subject to sorrow searches for what is subject to sorrow; someone who is subject to defilement searches for what is subject to defilement.
translations.mn26:6: And what, monks, is the search for what is subject to birth? The search for sons and daughters, the search for slaves and servants, the search for goats and sheep, the search for chickens and pigs, the search for elephants and cattle, the search for gold and silver. These, monks, are the acquisitions that are subject to birth. A person who is subject to birth, having acquired these things, is bound to them, and having become bound to them, searches for what is subject to birth.
translations.mn27:12: A householder or a householder's son or someone from another family hears that Dhamma. Having heard that Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata. He thinks to himself: 'The household life is confining and dusty, and the life of a homeless wanderer is open and free. It is not easy for one living at home to lead a holy life that is totally perfect and pure, like a polished shell. What if I were to shave my head and beard, put on the yellow robes, and go forth from home to homelessness?' Later, he abandons a small or large amount of wealth, and a small or large circle of relatives, shaves his head and beard, puts on the yellow robes, and goes forth from home to homelessness.
translations.mn27:13: Having gone forth, a monk lives having renounced the killing of living creatures. With rod and sword laid aside, he is conscientious, full of sympathy, and takes care to do no harm to any living creatures. He lives having renounced taking what is not given, and takes only what is given. He is clean-handed, and takes only what is given, and takes only what is given with a clean hand. Having renounced uncelibacy, he lives a celibate life, aloof, and refrains from sexual intercourse, the common way of the world. Having renounced false speech, he speaks the truth, and is trustworthy and reliable, and does not deceive the world. Having renounced malicious speech, he does not repeat what he has heard to cause division, and does not create divisions. He brings people together, and speaks words that are conciliatory and bring people together, words that are pleasant to hear, and loveable, and that promote unity among the people. Having renounced harsh speech, he speaks words that are gentle, pleasing to the ear, and loveable, and that go to the heart. Having renounced idle chatter, he speaks at the right time, and speaks words that are valuable, and that are connected with the Dhamma. He abstains from injuring seeds and plants, and takes only one meal a day, and eats in the evening. He abstains from watching dancing and other shows, and from using perfumes and adornments. He sleeps on a low bed, and abstains from accepting gold and silver, and from accepting raw grain or raw meat, and from accepting women or girls, and from accepting bondservants or goats or sheep, and from accepting fowl or pigs, and from accepting elephants or cattle or horses, and from accepting fields or land. He abstains from acting as a messenger or as an emissary, and from buying and selling, and from using false weights and measures, and from cheating and deceiving.
translations.mn27:14: He is content with his robes, his almsfood, and his lodgings. Just as a bird takes flight with its wings, and leaves its nest, so a monk is content with his robes, his almsfood, and his lodgings, and goes on his way. He takes pleasure in his own practice of the Dhamma, and is free from remorse.
translations.mn27:15: When he sees a form with his eye, he does not become entranced by its general features or its details. He guards his eye, and does not allow unwholesome states to arise. When he hears a sound with his ear, when he smells an odor with his nose, when he tastes a flavor with his tongue, when he feels a tactile sensation with his body, when he knows a mental phenomenon with his mind, he does not become entranced by its general features or its details. He guards his mind, and does not allow unwholesome states to arise. He takes pleasure in his own practice of the Dhamma, and is free from remorse.
translations.mn27:16: He acts with mindfulness when going forward or backward, when looking ahead or around, when bending or stretching, when wearing his robes or carrying his bowl, when eating or drinking, when urinating or defecating, when walking or standing or sitting or lying down, when speaking or remaining silent.
translations.mn27:17: With this noble moral practice, this noble contentment, this noble restraint of the senses, and this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension, he resorts to a secluded resting place, such as a forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a glade, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.
translations.mn27:18: After his meal, he sits down, crossing his legs, and with his body straight, and establishes mindfulness in front of him. He gives up covetousness, and with a mind free from covetousness, he purifies his mind. He gives up ill-will and hatred, and with a mind free from ill-will, he purifies his mind. He gives up dullness and drowsiness, and with a mind free from dullness and drowsiness, he purifies his mind. He gives up restlessness and worry, and with a mind free from restlessness and worry, he purifies his mind. He gives up doubt, and with a mind free from doubt, he purifies his mind.
translations.mn27:19: Having given up these five hindrances, and having put aside the corruptions of the mind, he lives having removed himself from sensual desires, and from unwholesome states, and with initial and sustained application of the mind, and with joy and pleasure born of seclusion, he enters the first jhana. This, brahmin, is called the Tathagata's path, the Tathagata's practice, the Tathagata's way. But a noble disciple does not yet reach the end: 'The Blessed One is the fully awakened one, the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, the Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing well.'
translations.mn27:2: Now at that time the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi was driving out of Sāvatthī in a fully equipped carriage to go to his own park for the day. He saw the wanderer Pilotika coming from a distance. Having seen him, he said to Pilotika: 'From where are you coming, good Vacchāyana, so early in the morning?' 'I am coming, sir, from the presence of the ascetic Gotama.' 'What does the good Vacchāyana think about the ascetic Gotama's wisdom? Does he consider him wise?' 'Who am I, sir, to know the ascetic Gotama's wisdom? Only one like him could know it.' 'The good Vacchāyana certainly praises the ascetic Gotama with high praise.' 'Who am I, sir, to praise the ascetic Gotama? The ascetic Gotama is esteemed by the people, the best of gods and men.' 'What, good Vacchāyana, has the ascetic Gotama done to deserve such esteem?'
translations.mn27:20: Again, a monk, with the subsiding of thinking and pondering, enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and singleness of mind without thinking and pondering, and has joy and happiness born of concentration. This, too, is called ... a well-taught Bhagavā's disciple.
translations.mn27:21: Again, a monk, with the fading away of joy, dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body, and enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: 'He dwells happily with equanimity and mindfulness.' This, too, is called ... a well-taught Bhagavā's disciple.
translations.mn27:22: Again, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and sadness, enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is without pleasure and pain, and has pure equanimity and mindfulness. This is called the Tathāgata's footstep, the Tathāgata's way, the Tathāgata's path. But a noble disciple has not yet reached the end: 'The Blessed One is the fully awakened one, the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, the Blessed One's disciple community is well-practiced.'
translations.mn27:3: Just as a skilled elephant hunter would enter an elephant forest, and he would see a large elephant footprint, long from one end to the other and broad from one side to the other. He would come to the conclusion: 'This is a big bull elephant.' In the same way, I, sir, have seen the four factors in the ascetic Gotama, and I have come to the conclusion: 'The Blessed One is the fully awakened one, the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, the Blessed One's disciple community is well-practiced.'
translations.mn27:4: What are the four factors? Here, sir, I see some aristocrats who are wise, clever, and experienced in controversy and debate, who wander about breaking the syllogisms of others with their own syllogisms. They hear: 'The ascetic Gotama will come to a certain village or town.' They plan a question: 'We will approach the ascetic Gotama and ask him this question. If he answers us like this, we will argue with him like this. If he answers us like that, we will argue with him like that.' They hear: 'The ascetic Gotama has come to a certain village or town.' They approach the ascetic Gotama. The ascetic Gotama instructs them, rouses them, and gladdens them with a Dhamma talk. Those instructed, roused, and gladdened by the ascetic Gotama do not ask him a question or argue with him. They become his disciples. When I, sir, saw the first factor in the ascetic Gotama, I came to the conclusion: 'The Blessed One is the fully awakened one, the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, the Blessed One's disciple community is well-practiced.'
translations.mn27:9: Then the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged greetings, he sat down at one side. As he was sitting down, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi told the Blessed One the entire conversation he had with the wanderer Pilotika. The Blessed One said to the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi: 'The elephant footprint simile is not yet fully explained. But, brahmin, listen to how the elephant footprint simile is fully explained, and pay attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, sir,' the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.mn28:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. There the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the monks: 'Friends, monks.' 'Friends,' the monks replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said:
translations.mn28:10: For a monk who recollects the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha in this way, his mindfulness based on equanimity does not become established. He feels a sense of urgency and anxiety: 'I have not gained what I should have, I have not achieved what I should have achieved, it is not enough for me, I have not attained what I should have attained, when I recollect the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha in this way and my mindfulness based on equanimity does not become established.' Just as a dog, on seeing a butcher, feels a sense of urgency and anxiety, so too, for a monk who recollects the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha in this way, and his mindfulness based on equanimity does not become established, he feels a sense of urgency and anxiety: 'I have not gained what I should have, I have not achieved what I should have achieved, it is not enough for me, I have not attained what I should have attained, when I recollect the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha in this way and my mindfulness based on equanimity does not become established.' But for a monk who recollects the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha in this way, and his mindfulness based on equanimity becomes established, he is satisfied with that. To this extent, a monk's efforts are fruitful.
translations.mn28:12: There comes a time, friend, when the external water element is stirred up. It sweeps away a village, a town, a city, a district, and a country. There comes a time when the great ocean, a hundred yojanas wide, two hundred yojanas wide, three hundred yojanas wide, four hundred yojanas wide, and five hundred yojanas wide, is stirred up. There comes a time when the great ocean is filled with water up to the height of seven palm trees, six palm trees, five palm trees, four palm trees, three palm trees, two palm trees, and one palm tree. There comes a time when the great ocean is filled with water up to the height of seven porises, six porises, five porises, four porises, three porises, two porises, and one porise. There comes a time when the great ocean is filled with water up to the height of a man's head, his neck, his waist, his knees, and his ankles. There comes a time when the great ocean is not even knee-deep. And it is in this external water element that the impermanence, the suffering, the emptiness, and the non-self of this great body will be seen.
translations.mn28:13: What is there to be known or seen in this foul body, which is subject to craving, that one could think: 'I am this' or 'this is mine'?
translations.mn28:14: For a monk who recollects the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha in this way, and his mindfulness based on equanimity becomes established, he is satisfied with that.
translations.mn28:17: There comes a time, friend, when the external fire element is stirred up. It burns a village, a town, a city, a district, and a country. It burns a fertile land, a wilderness, a rocky land, a land with water, and a beautiful land, and it is extinguished without leaving any fuel. There comes a time when people search for a place to cook even a single pot of food. And it is in this external fire element that the impermanence, the suffering, the emptiness, and the non-self of this great body will be seen. What is there to be known or seen in this foul body, which is subject to craving, that one could think: 'I am this' or 'this is mine'?
translations.mn28:18-20: But if one does not find satisfaction in that, for a monk who recollects the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha in this way, and his mindfulness based on equanimity becomes established, he is satisfied with that. To this extent, a monk's efforts are fruitful.
translations.mn28:2: Just as all the footprints of living beings that walk on land are contained within the footprint of the elephant, which is considered the largest of them, so too, all wholesome things are contained within the Four Noble Truths. What are the Four Noble Truths? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn28:22: There comes a time, friend, when the external wind element is stirred up. It sweeps away a village, a town, a city, a district, and a country. There comes a time when, in the last month of the hot season, people search for a breeze even with a fan, and they do not want to sit in the shade. And it is in this external wind element that the impermanence, the suffering, the emptiness, and the non-self of this great body will be seen. What is there to be known or seen in this foul body, which is subject to craving, that one could think: 'I am this' or 'this is mine'? But if one does not find satisfaction in that,
translations.mn28:23: If others abuse, insult, and harass him, he understands: 'This painful feeling that has arisen is born of contact.' He sees that it is impermanent, that the feeling is impermanent, the perception is impermanent, the mental formations are impermanent, and the consciousness is impermanent. His mind leaps up, is pleased, and is satisfied and delighted with the dhātu, the elements.
translations.mn28:24: If, friend, others abuse, revile, and scold a bhikkhu with unwelcome, unpleasant, and unpleasing words, even with blows of the fist, sticks, and swords. He understands thus: ‘This body is such that blows with the fist, sticks, and swords, and even a shower of arrows, affect it. My energy will be aroused, mindfulness will be established, and my body will be tranquil and unrepelled, my mind will be concentrated and one-pointed. Let blows with the fist, sticks, and swords, and even a shower of arrows affect this body. This is the practice taught by the Buddhas.’
translations.mn28:26: Just as, friend, space is enclosed by timber and clay and rocks and mortar, and it comes to be called ‘house’; so too, friend, space is enclosed by bone and sinew and flesh and skin, and it comes to be called ‘form’.
translations.mn28:27: If, friend, the internal eye is intact and external forms do not come into its range, and there is no corresponding engagement, then there is no manifestation of consciousness. If the internal eye is intact and external forms do come into its range, but there is no corresponding engagement, then there is no manifestation of consciousness. But when the internal eye is intact and external forms come into its range, and there is a corresponding engagement, then there is a manifestation of consciousness.
translations.mn28:28: The form of one who has come to be is included in the form clinging-aggregate; the feeling of one who has come to be is included in the feeling clinging-aggregate; the perception of one who has come to be is included in the perception clinging-aggregate; the volitional formations of one who has come to be are included in the volitional formations clinging-aggregate; the consciousness of one who has come to be is included in the consciousness clinging-aggregate. He understands thus: ‘It is in this way that the inclusion, the coming together, the convergence of these five clinging-aggregates is to be understood.’ It has been said by the Blessed One: ‘He who sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma; he who sees the Dhamma sees dependent origination.’ And these five clinging-aggregates are dependently arisen.
translations.mn28:3: And what, friend, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering; not getting what one wants is suffering; in short, the five clinging-aggregates are suffering. And what, friend, are the five clinging-aggregates? They are: form clinging-aggregate, feeling clinging-aggregate, perception clinging-aggregate, volitional formations clinging-aggregate, and consciousness clinging-aggregate.
translations.mn28:37: The mind is intact, and external phenomena do not come into its range, and there is no corresponding engagement, then there is no manifestation of consciousness.
translations.mn28:7: There is a time, friend, when the external water element is disturbed. At that time the external earth element is tranquil. The impermanence, the suffering, and the change of the external earth element can be known. What has this large body, which is the basis of the clinging to the notion ‘I am,’ to do with it? It is not worth considering.
translations.mn29:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Rājagaha, on Mount Gijjhakūṭa, not long after Devadatta’s departure.
translations.mn29:3: Here, monks, some clansman goes forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness, thinking: ‘I am oppressed by birth, aging, and death, by sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; I am oppressed by suffering, afflicted by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering and sorrow can be known.’
translations.mn2:10: And what, monks, are the things that should not be attended to, that one should not attend to? When one attends to things that should not be attended to, unarisen sensual desire arises, and arisen sensual desire increases; unarisen desire for existence arises, and arisen desire for existence increases; unarisen ignorance arises, and arisen ignorance increases. These are the things that should not be attended to, that one should not attend to. And what, monks, are the things that should be attended to, that one should attend to? When one attends to things that should be attended to, unarisen sensual desire does not arise, and arisen sensual desire is abandoned; unarisen desire for existence does not arise, and arisen desire for existence is abandoned; unarisen ignorance does not arise, and arisen ignorance is abandoned. For one who attends to things that should not be attended to and does not attend to things that should be attended to, unarisen corruptions do not arise, and arisen corruptions are abandoned.
translations.mn2:11: He attends to the idea: 'This is suffering' in the appropriate way, 'This is the origin of suffering' in the appropriate way, 'This is the cessation of suffering' in the appropriate way, 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering' in the appropriate way. For one who attends to things in the appropriate way, three fetters are abandoned: personality view, doubt, and dependence on rituals and practices. These are called the corruptions that should be abandoned by seeing.
translations.mn2:12: And what, monks, are the corruptions that should be abandoned by restraint? Here, a monk, having reflected, lives restrained with regard to the eye faculty. For one who lives unrestrained with regard to the eye faculty, corruptions, vexations, and fevers might arise. For one who lives restrained with regard to the eye faculty, such corruptions, vexations, and fevers do not arise. Having reflected, he lives restrained with regard to the ear faculty... the nose faculty... the tongue faculty... the body faculty... the mind faculty. For one who lives unrestrained with regard to the mind faculty, corruptions, vexations, and fevers might arise. For one who lives restrained with regard to the mind faculty, such corruptions, vexations, and fevers do not arise. These are called the corruptions that should be abandoned by restraint.
translations.mn2:14: Having reflected, he uses alms food: 'Not for amusement, not for intoxication, not for beautification, not for embellishment, but only for the maintenance and nourishment of this body, for the ending of discomfort, and for assisting the holy life, so that I will put an end to old feelings and not create new ones, and so that I will be healthy and blameless, and will live in comfort.'
translations.mn2:16: Having reflected, he uses medicine and provisions for the sick: 'Only to the extent necessary for the ending of old feelings and the prevention of new ones.'
translations.mn2:17: For one who does not use them, corruptions, vexations, and fevers might arise. For one who uses them, such corruptions, vexations, and fevers do not arise. These are called the corruptions that should be abandoned by using.
translations.mn2:3: I say, monks, that the destruction of the corruptions comes from knowing and seeing, not from not knowing and not seeing. What is it that I say comes from knowing and seeing?
