Just as, Māgaṇḍiya, beings who are not free from sensual desire, being consumed by sensual craving, being tormented by sensual fever, and indulging in sensual pleasures, have a greater and greater sensual craving, a greater and greater sensual fever, and a greater and greater pleasure and pain, all based on the five cords of sensual pleasure.
translations.mn75:18: What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya? Have you seen or heard of a king or a king's minister who, being endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure, being attended upon, being ministered to, having abandoned sensual craving, having removed sensual distress, being without thirst, having a tranquil mind, dwells or lives or will live internally?
translations.mn75:2: Then the Bhagavā, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, went into Kammāsadhamma for alms. Having walked for alms in Kammāsadhamma, after his meal, he returned from his alms round and approached a certain forest grove for the day's abiding. Having entered that forest grove, he sat down at the root of a certain tree for the day's abiding.
translations.mn75:22: 'I am pleased with the Bhagavā, Gotama. May the Bhagavā, Gotama, teach the Dhamma so that I may know health and see nibbāna.' 'Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, a person was born blind; he would not see dark or light forms, black or white forms, ... . His friends and relatives, kinsmen, would attend upon a surgeon. The surgeon would administer medicine to him. The medicine would not create eyes for him, nor would it purify his eyes. What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya? Would that surgeon be a sharer in the fatigue and distress of that person?' 'Yes, venerable sir.' 'In the same way, Māgaṇḍiya, if I were to teach the Dhamma to you, saying: 'This is health, this is nibbāna,' you would not know health, you would not see nibbāna.'
translations.mn75:24: In the same way, Māgaṇḍiya, if I were to teach the Dhamma to you, saying: 'This is health, this is nibbāna.' You would know health, you would see nibbāna. For you, together with the arising of the eye, the passion for the five aggregates of clinging would be abandoned; and you would think: 'For a long time, I have been deceived and obstructed by this mind. I have taken form as clinging, I have taken feeling as clinging, I have taken perception as clinging, I have taken volitional formations as clinging, I have taken consciousness as clinging. My clinging has become the cause of becoming, becoming has become the cause of birth, birth has become the cause of old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.'
translations.mn75:25: 'I am pleased, venerable Gotama. May the Bhagavā, Gotama, teach the Dhamma so that I may rise from this seat without illness.' 'You should, Māgaṇḍiya, associate with good people. When you associate with good people, you will hear the true Dhamma; when you hear the true Dhamma, you will practice in accordance with the Dhamma; when you practice in accordance with the Dhamma, you will know and see for yourself - these diseases, tumors, and darts. Here, these diseases, tumors, and darts are completely removed. The cessation of my clinging is the cessation of becoming, the cessation of becoming is the cessation of birth, the cessation of birth is the cessation of old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.'
translations.mn75:26: When this was said, the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya said to the Bhagavā: 'Excellent, venerable Gotama, excellent! Just as if one were to turn upright what had been turned upside down, or to reveal what had been concealed, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to hold a lamp in the darkness, saying: 'Those with eyes will see forms'; in the same way, the Dhamma has been revealed by the Bhagavā in many ways. I go to the Bhagavā, Gotama, for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the community of bhikkhus. May I receive the going forth and the higher ordination in the presence of the Bhagavā, Gotama?'
translations.mn75:27: 'Whoever, Māgaṇḍiya, having formerly belonged to another sect, desires the going forth and ordination in this Dhamma and Vinaya, he dwells for four months; at the end of the four months, if the bhikkhus are pleased, they will give him the going forth and ordination as a bhikkhu. And here, the individual's character is known.' 'If, venerable sir, those who have formerly belonged to another sect and desire the going forth and ordination in this Dhamma and Vinaya dwell for four months, and at the end of the four months, if the bhikkhus are pleased, they give them the going forth and ordination as bhikkhus, I will dwell for four years; at the end of the four years, if the bhikkhus are pleased, let them give me the going forth and ordination as a bhikkhu.'
translations.mn75:3: Now on that occasion the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya was wandering from village to village, from town to town, and he came to the park of the brahmin Bhāradvājagotta. Māgaṇḍiya saw a grass mat spread out at the brahmin Bhāradvājagotta’s park. Having seen it, he said to Bhāradvājagotta: “To whom, sir, does this grass mat belong in the park of Bhāradvājagotta, which seems to be reserved for a recluse?”
translations.mn75:6: The Buddha heard this conversation between Bhāradvājagotta and the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya with his divine ear, which is purified and surpasses that of humans. In the evening, the Buddha emerged from seclusion and went to the park of Bhāradvājagotta, where he sat down on the prepared grass mat. Bhāradvājagotta went to the Buddha, exchanged greetings, and sat down to one side. The Buddha asked him: “Bhāradvāja, what was the conversation you had with the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya about this grass mat?”
translations.mn75:7: This is what Bhāradvājagotta and the Buddha were discussing in private. The wanderer Māgaṇḍiya was wandering from village to village, from town to town, and he came to the park of Bhāradvājagotta and the Buddha, where he exchanged greetings and sat down to one side. The Buddha asked him:
translations.mn77:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Buddha was staying in Rājagaha, at the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground.
translations.mn77:10: There are, Udāyī, five other things that my disciples honor, respect, and venerate me with, and having honored, respected, and venerated me, they live in dependence on me. What five? My disciples honor, respect, and venerate me with the thought: ‘The recluse Gotama is virtuous, with a high code of virtue and a high code of practice.’
translations.mn77:15: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have taught my disciples the practice so that, practicing accordingly, my disciples cultivate the four establishments of mindfulness. A bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body as body, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having put aside covetousness and displeasure in the world; he dwells contemplating feelings as feelings, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having put aside covetousness and displeasure in the world; he dwells contemplating the mind as mind, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having put aside covetousness and displeasure in the world; he dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having put aside covetousness and displeasure in the world. Many of my disciples, having practiced accordingly, dwell having realized the fruit of wisdom and liberation.
translations.mn77:16: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have taught my disciples the practice so that, practicing accordingly, my disciples cultivate the four right endeavors. A bhikkhu generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states, makes an effort, applies his mind, and exerts himself; he generates desire for the abandoning of arisen unwholesome states, makes an effort, applies his mind, and exerts himself; he generates desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome states, makes an effort, applies his mind, and exerts himself; he generates desire for the maintenance, non-decline, increase, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states, makes an effort, applies his mind, and exerts himself. Many of my disciples, having practiced accordingly, dwell having realized the fruit of wisdom and liberation.
translations.mn77:17: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have taught my disciples the practice so that, practicing accordingly, my disciples cultivate the four bases of psychic power. A bhikkhu cultivates the basis of psychic power that has will as its vehicle, concentration as its basis, and mental development as its equipment; he cultivates the basis of psychic power that has effort as its vehicle, concentration as its basis, and mental development as its equipment; he cultivates the basis of psychic power that has consciousness as its vehicle, concentration as its basis, and mental development as its equipment; he cultivates the basis of psychic power that has investigation as its vehicle, concentration as its basis, and mental development as its equipment. Many of my disciples, having practiced accordingly, dwell having realized the fruit of wisdom and liberation.
translations.mn77:18: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have taught my disciples the practice so that, practicing accordingly, my disciples cultivate the five spiritual faculties. A bhikkhu cultivates the faculty of faith, which leads to peace, leads to enlightenment; he cultivates the faculty of energy, which leads to peace, leads to enlightenment; he cultivates the faculty of mindfulness, which leads to peace, leads to enlightenment; he cultivates the faculty of concentration, which leads to peace, leads to enlightenment; he cultivates the faculty of wisdom, which leads to peace, leads to enlightenment. Many of my disciples, having practiced accordingly, dwell having realized the fruit of wisdom and liberation.
translations.mn77:2: At that time a number of well-known wanderers, including Annabhāro, Varadhara, and Sakuludāyī, were residing in the wanderers’ park at Moranivāpa.
translations.mn77:20: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have taught my disciples the practice so that, practicing accordingly, my disciples cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment. A bhikkhu cultivates the factor of mindfulness as a factor of enlightenment, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, and based on cessation, leading to letting go; he cultivates the factor of investigation of phenomena as a factor of enlightenment, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, and based on cessation, leading to letting go; he cultivates the factor of energy as a factor of enlightenment, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, and based on cessation, leading to letting go; he cultivates the factor of joy as a factor of enlightenment, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, and based on cessation, leading to letting go; he cultivates the factor of tranquility as a factor of enlightenment, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, and based on cessation, leading to letting go; he cultivates the factor of concentration as a factor of enlightenment, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, and based on cessation, leading to letting go; he cultivates the factor of equanimity as a factor of enlightenment, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, and based on cessation, leading to letting go. Many of my disciples, having practiced accordingly, dwell having realized the fruit of wisdom and liberation.
translations.mn77:21: Again, Udayi, I have taught the practice of my disciples, so that my disciples who proceed rightly develop the noble eightfold path. Here, Udayi, a monk develops right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. And many of my disciples, having developed these, dwell having reached the culmination of the spiritual path.
translations.mn77:22: Again, Udayi, I have taught the practice of my disciples, so that my disciples who proceed rightly develop the eight liberations. Having form, one sees forms, this is the first liberation; being percipient of the internal and external, one sees forms, this is the second liberation; being possessed of joy, this is the third liberation; having completely transcended perceptions of form, having disappeared perceptions of sensory impact, having not paid attention to perceptions of diversity, one enters and dwells in the base of infinite space, this is the fourth liberation; having completely transcended the base of infinite space, one enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness, this is the fifth liberation; having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, one enters and dwells in the base of nothingness, this is the sixth liberation; having completely transcended the base of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the base of neither perception nor non-perception, this is the seventh liberation; having completely transcended the base of neither perception nor non-perception, one enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling, this is the eighth liberation. And many of my disciples, having developed these, dwell having reached the culmination of the spiritual path.
translations.mn77:24: Again, Udayi, I have taught the practice of my disciples, so that my disciples who proceed rightly develop the ten bases of kasina. One perceives the earth kasina above, below, across, and undivided, as boundless; one perceives the water kasina... the fire kasina... the air kasina... the blue kasina... the yellow kasina... the red kasina... the white kasina... the space kasina... the consciousness kasina above, below, across, and undivided, as boundless. And many of my disciples, having developed these, dwell having reached the culmination of the spiritual path.
translations.mn77:25: Again, Udayi, I have taught the practice of my disciples, so that my disciples who proceed rightly develop the four jhanas. Here, Udayi, a monk, having separated from sensual desires, having separated from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhana, which is accompanied by thought and examination, and is filled with joy and pleasure born of seclusion. He drenches, steeps, and fills his body with the joy and pleasure born of seclusion, so that no part of his body is untouched by the joy and pleasure born of seclusion. Just as, Udayi, a skilled bathman or his apprentice, having sprinkled bath powder on a bronze dish, would drop water on it and circularly knead it, so that the bath powder would be absorbed and the water would penetrate every part, and no part of the dish would be untouched by the bath powder; in the same way, Udayi, the monk drenches, steeps, and fills his body with the joy and pleasure born of seclusion, so that no part of his body is untouched by the joy and pleasure born of seclusion.
translations.mn77:26: Again, Udayi, the monk, having suppressed thought and examination, enters and dwells in the second jhana, which is accompanied by internal confidence and joy, and is filled with pleasure born of concentration. He drenches, steeps, and fills his body with the pleasure born of concentration, so that no part of his body is untouched by the pleasure born of concentration. Just as, Udayi, a deep lake, with water welling up from below, would have no current flowing to the east, west, north, or south, and no water would be poured in or taken out, and the cool water would drench, steep, and fill the lake, so that no part of the lake would be untouched by the cool water; in the same way, Udayi, the monk drenches, steeps, and fills his body with the pleasure born of concentration, so that no part of his body is untouched by the pleasure born of concentration.
translations.mn77:27: Again, Udayi, the monk, having given up pleasure, enters and dwells in the third jhana, where, being free from pleasure, one is equable, mindful, and fully aware, and one experiences pleasure with the body. He drenches, steeps, and fills his body with the pleasure that is free from pleasure, so that no part of his body is untouched by the pleasure that is free from pleasure. Just as, Udayi, a lotus or a water lily or a blue lotus, having grown in the water, having been nourished by the water, and having been immersed in the water, would be drenched, steeped, and filled with the cool water, from the tips of the roots to the tips of the leaves, and no part of the lotus or water lily or blue lotus would be untouched by the cool water; in the same way, Udayi, the monk drenches, steeps, and fills his body with the pleasure that is free from pleasure, so that no part of his body is untouched by the pleasure that is free from pleasure.
translations.mn77:28: Again, Udayi, the monk, having given up pleasure and pain, and having previously abandoned joy and displeasure, enters and dwells in the fourth jhana, which is beyond pleasure and pain, and is accompanied by equanimity and mindfulness. He sits having drenched, steeped, and filled his body with a pure and cleansed mind, so that no part of his body is untouched by the pure and cleansed mind. Just as, Udayi, a man would sit having wrapped himself in a white cloth, and no part of his body would be untouched by the white cloth; in the same way, Udayi, the monk sits having drenched, steeped, and filled his body with a pure and cleansed mind, so that no part of his body is untouched by the pure and cleansed mind. And many of my disciples, having developed these, dwell having reached the culmination of the spiritual path.
translations.mn77:3: Now, the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms. Then, the Blessed One thought: 'Rājagaha is too crowded for me to go for alms now. Let me go to the park where the wanderer Moraniya lives, and the park where the wanderer Sakuludāyī lives.'
translations.mn77:32: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have taught the disciples the path, and those of my disciples who practice accordingly, with a divine ear that is pure and surpasses that of humans, hear both divine and human sounds, near and far. Just as a powerful drum can be heard in all four directions, so too, Udāyī, I have taught the disciples the path, and those of my disciples who practice accordingly, with a divine ear that is pure and surpasses that of humans, hear both divine and human sounds, near and far. And many of my disciples live having achieved the perfection of wisdom.
translations.mn77:34: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have taught the disciples the path, and those of my disciples who practice accordingly, recollect their many past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many aeons of world-contraction and expansion. 'I was such a name, such a clan, such a color, such a food, such a pleasure and pain, such a life-span, and such a destiny. Having died there, I was reborn here; having died here, I was reborn there.' Thus, they recollect their many past lives with their modes and details. Just as a man might go from his own village to another village, and then from that village to another, and then return to his own village, he would think: 'I went from my own village to that village, and there I stood, sat, spoke, and remained silent; then I went to another village, and there I stood, sat, spoke, and remained silent; and now I have returned to my own village.' In the same way, Udāyī, I have taught the disciples the path, and those of my disciples who practice accordingly, recollect their many past lives, that is, one birth, two births... and they recollect their many past lives with their modes and details. And many of my disciples live having achieved the perfection of wisdom.
translations.mn77:35: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have taught the disciples the path, and those of my disciples who practice accordingly, with a divine eye that is pure and surpasses that of humans, see beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in good or bad destinations, according to their actions. They understand: 'These beings, who were immoral in their actions, speech, and thoughts, and who reviled the noble ones, and held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views, have, after the breakup of the body, been reborn in a bad destination, in a state of suffering, in hell; while those beings who were moral in their actions, speech, and thoughts, and who did not revile the noble ones, and who held right views, and undertook actions based on right views, have, after the breakup of the body, been reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.' Thus, with a divine eye that is pure and surpasses that of humans, they see beings passing away and being reborn... according to their actions. Just as a man with good eyesight standing between two houses with open doors might see people entering and leaving, walking back and forth, and wandering about, so too, Udāyī, I have taught the disciples the path, and those of my disciples who practice accordingly, with a divine eye that is pure and surpasses that of humans, see beings passing away and being reborn... according to their actions... And many of my disciples live having achieved the perfection of wisdom.
translations.mn77:36: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have taught the disciples the path, and those of my disciples who practice accordingly, having destroyed the corruptions, live in the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for themselves in this very life. Just as a man with good eyesight standing on the bank of a clear and calm lake might see shells, pebbles, and fish swimming about or standing still, he would think: 'This lake is clear and calm, and there are shells, pebbles, and fish swimming about or standing still.' In the same way, Udāyī, I have taught the disciples the path, and those of my disciples who practice accordingly, having destroyed the corruptions, live in the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for themselves in this very life. And many of my disciples live having achieved the perfection of wisdom.
translations.mn77:5: Then, the Blessed One approached the park where the wanderer Sakuludāyī lived. The wanderer Sakuludāyī saw the Blessed One coming from afar and said: 'Come, Bhante, come, Bhagavā. You are welcome, Bhagavā. It has been a long time since you have taken the opportunity to come here. Please sit down, Bhagavā; this seat is prepared.' The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Sakuludāyī, the wanderer, took another, lower seat and sat down to one side.
translations.mn77:7: How many things, Udāyī, do you see in my teaching that my disciples honor, respect, and venerate, and which they use as a basis for their spiritual practice?
translations.mn77:9: If my disciples were to honor, respect, and venerate me because I am one who eats little, and they were to live in dependence on that, there are some of my disciples who eat little and some who eat a lot. But if my disciples were to honor, respect, and venerate me because I am one who eats little, and they were to live in dependence on that, those of my disciples who eat little would not honor, respect, and venerate me, nor would they live in dependence on that. If my disciples were to honor, respect, and venerate me because I am satisfied with any old robe, and they were to live in dependence on that, there are some of my disciples who wear rag robes and some who wear good robes. But if my disciples were to honor, respect, and venerate me because I am satisfied with any old robe, and they were to live in dependence on that, those of my disciples who wear rag robes would not honor, respect, and venerate me, nor would they live in dependence on that. If my disciples were to honor, respect, and venerate me because I am satisfied with any old almsfood, and they were to live in dependence on that, there are some of my disciples who go on almsround and some who do not. But if my disciples were to honor, respect, and venerate me because I am satisfied with any old almsfood, and they were to live in dependence on that, those of my disciples who go on almsround would not honor, respect, and venerate me, nor would they live in dependence on that. If my disciples were to honor, respect, and venerate me because I am satisfied with any old lodging, and they were to live in dependence on that, there are some of my disciples who live in the wilderness and some who live in the village. But if my disciples were to honor, respect, and venerate me because I am satisfied with any old lodging, and they were to live in dependence on that, those of my disciples who live in the wilderness would not honor, respect, and venerate me, nor would they live in dependence on that. If my disciples were to honor, respect, and venerate me because I live in solitude, and they were to live in dependence on that, there are some of my disciples who live in solitude and some who live with others. But if my disciples were to honor, respect, and venerate me because I live in solitude, and they were to live in dependence on that, those of my disciples who live in solitude would not honor, respect, and venerate me, nor would they live in dependence on that. Thus, my disciples do not honor, respect, and venerate me, nor do they live in dependence on these five things.
translations.mn7:11: When one has given up the corruptions, one gains knowledge and vision, one gains a sense of spiritual urgency, joy arises, and the mind becomes concentrated.
translations.mn7:13: He dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, and likewise the second, the third, and the fourth. In this way he dwells pervading above, below, and all around, everywhere, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, and without ill will.
translations.mn7:17: He understands: 'There is what is low, there is what is excellent, and there is the escape from this whole field of perception.'
translations.mn7:18: For one who knows and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of being, and from the taint of ignorance. When it is liberated, there is the knowledge: 'It is liberated.' He understands: 'Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming back to this state.' This, monks, is called a monk who is quenched by his own knowledge.
translations.mn7:19: Now at that time the brahmin Sundarika-Bharadvaja was sitting not far from the Blessed One. Then the brahmin Sundarika-Bharadvaja said to the Blessed One: 'Does Master Gotama intend to go to the river Bāhuka to bathe?' 'What is the use, brahmin, of the river Bāhuka? What is the use of the river Bāhuka to you?' 'The river Bāhuka, Master Gotama, is considered holy by the people, and many people wash away their evil deeds there.'
translations.mn7:2: Suppose a cloth is stained and dirty, and a dyer wants to dye it blue, or yellow, or red, or purple. If the cloth is not clean, it will not take the dye properly. Why is that? Because the cloth is not clean. In the same way, if the mind is stained, it will not shine. Suppose a cloth is clean and pure, and a dyer wants to dye it blue, or yellow, or red, or purple. If the cloth is clean, it will take the dye properly. Why is that? Because the cloth is clean. In the same way, if the mind is clean, it will shine.
translations.mn7:20: Then the Blessed One, addressing the brahmin Sundarika-Bharadvaja in verse, said: 'The Bāhuka, the Sundarika, the Sarassati, the Payaga, and the Bāhumati - a fool, a simpleton, cannot be cleansed by them. What can the Sundarika do, what can the Payaga do, what can the Bāhuka do? They cannot cleanse a man who has done evil, a man with evil deeds. For one who is pure, the day is always a festival, the day is always a holy day; for one who is pure, the mind is always pure, the mind is always clear. Do good, brahmin, and make merit; make merit and do good. If you do not speak falsely, if you do not harm living beings, if you do not take what is not given, if you are faithful and not stingy, what is the use of going to Gayā, what is the use of bathing in the river?'
translations.mn7:3: And what, monks, are the corruptions of the mind? Greed is a corruption of the mind, hatred is a corruption of the mind, delusion is a corruption of the mind, anger is a corruption of the mind, hostility is a corruption of the mind, denigration is a corruption of the mind, domineering is a corruption of the mind, envy is a corruption of the mind, miserliness is a corruption of the mind, deceit is a corruption of the mind, quarrelsomeness is a corruption of the mind, stubbornness is a corruption of the mind, conceit is a corruption of the mind, arrogance is a corruption of the mind, intoxication is a corruption of the mind, heedlessness is a corruption of the mind.
translations.mn7:6: He has confidence in the Dhamma, having come to know it by his own experience: 'The Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One, it is directly visible, timeless, inviting one to come and see, worthy of application, and to be personally experienced by the wise.'
translations.mn7:7: He has confidence in the Sangha, having come to know it by his own experience: 'The Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight individuals. This Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of respect; it is the supreme field of merit for the world.'
translations.mn82:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kuru people with a large community of monks, and arrived at a Kuru town called Thullakoṭṭhita.
translations.mn82:11: Then the friends and companions of the young man Raṭṭhapāla went to his parents and said: 'The young master Raṭṭhapāla has fallen down on the ground, saying:
translations.mn82:12: Then the young man Raṭṭhapāla got up and, having taken his bowl and robe, went to the Blessed One. Having gone to the Blessed One, he bowed down and sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the young man Raṭṭhapāla said to the Blessed One: 'I have been given permission by my parents to go forth from the household life into homelessness. Please, sir, ordain me.'
translations.mn82:13: Then the clansman Raṭṭhapāla went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, having bowed down to him, sat down to one side. The Blessed One, having instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened him with a talk on the Dhamma, got up from his seat and left. Then Raṭṭhapāla got up from his seat and, having bowed down to the Blessed One, circumambulated him and left. He wandered by stages, eventually arriving at Thullakoṭṭhita. There he stayed in the monastery of the brahman Kaṇṇa, the mango grove.
translations.mn82:14: Then, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and self-controlled, Raṭṭhapāla, before long, realized for himself, through his own effort, the goal for which clansmen rightly go forth from home to homelessness, and he abided in it. He directly knew: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no further becoming.' Then Raṭṭhapāla became one of the Arahants.
translations.mn82:16: Then Raṭṭhapāla got up from his seat, bowed down to the Blessed One, and having circumambulated him, took his bowl and robe, and left, wandering by stages, eventually arriving at Thullakoṭṭhita. There Raṭṭhapāla stayed in the monastery of the brahman Kaṇṇa, the mango grove. Then, in the morning, having put on his robes and, taking his bowl and outer robe, he went into Thullakoṭṭhita for alms.
translations.mn82:17: Now at that time Raṭṭhapāla's father was sitting in his high seat, having the door closed. He saw Raṭṭhapāla coming from afar and, having seen him, said: 'These shaven-headed menial monks have taken away my only son, dear and charming.' Then Raṭṭhapāla went to his father's house, but his father did not offer him a seat or invite him to sit down; instead, he scolded him.
translations.mn82:18: Now at that time a servant girl belonging to Raṭṭhapāla's relatives was about to throw away a meal of broken rice. Then Raṭṭhapāla said to her: 'If it is to be thrown away, sister, pour it into my bowl.' The servant girl poured the meal of broken rice into Raṭṭhapāla's bowl. Then the servant girl, having taken a sign from Raṭṭhapāla's hands, feet, and body, went to Raṭṭhapāla's mother and said: 'You should know, lady, that your son Raṭṭhapāla has arrived.' 'If what you say is true, I will give you this.' Then Raṭṭhapāla's mother went to his father and said: 'You should know, householder, that they say Raṭṭhapāla, our son, has arrived.'
translations.mn82:19: Then Raṭṭhapāla was eating the meal of broken rice near a certain wall. His father went to him and said: 'Raṭṭhapāla, my dear, do you eat that meal of broken rice? Don't you have a home to go to?' 'Where is the home for us, householder, who have gone forth from home to homelessness? We are homeless, householder. We went to your home, but we did not get a seat or an invitation to sit down; instead, we were scolded.' 'Come, dear Raṭṭhapāla, let's go home.' 'Enough, householder, I have finished my meal for today.' 'Then, dear Raṭṭhapāla, stay overnight and have a meal tomorrow.' Raṭṭhapāla consented in silence.
translations.mn82:20: Then Raṭṭhapāla's father, having known that Raṭṭhapāla had consented, went to his own house, had a large heap of gold and silver prepared, and had it covered with a cloth. He had Raṭṭhapāla's former wives adorn themselves with the same adornments with which they had been adorned when Raṭṭhapāla was a young man, dear and charming.
translations.mn82:21: Then Raṭṭhapāla's father had a delicious meal prepared in his own house towards the end of that night and announced to Raṭṭhapāla: 'It is time, dear Raṭṭhapāla, the meal is ready.'
translations.mn82:22: Then Raṭṭhapāla, early in the morning, having put on his robes and, taking his bowl and outer robe, went to his father's house and sat down in a prepared seat. Then Raṭṭhapāla's father uncovered the heap of gold and silver and said to Raṭṭhapāla: 'This, dear Raṭṭhapāla, is your mother's inheritance, this is your ancestral inheritance, and this is your paternal inheritance. You can enjoy the wealth and do meritorious deeds. Come, dear Raṭṭhapāla, having abandoned the homeless life, enjoy the wealth and do meritorious deeds.' 'If you, householder, will do as I say, load this heap of gold and silver on a cart, set it on fire, and sink it in the middle of the Ganges River.' 'Why is that? The things that will arise from that will be the cause of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.'
translations.mn82:23: Then the brahmin lady, Raṭṭhapāla's former wife, took his feet in her hands and said to Raṭṭhapāla: 'What kind of miracle is this, young master, that you have given up the holy life?' 'We did not give up the holy life, sister, for any miracle,' he replied. The women, rebuked by Raṭṭhapāla, sat down right there, disappointed.
translations.mn82:24: Then Raṭṭhapāla said to his father: 'If you have food to give, give it; don't annoy us.' 'Eat, dear Raṭṭhapāla, the meal is ready,' he replied. Then Raṭṭhapāla's father served and satisfied him with choice, hard, and soft foods. Then, after Raṭṭhapāla had eaten and washed his hands and bowl, he sat down at the base of a tree.
translations.mn82:26: Then Raṭṭhapāla, having spoken those verses, went to the park where King Korabya was, and sat down at the base of a certain tree for the day's abiding.
translations.mn82:27: Then King Korabya said to his game warden: 'Clean up the park, the pleasure garden; we will go to see the beautiful land.' 'Yes, your majesty,' the game warden replied, and cleaning up the park, he saw Raṭṭhapāla sitting at the base of a certain tree for the day's abiding. Having seen him, he went to King Korabya and said: 'The park is clean, your majesty. There is a young man of good family named Raṭṭhapāla, the son of a leading family in this very same Thullakoṭṭhika, who was often praised by you, sitting at the base of a certain tree.' 'Well then, game warden, never mind the pleasure garden. We will go to pay our respects to Raṭṭhapāla,' he said.
translations.mn82:28: Then King Korabya said: 'Distribute all the food and drink that has been prepared.' Having prepared fine carriages, he mounted a fine carriage and, with his fine carriages, he left Thullakoṭṭhika and went to see Raṭṭhapāla with a large retinue. As far as the carriage could go, he went by carriage, then he got down and, on foot, he approached Raṭṭhapāla. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with Raṭṭhapāla, and when they had concluded their greetings, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, King Korabya said to Raṭṭhapāla: 'Sit down, sir, on a seat.' 'Let the king sit down; I am already seated in my own seat,' he replied. The king sat down on a prepared seat.
translations.mn82:29: There are, Raṭṭhapāla, four kinds of people who have given up the household life for the homeless life, having shaved off their hair and beard, put on the yellow robes, and gone forth from the household life. What are the four? One who has given up the household life out of fear of old age, one who has given up the household life out of fear of illness, one who has given up the household life out of fear of poverty, and one who has given up the household life out of fear of death.
translations.mn82:3: Then the brahmin householders of Thullakoṭṭhika went to the Buddha, and having gone, some bowed down to the Buddha and sat down to one side; some exchanged greetings with him, and when they had concluded their greetings, sat down to one side; some, having raised their joined palms in salutation to the Buddha, sat down to one side; some announced their name and clan and sat down to one side; and some sat down to one side in silence. The Buddha instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened the brahmin householders of Thullakoṭṭhika with a Dhamma talk.
translations.mn82:34: These, Raṭṭhapāla, are the four kinds of people who have given up the household life for the homeless life, having shaved off their hair and beard, put on the yellow robes, and gone forth from the household life. You, Raṭṭhapāla, do not have these. Why, having seen, heard, and understood, did you give up the household life, Raṭṭhapāla?
translations.mn82:35: There are, your majesty, four Dhamma teachings, taught by the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Awakened One, which I, having seen, heard, and understood, have given up the household life. What are the four?
translations.mn82:4: At that time Raṭṭhapāla, a young man of a leading family in Thullakoṭṭhika, was sitting in the assembly. Then it occurred to Raṭṭhapāla: 'As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Buddha, it is not easy to lead the perfect and pure spiritual life as a layman, for it is not easy to fulfill the spiritual life while living in a home. What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on the yellow robes, and go forth from the household life?'
translations.mn82:6: Then the clansman Raṭṭhapāla approached the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down to one side. As he sat there, Raṭṭhapāla said to the Blessed One: "Whatever I have learned from the Blessed One's teachings, I know that it is not easy for one living in the household life to lead the perfectly complete, perfectly pure holy life, polished like a conch shell. I wish to shave off my hair and beard, don the ochre robe, and go forth from the household life into homelessness. May the Blessed One ordain me"
translations.mn95:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosalan country with a large Saṅgha of monks. He arrived at a Kosalan brahmin village called Opāsāda.
translations.mn95:10: Then the brahmin Caṅkī, together with a large group of brahmins, approached the Blessed One, and after exchanging greetings, he sat down to one side.
translations.mn95:11: At that time the Blessed One was sitting with a group of elderly brahmins, engaged in a discussion. A young man named Kāpaṭika, sixteen years old, learned in the three Vedas, was sitting in that assembly. The Blessed One said to Kāpaṭika: "Do not interrupt the discussion of these elderly brahmins. Come, Kāpaṭika, let us discuss the conclusion of the conversation."
translations.mn95:2: At that time the brahmin Caṅkī was living in the Opāsāda, having been given a grant of seven hundred pieces of money, a robe, and a bowl by King Pasenadi of Kosala.
translations.mn95:20: When one knows and sees that the Tathāgata's teaching is pure and free from defilements, then one places faith in him, and having faith, one approaches him, and having approached, one pays respect, and having paid respect, one lends an ear, and having lent an ear, one hears the Dhamma, and having heard the Dhamma, one remembers it, and having remembered it, one examines the meaning, and having examined the meaning, one comes to an understanding of the Dhamma, and having come to an understanding of the Dhamma, one's mind is inclined towards it, and having inclined one's mind, one makes an effort, and having made an effort, one weighs and balances, and having weighed and balanced, one strives, and having striven, one realizes with one's body the supreme truth, and having realized it, one sees it with wisdom.
translations.mn95:33: Caṅkī asked the Blessed One: "What is the benefit of approaching a teacher? We ask you, Gotama, to explain the benefit of approaching a teacher." The Blessed One replied: "Faith is the benefit of approaching a teacher. Without faith, one would not approach. Since faith arises, one approaches. Therefore, faith is the benefit of approaching a teacher."
translations.mn95:5: At that time Caṅkī the brahmin had gone up to the upper floor of the Opāsāda for his daytime rest. He saw the brahmin householders from the Opāsāda leaving the Opāsāda in a procession, heading north towards the Sāla forest, the Deer Park.
translations.mn9:11: What is nutrition, what is the origin of nutrition, what is the cessation of nutrition, and what is the path leading to the cessation of nutrition? There are four kinds of nutrition for the maintenance of beings, or for the assistance of those seeking existence. What four? Physical food, gross or subtle, is the first; contact is the second; mental volition is the third; and consciousness is the fourth. The origin of nutrition is the origin of craving; the cessation of nutrition is the cessation of craving; and the path leading to the cessation of nutrition is this noble eightfold path, that is, right understanding, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
translations.mn9:12: When a noble disciple thus understands nutrition, the origin of nutrition, the cessation of nutrition, and the path leading to the cessation of nutrition, he abandons the underlying tendency to lust, removes the underlying tendency to aversion, and uproots the underlying tendency to the view of self. Having abandoned ignorance and aroused true knowledge, he becomes one who in this very life makes an end of suffering— to this extent, a noble disciple is one of right view, with a view that is straight, with a view that is excellent, with a view that is beyond reproach.
translations.mn9:15: What, friend, is suffering, what is the origin of suffering, what is the cessation of suffering, what is the path leading to the cessation of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering, association with the unpleasant is suffering, separation from the pleasant is suffering, not getting what one wants is suffering — in short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. This is called suffering.
translations.mn9:16: What, friend, is the origin of suffering? It is craving that leads to rebirth, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking pleasure here and there — that is, sensual craving, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This is called the origin of suffering.
translations.mn9:17: What, friend, is the cessation of suffering? It is the complete fading away and cessation of that very craving, its abandonment, relinquishment, liberation, and release. This is called the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn9:18: What, friend, is the path leading to the cessation of suffering? It is this noble eightfold path, that is, right understanding, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This is called the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn9:2: 'Right understanding, right understanding,' it is said. In what way, friend, does a noble disciple have right understanding, undistorted understanding, and is endowed with the confidence that comes from understanding the teaching?
translations.mn9:20: The monks, delighting and rejoicing in the statement made by the Venerable Sāriputta, asked him a further question: 'Is there another way, friend, by which a noble disciple has right understanding, undistorted understanding, and is endowed with the confidence that comes from understanding the teaching?'
translations.mn9:3: When, friend, a noble disciple understands unwholesome and wholesome, and the root of unwholesome and wholesome, to that extent the noble disciple has right understanding, undistorted understanding, and is endowed with the confidence that comes from understanding the teaching.
translations.mn9:4: What, friend, is unwholesome, what is the root of unwholesome, what is wholesome, and what is the root of wholesome? Killing living beings is unwholesome, taking what is not given is unwholesome, sexual misconduct is unwholesome, false speech is unwholesome, divisive speech is unwholesome, harsh speech is unwholesome, idle chatter is unwholesome, covetousness is unwholesome, ill will is unwholesome, and wrong view is unwholesome. This is called unwholesome.
translations.mn9:5: What, friend, is the root of unwholesome? Greed is the root of unwholesome, hatred is the root of unwholesome, and delusion is the root of unwholesome. This is called the root of unwholesome.
translations.mn9:7: What, friend, is the root of wholesome? Non-greed is the root of wholesome, non-hatred is the root of wholesome, and non-delusion is the root of wholesome. This is called the root of wholesome.
translations.mn9:70: What, friend, are the taints, what is the origin of the taints, what is the cessation of the taints, and what is the path leading to the cessation of the taints? There are three taints: the taint of sensuality, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance. The origin of the taints is ignorance, the cessation of the taints is the cessation of ignorance, and the path leading to the cessation of the taints is this noble eightfold path, that is, right understanding, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
translations.mn9:8: When, friend, a noble disciple thus understands unwholesome, the root of unwholesome, wholesome, and the root of wholesome, he abandons the underlying tendency to lust, removes the underlying tendency to aversion, and uproots the underlying tendency to ignorance. By abandoning ignorance and developing knowledge, he becomes one who destroys suffering in this very life — to that extent the noble disciple has right understanding, undistorted understanding, and is endowed with the confidence that comes from understanding the teaching.
translations.sn1.10:2: For those who live in the wilderness, who are tranquil, and who are brahmins, what is the beauty of their life, living on one meal a day?
translations.sn1.10:3: They do not lament about the past, nor do they long for the future. They find joy in the present moment, and that is the beauty of their life.
translations.sn1.17:1: It is difficult and painful to live a life of restraint, to live a life of self-control, and to live a life of renunciation; there are many obstacles, and the foolish person is distressed by them.
translations.sn1.17:2: How should one live a life of self-control, without restraining one's mind? One would be distressed at every step, and would be under the control of one's thoughts.
translations.sn1.17:3: Just as a pot is broken into pieces, so too the mind of one who is not self-controlled is broken. One who is not self-controlled is not free from others, and is like a dead person, without any freedom.
translations.sn1.18:1: A person who is restrained by shame, who is wise, and who is self-controlled, is rare in the world. Such a person is like a good horse, and is praised by the wise.
translations.sn1.18:2: Those who are restrained by shame, who are self-controlled, and who are always mindful, can attain the end of suffering, and can live a peaceful life, free from trouble.
translations.sn1.1:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Blessed One was living in Sāvatthī, at Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then, in the middle of the night, a certain deity, whose beauty was surpassing, illuminated the entire Jeta's Grove with his radiance, and approached the Blessed One. Having approached the Blessed One, he bowed down to him and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the deity asked the Blessed One: 'How is it that you have crossed the flood, sir?' 'I have crossed the flood, friend, without being submerged, without being swept away,' the Blessed One replied.
translations.sn1.1:2: The deity asked: 'But how is it that you have crossed the flood, sir, without being submerged, without being swept away?' The Blessed One replied: 'When I stand, I stand firmly; when I sit, I sit firmly; when I lie down, I lie down firmly. In this way, I have crossed the flood, friend, without being submerged, without being swept away, and I am not bound by the three worlds.'
translations.sn1.1:3: The deity, having delighted in the Blessed One's words, bowed down to him, circumambulated him, and disappeared right there.
translations.sn1.20:1: Thus I have heard—on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Tapoda monastery. Then, when the night was far advanced, the Venerable Samiddhi rose from his seat and, after washing his feet, stood outside, holding his robe and bowl. After washing his feet and standing outside, holding his robe and bowl, a certain deity, of stunning beauty, illuminating the entire Tapoda monastery, approached the Venerable Samiddhi; having approached, she stood in the air and addressed the Venerable Samiddhi with a verse:
translations.sn1.20:2: “You are a bhikkhu without having asked, you are not a bhikkhu because you have asked; Having asked, you should be a bhikkhu, do not let that time pass”
translations.sn1.20:20: “Beings are stuck in what can be expressed, established in what can be expressed; Not fully understanding what can be expressed, they are tormented by death”
translations.sn1.20:21: And having fully understood what can be expressed, one does not think in terms of expression; That does not exist for them, what they do not speak of does not exist for them; If you understand, tell me, demon”
translations.sn1.20:22: “I do not understand, venerable sir, the meaning of what the Blessed One has said in brief. May the Blessed One explain it to me in such a way that I can understand the detailed meaning of what the Blessed One has said in brief”
translations.sn1.20:23: “One who thinks 'equal and unequal' would quarrel with that; Unshaken in the three times, one is not 'equal and unequal'; If you understand, tell me, demon”
translations.sn1.20:25: “Having abandoned conceit, not dependent on a hut, having cut off craving here in name and form; That which is without bonds, without distress, and without support, I have searched for but not found, in the world of humans or in heaven”
translations.sn1.20:3: “I do not know the time, the time is not visible; Therefore, I ask without knowing the time, do not let the time pass me by”
translations.sn1.20:4: Then that deity, having placed herself on the ground, said to the Venerable Samiddhi: 'You are young, bhikkhu, newly ordained, with black hair, endowed with the blessings of youth, in the prime of life, not having indulged in sensual pleasures. Enjoy human sensual pleasures, bhikkhu; do not abandon what can be seen and run after what is to be seen in the future'
translations.sn1.20:5: “I do not abandon what can be seen and run after what is to be seen in the future. I abandon what is to be seen in the future and run after what can be seen. For what can be seen in the future, bhikkhu, has been spoken of by the Blessed One as sensual pleasures, which are many and bring much suffering; the drawbacks are more. This Dhamma is visible here and now, without delay, inviting one to come and see, to be seen for oneself by the wise”
translations.sn1.20:6: “And how, bhikkhu, have sensual pleasures been spoken of by the Blessed One as many and bringing much suffering, with more drawbacks? And how is this Dhamma visible here and now, without delay, inviting one to come and see, to be seen for oneself by the wise?”
translations.sn1.20:7: “I am new to this Dhamma and Vinaya, having recently ordained. I am not able to explain it in detail. The Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Awakened One, is dwelling at Rājagaha in the Tapoda monastery. Having approached the Blessed One, ask him about this matter. As the Blessed One explains it, you should remember it”
translations.sn1.20:8: “It is not easy, bhikkhu, for us to approach the Blessed One, as he is surrounded by other powerful deities. If you approach the Blessed One and ask him about this matter, we will also come to hear the Dhamma”
translations.sn1.21:2: “Like a spear stuck in the throat, burning, a bhikkhu, mindful, should wander for the abandonment of sensual desire”
translations.sn1.21:3: “Like a spear stuck in the throat, burning, a bhikkhu, mindful, should wander for the abandonment of the view of self”
translations.sn1.25:1: “A bhikkhu who is an Arahant, who has completed his task, whose corruptions are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, who has done what had to be done, who has laid down the burden, who has attained his goal, who has destroyed the fetters of existence, who is liberated by perfect knowledge—I call him one who speaks of 'I' and 'mine'”
translations.sn1.25:2: “A bhikkhu who is an Arahant, who has completed his task, whose corruptions are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, who has done what had to be done, who has laid down the burden, who has attained his goal, who has destroyed the fetters of existence, who is liberated by perfect knowledge—I call him one who speaks of 'I' and 'mine'; Having understood the designation in the world, he uses it with a knowledge that is not tied to it”
translations.sn1.25:3: “A bhikkhu who is an Arahant, who has completed his task, whose corruptions are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, who has done what had to be done, who has laid down the burden, who has attained his goal, who has destroyed the fetters of existence, who is liberated by perfect knowledge—Would such a bhikkhu, having approached conceit, say 'I speak' and 'I am spoken to'?”
translations.sn1.25:4: “For one who has abandoned conceit, there are no bonds; All the bonds of conceit have been cut off; That wise one, having overcome conceit, would say 'I speak'”
translations.sn1.25:5: “And 'I am spoken to', having understood the designation in the world, with a knowledge that is not tied to it; He would use it with a mere indication, without any attachment”
translations.sn1.2:1: At Sāvatthī. Then, when the night was far advanced, a certain deity, of stunning beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta's Grove, approached the Blessed One; having approached, she bowed down to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity addressed the Blessed One with a verse:
translations.sn1.2:5: “With the complete destruction of delight and existence, the cessation of perceptions and consciousness; With the cessation of feelings, peace; Thus, venerable sir, I know the emancipation and liberation of beings”
translations.sn1.36:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then, when the night was far advanced, a large number of devas, of stunning beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta’s Grove, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they bowed down to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, one of the deities addressed the Blessed One with a verse:
translations.sn1.36:2: “Faith is the second thing for a person, if they do not rely on what is not to be relied on; And they have fame and renown, and they go to heaven, leaving the body behind”
translations.sn1.36:4: “One should abandon anger, completely give up pride; One should transcend all bonds; That which is without acquisitions, not coming under the control of any acquisitions, is not attached to name and form”
translations.sn1.36:5: “The foolish and ignorant run after negligence; The wise and intelligent guard diligence as their greatest treasure”
translations.sn1.36:6: “Do not run after negligence, do not indulge in sensual pleasure; One who is diligent, meditating, attains the highest happiness”
translations.sn1.38:1: Thus have I heard— on one occasion the Blessed One was living in the bamboo grove, the Migāra’s mother’s mansion, in Rājagaha.  At that time the Blessed One’s foot had been injured by a stone splinter.  Severe pains assailed the Blessed One, bodily feelings that were painful, sharp, and bitter; yet the Blessed One endured them, mindful and fully aware, without becoming distressed.
translations.sn1.38:10: Those who are dominated by craving, bound by the fetters of behavior, roam about for a hundred years, their minds not well-released; they are of lowly character, not crossers of the flood.
translations.sn1.38:11: Taming the mind does not come about through conceit, nor does it come about through lack of mindfulness in one who is not concentrated; one who lives in the wilderness, heedless, cannot cross the realm of death.
translations.sn1.38:12: Having abandoned conceit, well-concentrated, with a mind completely freed from all things, one who lives in the wilderness, heedful, can cross the realm of death.
translations.sn1.38:2: Then, when the night had advanced, seven hundred devas of stunning beauty, having outshone the entire Maddakucchi, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they bowed down to the Blessed One and stood to one side.  One of those devas, standing to one side, spoke this verse in the Blessed One’s presence: 'The ascetic Gotama is indeed a bull elephant; the bodily feelings that arise in him are painful, sharp, and bitter, but he endures them, mindful and fully aware, without becoming distressed.'
translations.sn1.38:3: Then another deva spoke this verse in the Blessed One’s presence: 'The ascetic Gotama is indeed a lion; the bodily feelings that arise in him are painful, sharp, and bitter, but he endures them, mindful and fully aware, without becoming distressed.'
translations.sn1.38:8: Then another deva spoke this verse in the Blessed One’s presence: 'Look at his concentration, well-developed, his mind well-released, not excited, not slack, not restrained by force, not artificially produced.  Whoever thinks that one should cross beyond a man who is like this, a bull of a man, a lion of a man, a man of great wisdom, a man of great intelligence, a man of great power, should think of it as not seeing.'
translations.sn1.38:9: For five hundred years, ascetics and brahmins roam about, their minds not well-released; they are of lowly character, not crossers of the flood.
translations.sn1.41:1: Thus have I heard— on one occasion the Blessed One was living in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery, in Sāvatthi.  Then a certain deva, of stunning beauty, having outshone the entire Jeta Grove, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he bowed down to the Blessed One and stood to one side.  Standing to one side, that deva spoke these verses in the Blessed One’s presence:
translations.sn1.41:4: The gift bears fruit as happiness, not the non-gift in the same way; thieves steal it, kings take it, fire burns it.
translations.sn1.41:5: Then, having relinquished the end, the body with all its accessories; having understood this, the wise one enjoys and gives; having given and having become, according to one’s experience, one goes to a state of bliss, unrebuked.
translations.sn1.42:1: 'What is it that gives strength, what is it that gives beauty? What is it that gives pleasure, what is it that gives eyesight? Who is it that gives everything, tell me when asked?'
translations.sn1.42:2: 'Food gives strength, clothing gives beauty; a vehicle gives pleasure, a lamp gives eyesight. He who gives a dwelling is the giver of everything; the gift of the deathless is the best gift, the one who teaches the Dhamma.'
translations.sn1.42:3: He is the giver of everything, the one who gives a dwelling; the gift of the deathless is the best gift, the one who teaches the Dhamma.
translations.sn1.51:1: 'What is good even for a long time, what is good when established? What is the jewel of men, what is it that thieves cannot steal?'
translations.sn1.51:2: 'Virtue is good even for a long time, faith is good when established; wisdom is the jewel of men, merit is what thieves cannot steal.'
translations.sn1.55:1: 'What generates a person, what is their divider? What is the origin of the round of rebirths, what is their great fear?'
translations.sn1.55:2: 'Craving generates a person, the mind is their divider; the living being is the origin of the round of rebirths, suffering is their great fear.'
translations.sn1.56:1: 'What generates a person, what is their divider? What is the origin of the round of rebirths, by what means do they not cross over?'
translations.sn1.56:2: 'Craving generates a person, the mind is their divider; the living being is the origin of the round of rebirths, they do not cross over due to suffering.'
translations.sn1.57:1: 'What generates a person, what is their divider? What is the origin of the round of rebirths, what is their destination?'
translations.sn1.57:2: 'Craving generates a person, the mind is their divider; the living being is the origin of the round of rebirths, action is their destination.'
translations.sn1.59:1: 'What is the second thing for a person, what is their expansion? Whose delight is death, and by whom are all sufferings destroyed?'
translations.sn1.59:2: 'Faith is the second thing for a person, wisdom is their expansion; one who delights in Nibbana, death destroys all sufferings.'
translations.sn1.62:1: 'By what is the world led, by what is it defiled? By what is it one-dhamma, and all of it under control?'
translations.sn1.62:2: 'The world is led by the mind, the world is defiled by the mind; the mind is one-dhamma, and all of it is under control.'
translations.sn1.63:2: 'The world is led by craving, the world is defiled by craving; craving is one-dhamma, and all of it is under control.'
translations.sn1.64:1: 'What is the bond of the world, what is its examination? By the removal of what is Nibbana spoken of?'
translations.sn1.64:2: 'The bond of the world is delight, the examination is of thought; by the removal of craving is Nibbana spoken of.'
translations.sn1.65:1: 'What is the connection of the world, what is its examination? By the removal of what does one cut off all bonds?'
translations.sn1.65:2: 'The connection of the world is delight, the examination is of thought; by the removal of craving does one cut off all bonds.'
translations.sn1.69:1: 'By what is the world bound, by what is it freed? By the removal of what does one cut off all bonds?'
translations.sn1.69:2: 'The world is bound by desire, it is freed by the freedom from desire; by the removal of desire does one cut off all bonds.'
translations.sn1.71:2: 'What is it that one should destroy to attain happiness, what is it that one should destroy to not sorrow? By the removal of what single dhamma does one delight in destruction, Gotama?'
translations.sn1.71:3: 'One should destroy anger to attain happiness, one should destroy anger to not sorrow; the noble ones praise the destruction of anger, which is bitter and unpleasant, and they do not sorrow over it.'
translations.sn1.73:1: 'What is the best wealth for a person, what is the best thing to accumulate for happiness? What is the best taste for the tongue, what is the best life to live?'
translations.sn1.73:2: The wealth of a person is their faith, The Dhamma is well-practiced, it brings happiness; Truth is the most excellent of tastes, They call the life of wisdom the best.
translations.sn1.7:2: For those whose teachings are not well-understood, They are led astray by the doctrines of others; Those people do not awaken to the teachings, It is time for them to awaken.
translations.sn1.7:3: For those whose teachings are well-understood, They are not led astray by the doctrines of others; Those fully awakened ones, with proper understanding, roam in the uneven.
translations.sn1.8:2: For those whose teachings are well-taught, They are led astray by the doctrines of others; Those people do not awaken to the teachings, It is time for them to awaken.
translations.sn1.8:3: For those whose teachings are not well-taught, They are not led astray by the doctrines of others; Those fully awakened ones, with proper understanding, roam in the uneven.
translations.sn11.14:1: At one time the Bhagava was living in the bamboo grove in Rajagaha. There the Bhagava addressed the monks: 'Monks.' 'Venerable sir,' those monks replied to the Bhagava. The Bhagava said this:
translations.sn11.14:3: Then, monks, Sakka, the lord of the gods, addressed the gods of the Thirty-Three: 'Do not, monks, despise this young god. This young god, formerly a human, had faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom in the Dhamma and Vinaya as taught by the Tathagata. Having had faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom in the Dhamma and Vinaya as taught by the Tathagata, after the break-up of the body, after death, he was reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world, and became one of the gods of the Thirty-Three. He surpasses other gods in beauty and fame.', Then, monks, Sakka, the lord of the gods, being pleased, at that time, spoke these verses:
translations.sn11.14:6: Therefore, a wise person should attend to faith and virtue, To serenity and a knowledge of the teaching; They should attend to the dispensation of the Buddhas.
translations.sn11.15:1: At Savatthi, in Jeta's grove. Then Sakka, the lord of the gods, approached the Bhagava; having approached, he bowed down to the Bhagava and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, the lord of the gods, said to the Bhagava: 'What, venerable sir, is delightful?
translations.sn11.15:2: A park, a woodland, a lake, A created pleasure grove; For one who delights in people, Fifty years is not a long time.
translations.sn11.22:1: At Savatthi, in Jeta's grove. There ... said this: 'Monks, formerly a certain wicked yakkha, rough and violent, was sitting on the seat of Sakka, the lord of the gods. There, monks, the gods of the Thirty-Three were annoyed, irritated, and disgusted: 'It is wonderful, sir, it is marvelous, sir. This yakkha, rough and violent, is sitting on the seat of Sakka, the lord of the gods.' As, monks, the gods of the Thirty-Three were annoyed, irritated, and disgusted, so that yakkha became more handsome, more lovely, and more pleasing to see.
translations.sn11.22:3: Then, monks, Sakka, the lord of the gods, approached that yakkha who was rough and violent; having approached, he arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his right knee, and, with his right hand, touched the ground. With his palm together, he greeted the yakkha three times, saying: 'I am Sakka, the lord of the gods, I am Sakka, the lord of the gods.' As, monks, Sakka, the lord of the gods, greeted the yakkha, so that yakkha became more rough and violent. Being more rough and violent, he disappeared right there. Then, monks, Sakka, the lord of the gods, having sat down on his own seat, being pleased, at that time, spoke these verses to the gods of the Thirty-Three:
translations.sn11.22:4: I am not one with a corrupted mind, Nor am I one with a corrupted speech; I do not get angry for a long time, Anger does not persist in me.
translations.sn11.22:5: I do not speak harshly, Nor do I proclaim the teachings; I gather myself, I see my own benefit.
translations.sn11.24:2: There are, monks, two fools. One who does not see the danger in danger, and one who does not accept the teaching as taught - these, monks, are two fools. There are, monks, two wise people. One who sees the danger in danger, and one who accepts the teaching as taught - these, monks, are two wise people.
translations.sn11.24:3: Formerly, monks, Sakka, the lord of the gods, being pleased, at that time, spoke this verse to the gods of the Thirty-Three in the Sudhamma assembly hall:
translations.sn11.24:4: Let anger be under your control, Let there not be decay among your friends; Do not blame the household, Do not speak falsely; For anger is a bad person, It harasses like a mountain.
translations.sn11.3:1: At Savatthi. There the Bhagava addressed the monks: 'Monks.' 'Venerable sir,' those monks replied to the Bhagava. The Bhagava said this:
translations.sn11.3:10: If you do not remember me, remember the Dhamma: 'The Dhamma is well-taught by the Bhagava, visible, timeless, inviting, to be personally known by the wise.' For, monks, when you remember the Dhamma, any fear, trepidation, or horror that may arise will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:11: If you do not remember the Dhamma, remember the Sangha: 'The Sangha of the Bhagava's disciples is practicing well, practicing straight, practicing rightly, practicing properly, that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight individuals. This Sangha of the Bhagava's disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of respect, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.' For, monks, when you remember the Sangha, any fear, trepidation, or horror that may arise will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:12: What is the reason for this? The Tathagata, monks, is an arahant, a fully awakened one, without lust, without hatred, without delusion, without fear, without trepidation, without anxiety, without fleeing.
translations.sn11.3:13: In the forest, at the foot of a tree, Or in an empty hut, monks; Remember the Awakened One, Fear will not come to you.
translations.sn11.3:14: If you cannot remember the Buddha, The best in the world, the bull of men; Then remember the Dhamma, Leading to the end, well-taught.
translations.sn11.3:15: If you cannot remember the Dhamma, Leading to the end, well-taught; Then remember the Sangha, The unsurpassed field of merit.
translations.sn11.3:16: Thus, monks, remembering the Buddha, The Dhamma, and the Sangha; Fear, trepidation, or horror Will not arise.
translations.sn11.3:2: In the past, monks, a war between the gods and the demons broke out. Then Sakka, the lord of the gods, addressed the gods who had gathered:
translations.sn11.3:3: ‘If, monks, fear or trepidation or hair-standing-on-end should arise in you when you have gone to war with the gods, then at that time look up to my banner. For it is my banner that you look up to that will dispel any fear or trepidation or hair-standing-on-end that may arise in you.
translations.sn11.3:4: If you do not look up to my banner, then look up to the banner of Pajāpati, the king of the gods. For it is Pajāpati, the king of the gods, whose banner you look up to that will dispel any fear or trepidation or hair-standing-on-end that may arise in you.
translations.sn11.3:8: What is the reason for this? Sakka, the lord of the gods, is without lust, without hatred, without delusion, fearful, timid, and runs away.
translations.sn11.3:9: And I, monks, say this: ‘If fear or trepidation or hair-standing-on-end should arise in you who dwell in the forest or at the foot of a tree or in an empty hut, then at that time recall me: “That Blessed One is worthy and rightly self-awakened, consummate in knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the cosmos, unexcelled trainer of those to be tamed, teacher of those who need training, awakened, blessed.” For it is I whom you recall that will dispel any fear or trepidation or hair-standing-on-end that may arise in you.
translations.sn11.5:12: He wanders for the benefit of both himself and others, knowing the other's mind, and being mindful, he is at peace.
translations.sn11.5:14: When Sakka, the lord of the gods, had spoken these verses, the gods were delighted, but the demons were displeased. Then the retinue of the gods and the demons said: ‘The verses spoken by the demon Vepacitti are provocative and lead to strife and dispute. The verses spoken by Sakka, the lord of the gods, are gentle and lead to non-strife and non-dispute. The victory is with Sakka, the lord of the gods, who spoke well.’ Thus, monks, the victory was with Sakka, the lord of the gods, who spoke well.
translations.sn11.5:2: ‘The foolish are many, but there is no one to restrain them; therefore the wise restrain the foolish with a strong rod.’
translations.sn11.5:3: When the demon Vepacitti had spoken this verse, the demons were delighted, but the gods were displeased. Then Vepacitti, the demon, said to Sakka, the lord of the gods: ‘Speak a verse, lord of the gods.’
translations.sn11.5:4: ‘This, I think, is the way to restrain a fool: knowing the other's mind, and being mindful, one is at peace.’
translations.sn11.5:5: When Sakka, the lord of the gods, had spoken this verse, the gods were delighted, but the demons were displeased. Then Sakka, the lord of the gods, said to Vepacitti, the demon: ‘Speak a verse, Vepacitti.’
translations.sn11.5:6: ‘I see only one way to endure, O Vāsava, that is to see the fault; when a fool thinks, “I will endure the fear,” the foolish one endures, but the wise one does not. The foolish one is led astray, and like a cow, runs away in fear.’
translations.sn11.5:8: ‘Let one think, “I will endure the fear,” or not, the wise one endures with patience, for there is no other benefit greater than patience.’
translations.sn12.11:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. ‘There are, monks, these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings, or for the support of those seeking rebirth. Which four? Physical nutriment, gross or refined; contact as the second; mental intention as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings, or for the support of those seeking rebirth.
translations.sn12.12:1: The Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī. ‘There are, monks, these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings, or for the support of those seeking rebirth. Which four? Physical nutriment, gross or refined; contact as the second; mental intention as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings, or for the support of those seeking rebirth.
translations.sn12.15:1: The Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī. Then Ven. Kaccānagotta went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, having bowed down, sat to one side. As he was sitting there, he said to the Blessed One: ‘“Right view, right view,” is spoken of, Lord. Defined in what way is right view?
translations.sn12.15:2: ‘The world, Kaccāna, for the most part, relies on the dual notions of existence and non-existence. But when one sees the world as it has come to be, with the right understanding of the way it has come to be, then the notions of non-existence with regard to the world do not occur. When one sees the world as it has come to be, with the right understanding of the way it has come to be, then the notions of existence with regard to the world do not occur. The world, Kaccāna, is for the most part fastened by and attached to the notions of existence and non-existence. The world, Kaccāna, is for the most part fastened by and attached to the notions of existence and non-existence. The world, Kaccāna, is for the most part fastened by and attached to the notions of existence and non-existence. One does not take a stand about “my self,” and one does not take a stand about “my self.” One does not take a stand about “my self.” One does not take a stand about “my self.” When one sees that “suffering is arising,” one does not doubt, one does not vacillate, and one's knowledge is not dependent on others. This, Kaccāna, is the extent to which there is right view.’
translations.sn12.17:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground. Now on that occasion the Blessed One had gone for alms in Rājagaha, and after the alms round, on returning from his alms round, he sat down at the root of a tree. The naked ascetic Kassapa saw the Blessed One sitting at the root of the tree from afar, and on seeing him, he went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. After the greetings and polite conversation, he stood to one side and said to the Blessed One: ‘We would like to ask the Blessed One Gotama a question, if the Blessed One would allow us to do so.’ ‘It is not the right time, Kassapa, to ask a question. I have just entered a village and my bowl is full.’
translations.sn12.17:5: ‘He acts, he experiences’ — thus, Kassapa, from the beginning, the deluded declare the self-made suffering to be eternal. ‘Another acts, another experiences’ — thus, Kassapa, the deluded, experiencing feelings, declare the other-made suffering to be annihilated. These two extremes, Kassapa, are not to be adhered to by the Tathagata when teaching the Dhamma: ‘With ignorance as condition, formations; with formations as condition, consciousness … thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. With the complete cessation of ignorance, the cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations, the cessation of consciousness … thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’
translations.sn12.17:6: When this was said, the naked ascetic Kassapa said to the Bhagava: ‘Excellent, Bhante! Excellent, Bhante! Just as if one were to turn upright what had been turned upside down … one would say: “The eye sees forms.” So too, the Bhagava has revealed the Dhamma in many ways. I go to the Bhagava for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of bhikkhus. May I receive the going forth and the higher ordination in the Bhagava’s presence?’
translations.sn12.17:7: ‘Whoever, Kassapa, formerly belonged to another sect and desires the going forth and ordination in this Dhamma and Vinaya, let him wait four months. At the end of the four months, if the bhikkhus are satisfied with him, they will give him the going forth and ordination into bhikkhuhood. And I know individuals by their character.’
translations.sn12.18:1: The Bhagava was dwelling at Savatthi. Then the wanderer Timbaruka approached the Bhagava; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Bhagava. Having exchanged greetings, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the wanderer Timbaruka said to the Bhagava:
