translations.sn12.18:4: ‘That feeling, that experiencer’ — thus, Timbaruka, from the beginning, the deluded declare the self-made pleasure and pain to be eternal. ‘Another feeling, another experiencer’ — thus, Timbaruka, the deluded, experiencing feelings, declare the other-made pleasure and pain to be annihilated. These two extremes, Timbaruka, are not to be adhered to by the Tathagata when teaching the Dhamma: ‘With ignorance as condition, formations; with formations as condition, consciousness … thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. With the complete cessation of ignorance, the cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations, the cessation of consciousness … thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’
translations.sn12.19:1: The Bhagava was dwelling at Savatthi. ‘This body, bhikkhus, has arisen dependent on ignorance, shackled by craving. And this name-and-form, external and internal, has arisen dependent on this duality. Dependent on the duality, contact; dependent on contact, the six sense bases. The fool, contacted by these, experiences pleasure and pain, or something else among these.’
translations.sn12.19:2: ‘This body, bhikkhus, has arisen dependent on ignorance, shackled by craving. And this name-and-form, external and internal, has arisen dependent on this duality. Dependent on the duality, contact; dependent on contact, the six sense bases. The wise person, contacted by these, experiences pleasure and pain, or something else among these.’
translations.sn12.19:3: ‘What distinction, bhikkhus, what superiority, what difference is there between the wise person and the fool?’ ‘We have the Bhagava as our root, Bhante, the Bhagava as our guide, the Bhagava as our resort. May the Bhagava explain the meaning of what has been said. The bhikkhus will listen.’
translations.sn12.19:5: ‘The body, bhikkhus, of one enveloped in ignorance and shackled by craving has arisen. That ignorance of the fool is not abandoned, that craving is not removed. Why is that? The fool does not practice the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering. Therefore, with the breakup of the body, the fool comes under the control of the body; not having fully understood, the fool does not escape from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. I say that the fool does not escape from suffering.’
translations.sn12.23:5: ‘And what, bhikkhus, is the proximate cause of craving? It is to be said: “feeling.” … It is to be said: “contact.” … It is to be said: “the six sense bases.” … It is to be said: “name-and-form.” … It is to be said: “consciousness.” … It is to be said: “formations.” I say that formations are the proximate cause, not a remote cause. And what, bhikkhus, is the proximate cause of formations? It is to be said: “ignorance.”’
translations.sn12.23:6: ‘Thus, bhikkhus, ignorance is the proximate cause of formations, formations are the proximate cause of consciousness, consciousness is the proximate cause of name-and-form, name-and-form is the proximate cause of the six sense bases, the six sense bases are the proximate cause of contact, contact is the proximate cause of feeling, feeling is the proximate cause of craving, craving is the proximate cause of clinging, clinging is the proximate cause of existence, existence is the proximate cause of birth, birth is the proximate cause of suffering, suffering is the proximate cause of faith, faith is the proximate cause of joy, joy is the proximate cause of rapture, rapture is the proximate cause of tranquility, tranquility is the proximate cause of happiness, happiness is the proximate cause of concentration, concentration is the proximate cause of the knowledge and vision of things as they really are, the knowledge and vision of things as they really are is the proximate cause of disenchantment, disenchantment is the proximate cause of dispassion, dispassion is the proximate cause of liberation, liberation is the proximate cause of the knowledge of destruction.’
translations.sn12.23:7: ‘Just as, bhikkhus, the rain that falls on the upper reaches of a mountain flows down, filling the mountain clefts, gullies, and channels, and these, filled, fill the small rivers, and the small rivers, filled, fill the large rivers, and the large rivers, filled, fill the great ocean.’
translations.sn12.25:1: The Bhagava was dwelling at Savatthi. Then, in the evening, the Venerable Bhumiya, having emerged from seclusion, approached the Venerable Sariputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sariputta. Having exchanged greetings, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Bhumiya said to the Venerable Sariputta:
translations.sn12.25:10: ‘If, friend Ananda, there is a body, there arises, internally, a pleasant or painful feeling due to a deliberate act of body. If, friend Ananda, there is speech, there arises, internally, a pleasant or painful feeling due to a deliberate act of speech. If, friend Ananda, there is mind, there arises, internally, a pleasant or painful feeling due to a deliberate act of mind, due to ignorance.’
translations.sn12.25:11: Ananda, does one generate volitional formations in the body, depending on which pleasure and pain arise internally? Or do others generate volitional formations in the body, depending on which pleasure and pain arise internally? Does one generate volitional formations in the body while being mindful, depending on which pleasure and pain arise internally? Or does one generate volitional formations in the body while being unmindful, depending on which pleasure and pain arise internally?
translations.sn12.25:2: Some ascetics and brahmins, friend Sāriputta, declare that pleasure and pain are self-made. Some ascetics and brahmins declare that pleasure and pain are made by others. Some ascetics and brahmins declare that pleasure and pain are both self-made and made by others. Some ascetics and brahmins declare that pleasure and pain are made neither by self nor by others, but are spontaneously arisen. Here, friend Sāriputta, what does the Blessed One say, what does he teach, how should we explain it so that we do not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is not true, do not attribute to him what he did not say, and speak in accordance with the Dhamma, and so that no fellow follower of the Dhamma will be led to criticise our explanation?
translations.sn12.25:3: The Blessed One has said, friend, that pleasure and pain are dependently arisen. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact. If one explains it in this way, one explains it in accordance with the Blessed One's words, does not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is not true, and speaks in accordance with the Dhamma, and no fellow follower of the Dhamma will be led to criticise such an explanation.
translations.sn12.25:4: In this case, friend, those ascetics and brahmins who declare that pleasure and pain are self-made, that too is dependent on contact. And those who declare that pleasure and pain are made by others, that too is dependent on contact. And those who declare that pleasure and pain are both self-made and made by others, that too is dependent on contact. And those who declare that pleasure and pain are made neither by self nor by others, but are spontaneously arisen, that too is dependent on contact.
translations.sn12.25:5: In this case, friend, those ascetics and brahmins who declare that pleasure and pain are self-made, they must feel it apart from contact. But that is not possible. And those who declare that pleasure and pain are made by others, they must feel it apart from contact. But that is not possible. And those who declare that pleasure and pain are both self-made and made by others, they must feel it apart from contact. But that is not possible. And those who declare that pleasure and pain are made neither by self nor by others, but are spontaneously arisen, they must feel it apart from contact. But that is not possible.
translations.sn12.25:6: Then Venerable Ānanda heard this conversation between Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Bhūmiya. Then Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, bowed down to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Ānanda reported the entire conversation between Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Bhūmiya to the Blessed One.
translations.sn12.25:7: Well said, well said, Ānanda, Sāriputta has explained it correctly. I have said that pleasure and pain are dependently arisen. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact. If one explains it in this way, one explains it in accordance with my words, does not misrepresent me with what is not true, and speaks in accordance with the Dhamma, and no fellow follower of the Dhamma will be led to criticise such an explanation.
translations.sn12.2:11: And what, monks, is name-and-form? Feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention - this is called name. The four great elements and the form derived from them - this is called form. This is name, this is form. This, monks, is called name-and-form.
translations.sn12.2:12: And what, monks, is consciousness? These six are classes of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. This, monks, is called consciousness.
translations.sn12.2:13: And what, monks, are the volitional formations? There are three volitional formations: bodily volitional formation, verbal volitional formation, and mental volitional formation. These, monks, are called the volitional formations.
translations.sn12.2:14: And what, monks, is ignorance? Not knowing suffering, not knowing the origin of suffering, not knowing the cessation of suffering, and not knowing the way leading to the cessation of suffering - this, monks, is called ignorance.
translations.sn12.2:5: And what, monks, is becoming? There are three kinds of becoming: sensual becoming, form becoming, and formless becoming. This, monks, is called becoming.
translations.sn12.2:6: And what, monks, is clinging? There are four kinds of clinging: sensual clinging, view clinging, practice clinging, and self clinging. This, monks, is called clinging.
translations.sn12.31:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī. Then the Blessed One addressed Venerable Sāriputta: 'I have said this, Sāriputta, in the Pārāyana, the question of Ajita:
translations.sn12.31:2: 'Those who are skilled in the doctrine, and those who are trainees here; I ask about their deportment, tell me, O Mārisa'
translations.sn12.31:3: How, Sāriputta, should the meaning of this brief statement be explained in detail?
translations.sn12.31:7: 'Do you see, Sāriputta, what is real as it really is?' 'Yes, venerable sir, one who sees what is real as it really is, sees it with proper understanding. Having seen what is real as it really is with proper understanding, one practises for the disenchantment, the fading away, and the cessation of what is real. One sees the origin of what is real with proper understanding. One sees the origin of what is real with proper understanding, and practises for the disenchantment, the fading away, and the cessation of the origin of what is real. One sees the cessation of the origin of what is real with proper understanding. One sees the cessation of the origin of what is real with proper understanding, and practises for the disenchantment, the fading away, and the cessation of the cessation of the origin of what is real. Thus, venerable sir, one is a trainee.'
translations.sn12.31:8: And how, venerable sir, is a conditioned phenomenon? 'It has come to be,' one sees it as it really is with proper wisdom. Having seen it as it really is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with it, detached from it, freed from it, and independent of it. The same with the origin of nutriment: one sees it as it really is with proper wisdom. Having seen it as it really is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with it, detached from it, freed from it, and independent of it. The same with the cessation of nutriment: one sees it as it really is with proper wisdom. Having seen it as it really is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with it, detached from it, freed from it, and independent of it. Thus, venerable sir, is a conditioned phenomenon.
translations.sn12.35:1: The Buddha was staying near Savatthi. 'With ignorance as condition, formations arise; with formations as condition, consciousness arises... Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.' When this was said, a certain monk asked the Buddha: 'What is aging-and-death, and whose is this aging-and-death?' 'This is not a question to be asked,' the Buddha replied. 'If anyone were to say,
translations.sn12.35:2: What, venerable sir, is birth, and what is the origin of birth?
translations.sn12.38:1: Whatever one intends, whatever one plans, whatever one dwells on, that becomes the basis for the persistence of consciousness. With a basis, there is a support for consciousness. When consciousness has a support and grows, there is the production of future birth. With the production of future birth, there are aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair. This is the origin of the entire mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.38:2: If one does not intend and does not plan, but dwells on something, that becomes the basis for the persistence of consciousness. With a basis, there is a support for consciousness. When consciousness has a support and grows, there is the production of future birth. With the production of future birth, there are aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair. This is the origin of the entire mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.35:4: What, venerable sir, are formations, and what is the origin of formations?
translations.sn12.35:7: With the complete cessation of ignorance, the things that are cankered, that are corrupted, that are defiled are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm tree whose head has been destroyed, unable to arise in the future.
translations.sn12.35:3: What, venerable sir, is becoming, and what is the origin of becoming?
translations.sn12.35:5: With the complete cessation of ignorance, the things that are cankered, that are corrupted, that are defiled are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm tree whose head has been destroyed, unable to arise in the future. 'What is aging and death, and what is the origin of aging and death?' or 'Is aging and death one thing, and its origin another?' or 'Is the soul one thing, and the body another?' All these things are abandoned.
translations.sn12.44:1: I will teach you, monks, the origin and the passing away of the world. Listen and pay attention, I will speak.
translations.sn12.44:2: And what, monks, is the origin of the world? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, there is feeling; with feeling as condition, there is craving; with craving as condition, there is clinging; with clinging as condition, there is becoming; with becoming as condition, there is birth; with birth as condition, there is aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. This, monks, is the origin of the world.
translations.sn12.44:3: Dependent on the ear and sounds, ear-consciousness arises... Dependent on the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, there is feeling... With birth as condition, there is aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. This, monks, is the origin of the world.
translations.sn12.44:4: And what, monks, is the cessation of the world? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, there is feeling; with feeling as condition, there is craving. But with the complete fading away and cessation of that craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases... and so the complete cessation of the aggregate of suffering occurs. This, monks, is the cessation of the world.
translations.sn12.46:1: The Buddha was staying near Savatthi. Then a certain brahmin approached the Buddha, exchanged greetings, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the brahmin said to the Buddha:
translations.sn12.46:2: 'Does the one who acts also experience the result?' 'The one who acts also experiences the result,' monks, this is one extreme.
translations.sn12.46:3: 'Or does another act and another experience the result?' 'Another acts and another experiences the result,' monks, this is the second extreme. Without taking up either of these extremes, the Tathagata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: 'With ignorance as condition, formations; with formations as condition, consciousness... and so the origin of the aggregate of suffering occurs. With the complete fading away and cessation of ignorance, formations cease; with the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases... and so the cessation of the aggregate of suffering occurs.'
translations.sn12.51:10: He experiences a pleasant feeling, knowing it as impermanent, knowing it as not to be clung to, knowing it as not to be delighted in. He experiences a painful feeling, knowing it as impermanent, knowing it as not to be clung to, knowing it as not to be delighted in. He experiences a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, knowing it as impermanent, knowing it as not to be clung to, knowing it as not to be delighted in. He experiences a pleasant feeling, detached from it. He experiences a painful feeling, detached from it. He experiences a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, detached from it.
translations.sn12.51:11: When experiencing a feeling limited to the body, he knows it as limited to the body. When experiencing a feeling limited to life, he knows it as limited to life. With the breakup of the body, after life has ended, all his feelings will have disappeared, and his body will have lain down.
translations.sn12.51:12: Just as a man might take a hot pot out of a kiln and put it down on a level surface, where the heat would gradually dissipate, and the pot would eventually become cool. In the same way, a monk experiences a feeling limited to the body, knowing it as limited to the body... With the breakup of the body, after life has ended, all his feelings will have disappeared, and his body will have lain down.
translations.sn12.51:13: 'What do you think, monks? Can a monk who has eliminated the corruptions create a meritorious formation, a demeritorious formation, or an imperturbable formation?' 'No, sir.'
translations.sn12.51:14: 'Or is it the case that, in the complete absence of formations, consciousness would still be discerned?' 'No, sir.'
translations.sn12.51:2: 'How far, monks, should a monk investigate in order to completely understand suffering?' 'The Blessed One is our teacher, the Dhamma is our guide. Please, sir, explain this matter, and the monks will listen and remember it.' 'Listen, monks, and pay attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, sir,' the monks replied.
translations.sn12.51:4: He understands aging-and-death, understands the origin of aging-and-death, understands the cessation of aging-and-death, and understands the path leading to the cessation of aging-and-death. Being thus practiced, he practices in accordance with the Dhamma; this is called a monk who is fully and utterly practicing for the complete destruction of suffering, for the cessation of aging-and-death.
translations.sn12.51:5: Investigating further, he investigates: 'What is the origin of this birth? What is its cause? What is its origin? What is its condition? When what exists does birth exist, and when what does not exist does birth not exist?' Investigating in this way, he understands: 'Birth has existence as its origin, the origin of birth is existence, existence is the condition of birth; when existence exists, birth exists, and when existence does not exist, birth does not exist.'
translations.sn12.51:6: He perceives birth and he perceives the origin of birth, he perceives the cessation of birth, and the path leading to the cessation of birth; thus he is a practitioner who lives according to the teachings, and this is called a monk who has fully and utterly practiced for the sake of the complete cessation of suffering, for the cessation of birth.
translations.sn12.51:7: Then, investigating further, he investigates: 'What is the origin of this existence? ... What is the origin of this clinging? ... What is the origin of this craving? ... What is the origin of this feeling? ... What is the origin of this contact? ... What is the origin of this sixfold base? ... What is the origin of this name-and-form? ... What is the origin of this consciousness? ... What are the origins, conditions, and arisings of these formations? In what do they arise, and in what do they not arise?' Investigating in this way, he understands: 'Formations arise from ignorance, are conditioned by ignorance, and have ignorance as their origin and cause; when ignorance exists, formations exist, and when ignorance does not exist, formations do not exist.'
translations.sn12.51:8: He perceives the formations and he perceives the origin of the formations, he perceives the cessation of the formations, and the path leading to the cessation of the formations; thus he is a practitioner who lives according to the teachings, and this is called a monk who has fully and utterly practiced for the sake of the complete cessation of suffering, for the cessation of formations.
translations.sn12.51:9: A person, monks, who is immersed in ignorance, creates a meritorious formation, and his consciousness is headed for merit. He creates a demeritorious formation, and his consciousness is headed for demerit. He creates an imperturbable formation, and his consciousness is headed for imperturbability. But when a monk's ignorance has been abandoned and knowledge has arisen, he does not create a meritorious formation, nor a demeritorious formation, nor an imperturbable formation. Not creating, not willing, he does not cling to anything in the world; not clinging, he is not anxious, and without anxiety, he personally attains Nibbana. 'My birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no further becoming,' he knows.
translations.sn12.52:2: Suppose, monks, a large tree with a trunk, branches, and leaves stands for a hundred years, or two hundred years, or three hundred years, or four hundred years. A man would from time to time remove the dried leaves, dried branches, and dried trunk. Similarly, a large mass of suffering stands for a long time, and a man would from time to time remove the dried leaves of suffering, the dried branches of suffering, and the dried trunk of suffering. In the same way, monks, when one dwells observing the attractiveness of things that can be clung to, craving increases. Craving conditions clinging ... and thus there arises the entire mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.52:3: When one dwells observing the unattractiveness of things that can be clung to, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases; with the cessation of becoming, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. And thus there is the cessation of the entire mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.55:1: He was staying at Savatthi. 'When one dwells observing the attractiveness of things that can be clung to, craving increases. Craving conditions clinging ... and thus there arises the entire mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.55:2: Suppose, monks, a large tree. Its roots, its trunk, its branches, and its leaves all receive nourishment. Similarly, a large mass of suffering stands for a long time, and it is nourished by clinging. In the same way, monks, when one dwells observing the attractiveness of things that can be clung to, craving increases. Craving conditions clinging ... and thus there arises the entire mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.55:3: When one dwells observing the unattractiveness of things that can be clung to, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases ... and thus there is the cessation of the entire mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.61:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Savatthi in Jeta's Grove, Anathapindika's monastery. 'An untaught ordinary person, monks, does not feel disgust with this body, composed of the four great elements, and does not become dispassionate towards it, and is not liberated from it. What is the reason? This body, composed of the four great elements, has the nature of decay and dissolution, and it has the nature of being taken up and put down.
translations.sn12.61:2: And this, monks, which is called mind, or consciousness, the untaught ordinary person is not able to feel disgust with it, and is not able to become dispassionate towards it, and is not able to be liberated from it. What is the reason? For a long time, monks, the untaught ordinary person has been attached to it, has been obsessed with it, and has been infatuated with it, thinking: 'This is mine, this is I, this is my self.'
translations.sn12.61:3: It would be better, monks, for the untaught ordinary person to regard this body, composed of the four great elements, as the self, rather than the mind. What is the reason? This body, composed of the four great elements, stands for one year, or two years, or three years, or four years, or five years, or ten years, or twenty years, or thirty years, or forty years, or fifty years, or a hundred years, or more.
translations.sn12.61:5: There, monks, a learned noble disciple reflects thus: 'When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases — that is, with ignorance as condition, formations; with formations as condition, consciousness … and so on. Thus, the entire mass of suffering originates. With the complete cessation of ignorance, formations cease; with the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases … and so on. Thus, the entire mass of suffering ceases.'
translations.sn12.62:3: There, monks, a learned noble disciple reflects thus: 'When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases.' A pleasant feeling, monks, arises in dependence on a pleasant contact. With the cessation of that pleasant contact, the pleasant feeling that arose in dependence on it ceases and subsides. A painful feeling, monks, arises in dependence on a painful contact. With the cessation of that painful contact, the painful feeling that arose in dependence on it ceases and subsides. A neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, monks, arises in dependence on a neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact. With the cessation of that neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that arose in dependence on it ceases and subsides.
translations.sn12.62:4: Just as, monks, when two sticks are rubbed together, heat is generated and fire is produced. And when those two sticks are separated, the heat that was produced and the fire that was produced cease and subside. So too, monks, a pleasant feeling arises in dependence on a pleasant contact. With the cessation of that pleasant contact, the pleasant feeling that arose in dependence on it ceases and subsides … and so on. A painful feeling arises in dependence on a painful contact. A neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises in dependence on a neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact. With the cessation of that neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that arose in dependence on it ceases and subsides.
translations.sn12.63:3: What do you think, monks? Do you eat food for the sake of pleasure, or for the sake of intoxication, or for the sake of beautification, or for the sake of adornment?
translations.sn12.63:4: And how, monks, should one regard the nutriment of contact? Suppose a cow were standing on a field, and the creatures that depend on the cow would feed on it. If the cow were to stand on a tree, the creatures that depend on the cow would feed on it. If the cow were to stand on water, the creatures that depend on the cow would feed on it. If the cow were to stand on air, the creatures that depend on the cow would feed on it. Wherever the cow might stand, the creatures that depend on it would feed on it. So too, monks, I say that one should regard the nutriment of contact. When one has fully understood the nutriment of contact, the three feelings are fully understood. I say that there is nothing further to be done by a noble disciple who has fully understood the three feelings.
translations.sn12.63:5: And how, monks, should one regard the nutriment of mental volition? Suppose a man were to be taken and thrown into a pit of glowing embers. He would wriggle and struggle, but the more he wriggles and struggles, the more he would get burned. So too, monks, I say that one should regard the nutriment of mental volition. When one has fully understood the nutriment of mental volition, the three kinds of craving are fully understood. I say that there is nothing further to be done by a noble disciple who has fully understood the three kinds of craving.
translations.sn12.64:2: If, monks, there is passion, delight, and craving for the nutriment of edible food, consciousness becomes established and grows. Where consciousness becomes established and grows, there is a descent of name-and-form. Where there is a descent of name-and-form, there is an increase of formations. Where there is an increase of formations, there is future birth, aging, and death. Where there is future birth, aging, and death, that is a source of suffering, a source of despair, I say.
translations.sn12.64:4: Just as, monks, a laundryman or a dyer, with dye-stuffs of various kinds, if he wants to dye a cloth black, first makes it blue; if he wants to dye it red, first makes it yellow; if he wants to dye it of a dark brown color, first makes it of a brown color; if he wants to dye it of a yellow color, first makes it green; if he wants to dye it of a dark green color, first makes it blue-green; if he wants to dye it of a crimson color, first makes it of a red color; if he wants to dye it of a brown color, first makes it of a dark brown color; if he wants to make a picture of a man or a woman, first makes the outline on the wall or on the cloth or on the paper; in the same way, monks, if there is passion, delight, and craving for nutriment, consciousness becomes established there and grows. Wherever consciousness becomes established and grows, there is a descent of name-and-form. Where there is a descent of name-and-form, there is an increase of volitional formations. Where there is an increase of volitional formations, there is the production of future birth and future death. Where there is the production of future birth and future death, there is the production of future birth, aging, and death. Where there is the production of future birth, aging, and death, I say that is with sorrow, with lamentation, with pain, with grief, and with despair.
translations.sn12.64:6: Just as, monks, a laundryman or a dyer, with dye-stuffs of various kinds, if he does not want to dye a cloth black, does not make it blue; if he does not want to dye it red, does not make it yellow; if he does not want to dye it of a dark brown color, does not make it of a brown color; if he does not want to dye it of a yellow color, does not make it green; if he does not want to dye it of a dark green color, does not make it blue-green; if he does not want to dye it of a crimson color, does not make it of a red color; if he does not want to dye it of a brown color, does not make it of a dark brown color; if he does not want to make a picture of a man or a woman, does not make the outline on the wall or on the cloth or on the paper; in the same way, monks, if there is no passion, no delight, and no craving for nutriment, consciousness does not become established there and does not grow. Wherever consciousness does not become established and does not grow, there is no descent of name-and-form. Where there is no descent of name-and-form, there is no increase of volitional formations. Where there is no increase of volitional formations, there is no production of future birth and future death. Where there is no production of future birth and future death, there is no production of future birth, aging, and death. Where there is no production of future birth, aging, and death, I say that is without sorrow, without lamentation, without pain, without grief, and without despair.
translations.sn12.64:8: Just as, monks, when the sun rises in the east, west, south, or north, and its rays enter through a window or a crack in the wall, they do not stand on the western wall, do they? 'No, venerable sir.' 'If they do not stand on the western wall, where do they stand?' 'On the ground, venerable sir.' 'If they do not stand on the ground, where do they stand?' 'On the water, venerable sir.' 'If they do not stand on the water, where do they stand?' 'They do not stand, venerable sir.' In the same way, monks, if there is no passion, no delight, and no craving for nutriment ...
translations.sn12.65:1: I lived at Savatthi. Before my enlightenment, when I was still an unenlightened Bodhisatta, the thought occurred to me: 'This world is beset by birth, aging, and death. But it does not know the escape from suffering, from aging and death. How can the escape from this suffering, from aging and death, be known?' Then it occurred to me: 'What is the cause of aging and death? What is the condition for aging and death?' Then, through careful attention, I had a breakthrough, an understanding: 'Aging and death arise from birth; they have birth as their condition.'
translations.sn12.65:3: Then the thought occurred to me: 'This consciousness does not go beyond name-and-form; it is tied to name-and-form. To the extent that name-and-form exist, consciousness exists, conditioned by name-and-form; name-and-form exist, conditioned by consciousness; the six sense bases exist, conditioned by name-and-form; contact exists, conditioned by the six sense bases ... Thus the entire mass of suffering arises.' 'Arising, arising' - this knowledge, this vision, this understanding, this light, this wisdom arose in me regarding things I had not heard before.
translations.sn12.65:5: Then the thought occurred to me: 'What is the condition for the existence of consciousness? What is the condition for the cessation of consciousness?' Then, through careful attention, I had a breakthrough, an understanding: 'Consciousness exists when name-and-form exist; consciousness ceases with the cessation of name-and-form.'
translations.sn12.65:6: Then the thought occurred to me: 'I have discovered the path to enlightenment, which is the cessation of name-and-form, the cessation of consciousness; the cessation of consciousness, the cessation of name-and-form; the cessation of name-and-form, the cessation of the six sense bases; the cessation of the six sense bases, the cessation of contact ... Thus the entire mass of suffering ceases.' 'Cessation, cessation' - this knowledge, this vision, this understanding, this light, this wisdom arose in me regarding things I had not heard before.
translations.sn12.65:7: Just as, monks, a man walking in the forest sees an old path, an old road, traveled by people in the past. He follows it and sees an old city, an old capital, inhabited by people in the past, with parks, gardens, ponds, and ramparts, delightful and charming. Then he informs the king or the king's minister: 'Your majesty, I have seen an old path, an old road, traveled by people in the past. I followed it and saw an old city, an old capital ... Please, your majesty, restore that city.' Then the king or the king's minister restores that city. Later on, that city becomes successful, prosperous, filled with people, and well-developed. In the same way, monks, I saw the old path, the old road, traveled by the Fully Enlightened Ones of the past.
translations.sn12.66:1: I have heard that the Blessed One was living in the Kuru country at a town called Kammasadhamma. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Monks.' 'Venerable sir,' the monks replied. The Blessed One said: 'Let us practice mindfulness of the body, monks.' When this was said, a certain monk said to the Blessed One: 'I will practice mindfulness of the body, venerable sir.' 'But how do you practice mindfulness of the body?' The monk replied, but the Blessed One was not pleased with his reply.
translations.sn12.66:2: When this was said, Venerable Ānanda said to the Bhagavā: 'It is time, Bhagavā; it is time, Sugata, for the Bhagavā to explain the intermediate. The monks will listen.', 'Then, Ānanda, listen and pay close attention, I will speak.', 'Yes, Bhante', those monks replied to the Bhagavā. The Bhagavā said:
translations.sn12.66:5: Then, examining further, he examines the intermediate: 'Where does this craving, when it arises, arise? Where does it, when it settles, settle?' He examines and knows thus: 'In the world, the pleasing and charming, that is where craving, when it arises, arises, and that is where, when it settles, it settles. And what in the world is pleasing and charming? The eye in the world is pleasing and charming, that is where craving, when it arises, arises, and that is where, when it settles, it settles. The ear in the world is pleasing and charming... the nose in the world is pleasing and charming... the tongue in the world is pleasing and charming... the body in the world is pleasing and charming... the mind in the world is pleasing and charming, that is where craving, when it arises, arises, and that is where, when it settles, it settles.'
translations.sn12.66:6: Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past saw what is pleasing and charming in the world as permanent, saw it as pleasure, saw it as self, saw it as health, saw it as secure, they increased craving. Those who increased craving increased acquisitions. Those who increased acquisitions increased suffering. Those who increased suffering did not escape from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress, 'they did not escape suffering', I say.
translations.sn12.66:7: Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will see what is pleasing and charming in the world as permanent, will see it as pleasure, will see it as self, will see it as health, will see it as secure, they will increase craving. Those who increase craving will increase acquisitions. Those who increase acquisitions will increase suffering. Those who increase suffering will not escape from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress, 'they will not escape suffering', I say.
translations.sn12.66:8: Whatever ascetics or brahmins at present see what is pleasing and charming in the world as permanent, see it as pleasure, see it as self, see it as health, see it as secure, they increase craving. Those who increase craving increase acquisitions. Those who increase acquisitions increase suffering. Those who increase suffering do not escape from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress, 'they do not escape suffering', I say.
translations.sn12.67:1: On one occasion the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita were dwelling near Bārāṇasī at Isipatana in the Deer Park. Then, in the evening, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita emerged from seclusion and approached the Venerable Sāriputta. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta and, after the exchange, sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita said to the Venerable Sāriputta: 'What, friend Sāriputta, is aging and death self-made, other-made, or both self-made and other-made, or is it without a maker, arisen spontaneously?' 'Aging and death are not self-made, friend Koṭṭhika, nor other-made, nor both self-made and other-made, nor without a maker, arisen spontaneously. But rather, aging and death come from birth.'
translations.sn12.67:2: 'What, friend Sāriputta, is birth self-made, other-made, or both self-made and other-made, or is it without a maker, arisen spontaneously?' 'Birth is not self-made, friend Koṭṭhika, nor other-made, nor both self-made and other-made, nor without a maker, arisen spontaneously. But rather, birth comes from existence.'
translations.sn12.67:4: 'What, friend Sāriputta, is consciousness self-made, other-made, or both self-made and other-made, or is it without a maker, arisen spontaneously?' 'Consciousness is not self-made, friend Koṭṭhika, nor other-made, nor both self-made and other-made, nor without a maker, arisen spontaneously. But rather, consciousness comes from name-and-form.'
translations.sn12.67:5: 'We understand the statement made by the Venerable Sāriputta thus: 'Name-and-form is not self-made, friend Koṭṭhika, nor other-made, nor both self-made and other-made, nor without a maker, arisen spontaneously. But rather, name-and-form comes from consciousness.'
translations.sn12.67:7: How, friend Sāriputta, is the meaning of this statement to be understood?  'I will give you an analogy, friends.  For by means of an analogy, wise men understand the meaning of what has been said.  It is just as if two sheaves of reeds were to stand leaning against each other.  Just so, friend Sāriputta, from name-and-form as condition, consciousness arises; from consciousness as condition, name-and-form; from name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; from the six sense bases as condition, contact ...  Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.  If one were to pull away one of those sheaves of reeds, the other would fall; if one were to pull away the other, the first would fall.  Just so, friend Sāriputta, from the cessation of name-and-form, the cessation of consciousness; from the cessation of consciousness, the cessation of name-and-form; from the cessation of name-and-form, the cessation of the six sense bases; from the cessation of the six sense bases, the cessation of contact ...  Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.67:8: Wonderful, friend Sāriputta!  Marvelous, friend Sāriputta!  This has been well spoken by the venerable Sāriputta.  And we are pleased with the venerable Sāriputta's statement, which is accompanied by these thirty-six grounds.
translations.sn12.68:13: 'Is the venerable Nārada an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed?'  'As to that, friend, I do not know whether I am an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed.  Just as if there were a pool of water, but no water-bird or fish, and a man were to come along, parched and thirsty, and were to look into the pool.  He would know, 'There is water', but he would not stay there.  Just so, friend, I know, 'The cessation of existence is nibbāna', but I am not an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed.
translations.sn12.68:6: 'Is the venerable Musīla an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed?'  To this, the venerable Musīla remained silent.
translations.sn12.69:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Blessed One was living in Sāvatthī, at Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.  There the Blessed One addressed the monks, 'The great ocean, monks, becomes the source of many great rivers; the great rivers become the source of many small rivers; the small rivers become the source of many great streams; the great streams become the source of many small streams.  Just so, monks, ignorance becomes the source of volitional formations; volitional formations become the source of consciousness; consciousness becomes the source of name-and-form; name-and-form becomes the source of the six sense bases; the six sense bases become the source of contact; contact becomes the source of feeling; feeling becomes the source of craving; craving becomes the source of clinging; clinging becomes the source of existence; existence becomes the source of birth; birth becomes the source of aging-and-death.',
translations.sn12.70:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Blessed One was living in Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground.  At that time the Blessed One was honored, respected, revered, and venerated by the people of Rājagaha, who offered him robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines.  The Saṅgha, too, was honored, respected, revered, and venerated by the people of Rājagaha, who offered it robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines.  But the wanderers of other sects were not honored, respected, revered, or venerated by the people of Rājagaha, who did not offer them robes, almsfood, lodgings, or medicines.
translations.sn12.70:10: 'But do you, venerable sirs, know and see those who are freed, who have gone beyond the material and immaterial worlds, and who, having realized them with the body, dwell in them?'  'No, friend.',
translations.sn12.70:11: 'Here, venerable sirs, is a matter that is not clear to us.  Please clarify it for us.'  'We are freed by wisdom, friend.',
translations.sn12.70:12: 'I do not know the meaning of the venerable ones' brief statement.  Please, venerable sirs, explain it to me so that I may understand the meaning of the venerable ones' brief statement.'  'You may or may not understand, friend, but we are freed by wisdom.',
translations.sn12.70:13: Then the venerable Susīma got up from his seat, went to the Blessed One, and, after paying homage to him, sat down to one side.  As he sat there, he reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation that had taken place among the monks.  'First, Susīma, comes knowledge of the truth, and afterwards, knowledge of nibbāna.',
translations.sn12.70:14: 'I do not know, Bhante, the meaning of the Blessed One's brief statement.  Please, Bhante, explain it to me so that I may understand the meaning of the Blessed One's brief statement.'  'You may or may not understand, Susīma, but first comes knowledge of the truth, and afterwards, knowledge of nibbāna.',
translations.sn12.70:16: 'Therefore, Susīma, whatever form, past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'  Whatever feeling, past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'  Whatever perception, whatever volitional formations, past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'  Whatever consciousness, past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'
translations.sn12.70:17: Seeing thus, a noble disciple is disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, they become dispassionate. Through dispassion, they are liberated. When liberated, there is the knowledge that they are liberated. They understand: 'Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming back to any state of being.'
translations.sn12.70:18: 'Do you see, Susima, 'With birth as condition, aging-and-death?' 'Yes, sir.' 'Do you see, Susima, 'With existence as condition, birth?' 'Yes, sir.' 'Do you see, Susima, 'With clinging as condition, existence?' 'Yes, sir.' 'Do you see, Susima, 'With craving as condition, clinging?' 'Yes, sir.' 'With feeling as condition, craving... With contact as condition, feeling... With the six sense bases as condition, contact... With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases... With consciousness as condition, name-and-form... With volitional formations as condition, consciousness... With ignorance as condition, volitional formations, Susima, do you see?' 'Yes, sir.'
translations.sn12.70:2: Now at that time the wanderer Susima was living in Rājagaha with a large group of wanderers. Then the wanderer Susima's group said to him: 'Come, friend Susima, let's live the holy life under the ascetic Gotama. You can master the doctrine and then teach it to us. We can then teach it to the laypeople. In that way, we too will be respected, revered, honored, and venerated, and we will receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites.' 'Yes, friends,' Susima replied, and having agreed to his group, he went to Venerable Ānanda and, on arrival, exchanged courteous greetings with him. After an exchange of friendly greetings, he sat to one side. As he was sitting there, he said to Venerable Ānanda: 'I want to live the holy life in this doctrine and discipline.'
translations.sn12.70:21: 'But do you, Susima, see — by means of the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human — both kinds of sounds, divine and human, whether near or far?' 'No, sir.'
translations.sn12.70:25: 'But do you, Susima, see — by means of the body — those peaceful immaterial deliverances, surpassing forms, which are completely immune to the material world?' 'No, sir.'
translations.sn12.70:27: Then Venerable Susima, having bowed down to the Blessed One's feet, said to him: 'I have committed an offense, sir, in that I was foolish, incompetent, and unskilled, having claimed to be a speaker on the doctrine in this well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya. May the Blessed One please accept my offense as an offense, so that I may restrain myself in the future.'
translations.sn12.70:3: Then Venerable Ānanda, taking Susima the wanderer, went to the Blessed One and, on arrival, bowed down to him and sat to one side. As he was sitting there, he said to the Blessed One: 'This, sir, is the wanderer Susima, who says: 'I want to live the holy life in this doctrine and discipline.' 'Then, Ānanda, let Susima go forth.' There Susima the wanderer received the going forth and the full acceptance in the Blessed One's presence.
translations.sn12.70:5: 'But do you, venerable sirs, see — by means of the various kinds of psychic power — having been one, you become many; having been many, you become one? You appear and vanish; you go unhindered through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through air; you dive in and out of the earth as if it were water; you walk on water as if it were earth; you sit cross-legged in the air like a bird; with your hands you touch and stroke the sun and the moon, so powerful and mighty; you exercise mastery with your body as far as the Brahmā world?' 'No, friend.'
translations.sn12.70:6: 'But do you, venerable sirs, see — by means of the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human — both kinds of sounds, divine and human, whether near or far?' 'No, friend.'
translations.sn12.70:7: 'But do you, venerable sirs, see — by means of the mind — the minds of other beings, other persons, having encompassed them with your own mind? You see a mind with passion and a mind without passion... a mind with aversion and a mind without aversion... a mind with delusion and a mind without delusion... a restricted mind and an expanded mind... a mind that is not composed and a mind that is composed... a mind that is liberated and a mind that is not liberated?' 'No, friend.'
translations.sn12.70:8: 'But do you, venerable sirs, see — by means of the various kinds of recollection of past lives — having recollected your manifold past lives, thus: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of cosmic contraction, many eons of cosmic expansion, many eons of cosmic contraction and expansion: 'There I was, by such a name, by such a clan, by such a caste, by such a food, experiencing such pleasure and pain, with such a life-span; having died there, I was reborn here'?' 'No, friend.'
translations.sn12.70:9: Do you, venerable sirs, having such knowledge, having such vision, with the divine eye, which is pure and surpasses that of humans, see beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good or bad destination, according to their actions? You see beings who are possessed of wrong conduct of body, speech, and mind, who revile the noble ones, who are wrong in their views, who are given to wrong views, who are of wrong actions, and on the break-up of the body, after death, have appeared in a state of woe, in a bad destination, in the lower world, in hell. And you see beings who are possessed of good conduct of body, speech, and mind, who do not revile the noble ones, who are right in their views, who are given to right views, who are of right actions, and on the break-up of the body, after death, have appeared in a good destination, in the heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye, which is pure and surpasses that of humans, you see beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good or bad destination, according to their actions.
translations.sn16.11:1: On one occasion the Venerable Mahākassapa was living in Rājagaha in the Veluvana, the bamboo grove of Kalandaka.
translations.sn16.11:10: Therefore, Kassapa, you should train thus: 'May I have a keen sense of conscience and a keen sense of fear of wrongdoing towards my companions in the holy life, the elders and my peers.' That's how you should train, Kassapa.
translations.sn16.11:11: Therefore, Kassapa, you should train thus: 'Whatever Dhamma teaching I hear that is conducive to the wholesome, I will retain it in mind, attend to it, and examine it with all my mind, and I will hear the Dhamma with a willing ear.' That's how you should train, Kassapa.
translations.sn16.11:12: Therefore, Kassapa, you should train thus: 'May my mindfulness of the body be established and not forgotten.' That's how you should train, Kassapa.
translations.sn16.11:13: Then, venerable sir, the Bhagava, having advised me with this advice, rose from his seat and left. I, venerable sir, having eaten the almsfood in the village of Sarana, set out on a seven-day journey.
translations.sn16.11:14: Then, venerable sir, the Bhagava went by the road to the root of a certain tree and sat down on a prepared seat. Having sat down, the Bhagava said to me: 'This rug made of antelope hide is soft, Kassapa.' 'May the Bhagava accept this rug made of antelope hide out of compassion.' 'Will you wear the worn-out robes, the rag-robes, Kassapa?' 'I will wear them, venerable sir.' So I spread out the rug made of antelope hide for the Bhagava and I wore the worn-out robes, the rag-robes.
translations.sn16.11:17: I, venerable sir, having destroyed the corruptions, having realized the corruption-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having known and realized it for myself in this very life, live having known and realized it. The seven gems, venerable sir, or the eight-gemmed wheel, or the canopy with its thousand spokes, are not worth one-sixteenth of the six higher knowledges.
translations.sn16.11:2: At that time the Venerable Ānanda had three times the number of attendants, and most of them were young monks who had given up their training in the lower teachings.
translations.sn16.11:3: There are three occasions, venerable Kassapa, on which the Bhagava has allowed a meal of three dishes in a family: for the purpose of restraining those of evil desires, for the comfort of the monks, so that they may not be divided by the evil desires of the factions, and for the purpose of helping the families.
translations.sn16.11:4: But what, venerable Ānanda, do you do, wandering with these new monks who are uncontrolled in their senses, who are immoderate in eating, and who are not intent on vigilance? I think you are wandering for the sake of gain, I think you are wandering for the sake of a family. Your retinue is increasing, venerable Ānanda, your new monks are increasing. This young man is not mindful.
translations.sn16.11:6: The nun Thullanandā heard: 'The Venerable Ānanda, the wise one, has been offended by the Venerable Mahākassapa with a young man's words.'
translations.sn16.11:7: Then the nun Thullanandā, being displeased, spoke these words: 'What has the Venerable Mahākassapa, who is a former member of another sect, to do with offending the Venerable Ānanda, the wise one, with a young man's words?' The Venerable Mahākassapa heard the nun Thullanandā speaking these words.
translations.sn16.11:8: Then the Venerable Mahākassapa said to the Venerable Ānanda: 'The bhikkhuni Thullanandā spoke rashly, without reflection. As for me, since I shaved my head, put on these yellow robes, and went forth from home to homelessness, I do not know of any other teacher except the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Awakened One. Formerly, when I was a layman, it occurred to me: 'Life in a home is confining, a path of dust; the life of a bhikkhu is the open air. It is not easy, living in a home, to lead the fully perfected, totally pure holy life. What if I were to shave my head, put on these yellow robes, and go forth from home to homelessness?' And so, I shaved my head, put on these yellow robes, and went forth from home to homelessness, out of faith in the arahants in this world.
translations.sn16.13:2: Just as, Kassapa, the disappearance of gold does not occur as long as no counterfeit of gold has appeared in the world, but when a counterfeit of gold has appeared, then the disappearance of gold occurs, so too, Kassapa, the disappearance of the good Dhamma does not occur as long as no counterfeit of the good Dhamma has appeared, but when a counterfeit of the good Dhamma has appeared, then the disappearance of the good Dhamma occurs.
translations.sn16.13:4: There are, Kassapa, these five things that conduce to the decline and disappearance of the good Dhamma. What five? Here, Kassapa, bhikkhus, bhikkhunis, male and female lay followers live without respect, without reverence for the Teacher, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and without respect for the training. These five things, Kassapa, conduce to the decline and disappearance of the good Dhamma.
translations.sn16.2:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Venerable Mahākassapa and the Venerable Sāriputta were living near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground. Then, in the late afternoon, the Venerable Sāriputta emerged from his seclusion and approached the Venerable Mahākassapa. On arriving, he exchanged greetings with Mahākassapa and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, he said to Mahākassapa: 'It is said, friend Kassapa,
translations.sn21.10:1: At one time the Buddha was staying in the bamboo grove in Rājagaha. At that time a certain senior monk, living alone, was a praise-winner among those living alone. He would enter a village alone for alms, would return alone, would sit alone in a private place, and would walk alone on his walking path. Then a number of monks approached the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those monks said to the Buddha: "There is, sir, a certain senior monk, living alone, who is a praise-winner among those living alone."
translations.sn16.2:3: And how, friend, is one shameless? Here, a monk does not feel shame at unarisen unwholesome unskillful phenomena arising in him, which would be unbeneficial and stressful. He does not feel shame at arisen unwholesome unskillful phenomena not being abandoned in him, which would be unbeneficial and stressful. He does not feel shame at unarisen wholesome skillful phenomena not arising in him, which would be unbeneficial and stressful. He does not feel shame at arisen wholesome skillful phenomena ceasing in him, which would be unbeneficial and stressful. That's how one is shameless. That's how one is without shame or fear of wrongdoing, and incapable of enlightenment, incapable of nibbāna, and incapable of attaining the unsurpassed, safe-from-temptation security.
translations.sn21.10:3: "I say, elder, that there is no such thing as living alone. But, elder, listen to and pay attention to how one lives alone in a full and thorough way: whatever is past is abandoned, whatever is future is rejected, and in the present, one's own existence is clearly seen with desire removed. That's how one lives alone in a full and thorough way."
translations.sn21.1:1: I have heard that at one time the Buddha was staying in Sāvatthī at Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. There Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the monks: "Friends, monks..." "Yes, friend," the monks replied to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
translations.sn16.2:4: And how, friend, is one ardent? Here, a monk feels a sense of urgency at unarisen unwholesome unskillful phenomena arising in him, which would be unbeneficial and stressful. He feels a sense of urgency at arisen unwholesome unskillful phenomena not being abandoned in him, which would be unbeneficial and stressful. He feels a sense of urgency at unarisen wholesome skillful phenomena not arising in him... He feels a sense of urgency at arisen wholesome skillful phenomena ceasing in him... That's how one is ardent.
translations.sn16.5:1: I have heard that... the Buddha was staying in Rājagaha in the bamboo grove. Then Venerable Mahākassapa approached the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Buddha said to Venerable Mahākassapa: "You are old now, Kassapa, and these worn-out, tattered, and frayed robes are not suitable for you. So accept robes from householders, and also eat their invitations. And live near me."
translations.sn21.1:2: There I, friend, being alone and withdrawn from the crowd, had this thought: 'What is noble silence? What is noble silence?' Then it occurred to me: 'A monk who has attained the second jhana, with the subsiding of thinking and pondering, and has inner peace, one-pointedness of mind, without thinking and pondering, and has pleasure and happiness born of concentration, dwells in this way. This is called noble silence.' I, friend, having attained the second jhana, with the subsiding of thinking and pondering, and having inner peace, one-pointedness of mind, without thinking and pondering, and having pleasure and happiness born of concentration, dwelt in this way. As I was dwelling in this dwelling, perceptions associated with thinking arose in me.
translations.sn21.2:1: At Savatthi. Then the Venerable Sariputta addressed the monks: 'Friends, monks.' 'Friend,' those monks replied to the Venerable Sariputta. The Venerable Sariputta said:
translations.sn21.2:2: 'There I, friend, being alone and withdrawn from the crowd, had this thought:
translations.sn21.3:6: ‘Sāriputta’s wisdom, his virtue, and his peace; and also a monk who has gone to the other shore, that would be the highest’.”
translations.sn21.8:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Nanda, the Buddha’s nephew, having wrapped his robe around him, having put on his bowl, and having saluted the Buddha, sat down to one side. The Buddha said to the Venerable Nanda: “It is not fitting for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness, Nanda, that you should wear a robe that has been wrapped around you, or that you should anoint your eyes, or that you should carry a staff. It is fitting for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness, Nanda, that you should live in the wilderness, and that you should be an almsman, and that you should wear rag-robes, and that you should be dependent on others for your food, and that you should be unrestrained in your senses.”
translations.sn21.3:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Buddha was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. At that time the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna were dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground, in a single dwelling. Then the Venerable Sāriputta, having emerged from his daytime meditation, went to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Having gone there, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Having finished the exchange of greetings and friendly conversation, he sat down to one side. The Venerable Sāriputta said to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
translations.sn21.6:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Lakuṇḍakabhaddiya went to the Buddha. The Buddha saw the Venerable Lakuṇḍakabhaddiya coming from afar. Having seen him, he said to the monks: “Do you see, monks, that monk coming, ugly, unsightly, and repulsive to the monks, with a distorted body?” “Yes, sir.” “This monk, monks, is of great power and great might, and the attainment that he has not yet attained is not easily attainable. For the sake of which clansmen go forth from the household life into homelessness, that is the highest goal of the holy life, which he has seen for himself, and having known and realized it, he dwells having attained it.”
translations.sn21.6:2: “Swans, peacocks, and pheasants, and elephants, and horses, and deer; all are afraid of the lion, there is no comparison with his body.”
translations.sn21.3:3: “Here, friend, I asked the Buddha: ‘What is meant by “one who has aroused energy”, venerable sir? How far does one who has aroused energy go?’ The Buddha said to me: ‘Here, Moggallāna, a monk dwells having aroused energy—let his skin, sinew, and bones remain, let his flesh and blood dry up, and yet he will not lose his energy as long as his body will allow him to do what a man can do with his energy.’ That, friend, is how far one who has aroused energy goes.” That is how my discussion with the Buddha went.”
translations.sn21.3:2: “Your faculties are clear, friend Moggallāna; your facial complexion is pure and bright, and you are living in a peaceful state today.” “Today, friend, I lived in a peaceful state. And I also had a discussion about the teaching.” “With whom did the Venerable Moggallāna have a discussion about the teaching?” “I had a discussion about the teaching with the Buddha.” “But the Buddha is far away, friend, dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Did the Venerable Moggallāna go to the Buddha through psychic power, or did the Buddha go to the Venerable Moggallāna through psychic power?” “I did not go to the Buddha through psychic power, friend, nor did the Buddha come to me through psychic power. But as far as the Buddha is concerned, my divine eye is purified, and my divine ear is also purified. And as far as I am concerned, the Buddha’s divine eye is also purified, and his divine ear is also purified.” “How did the Venerable Moggallāna have a discussion about the teaching with the Buddha?”
translations.sn21.8:2: “When shall I see Nanda, living in the wilderness, wearing rag-robes, and dependent on others for his food, and unrestrained in his senses?”
translations.sn21.9:1: He was living in Savatthi. Then the Venerable Tissa, the Buddha's nephew, approached the Buddha, and after paying homage to him, sat down to one side, unhappy, disappointed, and crying. The Buddha said to the Venerable Tissa: 'Why are you sitting to one side, unhappy, disappointed, and crying?' 'The monks, sir, are harassing me with their words and I am not able to reply to them.', 'You, Tissa, speak but are not able to reply. It is not fitting for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith from the household life to the homeless life, that you speak but are not able to reply. It is fitting for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith from the household life to the homeless life, that you speak and are able to reply.'
translations.sn22.100:2: Do you see, monks, the movement of the mind called 'mind'?
translations.sn22.100:3: I do not see, monks, any other single thing that is as much responsible for the corruption of beings as the mind. The mind is corrupted by lust, hatred, and delusion. Therefore, monks, the mind should be constantly examined: 'For a long time this mind has been corrupted by lust, hatred, and delusion.' The corruption of the mind corrupts beings; the purification of the mind purifies beings.
translations.sn22.101:1: The teaching of Savatthi. 'I teach, monks, the destruction of the corruptions only to one who knows and sees, not to one who does not know and does not see. And what is it, monks, that one who knows and sees should know and see for the destruction of the corruptions? 'Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the cessation of form; such is feeling ... such is perception ... such is mental formations ... such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the cessation of consciousness.' Thus, monks, one who knows and sees should know and see for the destruction of the corruptions.
translations.sn22.101:2: When a monk who is not devoted to development lives without exerting himself, the thought may occur to him: 'O that, without having to rely on others, my mind might be free from the corruptions!' But his mind is not freed from the corruptions. Why is that? Because of his failure to develop (the path). What is the failure to develop? The failure to develop the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of success, the five spiritual faculties, the five spiritual powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
translations.sn22.101:3: Just as a hen, monks, has eight or ten or twelve eggs, but if she does not sit on them, or hatch them, or keep them warm, they will not develop and will not produce chicks. Even if the hen wishes: 'May my chicks emerge from the eggs, peck at the shell with their beaks, and come out,' still the chicks will not emerge. Why is that? Because the hen has not sat on the eggs, or hatched them, or kept them warm. In the same way, monks, when a monk who is not devoted to development lives without exerting himself, the thought may occur to him: 'O that, without having to rely on others, my mind might be free from the corruptions!' But his mind is not freed from the corruptions. Why is that? Because of his failure to develop (the path). What is the failure to develop? The failure to develop the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of success, the five spiritual faculties, the five spiritual powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
translations.sn22.1:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Buddha was living in the Bhagga country at the village of Susumara, in the Bhesakala forest, at the deer park. Then Nakula's father, the householder, went to the Buddha and, on arrival, bowed down to him and sat to one side. As he was sitting there, he said to the Buddha:
translations.sn22.1:10: One regards feeling as self, or self as devoid of feeling, or feeling as in self, or self as in feeling. One is possessed by the idea: 'I am feeling, feeling is mine.' The feeling that one is so possessed of changes and varies. With the change and variation of feeling, there arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
translations.sn22.1:11: One regards perception as self, or self as devoid of perception, or perception as in self, or self as in perception. One is possessed by the idea: 'I am perception, perception is mine.' The perception that one is so possessed of changes and varies. With the change and variation of perception, there arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
translations.sn22.1:12: One regards mental formations as self, or self as devoid of mental formations, or mental formations as in self, or self as in mental formations. One is possessed by the idea: 'I am mental formations, mental formations are mine.' The mental formations that one is so possessed of change and vary. With the change and variation of mental formations, there arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
translations.sn22.1:13: He perceives consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness. He is obsessed with the idea: 'I am consciousness, consciousness is mine.' As for him, being obsessed with the idea 'I am consciousness, consciousness is mine,' the consciousness changes and becomes different. With the change and difference in consciousness, there arise in him sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Thus, householder, he feels bodily discomfort and mental discomfort.
translations.sn22.1:14: And how, householder, does one feel bodily discomfort but not mental discomfort? Here, householder, a learned noble disciple who has heard the teaching, has seen the noble ones, is well-versed in the teaching of the noble ones, and has seen the good persons, is well-versed in the teaching of the good persons, does not perceive form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. He does not get obsessed with the idea: 'I am form, form is mine.' As for him, not getting obsessed with the idea 'I am form, form is mine,' the form changes and becomes different. With the change and difference in form, no sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in him.
translations.sn22.1:2: I am old, venerable, aged, advanced in years, and my life is at an end. I am an heir to the teachings of the Blessed One, and to the teachings of the monks. May the Blessed One teach me, may the Blessed One instruct me, for my long-term benefit and happiness.
translations.sn22.1:3: This is the way it is, householder. The body is sick, fragile, and sustained by effort. If one who is looking after this body were to experience even a moment's good health, that would be due to mere luck. Therefore, householder, you should train yourself: 'My body is sick, but my mind will not be sick.' That is how you should train yourself, householder.
translations.sn22.1:4: Then the householder Nakula's father, having delighted in and approved of the Blessed One's words, rose from his seat, bowed down to the Blessed One, and circumambulated him. He approached Ven. Sariputta and, having approached, bowed down to Ven. Sariputta and sat down to one side. As he sat down to one side, Ven. Sariputta said to him: 'Your faculties are clear, householder, your complexion is pure and bright. Is it not time now to hear the Dhamma from the Blessed One himself?'
translations.sn22.1:7: But, venerable sir, I do not think I should ask the Blessed One about this: 'For how long is one both bodily sick and mentally sick, and for how long is one bodily sick but not mentally sick?' Even if we were to come from a distance to ask Ven. Sariputta about the meaning of this statement, it would be good if Ven. Sariputta himself would explain the meaning of this statement.
translations.sn22.1:8: 'Listen, householder, and pay attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' replied the householder Nakula's father, and Ven. Sariputta said:
translations.sn22.1:9: And how, householder, is one both bodily sick and mentally sick? Here, householder, an unlearned ordinary person who has not seen the noble ones, is not versed in the teaching of the noble ones, and is not well-versed in the teaching of the good persons, perceives form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. He gets obsessed with the idea: 'I am form, form is mine.' As for him, getting obsessed with the idea 'I am form, form is mine,' the form changes and becomes different. With the change and difference in form, there arise in him sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
translations.sn22.22:2: And what, monks, is the burden-carrier? It is the person to be instructed. It is this venerable one of such name, such clan, and such personal name. This, monks, is called the burden-carrier.
translations.sn22.22:3: And what, monks, is the burden? It is the craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and greed, seeking pleasure here and there, that is, craving for sensual pleasure, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, monks, is called the burden.
translations.sn22.22:4: And what, monks, is the laying down of the burden? It is the complete destruction of that craving, the removal of the passion for it, the overcoming of it, the liberation from it, and the non-attachment to it. This, monks, is called the laying down of the burden.
translations.sn22.22:6: The five aggregates are the burden, the person is the burden-carrier; the burden is suffering in the world, the laying down of the burden is happiness.
translations.sn22.2:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Blessed One was living among the Sakyans at a town of the Sakyans named Devadaha. Then a number of monks who were returning from the countryside arrived at the Blessed One's presence, bowed down to him, and sat down to one side. As they sat down to one side, the monks said to the Blessed One: 'We wish to go to the countryside, to live in the countryside.'
translations.sn22.2:10: If, friend, one were to live having fully given up unwholesome things, and if, having seen the truth, there were to be happiness, unobstructed and without despair, and if, with the breakup of the body, after death, there were to be a good destination, the Blessed One would not praise the giving up of unwholesome things. But because, friend, one who lives having fully given up unwholesome things, and having seen the truth, experiences suffering, obstruction, and despair, and if, with the breakup of the body, after death, there is a bad destination, the Blessed One praises the giving up of unwholesome things.
translations.sn22.2:2: But, monks, have you seen Sariputta?
translations.sn22.2:3: Now at that time the Venerable Sāriputta was sitting not far from the Buddha in a certain cloister, on the edge of a pond. Then those monks, having delighted in and approved of the Buddha's words, rose from their seats, bowed down to the Buddha, and circled around him to the right. They approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta. Having exchanged greetings, they sat down to one side. As they were sitting to one side, those monks said to the Venerable Sāriputta: 'We wish, Venerable Sāriputta, to go to the Western country, to take up residence in the Western country. Our teacher has not permitted us.'
translations.sn22.2:5: 'Even from a distance, friend, we could come to the Venerable Sāriputta to ask about the meaning of what was said. Let the Venerable Sāriputta explain the meaning of what was said.' 'Then listen, monks, and pay attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, friend,' those monks replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said:
translations.sn22.36:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain monk approached the Buddha, sat down to one side, and said to him: 'Please, Bhante, teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Buddha, I might dwell alone, heedful, ardent, and resolute.'
