translations.sn36.31:5: And what, bhikkhus, is non-carnal happiness? Here, a bhikkhu, having separated himself from sensual pleasures, having separated himself from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhana, which is accompanied by thought and examination, and has the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. With the subsiding of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhana, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has the rapture and pleasure born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and fully aware, and he experiences happiness with the body, and enters upon the third jhana, which the noble ones declare: 'He dwells happily, in equanimity, and is mindful.' This, bhikkhus, is called non-carnal happiness.
translations.sn36.31:6: And what, bhikkhus, is the most excellent non-carnal happiness? The happiness that arises in a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, who has reviewed the mind and seen: 'My mind is liberated from sensuality, my mind is liberated from ill will, my mind is liberated from delusion.' This, bhikkhus, is called the most excellent non-carnal happiness.
translations.sn36.31:8: And what, bhikkhus, is non-carnal equanimity? Here, a bhikkhu, having given up pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and distress, enters and dwells in the fourth jhana, which has neither pleasure nor pain, and has purity of mindfulness and equanimity. This, bhikkhus, is called non-carnal equanimity.
translations.sn36.31:9: And what, bhikkhus, is the most excellent non-carnal equanimity? The equanimity that arises in a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, who has reviewed the mind and seen: 'My mind is liberated from sensuality, my mind is liberated from ill will, my mind is liberated from delusion.' This, bhikkhus, is called the most excellent non-carnal equanimity.
translations.sn36.4:2: One who does not tolerate these, when painful feelings arise; bodily feelings, born of the body, which the foolish person cannot tolerate.
translations.sn36.4:3: He wails and laments, weak in his will; he cannot stand firm, and does not attain the goal, nor does he attain the highest peace.
translations.sn36.6:2: A learned noble disciple, bhikkhus, when experiencing a painful feeling, does not sorrow, does not lament, does not weep, does not beat his breast, and does not become confused. He experiences one feeling - a bodily one, not a mental one.
translations.sn36.6:4: The wise person does not experience feeling, whether pleasant, painful, or neither, even if he has heard much. This, for the wise person, is the great distinction from the ordinary person.
translations.sn36.6:5: For one who has heard much and sees the conditioned things of the world and the next, the pleasant things do not delight his mind, and the unpleasant things do not disturb him.
translations.sn36.7:3: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu mindful? Here, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... the mind in the mind... mental phenomena in mental phenomena, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world. Thus, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu mindful.
translations.sn36.7:4: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu fully aware? Here, a bhikkhu, when going forward and returning, is fully aware; when looking ahead and looking away, he is fully aware; when bending and stretching, he is fully aware; when wearing his robes and carrying his alms bowl, he is fully aware; when eating, drinking, chewing, and savoring, he is fully aware; when defecating and urinating, he is fully aware; when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, talking, and keeping silent, he is fully aware. Thus, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu fully aware. A bhikkhu who is mindful, bhikkhus, is fully aware, and he will come to the end of suffering. This is our instruction to you.
translations.sn36.7:5: If a monk has a pleasant feeling, he knows: 'I have a pleasant feeling. It is impermanent, not permanent. What is impermanent, not permanent, is a condition for the arising of pleasant feeling. The body is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen. A pleasant feeling that arises dependent on the body, how can it be permanent?' He dwells observing the impermanence of the body and pleasant feeling, observing their disappearance, observing their fading away, observing their cessation, observing their letting go.
translations.sn36.7:8: When he feels a pleasant feeling, he knows it as impermanent, knows it as not to be delighted in, knows it as not to be attached to; when he feels a painful feeling, he knows it as impermanent, knows it as not to be delighted in, knows it as not to be attached to; when he feels a neither painful nor pleasant feeling, he knows it as impermanent, knows it as not to be delighted in, knows it as not to be attached to. When he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it without being attached; when he feels a painful feeling, he feels it without being attached; when he feels a neither painful nor pleasant feeling, he feels it without being attached. When he feels a feeling limited to the body, he knows: 'I feel a feeling limited to the body'; when he feels a feeling limited to life, he knows: 'I feel a feeling limited to life'. He knows: 'With the breakup of the body, after the ending of life, all feelings, not being delighted in, will become cool'
translations.sn4.13:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Rājagaha, in the Maddakucchi deer reserve. At that time the Blessed One's foot had been pierced by a splinter. Excruciating were the bodily feelings that developed within him — sharp, piercing, unwelcome, disagreeable — but the Blessed One endured them, mindful and alert, without becoming distressed. Then the Blessed One, having folded his robe four times, lay down on his right side in the lion's posture, with one foot placed on top of the other, mindful and alert, with his mind set on getting up.
translations.sn4.13:2: 'Are you sleeping, or are you lazy? Your aims are not being achieved, you are lying down alone in a secluded bed, like a weakling, snoring'
translations.sn4.13:3: 'I am not sleeping, nor am I lazy, I have achieved my aim, I am free from sorrow; I am lying down alone in a secluded bed, and I am sleeping, out of compassion for all beings'
translations.sn4.13:4: 'Some people have a dart in their chest, a dart in their head; they suffer, they feel pain; those with darts, with suffering, make a great noise; therefore I do not sleep, I am free from darts'
translations.sn4.13:5: 'I do not stumble, nor do I tremble, day and night I do not feel the heat; I do not see any decline anywhere in the world, therefore I sleep, out of compassion for all beings'
translations.sn4.18:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying in the Magadhan country at a village of the brahmins of Pañcasāla. At that time the brahmin girls of Pañcasāla were going to meet their grooms. The Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and entered Pañcasāla for alms. The brahmin women of Pañcasāla, having been possessed by Māra the Evil One, were saying: 'May the ascetic Gotama not get alms'
translations.sn4.18:2: Then the Blessed One, having walked for alms in Pañcasāla with his bowl in his hand, and having walked back with his bowl in his hand, Māra the Evil One approached him and said: 'Did you get alms, ascetic?' 'As you have made it, Evil One, so I did not get alms', the Blessed One said. 'Then, venerable sir, go for alms in Pañcasāla again. I will make it so that you get alms'
translations.sn4.19:4: 'Whatever they say, I say, whatever they think, they think of me; if their minds are like that, I will not be freed from them'
translations.sn4.19:5: 'What they say is not mine, what they think is not me; thus, Evil One, you should know, you do not know my path'
translations.sn4.1:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Blessed One was staying on the bank of the river Nerañjarā, at the root of the ajapāla banyan tree, after his enlightenment. Then the following thought occurred to the Blessed One, who was secluded and withdrawn: 'I am freed from the painful, troublesome, and miserable task. It is good that I am freed from the painful, troublesome, and miserable task. It is good that I have realized enlightenment'
translations.sn4.1:2: Then Māra the Evil One, knowing the Blessed One's thought, approached him and recited a verse:
translations.sn4.1:3: 'You have abandoned the ascetic practices by which men are purified, you think you are pure, but you are not on the path to purity'
translations.sn4.1:6: 'I develop virtue, concentration, and wisdom, the path to enlightenment; I have reached the highest purity, you are defeated, destroyer'
translations.sn4.1:7: Then Māra the Evil One thought: 'The Blessed One knows me, the Blessed One knows me', and he was unhappy and disappointed, and he disappeared right there.
translations.sn4.20:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying in the Kosalan country, in a forest hut in the Himalayan foothills. Then the following thought occurred to the Blessed One, who was secluded and withdrawn: 'Can a king, having killed his enemies, make a kingdom without killing, without violence, without a weapon, without a cry, by means of the Dhamma?'
translations.sn4.20:3: 'A mountain of gold, a mountain of silver, a mountain of jewels, a mountain of pearls, a mountain of corals, a mountain of rubies, a mountain of cat's eye; thus the wise wander'
translations.sn4.20:4: 'One who sees the origin of suffering, who sees the cause of suffering, how can that being be called a sensualist? Having known possessions, having known accumulation, that being is trained in self-control'
translations.sn4.21:1: Thus I have heard—on one occasion the Blessed One was living in the land of the Sakyans, in a forest near Silavati. At that time a large number of monks were living near the Blessed One, diligent, ardent, and resolute. Then the Evil One, Māra, having created a brahmanic appearance, with a large shaven head, dressed in a leather cloak, carrying an umbrella made of udumbara wood, approached those monks; having approached, he said to them: "Young monks, you have gone forth while young, with black hair, endowed with the blessings of youth. Enjoy human pleasures. Do not reject the visible pleasures, and do not run after the future ones." "We do not reject the visible pleasures and run after the future ones, brahman. We reject the future ones and run after the visible ones. The future pleasures, brahman, are said by the Blessed One to be full of much suffering and pain, and to have greater drawbacks. This Dhamma is visible here and now, timeless, inviting all to come and see, and is to be known personally by the wise." When this was said, the Evil One, Māra, shook his head, stuck out his tongue, raised his eyebrows, and, taking his umbrella, disappeared.
translations.sn4.24:1: Thus I have heard—on one occasion the Blessed One was living in Uruvela, on the bank of the river Nerañjarā, at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree. At that time the Evil One, Māra, had been following the Blessed One for seven years, watching for an opportunity to find fault. Then the Evil One, Māra, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he spoke to the Blessed One in verse:
translations.sn4.24:10: Not having obtained pleasure there, the wind blows away; Like a monkey on a mountain peak, Gotama is shaken.
translations.sn4.24:2: Are you sorrowful in the forest, having given up your sons? Have you lost your wealth, and are you searching for it? Have you committed some offense in the village, and is that why you do not make an effort? You do not make an effort, and no one is urging you on.
translations.sn4.24:3: I have destroyed the root of sorrow, and I meditate without sorrow. Having cut off all ties of existence and all longing, I meditate without any defilements, and I am not negligent.
translations.sn4.24:6: If you have understood the path, the safe passage to the deathless; then go alone, why do you instruct others?
translations.sn4.24:7: The people who are going to the other shore ask me, and I answer them according to what is true, without any distortion.
translations.sn4.24:8: Just as, sir, in a village or a town, there is a pond not far away. In it, there is a turtle. Then a number of boys and girls from the village or the town, having come out, approach the pond; having approached, they pull out the turtle from the water and put it on dry land. Whatever the turtle can do, the boys and girls cut it, break it, and tear it apart with sticks and stones. Just so, sir, the turtle, having been cut, broken, and torn apart by all those boys and girls, is unable to get back into the pond. In the same way, sir, whatever sensual pleasures have been indulged in, delighted in, and developed, all of them have been cut off, broken, and torn apart by the Blessed One. I am unable, sir, to approach the Blessed One again, expecting to find a foothold.
translations.sn4.24:9: The fat and the stone, the wind blows upon; We may find something soft, and it may be pleasant.
translations.sn4.25:10: The Worthy One, the Well-Gone One, is in the world, not attached by lust; Having transcended Māra's realm, I am sorrowful, for I have been defeated.
translations.sn4.25:12: Then Craving, Discontent, and Lust, the daughters of Māra, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they stood to one side. Standing to one side, Craving, the daughter of Māra, spoke to the Blessed One in verse:
translations.sn4.25:14: Having attained the goal, having found peace in the heart, having conquered the army of pleasant forms; I, alone, experience bliss, and I do not make an effort; no one is urging me on.
translations.sn4.25:16: How does the monk, who is often distracted, cross the flood, having gone beyond the sixth sense base? How does he meditate much, having perceptions of sensual pleasure, when he has not obtained what he wants?
translations.sn4.25:17: His body is tranquil, his mind is fully freed, he is without any mental constructs, mindful, and not dependent on anyone; he understands the Dhamma, and he does not get agitated, nor does he get excited, nor is he lethargic.
translations.sn4.25:2: Why are you sorrowful, dear? What person are you sorrowing for? We will bind him with the bond of lust, like an elephant in the forest, and we will bring him under our control; he will be our servant.
translations.sn4.25:20: The wanderer, the leader of the group, will overcome craving; many people will have faith in him, and he will wander alone, without any obstruction, and he will go to the other shore, the realm of the king of death.
translations.sn4.25:23: The foolish, like lotus stalks, will attack the mountain; they will dig into the rock with their fingernails, and they will eat the iron with their teeth.
translations.sn4.25:24: They will make the mountain peak a head, and they will take a stand in the underworld; they will eat the neck, and they will make Gotama tremble.
translations.sn4.25:4: Then Craving, Discontent, and Lust, the daughters of Māra, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they spoke to him: "We will pay homage to your feet, ascetic." Then the Blessed One did not consent, as one who has been fully freed from all attachments.
translations.sn4.25:5: Then Craving, Discontent, and Lust, the daughters of Māra, stepped aside and thought: "Men are prone to high and low things. What if we were to create a hundred, a hundred, a hundred beautiful young women?" Then Craving, Discontent, and Lust, the daughters of Māra, created a hundred, a hundred, a hundred beautiful young women, and approached the Blessed One; having approached, they spoke to him: "We will pay homage to your feet, ascetic." The Blessed One did not consent, as one who has been fully freed from all attachments.
translations.sn4.8:1: Thus I have heard—on one occasion the Blessed One was living in Sāvatthi, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Then the Evil One, Māra, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he spoke to the Blessed One in verse:
translations.sn4.8:2: A man delights in his sons, a cow delights in its calves; a man delights in his wealth, but one who has no attachments does not delight.
translations.sn4.8:3: He mourns for his son, saying, 'My son, my son!' He mourns for cattle, saying, 'My cattle, my cattle!' A person mourns due to possessions. One who has no possessions does not mourn.
translations.sn44.1:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Now on that occasion, the bhikkhuni Khemā was wandering on tour in the Kosi country and had arrived at a certain torana village. King Pasenadi of Kosala was also traveling from Sāketa to Sāvatthī and had arrived at that same torana village for the night. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala addressed a certain man: 'Come now, good man, find out if there is a monk or brahmin in this torana village whom I can visit today.'
translations.sn44.1:2: 'Yes, your majesty,' that man replied, and then he searched the entire torana village but did not find such a monk or brahmin who was suitable for King Pasenadi of Kosala to visit. He saw the bhikkhuni Khemā, who had arrived at the torana village. Having seen her, he approached King Pasenadi of Kosala and said to him:
translations.sn44.1:3: 'There is no monk or brahmin in this torana village, your majesty, who is suitable for you to visit. However, your majesty, there is a bhikkhuni named Khemā, a disciple of the Blessed One, an arahant, a fully awakened one. This lady Khemā has a good reputation in this way: 'She is wise, discerning, astute, and a good speaker.' Let your majesty visit her.'
translations.sn44.1:6: 'I will ask you about this, great king. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, great king? Is there a reckoner or a mathematician who can count the sand in the Ganges River—so many grains of sand, so many hundreds of grains, so many thousands of grains, or so many hundreds of thousands of grains?' 'No, venerable sir.' 'Is there a reckoner or a mathematician who can count the water in the great ocean—so many drops of water, so many hundreds of drops, so many thousands of drops, or so many hundreds of thousands of drops?' 'No, venerable sir.' 'Why is that?' 'The ocean is deep, venerable sir, immeasurable and unfathomable.' 'In the same way, great king, the Tathāgata has abandoned that form by which one could describe him, saying, 'The Tathāgata has this form' or 'The Tathāgata has that form.' The form by which one could describe him has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no longer subject to future arising. Freed from the form description, great king, the Tathāgata is deep, immeasurable, and unfathomable, like the great ocean. 'The Tathāgata exists after death' does not apply; 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death' does not apply; 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death' does not apply; 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death' does not apply.'
translations.sn44.1:9: The consciousness by which one could describe the Tathāgata has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no longer subject to future arising. Freed from the consciousness description, great king, the Tathāgata is deep, immeasurable, and unfathomable, like the great ocean. 'The Tathāgata exists after death' does not apply; 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death' does not apply; 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death' does not apply; 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death' does not apply.' Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, having delighted in and expressed his approval of the bhikkhuni Khemā's words, rose from his seat, bowed down to her, and departed.
translations.sn45.1:2: Bhikkhus, ignorance is the forerunner of the unwholesome states that arise with it, accompanied by shamelessness and a lack of fear of wrongdoing. For one affected by ignorance, wrong view arises; for one with wrong view, wrong intention arises; for one with wrong intention, wrong speech arises; for one with wrong speech, wrong action arises; for one with wrong action, wrong livelihood arises; for one with wrong livelihood, wrong effort arises; for one with wrong effort, wrong mindfulness arises; for one with wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration arises.
translations.sn45.2:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at a town of the Sakyans named Nagaraka. Then Ven. Ānanda approached the Blessed One and, on arrival, having bowed down to him, sat to one side. As he was sitting there, he said to the Blessed One: 'This holy life, sir, is lived with good friends, good companions, and good associates.'
translations.sn45.2:2: 'Do not say that, Ānanda. Do not say that. This holy life, Ānanda, is lived with good friends, good companions, and good associates. For a monk with good friends, good companions, and good associates, it is to be expected that he will develop and cultivate the noble eightfold path, and that he will develop and cultivate the noble eightfold path in a way that is progressive, not regressive.'
translations.sn45.2:3: 'But, Ānanda, how does a monk with good friends, good companions, and good associates develop and cultivate the noble eightfold path in a way that is progressive, not regressive? It is, Ānanda, when a monk develops right view, which is based on separation, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and is maturing in release; when he develops right intention, which is based on separation, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and is maturing in release... when he develops right concentration, which is based on separation, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and is maturing in release. It is in this way, Ānanda, that a monk with good friends, good companions, and good associates develops and cultivates the noble eightfold path in a way that is progressive, not regressive.'
translations.sn45.4:1: At Sāvatthī. Then, in the morning, the Venerable Ānanda dressed, and taking his bowl and outer robe, went into Sāvatthī for alms. The Venerable Ānanda saw a brahmin named Jaṇussoṇi, who was having a chariot harnessed with thoroughbreds, and who was leaving Sāvatthī. The chariot was white, with a white canopy, white horses, white reins, a white goad, a white umbrella, a white turban, and white sandals. The people who saw it said: 'This is a divine vehicle, indeed it is a divine vehicle.'
translations.sn45.4:10: He is not hostile, not violent; his weapon is withdrawal. He has patience as his covering, and is committed to the path to the end of suffering.
translations.sn45.4:2: Then the Venerable Ānanda, having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī and having eaten, went to the Blessed One after his meal, and having bowed down to the Blessed One, sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn45.4:4: It is possible, Ānanda,' said the Blessed One. 'This is the designation of the noble eightfold path: it is called the divine vehicle, the Dhamma vehicle, the unexcelled victory in battle.'
translations.sn45.4:8: For one who has faith and wisdom, the principles are in harmony, and are always carried on the shoulder; conscience and prudence are yoked, and mindfulness is the driver.
translations.sn45.4:9: The chariot is virtue, the charioteer is concentration, and the horses are the faculties. Evenness is the reins, and the chariot's canopy is dispassion.
translations.sn45.8:1: At Sāvatthī. 'I will teach you, monks, the noble eightfold path, and analyze it. Listen and pay attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' replied those monks to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.sn45.8:3: And what, monks, is right understanding? Knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, and knowledge of the way of practice leading to the cessation of suffering: this, monks, is called right understanding.
translations.sn45.8:4: And what, monks, is right intention? Intention of renunciation, intention of non-ill will, intention of harmlessness: this, monks, is called right intention.
translations.sn45.8:5: And what, monks, is right speech? Abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from idle chatter: this, monks, is called right speech.
translations.sn45.8:6: And what, monks, is right action? Abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from sexual misconduct: this, monks, is called right action.
translations.sn45.8:7: And what, monks, is right livelihood? Here, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, earns a living by right livelihood: this, monks, is called right livelihood.
translations.sn45.8:8: And what, monks, is right effort? Here, a monk generates desire, makes an effort, and exerts his mind to prevent the arising of unarisen unwholesome states, to abandon arisen unwholesome states, to generate unarisen wholesome states, and to maintain arisen wholesome states, to not forget them, to increase them, to develop them, and to perfect them: this, monks, is called right effort.
translations.sn45.8:9: And what, monks, is right mindfulness? Here, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure towards the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure towards the world. He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure towards the world. He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure towards the world: this, monks, is called right mindfulness.
translations.sn46.11:1: Just as, monks, the four modes of conduct of animals - going, standing, sitting, and lying down - all depend on the earth and are based on the earth, in the same way, a monk, based on virtue, established in virtue, develops and cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment.
translations.sn46.14:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel's Feeding Ground. At that time the Venerable Mahākassapa was living in the Pippali Cave, and he was sick, in pain, and severely ill. Then, in the late afternoon, the Blessed One came out of his seclusion and went to the Venerable Mahākassapa, and having sat down in the appointed seat, he said to the Venerable Mahākassapa:
translations.sn46.14:2: 'Can you bear it, Kassapa? Can you endure it? Are your painful feelings decreasing, not increasing? Are they decreasing, not increasing, as they are being endured?' 'I can bear it, venerable sir, I can endure it. But my painful feelings are severe, they are increasing, not decreasing; they are increasing, not decreasing, as they are being endured.'
translations.sn46.29:2: Here, monks, a monk develops the factor of mindfulness based on seclusion, and the factor of equanimity based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, leading to letting go. When these seven factors of enlightenment are thus developed and cultivated, they lead to the abandonment of the things that fetter.
translations.sn46.30:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sumbhe, in a town of the Sumbhans called Setaka. Then the Venerable Udāyī went to the Blessed One, and having bowed down to the Blessed One, sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Udāyī said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn46.30:2: It's amazing, sir. It's incredible, sir. I have great confidence in and respect for the Blessed One. Formerly, as a layman, I was not very learned in the Dhamma and the Saṅgha. But now, having seen the respect, reverence, shame, and fear of wrongdoing in the Blessed One, I have gone forth from the household life into homelessness. The Blessed One taught me the Dhamma: 'Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the cessation of form; such is feeling ... such is perception ... such is mental formation ... such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the cessation of consciousness.'
translations.sn46.30:3: I, sir, having gone to a solitary hut, having reflected on these five aggregates of clinging as they really are, understood: 'This is suffering,' 'This is the origin of suffering,' 'This is the cessation of suffering,' 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.' I have fully awakened to the Dhamma, and the path has been fully discovered by me. Whatever has been done, has been done for the purpose of enlightenment. I will live having understood: 'My birth has been destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming back to this world.'
translations.sn46.38:1: When, monks, a noble disciple listens to the Dhamma with a mind that is eager to hear, at that time these five hindrances do not exist. The seven factors of enlightenment are fully developed at that time.
translations.sn46.3:1: Those monks, monks, who are endowed with virtue, concentration, and wisdom, and who have gained liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation, I declare the service to them to be of great benefit; I declare the listening to them to be of great benefit; I declare the approaching them to be of great benefit; I declare the attendance on them to be of great benefit; I declare the recollection of them to be of great benefit; I declare the going forth under them to be of great benefit. Why is that? Because, monks, when those monks teach the Dhamma, one hears the Dhamma with both a bodily and mental clarity.
translations.sn46.3:2: When, monks, a monk, living with a mind that is clarified in both body and mind, recollects and reflects on that Dhamma, the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness is established in him at that time; he develops the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness at that time; the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness is fully developed in him at that time. Living thus mindful, he examines and investigates that Dhamma with wisdom.
translations.sn46.51:20: What, monks, is the nutriment for the non-arising of the unarisen factor of enlightenment that is effort, or for the fulfillment by development of the arisen factor of enlightenment that is effort? There is, monks, the element of initiative, the element of exertion, the element of struggle. Not giving attention to it is the nutriment for the non-arising of the unarisen factor of enlightenment that is effort, or for the fulfillment by development of the arisen factor of enlightenment that is effort.
translations.sn46.51:21: What, monks, is the nutriment for the non-arising of the unarisen factor of enlightenment that is joy, or for the fulfillment by development of the arisen factor of enlightenment that is joy? There are, monks, things that are the basis for the factor of enlightenment that is joy. Not giving attention to them is the nutriment for the non-arising of the unarisen factor of enlightenment that is joy, or for the fulfillment by development of the arisen factor of enlightenment that is joy.
translations.sn46.51:22: What, monks, is the nutriment for the non-arising of the unarisen factor of enlightenment that is tranquility, or for the fulfillment by development of the arisen factor of enlightenment that is tranquility? There is, monks, tranquility of body and tranquility of mind. Not giving attention to it is the nutriment for the non-arising of the unarisen factor of enlightenment that is tranquility, or for the fulfillment by development of the arisen factor of enlightenment that is tranquility.
translations.sn46.51:23: What, monks, is the nutriment for the non-arising of the unarisen factor of enlightenment that is concentration, or for the fulfillment by development of the arisen factor of enlightenment that is concentration? There is, monks, the sign of concentration, the sign of non-distraction. Not giving attention to it is the nutriment for the non-arising of the unarisen factor of enlightenment that is concentration, or for the fulfillment by development of the arisen factor of enlightenment that is concentration.
translations.sn46.52:1: Now, at that time, a number of monks, having dressed in the morning, took their bowls and robes and entered Sāvatthī for alms. Then it occurred to those monks: 'It is too early to go for alms in Sāvatthī. What if we were to go to the park of the wanderers of other sects?'
translations.sn46.52:10: What, monks, is the method by which the seven factors of enlightenment come to be fourteen? Whatever, monks, is the mindfulness directed to the Dhamma internally, that is the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness; whatever is the mindfulness directed to the Dhamma externally, that is the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness. The statement 'the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness' refers to this. This method is twofold.
translations.sn46.52:11: Whatever, monks, is the investigation of the Dhamma internally by wisdom, the examination of the Dhamma, the analysis of the Dhamma, that is the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of the Dhamma; whatever is the investigation of the Dhamma externally by wisdom, the examination of the Dhamma, the analysis of the Dhamma, that is the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of the Dhamma. The statement 'the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of the Dhamma' refers to this. This method is twofold.
translations.sn46.52:12: Whatever, monks, is the physical energy, that is the factor of enlightenment that is effort; whatever is the mental energy, that is the factor of enlightenment that is effort. The statement 'the factor of enlightenment that is effort' refers to this. This method is twofold.
translations.sn46.52:13: Whatever, monks, is the joy that is accompanied by thought and examination, that is the factor of enlightenment that is joy; whatever is the joy that is without thought and examination, that is the factor of enlightenment that is joy. The statement 'the factor of enlightenment that is joy' refers to this. This method is twofold.
translations.sn46.52:14: Whatever, monks, is the tranquility of body, that is the factor of enlightenment that is tranquility; whatever is the tranquility of mind, that is the factor of enlightenment that is tranquility. The statement 'the factor of enlightenment that is tranquility' refers to this. This method is twofold.
translations.sn46.52:15: Whatever concentration with applied thought and sustained thought is, that too is a factor of concentration. Whatever concentration without applied thought and sustained thought is, that too is a factor of concentration. This is the explanation of the term 'factor of concentration'. By this method, there are two kinds.
translations.sn46.52:2: Then those monks approached the park of the wanderers who were not followers of the Buddha; having approached, they exchanged greetings with those wanderers. Having exchanged greetings, they sat down to one side. As they were sitting down to one side, those wanderers who were not followers of the Buddha said to them:
translations.sn46.52:3: “The ascetic Gotama teaches his disciples the Dhamma in this way: 'Come, monks, having abandoned the five hindrances and the mental corruptions that weaken wisdom, develop the seven factors of enlightenment as they really are.' We too, friends, teach our disciples the Dhamma in this way: 'Come, friends, having abandoned the five hindrances and the mental corruptions that weaken wisdom, develop the seven factors of enlightenment as they really are.' What distinction, friends, or difference, or diversity can there be between the ascetic Gotama's teaching and ours, in regard to the teaching of the Dhamma or the explanation of the Dhamma?”
translations.sn46.52:4: Then those monks neither approved nor disapproved of the statement of those wanderers who were not followers of the Buddha; without approving or disapproving, they rose from their seats and left, saying: 'We will know the meaning of this statement after asking the Blessed One.' Then those monks, having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī, after the alms round, having returned from the alms round, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As they were sitting down to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn46.52:8: “One should say to those wanderers who are not followers of the Buddha: 'Is there a method by which the five hindrances become ten, and the seven factors of enlightenment become fourteen?' When asked thus, those wanderers who are not followers of the Buddha will not be able to give an answer, and they will meet with frustration. What is the reason for this? Because they are without a basis. I do not see anyone in the world with its gods, its Māras, its Brahmas, its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, who could satisfy the mind by explaining these questions, except for the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata or one who has heard it from them.
translations.sn46.52:9: And what, monks, is the method by which the five hindrances become ten? Whatever sensual desire there is, either internal or external, is a hindrance. 'The hindrance of sensual desire' is the explanation of this. By this method, there are two kinds. Whatever ill will there is, either internal or external, is a hindrance. 'The hindrance of ill will' is the explanation of this. By this method, there are two kinds. Whatever sloth and torpor there is, is a hindrance. 'The hindrance of sloth and torpor' is the explanation of this. By this method, there are two kinds. Whatever restlessness and remorse there is, is a hindrance. 'The hindrance of restlessness and remorse' is the explanation of this. By this method, there are two kinds. Whatever doubt there is, either internal or external, about the teachings, is a hindrance. 'The hindrance of doubt' is the explanation of this. By this method, there are two kinds. This, monks, is the method by which the five hindrances become ten.
translations.sn46.53:10: When the mind is excited, it is not the right time to develop the factor of enlightenment of investigation of Dhamma, or the factor of enlightenment of energy, or the factor of enlightenment of joy. What is the reason for this? Because an excited mind is not well composed by these things.
translations.sn46.53:11: Suppose a man wanted to make a large fire. If he were to put dry grass on it, and dry cow dung, and dry wood, and were to blow on it with his mouth, and not to cover it with ashes; would that man be able to make a large fire?
translations.sn46.53:14: Suppose a man wanted to make a large fire. If he were to put wet grass on it, and wet cow dung, and wet wood, and were to blow on it with a bellows, and to cover it with ashes; would that man be able to make a large fire?
translations.sn46.53:3: I do not see anyone in the world with its gods, its Māras, its Brahmas, its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, who could satisfy the mind by explaining these questions, except for the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata or one who has heard it from them.
translations.sn46.53:13: When, monks, the mind is restless, it is the right time to develop the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the enlightenment factor of concentration, and the enlightenment factor of equanimity. What is the reason for this? A restless mind, monks, is calmed by these things.
translations.sn46.53:2: Those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus, monks, should be asked: ‘In which case, friends, when the mind is sluggish, which of the enlightenment factors is it not the right time to develop, and which is it the right time to develop? And when the mind is restless, which of the enlightenment factors is it not the right time to develop, and which is it the right time to develop?’ When asked thus, monks, those ascetics and brahmins will not be able to reply and will furthermore be humiliated. What is the reason for this? Because they are without a basis, monks.
translations.sn46.53:4: On an occasion when the mind is slack, it is not the right time to develop the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the enlightenment factor of concentration, or the enlightenment factor of equanimity. What is the reason for this? When the mind is slack, it is not receptive to these things.
translations.sn46.53:5: Suppose a person wanted to make a small fire bigger. If they were to add wet sticks, wet cow dung, and green sticks to it, and then blow on it with a moist breath, and cover it with ashes; would they be able to make the small fire bigger?
translations.sn46.53:7: On an occasion when the mind is slack, it is the right time to develop the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, the enlightenment factor of effort, and the enlightenment factor of joy. What is the reason for this? When the mind is slack, it is receptive to these things.
translations.sn46.53:8: Suppose a person wanted to make a small fire bigger. If they were to add dry sticks, dry cow dung, and dry sticks to it, and then blow on it with a dry breath, and not cover it with ashes; would they be able to make the small fire bigger?
translations.sn46.54:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was living in the Koliyan country, in a Koliyan town called Haliddavasana. Then a number of bhikkhus, having dressed in the morning and taken their bowls and outer robes, went to Haliddavasana for alms. As they were walking for alms in Haliddavasana, it occurred to them: 'It is too early to walk for alms in Haliddavasana. What if we were to go to the park of the wanderers of other sects?'
translations.sn46.54:11: One should ask the wanderers of other sects who speak thus: 'How, friends, is the liberation of mind by loving-kindness developed, what is its purpose, its culmination, its fruit, and its final goal? How is the liberation of mind by compassion developed, what is its purpose, its culmination, its fruit, and its final goal? How is the liberation of mind by sympathetic joy developed, what is its purpose, its culmination, its fruit, and its final goal? How is the liberation of mind by equanimity developed, what is its purpose, its culmination, its fruit, and its final goal?' When asked thus, the wanderers of other sects will not be able to explain, and they will get into difficulties. What is the reason for this? It is because they have no knowledge of these things.
translations.sn46.54:12: How, bhikkhus, is the liberation of mind by loving-kindness developed, what is its purpose, its culmination, its fruit, and its final goal? Here, a bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness accompanied by loving-kindness... the enlightenment factor of equanimity accompanied by loving-kindness, based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in release. If he wishes, 'May I dwell with a mind free from hatred, and may I dwell with a mind of loving-kindness,' then he dwells with a mind of loving-kindness. I say that the liberation of mind by loving-kindness has the highest culmination, I say it has the highest fruit, and I say it has the highest final goal for a bhikkhu who has not penetrated to a higher liberation.
translations.sn46.54:13: How, bhikkhus, is the liberation of mind by compassion developed, what is its purpose, its culmination, its fruit, and its final goal? Here, a bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness accompanied by compassion... the enlightenment factor of equanimity accompanied by compassion, based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in release. If he wishes, 'May I dwell with a mind free from hatred, and may I dwell with a mind of compassion,' then he dwells with a mind of compassion... Having completely transcended perceptions of form, having overcome perceptions of sensory impingement, and not paying attention to perceptions of diversity, he dwells in the base of the infinity of space, having reached it through the cessation of perceptions of form. I say that the liberation of mind by compassion has the highest culmination, I say it has the highest fruit, and I say it has the highest final goal for a bhikkhu who has not penetrated to a higher liberation.
translations.sn46.54:14: How, bhikkhus, is the liberation of mind by sympathetic joy developed, what is its purpose, its culmination, its fruit, and its final goal? Here, a bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness accompanied by sympathetic joy... the enlightenment factor of equanimity accompanied by sympathetic joy, based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in release. If he wishes, 'May I dwell with a mind free from hatred, and may I dwell with a mind of sympathetic joy,' then he dwells with a mind of sympathetic joy... Having completely transcended the base of the infinity of space, he dwells in the base of the infinity of consciousness, having reached it through the cessation of the base of the infinity of space. I say that the liberation of mind by sympathetic joy has the highest culmination, I say it has the highest fruit, and I say it has the highest final goal for a bhikkhu who has not penetrated to a higher liberation.
translations.sn46.54:3: The ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma to his disciples in this way: 'Come, monks, having abandoned the five hindrances and the mental corruptions that weaken wisdom, dwell with a mind filled with loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, pervading one direction, then the second, then the third, then the fourth; above, below, and all around, everywhere, and to all beings, with a mind filled with loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, vast, exalted, measureless, without hatred, and without ill-will.'
translations.sn46.8:1: On one occasion the Venerable Upavāna and the Venerable Sāriputta were dwelling at Kosambī in the Ghositārāma. Then, in the evening, the Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and approached the Venerable Upavāna; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Upavāna and sat down to one side.
translations.sn46.8:2: 'Can it be known, friend Upavāna, that a monk has abandoned the hindrances and has well-developed the factors of enlightenment, which are conducive to a pleasant dwelling?' 'It can be known, friend Sāriputta, that a monk has abandoned the hindrances and has well-developed the factors of enlightenment, which are conducive to a pleasant dwelling.'
translations.sn47.10:1: Then the Venerable Ānanda, in the morning, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, approached a certain bhikkhunī's residence; having approached, he sat down in the appointed seat. Then several bhikkhunīs approached the Venerable Ānanda; having approached, they paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side.
translations.sn47.10:2: 'Here, Bhante Ānanda, several bhikkhunīs dwell with their minds well-established in the four establishments of mindfulness, and they know and see the superior and inferior of the past and the future.' 'So it is, sisters, so it is. For any monk or bhikkhunī who dwells with their mind well-established in the four establishments of mindfulness, this is to be expected: they will know and see the superior and inferior of the past and the future.'
translations.sn47.10:7: Again, Ānanda, a monk dwells contemplating feelings, mind, and phenomena as phenomena, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure towards the world. As he dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena, an object of phenomena arises in him, or a fever in his body, or a numbness in his mind, or his mind is distracted externally. Ānanda, a monk should direct his mind to some inspiring object. As he directs his mind to some inspiring object, joy arises. In one who is joyful, pleasure arises. In one who is pleased, the body becomes tranquil. In one who is tranquil, the mind becomes concentrated. He reflects: 'The purpose for which I directed my mind has been achieved. Now I will withdraw.' He withdraws, but does not think or reflect. He knows: 'I am without thought, without reflection, and I am mindful and at ease.' This, Ānanda, is how concentration is developed through directing the mind.
translations.sn47.10:9: Thus, Ānanda, I have taught the development of concentration through directing the mind and not directing the mind. What the Teacher should do out of compassion for his disciples, I have done for you. These are the roots of trees, these are empty huts. Practice jhāna, Ānanda, do not be heedless, do not be regretful later. This is our instruction to you.
translations.sn47.13:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. At that time the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling in the Magadha country at Nālakagāma, and he was sick, afflicted, and gravely ill. The novice Cunda was his attendant.
translations.sn47.13:2: Then the Venerable Sāriputta passed away, having attained final Nibbāna. The novice Cunda, taking the Venerable Sāriputta's bowl and robe, approached the Venerable Ānanda at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park; having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the novice Cunda said to the Venerable Ānanda: 'The Venerable Sāriputta has passed away, Bhante. This is his bowl and robe.'
translations.sn47.13:3: 'There is a matter to be discussed, friend Cunda, with the Blessed One. Come, friend Cunda, let us approach the Blessed One and report this matter to him.' 'Yes, Bhante,' the novice Cunda replied to the Venerable Ānanda.
translations.sn47.13:4: Then the Venerable Ānanda and the novice Cunda approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: 'This novice Cunda says:
translations.sn47.19:1: At one time the Buddha was living in the land of the Sumbhas, in a market town of the Sumbhas named Sedaka. There the Buddha addressed the monks: “Monks, in the past a bamboo acrobat, having raised up his bamboo pole, addressed his assistant Medakathālī: ‘Come, my good Medakathālī, having climbed up the bamboo pole, stand on my shoulders.’ ‘Yes, teacher,’ Medakathālī replied, and having climbed up the bamboo pole, she stood on the teacher’s shoulders. Then the bamboo acrobat said to his assistant Medakathālī: ‘You protect me, and I will protect you. Thus, protecting each other, we will show off our skills, and we will earn a profit, and safely get down from the bamboo pole.’ When this was said, Medakathālī replied to the bamboo acrobat: ‘This will not happen in this way, teacher. You protect yourself, and I will protect myself. Thus, each of us protecting ourselves, we will show off our skills, and we will earn a profit, and safely get down from the bamboo pole.’”
translations.sn47.19:2: The Buddha said: “That is the right way, monks, as Medakathālī said to the teacher. One should practice mindfulness in this way: ‘I will protect myself’ and ‘I will protect others.’ One who protects oneself protects others, and one who protects others protects oneself.
translations.sn47.20:1: I have heard that at one time the Buddha was living in the land of the Sumbhas, in a market town of the Sumbhas named Sedaka. There the Buddha addressed the monks: “Monks…” “Yes, Bhante,” the monks replied to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
translations.sn47.20:2: “Suppose, monks, that people were to gather from a country and say: ‘The daughter of the country is beautiful, the daughter of the country is beautiful. She is the most beautiful dancer and the most beautiful singer. The daughter of the country dances and sings.’ And a large crowd would gather to see her. Then a man would come along, desiring to live, desiring not to die, desiring pleasure, and averse to pain. They would say to him: ‘This bowl of oil is to be carried on your head between the great crowd and the daughter of the country, who is being exhibited. A man with a raised sword will follow you, and wherever you spill even a drop of oil, right there your head will be cut off.’ What do you think, monks? Would that man pay attention to that bowl of oil or would he be careless and distracted?” “No, Bhante.”
translations.sn47.25:1: I have heard that at one time the Buddha was living in Sāvatthī, at Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then a certain brahmin went to the Buddha, and after exchanging greetings, he sat down to one side. The brahmin said to the Buddha: “What is the reason, Master Gotama, what is the condition, that the good teaching does not last long after a Tathāgata has attained final nibbāna? What is the reason, Master Gotama, what is the condition, that the good teaching does last long after a Tathāgata has attained final nibbāna?”
translations.sn47.25:2: “The good teaching does not last long after a Tathāgata has attained final nibbāna, brahmin, when the four establishments of mindfulness are not developed and not practiced. The good teaching does last long after a Tathāgata has attained final nibbāna, brahmin, when the four establishments of mindfulness are developed and practiced.”
translations.sn47.29:2: Then Venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of the householder Sirivaḍḍha. Having gone there, he sat down in the appointed seat. Venerable Ānanda said to Sirivaḍḍha: “Are you bearing up, householder? Are you getting on? Are your bodily feelings fading away, not increasing?” “I am not bearing up, Bhante. I am not getting on. My bodily feelings are strong, they are increasing, not fading away.”
translations.sn47.29:3: “Therefore, householder, you should train in this way: ‘I will dwell observing the body in the body, ardent, with clear comprehension, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure towards the world. I will dwell observing feelings in feelings... I will dwell observing the mind in the mind... I will dwell observing phenomena in phenomena, ardent, with clear comprehension, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure towards the world.’ You should train in this way, householder.”
translations.sn47.33:1: “When the four establishments of mindfulness are developed, monks, the noble path that leads to the complete destruction of suffering is developed. When the four establishments of mindfulness are undeveloped, monks, the noble path that leads to the complete destruction of suffering is undeveloped.”
translations.sn47.37:1: “There are four establishments of mindfulness, monks. What four? Here a monk dwells observing the body in the body, ardent, with clear comprehension, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure towards the world. As he dwells observing the body in the body, the desire for the body is abandoned. With the abandonment of desire, the Deathless is realized.”
translations.sn47.37:2: “He dwells observing feelings in feelings, ardent, with clear comprehension, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure towards the world. As he dwells observing feelings in feelings, the desire for feelings is abandoned. With the abandonment of desire, the Deathless is realized.”
translations.sn47.37:3: “He dwells observing the mind in the mind, ardent, with clear comprehension, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure towards the world. As he dwells observing the mind in the mind, the desire for the mind is abandoned. With the abandonment of desire, the Deathless is realized.”
translations.sn47.38:1: “There are four establishments of mindfulness, monks. What four? Here a monk dwells observing the body in the body, ardent, with clear comprehension, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure towards the world. As he dwells observing the body in the body, the body is fully understood. With the full understanding of the body, the Deathless is realized.”
translations.sn47.38:2: “He dwells observing feelings in feelings, ardent, with clear comprehension, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure towards the world. As he dwells observing feelings in feelings, feelings are fully understood. With the full understanding of feelings, the Deathless is realized.”
translations.sn47.38:3: One dwells observing the mind in the mind, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure towards the world. For one dwelling observing the mind in the mind, the mind is known as it really is. Through the knowledge of the mind as it really is, the Deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.40:1: I will teach you, monks, the establishment of mindfulness and the development of mindfulness and the path leading to the development of mindfulness. Listen to this. And what, monks, is the establishment of mindfulness? Here, a monk dwells observing the body in the body, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure towards the world; he dwells observing feelings in feelings, ... he dwells observing the mind in the mind, ... he dwells observing phenomena in phenomena, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure towards the world. This is called the establishment of mindfulness.
translations.sn47.40:2: And what, monks, is the development of mindfulness? Here, a monk dwells observing the phenomenon of origination in the body, observing the phenomenon of passing away in the body, observing the phenomenon of origination and passing away in the body, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure towards the world. He dwells observing the phenomenon of origination in feelings, ... in the mind, ... in phenomena, observing the phenomenon of passing away in phenomena, observing the phenomenon of origination and passing away in phenomena, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure towards the world. This is called the development of mindfulness.
translations.sn47.4:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling in the Kosalan country at a town of the brahmins called Sālā.
translations.sn47.4:2: The Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Monks, I will teach you the development of the four establishments of mindfulness. These four are: Here, friends, a monk dwells observing the body in the body, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure towards the world; he dwells observing feelings in feelings, ... the mind in the mind, ... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure towards the world, for the sake of knowledge and understanding as they really are.
translations.sn47.4:3: Those monks who are trainees, who have not yet reached their goal but are striving for the supreme security from bondage, also dwell observing the body in the body, ... feelings in feelings, ... the mind in the mind, ... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure towards the world, for the sake of knowledge and understanding as they really are.
translations.sn47.4:4: Those monks who are arahants, whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their goal, destroyed the fetters of being, and are completely liberated through final knowledge, also dwell observing the body in the body, ... feelings in feelings, ... the mind in the mind, ... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, disjoined from the body, ... from feelings, ... from the mind, ... from phenomena.
translations.sn47.6:1: In the past, monks, a hunter caught a bird and the bird said to the hunter: 'We are unlucky, we are without merit, for we have wandered into the hunter's domain, into the domain of our own kin. If we had wandered into our own domain, into the domain of our kin, the hunter would not have had power over us, for the sake of a fight.' 'What is your domain, your kin's domain?' 'Plowing and sowing, and the place for oxen to lie down.'
translations.sn47.6:2: Then, monks, the hunter, being weak and unable to run, released the bird, saying: 'Go, bird, go wherever you like, but you will not escape me.' The bird went to the place where the oxen plowed and sowed, and climbed onto a large heap of plowed earth, and cried out to the hunter: 'Come and get me, hunter, come and get me.' The hunter, being weak and unable to run, went to the place, and the bird, knowing that the hunter was weak, seized the hunter and killed him. So it is, monks, for one who wanders into the domain of others, into the domain of one's own kin.
translations.sn47.6:3: Therefore, monks, do not wander into the domain of others, into the domain of one's own kin. For one who wanders into the domain of others, into the domain of one's own kin, Māra gains access, Māra gains a foothold. And what, monks, is the domain of others, the domain of one's own kin for a monk? The five cords of sensual pleasure.
translations.sn47.7:1: There are, monks, rugged and difficult regions in the Himalayas, the king of mountains, where neither monkeys nor humans can go. There are, monks, rugged and difficult regions in the Himalayas, the king of mountains, where monkeys can go, but not humans. There are, monks, pleasant and charming regions in the Himalayas, the king of mountains, where both monkeys and humans can go. In those regions, monks, hunters set traps to catch the monkeys.
translations.sn47.8:2: That foolish, untrained, and unskilled ordinary person does not recognize the sign of their own food: 'Today my food is delicious, I will eat a lot, I will eat a lot of this, I will praise this. The sour food is delicious, I will eat a lot of sour food, I will eat a lot of it, I will praise the sour food. The bitter food is delicious... the pungent food is delicious... the sweet food is delicious... the alkaline food is delicious... the non-alkaline food is delicious, I will eat a lot of non-alkaline food, I will eat a lot of it, I will praise the non-alkaline food.'
translations.sn47.8:4: That foolish, untrained, and unskilled monk does not gain the bliss of living in the present moment, nor does he gain mindfulness and clear comprehension. What is the reason for this? That foolish, untrained, and unskilled monk does not recognize the sign of his own mind.
translations.sn47.8:5: Just as a wise, skilled, and experienced cook, who is serving the king or the king's minister, is provided with various kinds of soups - sour, bitter, pungent, sweet, alkaline, and non-alkaline -
translations.sn5.10:1: At Savatthi. Then, in the morning, the bhikkhuni Vajira dressed, and taking her bowl and outer robe, went into Savatthi for alms. After walking for alms in Savatthi and returning, she went to the Andhavana for the day's abiding, and sat down at the foot of a certain tree. Then Mara the Evil One, wanting to arouse fear, trepidation, and horror in the bhikkhuni Vajira, wanting to make her fall away from concentration, approached her and addressed her in verse:
translations.sn5.10:2: 'What is this creature, and what is its origin? How does it arise, and how does it pass away?'
translations.sn5.10:3: Then the bhikkhuni Vajira thought: 'Who is this, a human or a non-human, speaking in verse?' Then the bhikkhuni Vajira thought: 'This is Mara the Evil One, who wants to arouse fear, trepidation, and horror in me, who wants to make me fall away from concentration, speaking in verse.' Then the bhikkhuni Vajira, knowing that it was Mara the Evil One, replied to him in verse:
translations.sn5.10:4: 'Why do you ask about the creature, Mara? Have you seen it? The pure and conditioned phenomenon is not found in this place.
translations.sn5.10:5: Just as the sound of a chariot is merely a term for the combination of its parts, so too the term 'creature' is merely a convention for the combination of the aggregates.
translations.sn5.10:6: Only suffering arises, and only suffering passes away. There is no other arising or passing away apart from suffering.'
translations.sn5.1:1: I have heard that on one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Savatthi, in Jeta's Grove, Anathapindika's monastery. Then, in the morning, the bhikkhuni Alavika dressed, and taking her bowl and outer robe, went into Savatthi for alms. After walking for alms in Savatthi and returning, she went to the Andhavana for the day's abiding, intent on seclusion. Then Mara the Evil One, wanting to arouse fear, trepidation, and horror in the bhikkhuni Alavika, wanting to make her fall away from seclusion, approached her and addressed her in verse:
translations.sn5.1:2: 'There is no escape in the world, why do you speak of seclusion? Enjoy the pleasures of the senses, do not be late.'
translations.sn5.1:3: Then the bhikkhuni Alavika thought: 'Who is this, a human or a non-human, speaking in verse?' Then the bhikkhuni Alavika thought: 'This is Mara the Evil One, who wants to arouse fear, trepidation, and horror in me, who wants to make me fall away from seclusion, speaking in verse.' Then the bhikkhuni Alavika, knowing that it was Mara the Evil One, replied to him in verse:
translations.sn5.1:4: 'There is an escape in the world, I have clearly seen it with wisdom. You, Evil One, do not know that state, you are a friend of the negligent.'
translations.sn5.1:5: 'The pleasures of the senses are like a spear, they pierce the aggregates. What you call pleasure, I call suffering.'
translations.sn5.1:6: Then Mara the Evil One thought: 'The bhikkhuni Alavika knows me,' and he was depressed and disappointed, and he vanished right there.
translations.sn5.2:2: 'What is to be attained by the sages, a state difficult to reach; it is not possible for a woman with two fingers to attain it.'
translations.sn5.2:4: 'What is the use of being a woman, when the mind is well-concentrated, and one is practicing mindfulness and insight into the Dhamma?
translations.sn5.3:2: 'Why are you, a young woman with a tear-stained face, going alone to the forest? Are you searching for a man?'
translations.sn5.3:3: Then the bhikkhuni Kisagotami thought: 'Who is this, a human or a non-human, speaking in verse?' Then the bhikkhuni Kisagotami thought: 'This is Mara the Evil One, who wants to arouse fear, trepidation, and horror in me, who wants to make me fall away from concentration, speaking in verse.'
translations.sn5.3:5: 'I have transcended my son, men are far from me; I do not grieve, I do not lament, I do not fear you, friend.'
translations.sn5.3:6: 'The bond of affection is fully destroyed, the mass of darkness is torn apart; having conquered the army of Death, I live without defilements.'
translations.sn5.3:7: Then Mara the Evil One thought: 'The bhikkhuni Kisagotami knows me,' and he was depressed and disappointed, and he vanished right there.
translations.sn5.4:1: At Savatthi. Then, in the morning, the bhikkhuni Vijaya dressed, and taking her bowl and outer robe, went into Savatthi for alms... and sat down at the foot of a certain tree. Then Mara the Evil One, wanting to arouse fear, trepidation, and horror in the bhikkhuni Vijaya, wanting to make her fall away from concentration, approached her and addressed her in verse:
translations.sn5.4:2: 'You are young and beautiful, and I am also young and handsome; come, let us enjoy ourselves with the five kinds of music.'
translations.sn5.4:4: 'Forms, sounds, tastes, smells, and tactile sensations are all delightful; I offer them to you, Mara, I am not attached to them.'
translations.sn5.4:5: With this rotten body, I will destroy the worldly, and having destroyed them, I will efface the craving for sensual pleasures.
translations.sn5.4:6: And those beings who are attached to form, and those who are attached to the formless; and the peaceful attainments - everywhere the darkness is destroyed.
translations.sn5.5:1: At Savatthi. Then, in the morning, the bhikkhuni Uppalavanna dressed, and taking her bowl and outer robe, went into Savatthi for alms.  ... She stood at the root of a certain tree in full bloom.  Then Mara the Evil One, wanting to arouse fear, trepidation, and horror in the bhikkhuni Uppalavanna, wanting to make her fall away from concentration, approached her and, having approached, recited a verse to her:
translations.sn5.5:2: “Having approached the tree in full bloom, bhikkhuni, you stand alone at the root of the sal tree; there is no second element of beauty for you, fool, do not be afraid of the thorns.”
translations.sn5.5:4: “Even if a hundred or a thousand fools were to come, they would all be like that; I do not tremble, I do not get excited, I do not fear even one of them, Mara.”
translations.sn5.5:6: I have mastered my mind, I have developed the bases of psychic power; I have cut off all ties, I do not fear him, friend.”
translations.sn5.5:7: Then Mara the Evil One, realizing, “The bhikkhuni Uppalavanna knows me,” sad and disappointed, disappeared right there.
translations.sn5.6:2: “What kind of birth is not pleasing to you, bhikkhuni, when one who is born enjoys sensual pleasures; who, then, would not like birth?”
translations.sn5.6:3: “For one who is born, death is certain; the born experience suffering; bondage, slaughter, and torment - therefore I do not like birth.”
translations.sn5.6:4: The Buddha taught the Dhamma, transcending birth; for the abandonment of all suffering, that has settled in me as a truth.”
translations.sn5.6:5: And those beings who are attached to form, and those who are attached to the formless; not knowing cessation, they come to renewed existence.”
translations.sn5.7:1: At Savatthi. Then, in the morning, the bhikkhuni Upacala dressed, and taking her bowl and outer robe, went into Savatthi for alms.  ... She sat down at the root of a certain tree for the day's abiding.  Then Mara the Evil One, wanting to arouse fear, trepidation, and horror in the bhikkhuni Upacala, wanting to make her fall away from concentration, approached her and, having approached, said to her: “Where do you want to be reborn, bhikkhuni?” “I do not want to be reborn anywhere, friend,” she replied.
translations.sn5.7:2: “The gods of the Thirty-three, the Yama gods, the Tusita gods, the gods who delight in creation, the gods who control others' creations - focus your mind on them, and you will experience delight.”
translations.sn5.7:3: “The gods of the Thirty-three, the Yama gods, the Tusita gods, the gods who delight in creation, the gods who control others' creations - they are bound by the bond of sensual desire, they come under the control of Mara again.”
translations.sn5.7:4: The whole world is ablaze, the whole world is smoking, the whole world is burning, the whole world is trembling.
translations.sn5.7:5: Unshaken, unburning, not serving the common people - where there is no path for Mara, my mind is delighted.”
translations.sn5.7:6: Then Mara the Evil One, realizing, “The bhikkhuni Upacala knows me,” sad and disappointed, disappeared right there.
translations.sn5.8:1: At Savatthi. Then, in the morning, the bhikkhuni Sisupacala dressed, and taking her bowl and outer robe, went into Savatthi for alms.  ... She sat down at the root of a certain tree for the day's abiding.  Then Mara the Evil One, wanting to arouse fear, trepidation, and horror in the bhikkhuni Sisupacala, wanting to make her fall away from concentration, approached her and, having approached, said to her: “What kind of sect do you like, bhikkhuni?” “I do not like any sect, friend,” she replied.
translations.sn5.8:2: “What do you shaven-headed one point to, appearing like a wanderer; you do not like any sect, what are you doing, bewildered?”
translations.sn5.8:3: “The sects outside are seen to be pleasing to those who have views; I do not like their Dhamma, they are unskilled in the Dhamma.”
translations.sn5.8:5: Everywhere freed, unstained, seeing all, having seen the destruction of all deeds, freed from the underlying tendencies; that is my Teacher, the Blessed One, and I like his teaching.”
translations.sn5.9:2: “What is this painted image, where is the creator of the image, where did the image arise, where does the image cease?”
translations.sn5.9:4: “This image is not created by oneself, nor is it created by another; it has arisen dependent on a cause, and it ceases with the cessation of the cause.”
translations.sn5.9:6: Similarly, the aggregates and the elements - these have arisen dependent on a cause, and they cease with the cessation of the cause.”
translations.sn56.11:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Baranasi in the Deer Park at Isipatana. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus of the group of five:
translations.sn56.11:10: When, bhikkhus, my knowledge and vision of these four noble truths as they really are in three turns and twelve modes was fully purified, then, bhikkhus, in the world with its gods, its Maras, and its Brahmas, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its princes and its people, I directly knew: ‘Unshakable is my liberation of mind; this is my last birth; there is no further becoming.’ And, bhikkhus, my knowledge and vision arose: ‘My liberation is unshakable; this is my last birth; there is no further becoming.’” This is what the Blessed One said. The bhikkhus of the group of five were satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.
translations.sn56.11:11: And while this discourse was being spoken, the stainless, immaculate vision of the Dhamma arose to the Venerable Kondañña: “Whatever is subject to origination is subject to cessation.”
translations.sn56.11:13: At that moment, at that instant, a tremendous sound went up as far as the Brahma-world, and the ten-thousandfold world system shook and trembled and quaked, and an immeasurable, splendid radiance appeared in the world, surpassing the divine majesty of the gods.
translations.sn56.11:2: “There are, bhikkhus, these two extremes which a renouncer should not follow. What two? The pursuit of sensual happiness in sensual pleasures, which is low, coarse, the way of ordinary people, unworthy, and unprofitable; and the pursuit of self-mortification, which is painful, unworthy, and unprofitable. Not having approached either of these extremes, the Tathagata has awakened to the middle way, which gives rise to vision, gives rise to knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbana.”
translations.sn56.11:3: And what, bhikkhus, is this middle way awakened to by the Tathagata? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, bhikkhus, is the middle way awakened to by the Tathagata, which gives rise to vision, gives rise to knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbana.”
translations.sn56.11:4: This, monks, is the noble truth of suffering—birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering, association with the unpleasant is suffering, separation from the pleasant is suffering, not getting what one wants is suffering—in short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. This, monks, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering—the craving that leads to rebirth, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking pleasure in this or that, namely, sensual craving, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering—the complete cessation, giving up, and relinquishing of that craving. This, monks, is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering—the noble eightfold path, namely, right understanding, …, right concentration.
translations.sn56.11:5: ‘This is the noble truth of suffering,’ monks, with regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, understanding, wisdom, and light. ‘This noble truth of suffering is to be fully understood,’ monks, with regard to things unheard before, …, there arose in me vision, knowledge, understanding, wisdom, and light. ‘This noble truth of suffering has been fully understood,’ monks, with regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, understanding, wisdom, and light.
translations.sn56.11:6: ‘This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering,’ monks, with regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, understanding, wisdom, and light. ‘This noble truth of the origin of suffering is to be abandoned,’ monks, with regard to things unheard before, …, there arose in me vision, knowledge, understanding, wisdom, and light. ‘This noble truth of the origin of suffering has been abandoned,’ monks, with regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, understanding, wisdom, and light.
translations.sn56.11:7: ‘This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering,’ monks, with regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, understanding, wisdom, and light. ‘This noble truth of the cessation of suffering is to be realized,’ monks, with regard to things unheard before, …, there arose in me vision, knowledge, understanding, wisdom, and light. ‘This noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized,’ monks, with regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, understanding, wisdom, and light.
translations.sn56.11:8: ‘This is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering,’ monks, with regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, understanding, wisdom, and light. ‘This noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering is to be developed,’ monks, with regard to things unheard before, …, there arose in me vision, knowledge, understanding, wisdom, and light. ‘This noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering has been developed,’ monks, with regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, understanding, wisdom, and light.
translations.sn56.11:9: For as long as, monks, my knowledge and vision of these four noble truths as they really are was not fully purified, I did not claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Mara, and Brahma, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans.
translations.sn56.20:1: There are, monks, these four noble truths that are actual, unerring, and not otherwise. What four? ‘This is suffering’—this, monks, is actual, unerring, and not otherwise; ‘this is the origin of suffering’—this, monks, is actual, unerring, and not otherwise; ‘this is the cessation of suffering’—this, monks, is actual, unerring, and not otherwise; ‘this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering’—this, monks, is actual, unerring, and not otherwise. These, monks, are the four noble truths that are actual, unerring, and not otherwise.
