translations.sn56.26:1: Those who are to be pitied, monks, and those who think they should be listened to—friends, companions, relatives, or family members—should be encouraged, inspired, and established in the knowledge and vision of these four noble truths as they really are.
translations.sn56.26:2: Which four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Those who are to be pitied, monks, and those who think they should be listened to—friends, companions, relatives, or family members—should be encouraged, inspired, and established in the knowledge and vision of these four noble truths as they really are.
translations.sn56.27:1: There are, monks, these four noble truths. What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering—these, monks, are the four noble truths that are actual, unerring, and not otherwise; therefore, they are called noble truths.
translations.sn56.28:1: There are, monks, these four noble truths. What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. The Tathagata, the noble one, is the highest in the world with its devas, Mara, and Brahma, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans; therefore, they are called noble truths.
translations.sn56.30:1: On one occasion, many elder monks were living in the Cetan forest. Then, after their alms round and meal, a number of elder monks assembled in the pavilion and sat down together. This discussion arose among them: ‘Which monk, friends, sees suffering, sees the origin of suffering, sees the cessation of suffering, and sees the path leading to the cessation of suffering?’
translations.sn56.31:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was living in the Kosiya kingdom, in a wooden dwelling in a wood of sīsa trees. Then the Blessed One, taking a few sīsa leaves in his hand, addressed the bhikkhus thus: "What do you think, bhikkhus? Which are more numerous, the few sīsa leaves that I have taken in my hand or those in the wood?" "The leaves that the Blessed One has taken in his hand are few, Lord; those in the wood are very numerous." "Just so, bhikkhus, the things that I have directly known but have not taught you are numerous. And why haven't I taught them? Because they are not useful, do not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna. That is why I have not taught them."
translations.sn56.31:2: And what, bhikkhus, have I taught? I have taught: 'This is suffering'; I have taught: 'This is the origin of suffering'; I have taught: 'This is the cessation of suffering'; I have taught: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.'
translations.sn56.31:3: And why, bhikkhus, have I taught this? Because it is useful, leads to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna. That is why I have taught it.
translations.sn56.35:1: Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were to say: 'I will not live in a house made of leaves, I will not live under a thatched roof, I will not live in a house with a peaked roof, I will not live in a mansion, until I have realized the unexcelled, sublime, perfect enlightenment.' He would be a long time living in such a place, bhikkhus. The life of a man is short, bhikkhus. He has just sixteen years, just sixteen years, bhikkhus, for one who lives a hundred years. One who lives a hundred years lives for just a hundred winters and a hundred summers. When one lives for just a hundred winters and a hundred summers, of what use are the things that are not useful, that do not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna?
translations.sn56.35:2: It is suitable, bhikkhus, for a clansman who has faith to live in this Dhamma and Discipline. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, the round of rebirths is without a known beginning; it is not possible to determine when a being first arose. Beings are beset by ignorance and fettered by craving. When this occurs to them, they are not freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. I say that the destruction of the taints is not achieved by them. But, bhikkhus, I say that the destruction of the taints is achieved by one who knows and sees, and not by one who does not know and see. What is it that he knows and sees? He knows and sees: 'This is suffering'; he knows and sees: 'This is the origin of suffering'; he knows and sees: 'This is the cessation of suffering'; he knows and sees: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.'
translations.sn56.36:1: Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were to take a wooden pole and throw it into a deep lake. If the pole were to sink, it would sink in the water; if it were to float, it would float on the water; if it were to be carried along, it would be carried along by the current. In the same way, bhikkhus, when a being has laid down this body and has taken up another body, I say that if his volitions were bad, they would lead him to a bad destination; if his volitions were good, they would lead him to a good destination. There are beings who are prone to anger, and they are reborn among the asuras; there are beings who are prone to enmity, and they are reborn among the petas; there are beings who are prone to delusion, and they are reborn among the animals.
translations.sn56.36:2: But, bhikkhus, there are also beings who are not prone to anger, who are not prone to enmity, who are not prone to delusion. They are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. Why is that? Because of the fineness of their existence. This, bhikkhus, is a great danger. But a person who has gained a foothold in the Dhamma, who has gained a foothold in the discipline, knows and sees: 'This is suffering'; he knows and sees: 'This is the origin of suffering'; he knows and sees: 'This is the cessation of suffering'; he knows and sees: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.'
translations.sn56.42:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was living in the city of Rājagaha, on the mountain called Paṇḍava. Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus thus: 'Come, bhikkhus, let us go to the Black Rock on the Isigili mountain to spend the day.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' those bhikkhus replied. Then the Blessed One, together with a number of bhikkhus, went to the Black Rock on the Isigili mountain. A certain bhikkhu saw a large drop of blood on the Black Rock and, having seen it, said to the Blessed One: 'This is a large drop of blood, venerable sir, a very large drop of blood. Is there, venerable sir, another drop of blood greater and more terrible than this?' 'There is, bhikkhu, another drop of blood greater and more terrible than this.'
translations.sn56.42:2: 'What, venerable sir, is the drop of blood greater and more terrible than this?' 'Those, bhikkhus, who do not know and see as it really is:
translations.sn56.45:1: At one time the Buddha was staying in the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof, in Vesālī. Then, in the morning, the Venerable Ānanda dressed, and taking his bowl and robe, went into Vesālī for alms. The Venerable Ānanda saw many Licchavi boys paying homage in a hall, throwing down a straw mat at a distance with a tiny pin, one after another, without a gap. Seeing this, he thought: 'These Licchavi boys are well-trained, very well-trained; for they throw down a straw mat at a distance with a tiny pin, one after another, without a gap.'
translations.sn56.45:3: 'What do you think, Ānanda? Which is more difficult and harder to do - to throw down a straw mat at a distance with a tiny pin, one after another, without a gap, or to penetrate the tip of a hair split into seven parts?' 'This is more difficult and harder to do, sir - to penetrate the tip of a hair split into seven parts.' 'Those who understand as it really is:
translations.sn56.46:1: 'There are, monks, dark and unguarded places in the world, where the moon and sun, which are so powerful and have such great influence, do not shine.'
translations.sn56.46:2: When this was said, a certain monk said to the Buddha: 'The darkness is great, sir, very great. Is there another darkness greater and more frightening than this?' 'There is, monk, another darkness greater and more frightening than this.'
translations.sn56.48:1: 'Suppose, monks, that this great earth were one ocean, and a man were to throw a yoke with a single hole into it. An east wind would drive it west, a west wind would drive it east, a north wind would drive it south, a south wind would drive it north. There would be a blind turtle that would come up once every hundred years. What do you think, monks? Would that blind turtle, coming up once every hundred years, put its neck through that yoke with a single hole?' 'It would be astonishing, sir, if the blind turtle ... were to put its neck through that yoke.'
translations.sn56.48:2: 'It is equally astonishing, monks, that a human state is attained. It is equally astonishing, monks, that a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Fully Awakened One, arises in the world. It is equally astonishing, monks, that the Dhamma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata appear in the world. And when a human state has been attained, a Tathāgata has arisen in the world, an Arahant, a Fully Awakened One, and the Dhamma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata appear in the world ...'
